Title: Yoginītantra.
First Chapter.
Om, salutation to Mahābhairava.
[I bow] to Śaṅkara, the Supreme Lord, who has ascended the peak of Kailāsa.
Pārvatī, the daughter of the mountain, questioned her beloved, the bull-bannered Lord.
The Goddess said:
O Blessed One, knower of all dharmas, Lord of all knowledge, O Teacher of the World, please explain to me that Yoginītantra which has been indicated [to me]. (2)
His majesty was proclaimed of old in the temple of Śrīśaila,
in Vārāṇasī, in Kāmarūpa [at Kāmākhyā], in Nepāla, and on Mount Mandara.
Īśvara said:
Listen, O Goddess, I shall proclaim the supreme Yoginī Tantra, which is purifying, most auspicious, and the bestower of the singular fruit of liberation. || 4 ||
"O beloved of my life, you must guard this with great effort;
O sweet-spoken one, act in such a way that no one else may obtain it. (5)
O lady of excellent hips, this tantra is very difficult for even gods and asuras to obtain;
all the deities desire to hear this unsurpassed tantra.
O Supreme Goddess, [these teachings] concerning the yakṣas and others have not been told by me to them;
yet, out of affection for you, I shall tell them to you, for I am bound to you by the highest [bond]. (7)

I bow to that Mother of the Universe, who possesses a row of teeth with a luster equal to lightning, who is like a crane amidst the clouds of the rainy season, whose radiance is like a fresh, glossy cloud,
and whose splendor is like a dark rain-cloud. (8)
She was beautiful with a garland of severed heads, with disheveled hair and naked;
her tongue was lolling, she made a terrible sound, and her three eyes were blood-red.
O Mistress of millions upon millions of digits, whose facial orb is shimmering;
O Thou whose radiant circle of a crown shines with the splendor of the digit of the New Moon.
She has two corpses as ear-ornaments, adorned with various jewels;
her ear-ornaments shine with a profusion of sun-stones and moon-stones.
With thousands of dead hands forming her girdle, she has a smiling face;
her countenance is made radiant by streams of blood trickling from both corners of her mouth.
Her four arms are beautifully adorned with a sword, a severed head, and the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness;
she is the supreme, eternal one, with a formidable form decorated with blood. || 13 ||
Mounted upon a corpse of Śiva, she stands atop Mahākāla;
her left foot is placed on the heart of Śiva, and her right marks the world.
Resembling ten million suns, it illuminated all the worlds.
He was resplendent with matted locks blazing with a luster equal to a mass of lightning. || 16 ||
The god, whose form is like a mountain of silver and whose body is a crystal peak. || 17 ||
Naked, most terrible, and adorned by the moon and the sun. || 18 ||
(3) Śambhu, richly adorned with various ornaments, with a radiant body of gold, possessing yogic sleep, and with a smiling lotus-face; || 19 ||
Constantly united with Mahākāla in inverted sexual union,
she is brilliantly radiant, illuminating the entire vessel of the cosmic egg.
She was surrounded by auspicious jackals of terrifying howls, appearing as if arisen at the time of universal dissolution,
her orb of faces eclipsing ten million times ten million autumn moons.
It was graced by yoginīs whose heads and hands were filled with hunger [and who were filled with nectar],
and likewise accompanied by those intoxicated by the wine from their slightly reddened mouths.
With terrible forms, great roars, and fearsome, fierce heats;
intent upon uttering cries of victory while clutching corpses and skeletons. || 23 ||
She was situated in the midst of the cremation ground, attended by Brahmā and other gods, while naked beings danced and played musical instruments incessantly.

Now listen, O Goddess of gods! I shall tell you the King of Tantras, which is very difficult to obtain; out of affection for you, I speak it, though it must never be disclosed under any circumstances. (25)
"O beloved, through devotion bound by extreme affection, I am your servant;
this scripture has its root in the Guru, and this world has its root in the Guru. (26)
The guru alone is the supreme Brahman; the guru alone is Śiva himself.
Even the gods bow down to him by whom the guru has been brought under control. (27)
Even if one should drink the water used for washing the feet of a person whose limbs are wasting away from disease, as if it were nectar, he shall go to the city of the Goddess.

Even if one who follows the injunctions for honoring a guru should drink liquor that has not been consecrated, there is no penance required even in that case; for he remains firmly established in the Veda. (29)
Even if something contrary to the Tantras is spoken by the Guru,
or if it is his own opinion based on the Vedas, it should be accepted as the word of Mahārudra.
Everything must be performed by the command of the Guru, except for the arrival of the ultimate reality (tattva).
There is non-duality with the deities and their lordship, but there is no non-duality with the Guru.
Non-duality does not float away as an effect; for me, there is nothing here in this world.
O Dear One, the Guru is the refuge, the Guru is the God, and the Guru is likewise the Goddess.
Whether in the world of the gods, the world of mortals, or the world of the nagas,
whether one possesses little knowledge or vast wisdom, the guru alone is the eternal refuge.
One should behave toward the sons of the guru as toward the guru himself, and toward his daughters and others likewise;
O Maheśānī, the wife of the guru is the guru himself—of this there is no doubt. (34)
O Dear Goddess, the remains of the Guru’s food, as well as the remains of his son’s food, must be eaten without doubt; if there is any alteration, there will be a downward fall.
O Great Goddess, the remains of the Guru (gurūcchiṣṭa) are very difficult even for Brahmā and the other gods to obtain;
thus the remains of the Guru are declared to be supremely pure, higher than the highest. (36)
O beloved, he who for twenty years eats even a mere handful of food that has been eaten by his guru, his guru’s wife, or his guru’s son,
shall live long, be freed from old age and disease, and in the end become Śiva.
If one should dwell in the presence of a supreme guru for fifty years, [he attains perfection].
Endowed with the conduct of Bhairava and serving at his feet, having enjoyed excellent pleasures here in this world, he shall in the end become a member of the host of goddesses. || 39 ||
Accompanied by hosts of Rudra-maidens endowed with beauty and youth, this Hero sports for as long as the moon, sun, and stars endure. (40)
That mortal who, having risen in the morning, performs a prostration with a staff before his guru, or bows down according to the prescribed rite to his son or his grandson; || 41 ||
He attains success, O lady of excellent hips; there is no need for deliberation on this point.
In whichever direction the Guru’s abode lies, he should always face that direction in the morning.
A person who, filled with devotion, bows down to the Guru, as well as his beloved wife, sons, and daughters, shall attain perfection; of this there is no doubt. (43)
For Kailāsa is the abode of the Guru, and his home is the dwelling of the Cintāmaṇi jewel;
the grove of trees is known as the row of Kalpa-trees, and the creeper is remembered as the Kalpa-creeper.
O Śivā, every water-pit is proclaimed to be equal to the Gaṅgā of heaven; indeed, everything is celebrated as being full of merit.
The female servants residing in the house of the Guru are proclaimed to be Bhairavīs. || 45 ||
The wise one should always contemplate his servants as having the form of Bhairava.
O Maheśvarī, by whomsoever the circumambulation of the Guru’s abode has been performed, [that merit is attained].
By him, the earth with its seven continents has been circumambulated.
The Śrī Devī said:
O Mahādeva, O Maheśāna, tell me, who is the Guru, O Compassionate One? This Guru whom you have proclaimed is indeed superior even to you. (47)
Īśvara said:
O Great Goddess, he who is known as Mahākāla is indeed Ādinātha;
O Queen of the Gods, he alone is now the supreme Guru in all mantras.
In the Śaiva, Śākta, Vaiṣṇava, Gāṇapatya, Aindra, Mahāśaiva, and Saura [traditions], he is the guru; of this there is no doubt. (49)
O Supreme Goddess, O Daughter of the Mountain, at the time of bestowing the mantra, he alone— and no other—
should be the speaker of the mantra among human beings.
O Śaṅkarī, that shall be the abode of Mahākāla;
therefore, O Goddess, there is no doubt that among humans, [the female] possesses greatness. (51)
O Goddess, just as Śiva, the giver of the mantra, bestows that knowledge upon the lotus of the Guru’s head,
so too does the disciple bestow that same knowledge upon the lotus of his own head.
Therefore, O Great Goddess, the Guru alone is traditionally held to be the one [source];
his human form, O Maheśvarī, serves as the locus of manifestation.
O Śaṅkarī, his greatness has been proclaimed in all the scriptures;
now I shall specifically describe the greatness pertaining to the Guru.
In the bestowing of mantras for the propitiation of deities, the lineage limit is ten generations;
however, for all the Mahāvidyās, it is considered to be fifty generations.
But in the bestowal of the yoga of Brahman—that is, the knowledge of Brahman—the limit is ten human lifetimes. || 55 ||
O Great Goddess, the Brahmayoga is proclaimed to reside in Bheruṇḍā;
the water from the feet of the Guru is meritorious, equivalent to bathing in all sacred pilgrimage sites.
Whatever fruit a man may obtain by bathing in all the sacred fords (tīrthas),
that same fruit a mortal obtains from a single drop of water from the feet of the Guru.
He who performs the ritual ablution with that water has effectively bathed in all the sacred fords.
Indeed, it purifies the body and cleanses it from all sins. || 58 ||
O Great Illusion, specifically, at that very moment he shall attain the state of Śiva;
so too the man who bears upon his head the dust from the feet of the Guru. (59)
He is liberated from all sins and becomes Śiva; of this there is no doubt.
O Goddess, he who applies a tilaka with that very dust [attains the same].
He who consumes even a single grain of its pollen for even a single day will undoubtedly become the four-armed Lord of Vaikuṇṭha.
He obtains the fruit of ten million great sacrifices; of this there is no doubt.
Thus, O Goddess, has this secret, which is the domain of the Guru, been told to you. It must be guarded with effort, like one's own family lineage and personal prowess. 62.
Thus ends the first chapter in the *Śrīyoginītantra*, the most excellent of all tantras, in the dialogue between the Goddess and the Lord, within the twenty-four thousand [verse] work.
The second chapter.
The illustrious Goddess said:
O Master of the moving and unmoving world, you who are a mass of supreme bliss!
I have heard from you the greatness of the Guru, which is more secret than the most secret.
And now I wish to hear about Kālī, who delivers one from all [sins];
that great vidyā which was taught as a perfected vidyā in the Yāmala.
O Great One, O Mahābrahmavidyā Cāmuṇḍā within the scope of the Tantra!
Command me, O Great God; out of compassion, O Śiva, reveal the secret.
Īśvara said:
This Kālikā is considered the great, supreme knowledge of Brahman;
having attained it, even the lowest of men reaches the liberation of Nirvāṇa. (4)
Her worshippers are indeed Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Śiva, and the others;
O Goddess, it is told as a secret that all the worlds are her worshippers.
By the grace of Kālikā, all partake in liberation and other blessings;
she is indeed equal to thousands of repetitions and tens of millions of recitations.
Therefore, by the power of fortune, one becomes fortunate who is intent upon the practice of Kālī;
for Kālī is established in all scriptures as the Mother of the worlds. (7)
He who indeed recites the mantra of Kālī is undoubtedly a son of Kālī;
you abandon this other [world], as well as the supreme Puruṣa. (8)
O You who pervade the universe, at times You abandon Your similarity [to the world];
yet, having attained the Kali-vidyā, You shall never abandon it.
The Śūdra-hood of the Śūdra has departed, as has the Brahmin-hood of the Brahmins;
indeed, by the mere act of receiving the mantra, all are truly equal to Śiva.
Just as those [rivers], upon reaching the Gaṅgā—which is no longer Vārāṇasī—become like it; so too, by the mere taking up of your mantra, all indeed become equal to Śiva. 11.
Moreover, if there were a woman equal to you and a man equal to me, his mother alone would be blessed and his father would be the best among the gods. (12)
His very ancestors go to heaven, O Goddess, because of that which is so difficult to attain:
by whose power of fortune that Kālī has been resorted to with devotion. (13)
For the ancestors of men who perform meritorious deeds indeed hope:
"When will a son in our lineage take refuge in the mantra of Kālī? (14)
Then, having reached the city of liberation, he indeed ceased forever,
just as Kālī and Tārā were severed, and likewise the Guru and the king.
They should be understood as one; if there is a division, one goes to hell.
A disciple of Tārā should abandon Kālī, and a disciple of Kālī should abandon Tāriṇī. (16)
The worship of Chinnāmahiṣamardinī is remembered as being performed at certain times;
O Goddess, if she is worshipped, one should indeed not worship any other [deity]. 17.
O Śivā, having conceived her as Kālī, one should worship her elsewhere;
she who is the supreme Vidyā Kālī is indeed Tārā, without a doubt. (18)
Indeed, through the state of differentiation between these two, various mantras arise;
that has been stated by me to you in the Kālikākalpa and the Tārākalpa. (19)
The illustrious Goddess said:
O Lord of Gods, O speaker of kind words, tell me of the various kinds [of recitation],
and especially, O Mahādeva, the secret concerning the core of japa.
Īśvara said:
The auspicious garland of letters has been described as bestowing all mantras;
O Goddess, its auspicious substitute is made of a great conch shell.
Success is not far off for one who holds a great conch in his hand;
in its absence, O you who are honored by heroes, a crystal [conch] bestows all accomplishments.
O Great Goddess, I shall tell you the number of jewels for the rosary:
with twenty-five [jewels] there is liberation, and with twenty-seven, nourishment. (23)
With thirty [recitations], there shall be the accomplishment of wealth; with fifty, for the sake of the accomplishment of mantras;
and with one hundred and eight, O Maheśvarī, every accomplishment indeed [is attained].
This has been declared as the general rule; now hear the specific [instruction] for those who possess desire.
A rosary of teeth should be used for recitation, and it is auspicious to wear it around the neck among men.
O beloved, if it is to be made with teeth, the number of teeth [to be used] should likewise be [as follows].
The garland that bestows all accomplishments [is strung] with the "king's tooth" as the Meru;
O Goddess of the Gods, in other cases as well, one should likewise designate [the central bead] as the Meru.
O Maheśānī, listen to the number [of recitations] for the mantra-vow (saṃkalpa) as well as for the recitation (japa) and the fire-oblation (homa); I shall explain it to you in due order. || 27 ||
A hundred, a thousand, ten thousand, a hundred thousand, and likewise a crore—
O Maheśvarī, in all these cases the enumeration is without distinction.
But in special cases, O Maheśānī! one should perform a special rite at times; when the count reaches a hundred or more, O Dear One! one should recite [the mantra] one hundred and eight times.
Having set aside the first and last two joints, one should then place the rosary upon the head of Śiva at the conclusion of the recitation, using the eight remaining joints.
The wise one should offer red flowers and water as an arghya-oblation to the Goddess, preceded by the sounding of drums and other instruments, as the fruit of his practice of recitation.
O Goddess of gods, the secret of the practice of recitation has been declared with all its primary and secondary limbs in the Sarasvatī-tantra; therefore, O beloved, you should know it.
O Maheśānī, the rosary [is formed] according to the sequence of Śiva and Śakti.
Listen, O Parameśānī, for the sake of the success of all tantras. || 33 ||
Beginning from the ring finger and the middle finger,
and starting from the little finger up to the base of the index finger, one should recite [the mantra] over ten joints.
One should regard the joint at the base of the middle finger as Mount Meru;
O Goddess, one should recite the mantra one hundred and eight times, omitting the first and the last pair [of syllables].
The Śivamālā has been fully described; now hear from me the Śaktimālā. It begins with the ring finger and the middle finger, and proceeds in order starting from the little finger.

O Supreme Goddess, one should recite over ten joints, from the base of the ring finger up to the root of the index finger; the two joints of the middle finger and the two joints of the index finger are also included.
Know Meru, O Goddess of gods; one should never touch those two [ends].
During the recitation of the hundred and eight [mantras] on a festival day, one should abandon the first and last pair.
One should always perform the recitation (japa) with the hand, but never that which is for the sake of specific desires (kāmya).
However, O beloved of mine, if a rosary is unavailable, one may perform even the recitation for specific desires with the hand.
The constant recitation performed as part of the daily rites is called "nityajāpa.
It includes the daily bath, the libations (tarpaṇa), the fire-oblation (homa), the offering of bali, and the act of satiation (tṛpti).
One should recite over all the rosaries both in forward and reverse order;
however, one should recite with the finger rosary only in the forward order.
O Goddess, one should mutter the male mantra with a rosary originating from Śiva;
O Goddess, one should mutter the female mantra with a rosary originating from Śakti.

O Goddess, without the Moon-mantra, one should mutter the Sāvitrī, the Mother of the Vedas; O Goddess, one should mutter the Sāvitrī with the hand using a rosary of Śiva-beads (or, according to another reading, a rosary of Śakti-beads). || 43 ||
O Goddess, one should mutter the mantra of Candra using the hand as a rosary;
for the muttering of the Sāvitrī, the hand-rosary is always recommended.
A rosary made of crystal, pearl, silk-cotton seeds, or even conch-shell is recommended for a Vaiṣṇava; for Gaṇeśvara, one made of elephant tusks is prescribed.
Rudrākṣas and red sandalwood are recommended for the recitation of Tripurā;
for the recitation of Dhūmāvatī, the seeds of the *dhuttūra* plant found in cremation grounds are recommended. (46)
Arising from the joints of the hand and strung upon a thread, it is highly praised for Bagalāmukhī; this is the truth, the absolute truth, O Maheśvarī! 47.

If that which was intended is not performed—whether it be deficient or excessive, or likewise whether the recitation (japa) is deficient or excessive—one will not partake of the full fruit; therefore, one should observe the prescribed rule. 48.

O Goddess, having taken a copper vessel filled with water, along with dūrvā grass, sesame seeds, kuśa grass, and fruit, one should perform the ritual sipping (ācamana) according to the prescribed rule.
And having worshipped the compassionate Śrī Guru upon the lotus of his head— whether he be one whose face is that of a Yakṣa, or even one whose face is that of the Lord of the Gods (Indra)— 50.

Having pronounced the month, the fortnight, the lunar day, as well as the festivals of the gods and so forth, and having uttered the time of beginning and end, along with the lineage and the names of the lovers (kāmin). || 51 ||
"I shall perform two rites; one should pour out water in the northeast.
The lunar month is used everywhere, but for the injunction regarding the lunar day (tithi), the solar month should be used. (52)
O Dear One, the lunar [day] is primary everywhere, but it is secondary for cruel rites;
likewise, it is [primary] for the giving and receiving of loans, as well as for nourishing, healing, and similar acts. (53)
O beloved, for bathing, giving, charity, and rites for prosperity or recovery, the lunar month is prescribed;
however, for the year and the [solar] festival, the solar month is declared.
Thus it has been declared in every age that in the Kali age, however, the solar month prevails in all respects;
initiation during a solar month is auspicious, but not in a lunar or a stellar month.
O Great Goddess, that [lunar month] is not for the sake of ritual recitation (sāvana), because it would be fruitless;
rather, the month of the moon (cāndra), which consists of ritual action and is rooted in the Vedas, is also praised.
Everything is auspicious during the bright fortnight and inauspicious during the other;
starting from the morning until midday, when the sun has reached its zenith. (57)
One who desires the proper fruit should perform actions for that long;
O Supreme Goddess, one may even perform cruel deeds during the remainder of that time.
When the first watch has passed, up until the third watch, that time is said to be for nocturnal recitation; now hear the time for worship. (59)
When half a watch has passed at night and half a watch remains, that hour is always the time for worship; it always bestows the fourfold aims of life.
Those two ghaṭikās which overlap the middle watches of the night are designated as the "Great Night" (mahārātri); whatever is performed then yields inexhaustible fruit.
Whatever has been recited, whatever has been offered in sacrifice, and whatever means for liberation has been performed—
all that becomes inexhaustible and conduces to infinity.
(14) O Goddess, one should not perform it at night during rites for Viṣṇu, Sūrya, Mahāsaura, or the ancestors;
nor, O Goddess, except at midday or during a lunar eclipse.
Initiation should be performed with effort according to the divisions of the bright fortnight;
one desiring liberation [should seek it] in the dark fortnight, while one desiring devotion likewise [seeks it] in the bright fortnight.
And for one desiring prosperity, the rite of Kṛṣṇa should be performed from the fifth day of the dark fortnight onwards;
at an auspicious time, one should perform all auspicious acts, and during times of distress, the inauspicious ones.
During an eclipse, at this great sacred site, no fault of the time exists;
especially in Vārāṇasī, one may perform all rites at all times.
There, the Kṛta Yuga is eternal and there is always the northern course of the sun;
and there is no distinction between day and night, nor between twilight and the dead of night. (67)

Fire is visibly seen in its form as a whirlpool in Śiva, yet it never arises in Kāśī due to the conjunction of the *sandhi* (the point of transition), O fair-faced one. [Regarding the *sandhi-yoga*: ] 68.

O Goddess, O auspicious one, for those crying out from two or three *krośas* away, Kāśī becomes five *krośas* in another birth; by its extent and its measure, this city is eternally and always auspicious.
O Śivā, this city of Nirvāṇa consists of supreme light;
there it establishes the cosmic egg, together with its peak and all material entities.
O Goddess, by wandering there one may attain nirvāṇa;
therefore, one should offer oneself as a brahmin at Vārāṇasī, even at the cost of all one's possessions.
In Vārāṇasī, there is the abode of the twice-born, as well as the yoga of Brahman and delight;
freedom from desire, the bondage of karma, and everything else—all these are causes for Nirvāṇa.

One who has died at a sacred site of liberation such as the Gaṅgā and others, through the application of knowledge and other means—or likewise through other yogas—should be brought to Kāśī and purified; thus liberated by my instruction, he attains release. (73)
I have no dwelling elsewhere, for there is no liberation for me without Kālikā;
whatever action is performed there, one shall obtain its infinite fruit. (74)
For everything shall indeed become inexhaustible, and one shall attain firm accomplishment;
therein lies the merit of conjunction, and therein one is truly liberated.
In that regard, O Śivā, I nourish [the world] through its true nature and not otherwise;
when the lunar day (tithi) is of short duration, the progression of the time for ritual action occurs accordingly.
Having indeed begun at the proper time, one may even complete it at an improper time;
however, if the twilight has fallen, one should recite the Gāyatrī ten times.
Then, having performed the twilight rites appropriate for the time, one should conclude the ritual action.
Thus has that which was asked by you, O daughter of the mountain, been told to you;
if there is anything further than this that remains in your mind, please speak it.
Thus ends the second chapter in the glorious Yoginītantra, the most excellent of all tantras, in the dialogue between the Goddess and the Lord, within the twenty-four thousand [verse] work.
The third chapter begins.
The Goddess said:
O Blessed One, Lord of the Pramathas, God of gods, Teacher of the world! O Lord, [please tell me] the prevention of war as well as the prevention of fevers and other ailments.
"O Lord, tell me out of your supreme compassion: how may [this] quickly come to pass?
O Supreme Lord, there is no savior for the worlds other than you. (2)
Īśvara said:
Out of affection for you, O daughter of the mountain, I shall quickly tell you this great armor that wards off battle as well as fever and other ailments.
I shall tell it in the vernacular tongue itself; listen to that.
Oṃ! Homage to the Blessed One, O Vajra-Chain! Slay! Devour! Eat!

Drink the blood from the skull-cup! O red-eyed one, O you clad in red garments, O you with eyes like ashes, O you whose body is smeared with ashes, O you who are encircled by a perimeter of vajra weapons! [Guard] the eastern direction!
May he bind [the spirits]; may he bind the southern direction, may he bind the western direction;

for the sake of the Nāgas and for wealth, may he bind the householders; may he bind the lord of names; may he protect from all those who are like sons—the Pretas, Bhūtas, Gandharvas, and whoever else there may be.
May it protect above, may it protect below; may it seal the fissure! O Jalamahābale, come, come! O you who possess the strength of a hundred crores of camels, O Vajra-fire-wreath of the thunderbolt!
HŪṂ PHAṬ HRĪṂ HRĪṂ ŚRĪṂ PHAṬ HUṂ HUṂ KRŪṂ PHAṂ PHAṂ.
"From all planetary influences (grahas), from all evil afflictions, Hrīṃ—may she protect me from everything.

O Goddess, this armor (kavaca), which is very difficult even for gods and asuras to obtain, should be employed against the fevers of the planets and other spirits, and in all ritual actions. || 4-5 ||
This armor must not be given to anyone whatsoever once it has issued from my mouth;
if it is given, there will be a loss of accomplishment, and one becomes a beast for the Yoginīs.
One should give it to one who is peaceful, heroic, steadfast, of noble birth, a practitioner of yoga, devoted to virtuous conduct, and who has conquered all enemies. || 7 ||
The Goddess said: (p.
17) "I have indeed heard the divine armor (kavaca) issued from the lotus of your mouth;
now I desire to hear the supreme [mantra] that brings the world under one's control."
Īśvara said: Listen, O Goddess, I shall proclaim this great [teaching] that causes delusion to the world,
which was formerly asked of me by Nārada on the summit of Kailāsa.
I have narrated this armor, which causes the delusion of all, to him;
by that very armor, Nārada, the son of Brahmā, [attained his power].
Having pierced through the three worlds, he who was fond of strife indeed deluded them;
observing that impossibility, Viṣṇu spoke to the son of Brahmā.
O Sage, tell me the reason why everything was deluded; how did all that come to pass in Viṣṇu? Viṣṇu spoke to the daughter of the ocean.
The wise Nārada, who is devoted to the welfare of all the worlds, questioned Mahādeva, the teacher of the universe, as he sat upon the peak of Kailāsa.
Nārada said:
O Lord, hear [let it be told] of the great Mahāvidyā of Kālikā, the most exalted [great] one.
O Lord, what is the fruit of this? What could be so deluding as this? || 14 ||
"O Śaṅkara, tell me by what means I may find protection in battle. The Lord said:
"O Goddess, that which was hidden during the three periods of time has now been revealed at this specific time. (15)
The goddess Kālī is naked and the enchantress of the world;
listen to that, O best of sages, for this is indeed the enchantment of the three worlds. (16)

p. 18) Kālabhairava is the seer (ṛṣi), Anuṣṭubh is the meter (chandaḥ), Śmaśānakālī is the deity (devatā), and the application (viniyoga) is for the purpose of deluding everywhere. Aiṃ hrāḥ hrūḥ hraḥ svāhā—may she always protect me in dispute; Klīṃ, may Dakṣiṇakālikā, the deity who grants victory in the midst of the assembly, [protect me]; Hrīṃ Hrīṃ.
O dark-bodied one, kill, kill the enemy! *Kṛṃ Klīṃ*, bring the three worlds under my control!
*Hrīṃ Śrīṃ Kṛṃ*, protect me, protect me! This supreme mantra of twenty-two syllables is effective in disputes and in the royal palace.
O Brahmarākṣasa, O Vetāla, O Rakṣas, protect me always! Wherever I am deprived of my armor, may Kālikā protect me there. 18.
"Protect me everywhere; may the Goddess, who is my own true nature, guard me.
This supreme delusion of these [beings] has been revealed through your good fortune. (19)
Whoever recites this constantly shall bring the three worlds under his control.
If one should worship the Vīrakāminī without knowing this armor (kavaca), [he gains no fruit]. (20)
He will always be afflicted by a great disease; of this there is no doubt.
He shall be short-lived and diseased—this has been told to you, O Nārada. (21)
The wearing of this armor, especially on birch bark, brings about the fulfillment of one's desires once the armor has been worn along with its mantra. || 22 ||
On the eighth day of the bright fortnight, the practitioner of mantra should draw [this armor] and wear it upon a golden leaf;
O great sage, the majesty of this armor is not capable of being fully described.
A yogin seeking the fruit should wear it on his crest or on his right arm;
O Goddess, this Kalpadruma is revealed out of affection for you. 24.
O Great Sage, it should be guarded with effort, recited, and caused to be recited. || 25 ||
Viṣṇu said:
"Thus, let this armor be constantly recited by Mahālakṣmī;
the three worlds, including all that is mobile and immobile, will certainly come under your control. (26)
Formerly, when Nārada desired the fruit [of his penance], Śiva spoke [this mantra];
by its recitation, even Nārada deluded all that is moving and unmoving.
The Goddess said:
O Sage, O Supreme Lord, adored by the world, Lord of the Pramathas, bestower of boons!
For the benefit of men, please explain Yoga in great detail. (28)
By which one quickly obtains a kingdom, by which one quickly obtains a son,
by which one quickly obtains knowledge, by which one quickly obtains wealth,
by which one quickly obtains fame, and by which one quickly obtains everything. (29)
Īśvara said:
Listen, O Goddess, I shall explain that which you ask of me;
it has been taught in detail in the Phetkāriṇītantra and the Nīlatantra.

Now, O Goddess of pure smiles, I shall explain this in detail: the sun might rise in the west, or the moon might fall to the earth. (Or rather: the sun or the moon might fall in the west to the earth. 31.
O Great Goddess, if the ocean were ever to dry up, this king of yogas of mine would never be in vain; it is indeed always unfailing.
Just as Viṣṇu’s discus is never in vain, just as my trident is,
and just as the thunderbolt of the King of the Gods is, so too is this yoga taught by me.
Just as the lotus-seated Brahmā is certain, O Goddess, so too is this yoga certain, O Goddess; there is no doubt in this matter. (34)
O Goddess, just as the wish-fulfilling tree (kalpavṛkṣa) fulfills all desires, so too, O Goddess, has this supreme yoga been proclaimed. (35)
O Goddess, for the sake of the kingdom, for the sake of the lineage, and for the sake of the son, one should set out on the journey upon a golden leaf measuring sixteen finger-breadths in length.

O auspicious goddess, it shines for the sake of sacrifice, for the sake of wealth, and for the sake of fame; likewise, O goddess, it is so when made of silver, and similarly when made of copper, though it leads to destruction.
O Supreme Goddess, O lady of excellent limbs, one should write the mantra of Tāriṇī— which bestows all accomplishments— either on gold or on birch bark for another's sake.
O Goddess, one who desires sovereignty, wealth, sons, fame,
or prosperity should draw this most beautiful [diagram] with a pen.

One should draw [the design] for the sake of knowledge with a golden rod eight finger-breadths long, using the root of *kuśa* grass; for other purposes, one should draw it with *dūrvā* grass according to the measurement of the little finger.
Having sipped water for purification and bowed before the Guru’s sandals, O Goddess,
one should face the northern direction and worship Tāriṇī.
Saffron, yellow pigment, jaṭāmāṃsī, and sandalwood; kāśmīra, musk, lac, and vermilion, O fair-faced one—42.
First, having unified everything, one should draw a hexagonal wheel;
in its center, one should inscribe the supreme Tārā consisting of four and a half syllables.

Or else, being absorbed in that [mantra], one should write the object of accomplishment (*sādhya*) situated within the *veda* (the square) using the five-and-a-half syllables; O beloved of Śambhu, listen now to what that object of accomplishment is.
"Subjugate such-and-such a person's speech; do it!
[And] accomplish such-and-such knowledge for such-and-such a person; do it! (45)
"O lustful woman, produce, produce a handsome son for such-and-such women! Give, give such-and-such wealth to such-and-such a man! 46.
In this very manner, having carefully inscribed the object of accomplishment (sādhya) in due order,
one should write the six long vowels, excluding the neuter *klī*, within the hexagon.
One should draw there a well-proportioned, beautiful, and very charming eight-petalled lotus,
with a pair of filaments on each of its eight petals.
Then, one should write the eight syllables on the eight petals as they will be described:
Vāgbhava, Bhuvaneśānī, Kāma, Huṃ, and likewise Praṇava.
Then one should write the *māyā-mantra* followed by *svāhā* in sequence starting from the east;
thus one should draw the yantra as a square with four gates. (50)
Upon the attainment of knowledge, even the supernatural powers (siddhis) arise; yet elsewhere, they do not exist except at the rising of the nectar [of immortality].
This applies when Jupiter, Venus, the Moon, Mars, or Mercury are present. (51)
When Tārā is favorable, one should recite the mantra with a concentrated mind;
having wrapped [the image] in yellow cloth, one should encircle it with lac.
The most excellent practitioner should bind it with a red silk cloth;
having placed it upon golden pedestals, the skillful one should perform the recitation.
One should never place it upon the surface of the ground, nor where it has come into contact with discarded flower offerings;
nor should one ever place it where it is cracked or stepped over. (54)
O Goddess, having set out on the length according to the measure of sixteen finger-breadths,
one should carefully fashion a jar that is enchanting to the sight of all.
One desiring sovereignty should fashion a jar with gold; one desiring a son, with silver; and one desiring victory in battle, with copper; otherwise, one may fashion it from clay. (56)
Having placed pearls, coral, gems, silver, gold,
and grain therein, one should cover its opening with sprouts.
Having covered it with a pair of red linen cloths, the wise and self-restrained practitioner [should place it] upon a square golden plate measuring eight finger-breadths on all sides.
Having written your mantra and carefully placed it inside a jar,
one should worship the supreme, auspicious Tārā with the sixty-four types of offerings.
O Queen, in the royal Puṣpaka chariot, there are sixteen layers of coverings in the lineage.
O Goddess, adorned with filaments and taking the offering as before,
the knower of mantras should present it with great skill using the bali-mantra.

Having bathed [the deity] with the five nectars (pañcāmṛta) and the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), the best of practitioners should worship and perform one thousand and eight oblations (homa). || 62 ||
O Goddess of the gods, one should place flowers and unbroken rice grains upon that vessel;
if the seeker of desire wishes for a kingdom, he should give land measuring the extent of a village.
O Maheśvarī, one who desires victory in battle [should give] a sacrificial fee consisting of two golden horses and a single Śālagrāma stone adorned with golden lines and other marks.
For the attainment of knowledge, however, one should give a cow and gold elsewhere;
the wise man should feed Brahmins and young maidens at Kalpapallava.

Then a man should place the yantra on his right arm, a woman on her left arm, and a child around the neck; thus has this beautiful [instruction] been told. One should not [discard] the deity even in a life-threatening crisis. (66)

Thus ends the third chapter in the *Śrīyoginītantra*, the great king of tantras, in the dialogue between the Goddess and the Lord, the most excellent of all tantras, within the twenty-four thousand [verse] work.
The fourth chapter.
The Goddess said:
O God of gods, O Lord of the world, who art saluted by gods and asuras,
I now desire to hear the means for accomplishing the six rites of the heroes.
Blessed are the kings who possess merit and enjoy sovereignty and other such splendors; and blessed is the woman who dwells in the abode of the Siddhas and delights in all yogic arts. (2)
The Lord said:

O Supreme Goddess, pacification (śānti), subjugation (vaśya), immobilization (stambhana), as well as inciting enmity (vidveṣa), eradication (uccāṭana), and killing (māraṇa)—this is proclaimed as the sixfold ritual action (ṣatkarma). || 3 ||
O Mother who pervades the universe, out of affection for you, I shall speak of the supreme means of attaining perfection—which brings swift success—concerning Tāriṇī, Kālikā, and Chinnā. 4.
Rati, Vāṇī, Ramā, Jyeṣṭhā, Mātaṅgī,
Kulakāminī, Durgā, and Bhadrakālī [should be worshipped] at the beginning of any rite for the successful accomplishment of that rite.
The hero should worship with the sixteen services according to his capacity,
either in an empty house, a great forest, or even in a temple of the deity.
One should perform the five rites; as for the rite of killing, it should be done upon a corpse.
In its absence, it should be performed on the ground of the ancestors. I shall now describe the garments to you. (7)
The primary [garment] is to be known as the sky-clad (naked state), and the second is a tiger skin;
in its absence, one may use red linen, but one should not employ any other cloth.
For the first [rite] gold is used, and for the second silver; for stambhana, a stone;
for vidveṣa and uccāṭana, copper; and for māraṇa, a skull is auspicious.
If a man other than a Brahmin is described as young and dark-complexioned,
and dies from causes other than famine or disease, a garland placed upon him brings auspiciousness.
In the absence [of these], O Dear One, one should perform the recitation with crystal beads, or one may recite with *indrākṣa* seeds;
or else, O Sovereign of the Gods, on a seat made of soft or tender materials.
O Goddess, O Beloved, [it may be] on a shaven head, or on a vulva, or on the skin of a tiger;
[measuring] one cubit, two cubits, or four cubits on all sides.
Remaining steady in posture, one should practice correctly and contemplate one's own fearlessness therein;
O Maheśānī, when fear arises, one should mutter the mantra spoken by Bhairava.
The pair of *viṣa*, then *vajrajāle*, followed by the pair of jaws (*hanu*);
then *sarvabhūtānataḥ* ending with the *kūrca* mantra—this is the Bhairava mantra. (14)
Then the practitioner should offer the bali-oblation to the spirits in accordance with the Dharma;
O Great Goddess, he should perform that ritual of the Dharma-stake using an *aśvattha* tree. (15)
One should perform the five rites according to the conjunctions of the days of the week beginning with Sunday;
and on Saturday, O Goddess, praised by heroes, the rite of killing is certain.
O lady of pure smiles, all the ritual actions should be performed during the conjunction of night;
first, the wise one should properly recite his own mantra ten thousand times over the corpse.
When the fruit of the ritual application has been obtained, it is a great protector of one's own voice;
therefore, on the day of the rite, when only one watch of the night has passed, the practitioner of mantra— (18)
One should worship the destroyer of the *kula* with these five substances along with the five deities beginning with Mā.
The *kulakaulika*, naked and with all his hair disheveled, [performs this]. 19.
Endowed with power, one should recite the Vidyā while always remembering you in the mind;
O Great Goddess, this should be done for a hundred thousand repetitions, preceded by the worship of Śakti.
Every day he should feed Brahmins, such as those belonging to the Kaula lineage and others, on alternating days;
likewise, he should offer meat, wine, and fish into the fire a hundred times each.
O Śāmbhavī, he should give a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to the Guru in the form of the Guru;
or, O best of heroes, according to the aforementioned injunction, [he may do so] from the various directions.
O Maheśānī, if one should perform this, one may lead even the gods [to such a state];
O Kāntā, no hesitation arises, and one will certainly partake of the fruit.
O Goddess of the gods, in the great ritual application, one should offer a black goat as a sacrifice;
at the conclusion of the worship, O Goddess, one should constantly honor the fire with its meat.

The ritual procedure is prescribed everywhere according to the sequence of the divine, the heroic, and the animal; one obtains the fruit through this sequence, but by transgressing it, one becomes a sinner.
Thus has the proper scope of the sixfold ritual been told to you;
it must be kept secret from the wicked, the corrupt, and in the presence of common cattle-herders.
The Goddess said: O Lord, what is the nature of the gods and others, and what is the auspicious power (śakti) like?
O ocean of compassion, tell me how they correspond appropriately to the six types of action (ṣaṭkarma).
Īśvara said: Mādhvī is declared to bring peace; for a Vaiśya, Sphāṭikī is auspicious.
For the rite of immobilization (stambhana), Ḍākinī is to be known [as the appropriate one]; for causing enmity (vidveṣa), Pauṣṭikī is considered [suitable]. (28)
Likewise, Gaudī is for eradication, and Bhairavī is considered for killing;
O Goddess, their characteristics have been told in the Kulamohana.
The Padminī is said to bestow peace, while the Śaṅkhinī is considered suitable for subjugation; O Goddess, the Nāgavallabhā is praised for paralyzing and expelling.
Likewise, the Teacher [taught] the slaying [rite], wherein the ḍākinī who bestows the death of enemies is fair-limbed, long-haired, and always speaks words of nectar. (31)

She who has red eyes, is of excellent character, and is a *padminī*, is auspicious for the practice of accomplishment (*sādhana*); indeed, she brings about success in mantra, as does she who is a *śaṅkhinī* and possesses such qualities. (32)
She who has long limbs is Śaṅkhinī, the one who causes the enchantment of the world;
she whose limbs are even is of the Śūdra body, neither short nor excessively tall.
Dīrghakeśī, Śatapuṣṭā, Madhyapuṣṭā, and Mṛdubhāṣā are Nāginīs;
Kṛṣṇāṅgī, Kṛśāṅgī, Danturā, and Madatāpitā are also [Nāginīs]. || 34 ||
She has short hair and a long nose, always speaking harshly;
she is perpetually angry, tall of body, and devoted to loud shrieks.
Shameless, devoid of laughter, sleep-prone, and a great eater—she is declared to be that Ḍākinī, who is praised in the yoga of death. (36)
O Goddess, these Śaktis arise from all castes;
they are accompanied by their offspring, are beautiful, and are auspicious with sons and other kin.
They should be accepted by those who delight in the Kula-essence and worshipped as beloved women with a spirit of devotion. (37)
The Goddess said: (p.
27) "O Maheśāna, if I am dear to you, [tell me] by which and which mantra a practitioner of mantras becomes a partaker of the six rites; [tell me] each of those mantras."
Īśvara said: The single-syllable mantra of Kālikā, the three-seed-mantra of Tārā, and the eleven-syllable mantra of Vajravairocanī—[these are the foremost]. (39)
And Manu is indeed declared to be the one who takes away all splendor;
what more need be said here? Listen, O beloved of my life! (40)
Endowed with power alone and composed in mind, one should recite the mantra of the Goddess;
one certainly attains the fruit, O Goddess praised by heroes, and not otherwise. 41.
O Maheśānī, if the wicked were to attain the fruit [of their actions], or if that which is fruitful were to become fruitless, then all of this would be in vain. (42)
O Śivā, daughter of the mountain, although I am the sustainer, the protector, and one striving for your protection, nevertheless, success has not been achieved; this is indeed a marvel.
O Goddess, I shall now describe to you specifically this method of slaying:
the peaceful [syllable] joined with fire and adorned with the left eye. (44)
Hrīṃ hu/ hu/ [Name], kill, kill, svāhā!
Then, O Goddess, the pair of kūrcas: [Name], kill, kill. || 45 ||
The fourteen-syllable mantra ending in *svāhā* is a destroyer of enemies.
Having taken charcoal from a *khadira* tree, especially on a Tuesday or the eighth lunar day, [one should perform the rite]. (46)
One should cause an effigy in the form of the enemy to be drawn upon an iron plate at night,
[inscribing the mantra] on its head, eyes, forehead, heart, and hand.
Having inscribed the syllables of the mantra at the navel, the secret place, the hips, the back, and the two feet in their sequential order, one should perform the consecration there. (48)
Having formed the *saṃhāramudrā*, one should meditate upon the Goddess who bestows victory—long of form, black in color, with her breasts and head perpetually raised. (49)
One should meditate upon the goddess who destroys enemies for the sake of the destruction of foes— she who is naked and is chewing a pair of human skulls in her hand.
Having meditated thus, O Śaṅkarī, with the powder of bricks using the left hand, one should offer it while saying, "Oṃ, obeisance to the destroyer of enemies," O Maheśvarī. (51)
One should offer a stream mixed with turmeric powder while reciting this mantra:
"Drink, drink the blood of [Name]!
followed by "Eat, eat the flesh! Hrīṃ Namaḥ! (52).
Having performed worship at midday or at midnight, one should recite [the mantra] one hundred and eight times on the eleventh day; then disease will surely arise—of this there is no doubt.
In the twenty-first year, increased by the number of syllables in the name, death from the enemy is certain;
or else, I shall describe another method for the destruction of the enemy. (54)
Having taken the excrement of a Puṅgīśa, one should worship it with warm water;
one should perform the recitation, worship, and other rites in reverse order.
One should collect the *puṅgī* fruit with the mantra "Salutation to Mahādeva," and one should perform the grinding with the mantra "Salutation to Śiva. (56)
Then, with the mantra "Salutation to Paśupati," one should stabilize the vital breaths.
O Maheśānī, having drawn an image of the enemy in an iron vessel using charcoal from Khadira wood, one should establish Śiva therein.
Then one should meditate upon Mahārudra; listen with a concentrated mind to the meditation:
[one should visualize] Rudra stationed upon the chest of the enemy, possessing a radiance like blazing fire. (58)
The god holds his hair with his left hand and draws in the vital breaths with his right;
he is clothed in human skin and entwined by great serpents and other creatures. (59)

Having invoked [the deity] with effort using "O wielder of the Pināka bow, come here," and so forth, the best of practitioners should bathe [the image] while saying, "Salutation to the Trident-bearer. (60)

One should worship with water for the feet and other offerings, saying "Salutation to Maheśvara. Likewise, O Maheśvarī, one should worship the forms beginning with Īśāna in reverse order, starting from the southeast corner and proceeding according to the manner of the Sun.

One should recite twenty-eight times the root mantra "Oṃ, salutation to Śiva, salutation to Śiva" (oṃ śivāya namaḥ śivāya namaḥ) followed by "huṃ. Then, one should dismiss [the deity] with the left hand while saying, "Forgive me. || 62 ||
"O Ajita, Keśava, Viṣṇu, Hare, Satya, Janārdana!
O Haṃsa, Nārāyaṇa! Svāhā!"—one should recite this mantra once.
"Homage to the Blessed Vāsudeva, Svāhā!"
Thus, one should recite "Śiva" or even "Namaḥ" just once.
In this way, O Goddess Trilocanā, by means of the Ekādaśāha rite, the intoxication of enemies occurs swiftly; it happens inevitably, truly, truly.
I shall describe, O Great Goddess, the supreme rite for paralyzing enemies:
one should fetch water from the house of a potter in a vessel [or a trident]. (66)
The best of practitioners clearly performs the "one" and "two" himself;
having brought from the middle of the fire-pot the aged ashes in that manner, [he proceeds]. (67)
O Goddess of the Gods, having placed a wide layer of dry reed leaves in a cooking pot and positioned it upon the ashes, one should place it within the enclosure. (68)
O Maheśvarī, having made an opening in the northeast on a Saturday, O Bhāvinī, again at midday when it is secluded; 69.
O beloved, from the vicinity of the pit in the enclosure on all four sides,
I shall protect that much ground from thieves.
O Goddess, with a joyful mind, one should perform the circumambulation on the ground; and then, O beautiful lady, that much ground should be traversed by turning to the left.
Having circumambulated, he should again go near the pit;
right there in that secluded pit, [he should place] a pin made of iron.
Having planted [the seed] and placed a pot with its saucer upon it,
and having filled that pit with earth, one should return home.
O Goddess, there shall indeed be a paralysis of movement for thieves and others;
O Goddess, this supreme yoga is difficult to obtain on the surface of the earth. (74)
The movement of piśācas, bhūtas, vetālas, kūṣmāṇḍas, brahmarākṣasas, dānavas,
and others is likewise obstructed there;
furthermore, the abundance of wealth and sons increases day and night.
Day by day, an increase in righteousness occurs; there is no doubt about this.
Thus ends the fourth chapter in the *Yoginītantra*, the supreme among all supreme tantras, in the dialogue between the Goddess and the Lord, within the twenty-four thousand [verse] work.
The fifth chapter begins.
The Goddess said: O Blessed One, knower of all dharmas, benefactor of the worlds,
[tell me] the practice of the universal mantra that fulfills all hopes.
Therefore, I wish to hear that; tell it to me, O Maheśvara.
Īśvara said:
First, I shall describe the most wonderful practice regarding the bed;
at the time when half a watch of the night has passed, the best of practitioners [should proceed].
Having become naked (digambara) and having properly sipped water according to the rules,
he should then sprinkle himself with the root mantra and lie down upon that bed.
Having worshipped the Guru, the Paraguru, the Parāparaguru, as well as the Parameṣṭhiguru, and Gaṇeśvara on the left; || 4 ||
And to the right, above the eyebrows, one should worship with "Salutation to the Dweller in the Cremation Ground," and then, O Śivā, with "Salutation to the Māyā-seat."
O Goddess, having written the Praṇava, the Vāgbhava, and Phaṭ upon the surface of the bed,
one should carefully perform the ritual sipping of water (ācamana) according to the procedure prescribed for one's own mantra.
The Praṇava, Maṇidhara, Vajriṇī, Mahāpada, and Pratisarā, joined with "rakṣa rakṣa māṃ hūṃ phaṭ svāhā. || 7 ||

O Goddess, having tied the topknot according to the rule with this mantra, one should perform the ritual placement on the limbs (aṅganyāsa), the ritual placement on the hands (karanyāsa), and likewise the ritual placement of the Mātṛkā letters.

Having performed the purification of the elements (bhūtaśuddhi) and other rites, the best of practitioners, having meditated with devotion upon the supreme Śivā in the lotus of the heart and worshipped her with mental offerings, [proceeds].
O fair-faced one, let it be placed upon the bed over the mantra;
then, O Goddess, [place] the *praṇava* and likewise "Salutation to the Vaṭukas. (10)
With this mantra, one should mentally worship Vaṭuka with water for the feet and other offerings;
thereafter, one should [protect] him on all sides with a stream of water using the fire-seed syllable (vahnibīja).
Having meditated upon the fire-fence and the resolve with reverence,
and having performed the recitation (japa), one should then offer it according to the prescribed rite, O Supreme Goddess.
O Goddess of gods, O Śivā, having formed the mental resolve once more, one should perform the entire sequence:
the fire-oblation (homa), the libation (tarpaṇa), and thereafter the consecration (abhiṣeka). 13.
If there is no food for the Brahmin, one should perform double the recitation;
having given gold as a sacrificial fee, one should perform the rite for the concealment of defects.
Having addressed Vaṭuka, O Goddess, saying "Forgive me," one should dismiss him.
Thus, O Great Goddess, has been described the supreme ritual for the preparation of the bed.
It swiftly brings about the accomplishment of mantras and bestows union with us;
now listen to the practice for three or four repetitions. (16)
Having gone to a place where three roads meet or a place where four roads meet, O fair-faced one,
she should worship her guru and prostrate before him with the mantra "Maṇidharī."
Having tied the knot at the end of the vajra, the supreme practitioner, free from fear, [should pray]:
"May all those gods, daityas, and bhairavas who dwell in the cremation ground show compassion; may they all become bestowers of siddhi upon me. (18)
One should bow down with devotion using this mantra beginning with the syllable *praṇava*;
thereafter, one should face either the east or the north.
Having sat down, performed the ritual sipping of water (ācamana), and recited the benediction (svasti-vācana), O Maheśvarī,
the wise practitioner should sweep that very spot and inscribe the seed-syllable of the preta (pretabīja) there.
O Great Goddess, one should spread out a seat upon the seed-syllable. Having sat there, O Queen of the Gods, one should meditate upon one’s chosen deity within the heart. (21)
O Maheśānī, having worshipped Kālī and the others according to the prescribed rite, one should offer oblations to the eight [deities] while propitiating them with a mind directed as one desires.

Kālī, Kapālinī, Kullā, Kurukullā, Virodhinī, Vipracittā, Nīlā, and Valākā—these are the enemies of the sages (or possessors of radiant wealth). They are worshipped with mantras beginning with *praṇava* (oṃ), ending with *namaḥ*, and including their respective names in the dative case (e.g., *kālīyai namaḥ*). This is performed according to the sequence of the *pūjāvalī*.
The offerings of worship, the bali-oblations, and so forth, are prescribed [for this purpose]. || 23 ||

Having made a formal resolve and recited the mantra one hundred and eight times, and having performed the rite for ensuring the absence of defects, he should leave that place, remember the Goddess, and go home.
Thus has been declared this sādhana, practiced for the attainment of all perfections;
it must not be given to just anyone, for it is the supreme benefit for practitioners. || 25 ||
Hereafter, O Maheśānī, I shall describe the practice of the root of the *bilva* tree; the *bilva* root is sixteen cubits in circumference.
O beautiful one, know that my matted locks are indeed like leaves;
O lady of lovely countenance, they consist of three leaves resembling the Ṛg, Yajur, and Sāma Vedas. (27)
Know, O lotus-eyed one, that all the scriptures are indeed branches [of this tree].
The Bilva tree is equal to the Kalpa-vṛkṣa; Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Śiva, and the others, as well as Mahālakṣmī, were born from the Bilva tree on the Śrīśaila mountain. (28)
The Goddess said: "How did that wife of Viṣṇu become a bilva tree?
O Compassionate One, tell me this most wonderful account. (29)
Īśvara said:
Listen, O Goddess, I shall relate a most wonderful account.
In the Satya Yuga, he worshipped the Liṅga named Rāmeśvara. (30)
Having prayed to my portion in the form of light, which is sought after by Brahmā and the other gods,
my speech there attained the state of being dear to everyone through my grace.
Sarasvatī was always exceedingly dear to Viṣṇu;
indeed, such affection as he felt for her was never produced even toward Lakṣmī by Keśava.
Thus lost in thought, Lakṣmī went to the supreme Śrīśaila;
having reached my Liṅga in a secluded spot, she performed most rigorous penance.
Nevertheless, O Supreme Goddess, if compassion had not arisen within me,
then that virtuous lady would have remained in the form of a tree before the Liṅga.
O Maheśānī, he worshipped [me] constantly with his own leaves, flowers, and fruits for ten million years; thereafter, grace descended upon me.
By that very grace, O Supreme Goddess, she shall abide upon the chest of Viṣṇu;
indeed, she shall always sport there forever.
For this reason, O Goddess Śivā, that beloved of Hari, being my devotee and peerless, has always worshipped me in that form.
Therefore, O Goddess, I remain stationed upon this tree day and night;
for I am always composed of all sacred fords and composed of all the gods.
O Supreme Goddess, for this very reason, there is no doubt that it is the Śrīvṛkṣa;
whoever worships with its fruits, its flowers, or its leaves [attains the goal]. (39)
Whether it be with that wood or with sandalwood, he who out of devotion wears that wood or sandalwood upon his forehead is my devotee; he is dear to me. (40)
Therefore, O Goddess, one should certainly not wear that sandalwood paste at any time, even if one bows down with a mind fixed on Śiva or filled with joy. (41)
One should never wear its leaf or its flower, O Maheśānī. As for that man who gives up his life at the root of the Bilva tree— [he attains liberation]. (42)
He will truly become the very body of Rudra, even if he is burdened by tens of millions of sins;
therefore, O Goddess, this sādhana brings pleasure to all.
Having gone there to the root of a *bilva* tree, O Goddess, one should diligently worship the four gurus as before, and having also fully honored the *kṣetrapāla*.
O illustrious guardian of the field, sovereign of the cremation ground, observer of noble vows!
Grant me success; O Creator of the World, grant me a place; salutations be unto you! (45)
Then, one should prostrate with this mantra beginning with the *praṇava*;
thereafter, O fair-faced one, having worshipped the site, one should draw [the diagram] there.
The best of practitioners should write the Vāgbhava syllable, the seed-syllable of the Preta, and again the Vāgbhava syllable; at the end of that, he should write the root mantra.
O Supreme Goddess, having worshipped Kālī and the others as before,
one should perform the ritual resolve (saṃkalpa), recite the mantra one hundred and eight times, and then attend to any omissions.
Then, having abandoned that place and remembering the Guru, one should go home.
Thus has been told to you the essence of essences, higher than the high. 49.
It must always be kept secret, O auspicious lady, especially among the multitude of worldly beings.
Now listen, O Goddess of gods, to the supreme practice of Muṇḍa-sādhana. 50.
O fair-faced one, having performed [the offering of] the three heads of a man, a buffalo, and a cat, the practitioner goes to the supreme state of the Great Goddess. (51)
Alternatively, O Supreme Goddess, one should respectfully offer three human skulls;
for you, O Great Mistress, arise from the offerings of jackals, snakes, dogs, men, and bulls. 52.
A human skull [or five skulls] should likewise be placed in the center; thus they are called the "five skulls.
Alternatively, O Supreme Goddess, one may use the five skulls of men.
Likewise, O Supreme Goddess, [one may offer] a hundred, a thousand, ten thousand, a hundred thousand, a million, or even ten million human heads.
Having placed a human skull upon the ground and having inflated it,
one should fashion the Goddess above it measuring one span (vitasti). O Goddess, for the lengthwise extension, one should employ four cubits (hasta).

One may perform [the rite] up to a thousand times or even a hundred thousand times with a sixteen-fingered [measure]; beyond that, O Great Goddess, one should proceed with a measure of one hundred cubits.
The preceptor should worship Bhūtanātha and the others in the four directions of that [mandala], using the previously mentioned mantra: "Obeisance to Bhūtanātha. (57)
Having worshipped with water for the feet and other offerings, one should diligently present the bali-oblation;
likewise, O Goddess, one should reverently worship the Lord of the Cremation Ground in the south.
And likewise, having worshipped the supreme Kālabhairava in the western part and similarly the cremation ground (śmaśāna) in the north, one should offer the sacrificial oblation (bali).
In the center of the altar, one should worship the seed-syllable of the preta (PHAṬ) immediately following that [mantra];
with this very [mantra], one should perform the worship of the sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas) using water for the feet and other offerings.
(37) Having written the seed-syllable of Caṇḍikā (*hrīṃ*) in the southwest, the best of practitioners should there worship with devotion Bhāratī in her own auspicious form. (61)

Having worshipped with this mantra—beginning with *vāgbhava* and ending with *namaḥ*, namely *vāgdevatā ṅeyutā* (or *vāgdevatābhagayutā*)—one should offer a sacrificial oblation (*bali*) to her. || 62 ||
O Hero, O Lord of the gods, O Lord of the world in the form of the Skull-bearer!
Have mercy, O illustrious one; become the bestower of perfection upon me as I bathe.
Upon the altar, one should likewise scatter three handfuls of flowers;
on the corpse, one should fashion the noose situated within the fire and endowed with a digit of the moon.
The seed-syllable of Māyā, followed by the seed-syllable of Kūrca and the syllable Phaṭ;
with this very [mantra], one should worship the sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas) with water for the feet and other offerings. || 65 ||
In the southwest, the preceptor [should worship] with the mantra "hrīṃ caṇḍikāyai namaḥ";
thereafter, in the northwest, with the mantra "hrīṃ bhadrakālyai namaḥ."
O Śāmbhavī, the practitioner [should worship] in the northeast with the mantra "Hrīṃ, obeisance to Bhadrakālī," and in the southeast with the mantra "Hrīṃ, obeisance to Caṇḍogrā. (67)
Having performed worship and offered the bali-oblation, he then stands up before them and says:
"Those gods and goddesses who dwell in the cremation ground, and the Bhairavas... (68)
"May they all show compassion; may they become bestowers of success upon me.
With this mantra beginning with the *praṇava*, one should cast three handfuls of flowers.
Then, having touched that place, one should say, "Become submissive.
O Maheśvarī, having spread out a seat of grass (viṣṭara-āsana) and sat down, [one should proceed].
Having performed ten thousand eight hundred recitations, one should observe the [daily] deficiencies;
having purified the place and bowed to the Goddess, one should go home while meditating upon her. (71)
O Goddess, O Śāmbhavī, hear the remainder regarding the procedure for *puraścaryā*:
one should never place a ritual peg (*kīlaka*) upon the three skulls at any time. (72)
In an empty house, on a riverbank, or on a mountain;
at a crossroads, at the foot of a bilva tree, in a cremation ground, or in a solitary, uninhabited place with a single linga. || 73 ||
One should cause these shaven heads to be placed upon them for the sake of accomplishing all desires and goals;
or, having thus placed a human shaven head according to the prescribed rite, [one should proceed].
"By this, one becomes the lord of all accomplishments; what need is there for many [other means], O lady of good vows?
Thus has the *sādhana* of the *muṇḍas* been told, O Goddess Śivā, by performing which one becomes the sovereign of all accomplished masters on earth. (75)
Thus ends the fifth chapter in the Yoginītantra, the supreme among all supreme tantras, in the dialogue between the Goddess and the Lord, within the twenty-four thousand [verse] work.
The sixth chapter.
The Goddess said:
O Blessed One, knower of all dharmas, proficient in all the Āgamas, you are the master of all mantras and an ocean of compassion. (1)

"You have made all phenomena [your own], O Sun within the lotus-heart of yogis. The divine state and the heroic state have been demonstrated by you through your greatness; tell me that specifically, O Moon-crested One. (2)
Īśvara said:
Two types of yoga have been proclaimed through the distinction between the divine (divya) and the heroic (vīra).
From that yoga, O Maheśvarī, the Kaula arose as both divine and heroic.
O Goddess, O beloved of the Kula, he who performs that rite without union with Her is not a practitioner of yoga; O Goddess, one who desires liberation should perform worship through the Great Union.
I shall speak this to you; having heard it, let it be worn as an ornament upon your ear.
One should contemplate the Self as the Supreme Brahman, or else not at all.
One should always contemplate one's own body as having one's desired form;
likewise, one should visualize the entire universe as having one's desired form.
O Goddess, guard this divine yoga with vigilance.
Listen now to this Vīrayoga, which is saluted by all the gods. One should first contemplate the three drops (bindus) pervaded by the Kalās.
Therefore, one should meditate upon the manifested form of a woman, sixteen years of age and so forth,
whose light illuminates the quarters of the sky like ten million rising suns.
The emergence of the upper *bindu* from the head down to the breast,
and the middle body from the *bindu* down to the throat, waist, and head.
One should contemplate [the deity] shining with two breasts, adorned with the three folds [of the waist], extending from the vulva down to the feet, and ending with the Kāma-mantra.
One should contemplate one’s own body as having the form of the *kāmakaḷā*, richly adorned with various ornaments and worshipped by Brahmā, Īśvara, and Viṣṇu. (11)
O Supreme Goddess, always listen to this yoga of the hero;
I shall describe their excellent conduct in brief. (12)
Meat, fish, mudrās, and sexual union—O Goddess, this is the conduct of the *paśu*, not of the *divya* or the *vīra*. (13)
O Maheśvarī, may he become a divine hero who follows the conduct of the gods;
O Maheśānī, if by fate wine and other such substances are not obtained.
On which day, O Goddess of gods, should one perform that rite for oneself?
Even so, O Śivā, this [specific day] regarding the sipping of water (ācamana) must not be disclosed.
Without the great intoxicant, the Kaula does not remain [awake] for even a moment;
therefore, O Goddess, wine and the like should be consumed day after day. (16)
I shall describe the procedure for practice; listen, O daughter of the mountain!
Having been initiated by a guru, one should perform the Kaula-nyāsa. (17)
The procedure for that is found in the Uttara-tantra and in this Kulārṇava;
I have taught it in due order—one should perform these two consecrations. (18)
Having received the name from the Guru as well, one should choose the supreme yoga—either the divine or the hero-yoga—according to one's past actions. (19)
At that very moment, having become beloved, he is liberated from time;
he who becomes divine is truly Viṣṇu—of this there is no doubt.
(41) Whoever shall become Rudra in the remainder [of the world] is indeed a hero, there is no doubt;
in whatever place a divine man or a preeminent hero should reside. (21)
O Goddess of the gods, that very family or that king of the land itself is designated as a field of accomplishment (siddhikṣetra) extending ten yojanas in every direction.
In that very place are all the sacred fords (tīrthas), and there is the Gaṅgā, the best of rivers;
it is difficult even for yoginīs, ḍākinīs, and serpents to attain.
By Brahma-rākṣasas, Vetālas, Kuṣmāṇḍas, Bhairavas, Śivas, Guhyakas, Dānavas, or even by Mārīs, Yakṣas, Kinnaras, and [Māyās]. (24)
Despite diseases, predatory beasts, famines, and swarms of serpents, there will certainly be auspiciousness and the expansion of that city. (25)
There will be abundance of food, security, and health; thus, for you, the treasury of Dharma shall constantly radiate all the scriptures from every source. (26)
That supreme practitioner is dearly beloved by Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Śiva, and the others;
for even trees live, but he alone truly lives as a living being among beasts and birds.
O Goddess, that preeminent hero whose mind is fixed on the duty of his lineage and who remains established in his own dharma—whether he dies anywhere at all—he becomes divine. || 28 ||
Right there, at that supreme level of knowledge, I place this Kula-dharma into your ear, O Goddess, which is to be practiced continuously. (29)
O Goddess, all the inhabitants of heaven, as well as the sages, humans, nāgas, siddhas, gandharvas, and kinnaras, are devoted to their respective family duties.
Whether they be sages, Vasus, Daityas, or even those who are the preeminent leaders of their lineages,
they all become the lords of their families through the grace of their family dharma.
Indra and the other gods, mounted upon their celestial vehicles, shall become long-lived.
In whatever manner people approach me, in that same manner they partake of the fruit [of their devotion]. (32)
A Brāhmaṇa, a Kṣatriya, or a Vaiśya—whether a student, a householder, a forest-dweller, or a recluse—these shall be the lineage-successors of the family. || 33 ||
O leader of the lineage, listen now from me to their procedure:
for a Brāhmaṇa, the liquor [surā] is made with jaggery and ginger juice. (34)
O fair-faced one, coconut water in a bronze vessel is for a Kṣatriya;
O woman of excellent complexion, honey placed in bronze is prescribed for a Vaiśya. (35)
Meat and fish are prescribed for all [the classes], along with salt and radish; likewise, birch bark, grain, and whatever else is said to be chewable [is permitted]. (36)
O Goddess, daughter of the mountain, that mudrā has been described for all;
the Brāhmaṇī belongs to the Brāhmaṇa, and the Kṣatriyā to the Kṣatriya. (37)
O Goddess, the rule for sexual union with a Vaiśya woman by a Vaiśya man is prescribed as praiseworthy;
likewise, O Maheśvarī, a Vaiśya woman or a Brāhmaṇī woman [is prescribed] for the three varṇas beginning with the Brāhmaṇa and Kṣatriya. (38)
O woman of excellent complexion, it has been stated that even a Kṣatriya may be the wife of a Brāhmaṇa;
or a Śūdra may be the wife of those of the three higher castes, such as Brāhmaṇas, in the absence [of others]. (39)
This is remembered as the vow for the Brahmins, Kṣatriyas, and Vaiśyas, as well as for those in the stages of life (āśramins).
Now listen to that which is prescribed for the ascetics (yatins) belonging to the three castes. 40.
O Śivā, the union of Kuṇḍalinī with the Bindu above the Sahasrāra is proclaimed as the supreme, divine sexual union (maithuna) for ascetics. 41.

O Śāmbhavī, listen as I describe the ritual procedure for one who belongs to the Avadhūta stage of life; for him, all intoxicants such as those used for nourishment and other purposes [are permitted]. 42.
O Goddess, his fish and meat—whether from aquatic, terrestrial, or aerial creatures—and the mudrā previously mentioned, shall be offered with devotion to that deity. (43)
Having abandoned the mother’s womb, one engages in sexual union with all types of wombs;
she whose womb has been violated should be beaten, but one must never beat her whose womb remains intact. 44.
O Goddess, from striking one who is unscarred (akṣata), the loss of spiritual power (siddhi) arises;
this lasts for twelve years, extending as far as sixty years. || 45 ||
Sexual intercourse with her is permitted only so long as she remains self-born; all those who follow the conduct of the Avadhūtas are declared to be equal to Śūdras.
I shall tell you the specific rule regarding sexual intercourse; listen to me.
Having abandoned women of the Brāhmaṇa, Kṣatriya, and Vaiśya castes, [one may approach] among all other castes. (47)
The wise man should engage in sexual union as an act performed with the nature of the deity;
he should be a householder, for he should never become one belonging to another stage of life.

This conduct is proclaimed for those of other castes as being like that of Śūdras; however, toward the two [higher] castes, it is like that toward a guru, and likewise toward the maternal grandfather's family. (49)
Sexual union is also well-prescribed even in the stage of the Avadhūta;
likewise for Kālī, Tārā, Chinnamastā, Sundarī, and Bhairavī. (50)
The Mātaṅgī-vidyā and likewise the Dhūmāvatī-vidyā—the conduct of the practitioners of these is traditionally held to be equal to that of the Avadhūtas. || 51 ||
In every stage of life, among all castes, and likewise in every yoga, O Auspicious One;
in all places and everywhere, there shall be no distinction whatsoever.
Bliss is the form of Brahman, and that is established within the body;
thus a Brahmin may offer the blood from his own limbs to the deity. (53)
There is no destruction of power nor any transformation in the offering of one’s own body-blood. (54)
O Goddess, substances such as [the sacrificial] materials are offered to it by those who observe the proper time;
O Goddess, all the rites beginning with purification constitute the latter half of the manifestation.
Through the first yoga alone, one who worships Kālī and others is accomplished;
through the second, [one attains] Bhairava; and through the third, Śiva-hood.
O Daughter of the Mountain, this is a marvel regarding the Lord of all Siddhis in the fourth [stage]:
he attains a state beyond the supreme; of this there is no doubt, he becomes equal to me.
But for those who have cultivated the reality of the Kula and clearly perceive the reality of the Kula, those Bhairavas do not arise; rather, they become Veśas who perceive that [reality] as equal.
Just as a house enveloped in darkness is seen [and dispelled] by means of a lamp, so too is the cycle of existence shrouded in illusion seen [and destroyed] by the lamp of knowledge. || 59 ||

For one who has cast aside the notion of duality regarding objects such as the pure and the impure, there is the state of being liberated while living; at the end of the body, he shall attain ultimate security.
Having drunk the *kula-rasa*, the hero should take recourse in the meditation on Brahman (*brahma-dhyāna*).
O Maheśānī, the meditation on Brahman is the cause of the nirvāṇa of Brahman. (61)
Listen to that, O Great Goddess, which is the essence of essences, higher than the highest:
that one's own life, body, and so forth, as well as the infinite universe, [are all but this]. (62)
Thus, O Goddess, whatever exists within the body, such as the great oceans and so forth—all that need not be contemplated; one should instead reflect that it does not exist. (63)
I am indeed like the great-splendored fisherman's net, pervading consciousness,
while being myself devoid of any supporting body.
O Goddess of gods, one should contemplate even one's own self as non-different from that [Brahman].
This is declared to be the meditation on Brahman, and it leads to extreme stability. (65)
Yogis serve the substance [of reality] and never otherwise;
he who performs self-contemplation for even a moment, thinking "I am Brahman," [attains it]. (66)
To him the Goddess shall grant the fruit; at its conclusion, it cannot be traversed by me, nor by Brahmā, nor even by Viṣṇu in any way whatsoever.
Therefore, O Great Goddess, one should never neglect the daily rites;
O Great Goddess, even in the absence of ritual materials, one should perform them with water alone.
Alternatively, one should constantly practice Kulayoga with the mind. O auspicious one, O lotus-faced lady, listen as I describe the ten-thousandfold rite. 69.
O Maheśānī, O fair-faced one, the supreme nectar that flows from the moon due to its union with Kuṇḍalī—the yogi should drink it; this is the truth, the very truth, Śiva himself.
This indeed is known as the Kulayoga, the Great Drink (mahāpāna); it is certainly remembered as such, O Great Goddess.
Having slain the animal of sin and merit with the sword of knowledge, O Śāmbhavī—this is the Great Drink. (71)
One should lead the mind into the Supreme Self; this is called "the eater" (palāśin).
Having restrained everything, including the mind and the senses, one should unite them within the Self. (72)
O my beloved, that yogi who eats fish becomes liberated from bondage;
he should dissolve the entire vessel of the universe into the Supreme Brahman.
The union of the self with that which is beyond the reach of others is not considered sexual intercourse in the context of *vīrya*.
Thus, O Goddess, I have told you the essence of essences, higher than the highest.
This, the means for attaining my very self, must be kept secret, kept secret. || 74 ||

Thus ends the sixth chapter in the *Śrīyoginītantra*, the great king of tantras [the most supreme among all tantras], in the dialogue between the Goddess and the Lord, within the twenty-four thousand [verse] work.
The seventh chapter.
The Goddess said: Salutations to you, O Mahādeva, the savior from the ocean of worldly existence;
O Lord of the universe, the remnant of my wife, O Īśvara who is affectionate toward your devotees. (1)
And the cause of the causes of the mass of supreme bliss—the two-fold yoga, distinguished as divine and heroic, has been heard by me. (2)

Now I desire to hear of the auspicious *vidyā* called Svāpnavatī, as well as the *vidyā* that revives the dead (*mṛtasañjīvanī*) and the Madhumatī; O Supreme Lord, tell me also the fruit and the method of practice for these. (3)
The Lord said: Listen, O Goddess, I shall declare that which you ask of me:
*Oṃ hrīṃ svapurāvāhi kāli svapne kathaya amukasya amukaṃ dehi krīṃ*.
Svāhā! || 4 ||
First, having extracted the Praṇava (Oṃ), then the Māyā-bīja (Hrīṃ); at the end of that, the two vocatives "svapurāvāhi Kāli. (5)
(47) After that, tell [the dream] in such a way: "In the dream, [I saw] so-and-so;
then, from the word 'give' (dehi), place the seed-syllable of Kālī, and likewise the consort of Fire (RA) at the end."
This Svāpnavatī-vidyā is extremely difficult to obtain in the three worlds;
it produces great wonder and was spoken by Mahākāla.
One should recite [the mantra] one hundred and eight times daily for four years;
