Flowers, barley-gruel, a conch, a kettle-drum, musical instruments, and the king [are auspicious omens]. (27)
A hundred cows, a chariot, a vehicle, and auspicious gifts on the right are prescribed; likewise, prepared food, a lump of meat, cooked rice, and a vessel for the preceptor. (28)
A ball of fish, food brought from elsewhere, and all auspicious things on the right side are favorable;
likewise, virgins, couples, courtesans, full jars, and women [are auspicious]. (29)
Cattle and birds moving to the left are bringers of auspiciousness;
a journey with curd and fruit ahead is proclaimed to bestow good fortune.
Likewise, when the curlews and peacocks move in pairs as one proceeds, then one should know that success is at hand; otherwise, one should predict an obstacle.
When vultures, hawks, and crows indeed approach one's side, a traveler should not undertake a journey; likewise, if crows are perched upon a tree, he should not set out.
One should never proceed after hearing the cry of a fallen person, harsh speech, the howling of a jackal or an iguana, or the sound of weeping and quarreling.
When Jupiter is eclipsed by the Sun, when Jupiter is in Leo, or when Venus has set, one should not perform the worship of deities, undertake journeys, or conduct consecrations. (34)
Likewise, one who initiates a vow, performs a marriage, builds a house or a temple, or undertakes the construction of ponds, wells, tanks, and the like, as well as mechanical devices; || 35 ||

Likewise, one should not plant a sacrificial tree— that is, the planting of a sacrificial tree— nor perform a grove-establishment, nor a vow to the gods, nor the ritual release of a bull, nor the commencement of a sacrifice. (36)
One should avoid the piercing of the ears, the initiation ceremony (*upanayana*), and the tonsure (*cūḍā*) for women;
one should never perform the first sight of them before the deities.

Prior to the commencement of vows, and for a journey lasting more than a year, as well as regarding the *vyālavrata*, one should indeed proceed constantly; there is no restriction of time in those cases, nor likewise in the *rohiṇīvrata*. (38)

On the occasion of the Śivarātri vow, at Prayāga (or for one from Prayāga), upon shaving the head, during a conflagration of the country, and during planetary afflictions, one may undertake an inauspicious rite. || 39 ||

The purification of the Sun is auspicious for Ujjayinī, and that of the Moon for the Middle Country; the purification of Mars is indeed for Nepāla, and that of Mercury for Avantī and [the breast-drinking place—meaning] the birthplace. (40)
In Gauḍa and Āndhra, the purification of Jupiter is prescribed; in Kāmarūpa, that of Venus;
in Mathurā, that of Saturn and Mercury; and in Aṅga and Vaṅga, that of Rāhu.
Likewise, the bow and arrow are situated at Oḍrapīṭha;
at Jālandhara there is the four-armed [deity], and at Hastapūrṇaka there is Ūrmikā.
In Kāmarūpa, the hand-measure is five; in Saumāra, it is one *tāra*;
in the Kolvapīṭha, it is four; and in Cauhāra, it shall be double that.
Know that Mahendra has four fingers (kalā), Śrīhaṭṭa has three fingers (vahni), and Upapīṭha in Pātāla has one finger (hasta). || 44 ||
On the Ratnapīṭha, at Ṣaḍhasta, and indeed in Lauhitya to the north, as well as at the hermitage of Baladeva and likewise in the hermitages of the maidens (Kanyā). || 45 ||
One should not approach the mouth of a yoginī; one should avoid bathing and meditative concentration.
Through a vehicle, one should know the fruit of wealth, and likewise through an umbrella and sandals.
Sexual intercourse and the eating of meat destroy the fruit of a pilgrimage;
however, by visiting a sacred site even incidentally, one may obtain the fruit of that site. (47)
But through knowledge one attains that [result], whereas for one devoid of knowledge it is fruitless.
One should avoid sipping water (ācamana) at a sacred ford (tīrtha), as well as washing the feet. (48)
Purity and ritual sipping of water, praising other sacred sites, delighting in other sacred sites, and always finding fault with one's own sacred sites. (49)
One should not discard impurity at a sacred ford (tīrtha), nor should one ever cast off hair there;
furthermore, one should not dwell on the bank of a sacred ford, especially on its southern side.
One should never bathe on the southern side of the holy ford;
likewise, on the northern side of the ford, there are eight thousand crores [of deities]. (51)
O beloved, there dwell sacred fords (tīrthas) and holy shrines (āyatanas) to the south of Kuṇḍatīrtha and on the left bank of the rivers;
among these tīrthas, one should never examine a Brāhmaṇa at all.
The twice-born who reside at whichever sacred ford (tīrtha) belongs to whichever deity should always be saluted and honored; through their word, one attains purification.
There is no restriction regarding the time for the śrāddha rite; however, one should avoid honey in the offering of the rice-balls (piṇḍa).
Having gone to a sacred ford (tīrtha), a wise man should not dwell on its bank for long;
this applies especially during an eclipse, at a sacred ford, and likewise on the day of the ancestors (śrāddha).
At the commencement and conclusion of a sacrifice, and especially during an earthquake,
that which is fit for giving to a Brahmin shall not be fit for a śrāddha rite.
It is proclaimed that no great gift (mahādāna) which is not given is fruitless;
likewise, there is no invocation (āvāhana), no water-offering (arghya), and no fire-oblation (agnīkaraṇa). || 57 ||
By the mere sprinkling of the purifier (pavitra), one should likewise ensure that [the water] is inexhaustible;
however, at a śrāddha performed at a sacred ford (tīrtha), one should not perform the offering of the garment or the sacred thread (vāsas-sūtra).
Then, at the times for offering the rice-balls, one should offer seventeen rice-balls;
having completed the śrāddha, one should never give away that [seventeenth] rice-ball.
One should perform ablutions; bathing should be performed at every pool and at every sacred ford—ten times, eight times, five times, seven times, and likewise three times a day.
Therefore, having performed an ablution, one should offer worship at a sacred ford—
at the Lauhitya, the Śoṇa, Gayā, and the Virajas.
One should likewise avoid the Maṇḍala in the hermitages of the Maidens (Kanyāśrama), at Agastya, on Mount Pāripātra, at Mukurāṅga, and at Ekāmra. || 62 ||
The mass of evil, however, flees and takes its stand upon the tip of the hair.
Therefore, one should abandon the crest-lock and place it at the base of the ear, or shave the base of the ear. 63.
At the end of a *ghaṭikā*, at the end of a month, at the end of six months,
and at the end of a year, or at the end of eight years, one should again perform the tonsure ceremony.
Then, having fashioned a Brahmin out of *kuśa* grass and placed him at the sacred bathing place (*tīrtha*),
the wise man, facing north, should cause his kinsmen to bathe.
One should bathe [the deity] three times with kuśa grass while reciting the mantra "kuśo nidhi.
There is no doubt that one will obtain a fourth part of the fruit of that sacred ford (tīrtha).
O twice-born one, having taken [the water] onto the lap and performed the immersion while reciting the name,
half of the fruit of the holy ford is ordained for the Brāhmaṇa.
Better is the sale of one's mother, better is the sale of one's father;
one should not cause a kinsman to bathe [at a sacred site], nor should one accept a gift at a holy ford. (68)
In sacred fields and holy fords, one should not utter a blessing for another;
nor, except in other circumstances, should one accept sesame seeds or a cow, especially so.

One should not accept from a Śūdra at a sacrifice, for he is excluded from the sacrifice; one might somehow become his sacrificial vessel. Whichever vessel belongs to whichever sacrifice, one becomes smeared by the sin of that [sacrifice].
Therefore, with every effort, one should avoid sacrificing for others.
Thus ends the second chapter in the second part of the upper section on Kāmarūpa in the *Śrīyoginītantra*, the great king of tantras in twenty-two thousand verses.
The third chapter.
The Blessed One said:
Kāmarūpa is the great sacred seat (pīṭha), the supreme secret among secrets;
there Śaṅkara always resides together with Pārvatī. (1)
The deity, when worshipped, becomes pleased upon that seat before long;
I shall now describe that seat, so listen, O beloved. (2)
At the time of the festival, a hundred rivers surrounded by ten million Liṅgas and hosts [of deities] will appear at the edge of Vāyukūṭa, measuring one dhanus and one hasta.
The moon remains in the form of wind; from it the vital air (māruta) issues forth.
By worshipping Tantuvāyu, one shall attain the world of Vāyu. || 4 ||
Formerly, to the east of Vāyugiri, there was a mountain known as Candrakūṭa;
in the middle was Godanta, and to the south was the auspicious Ṛṣyakrānta.
Mādhava is at Candrakūṭa, and Jaṭādhara is at Godanta;
Ṣaṇmukha and Jayanta are there, and Janārdana is at Aśvakrānta.
One should worship with honey and milk-rice using the respective seed-mantras;
he who resides at Vāyukūṭa shall become a lord of riches.
Residence on Candraśaila is subject to decay and not otherwise;
it is sinful at Godanta, but at Aśvakrānta it bestows liberation.
To the east of Candraśaila, slightly in the southeastern direction,
O Goddess of Devas, within the Lohitya [region], at a distance of thirty bow-lengths.

Residing there at the place known as Indraśaila yields great fruit. Between Indraśaila and Candraśaila, slightly toward the southern side and to the north of Candraśaila, the wise man should abandon a distance of six bow-lengths.
In its layout, it measures three bow-lengths, while the lake known as Candrakuṇḍa is considered to be one hundred bow-lengths in width and twenty-five in length.
Having bathed and drunk there, a man attains absolute liberation (kaivalya).
The great sacred ford Candratīrtha is equal to the sacred ford Piṇḍāraka.
Having bathed with this mantra, one dispels even the sin of killing a Brahmin:
"O you who are born from the lineage of Sudhīśa, O giver of pleasure to Mādhava! (13)
O remover of sin, salutations to you who bring delight to the ears of the wise! Bhṛgu [recited] almost all the yugas, accompanied by the initial series.

Above that is Bhṛgu with the staff (the letter *da*), ending with *ja* (i.e., *dja*), accompanied by Śakti (*ī*) and Surā (*u*). It is joined with Nāda (*m*) and Bindu (*n*), and again ending with *ja*, it is the Subhāvika. (15)
Having recited the eight-syllable mantra, one should offer the *arghya* with the *kakkola* mantra. Reciting the *kāma-mantra* at night on the full moon day of the months of Meṣa or Mīna, || 16 ||
Having bathed, one attains the status of Brahman and does not encounter an evil fate;
one should perform the bath during the day, for it destroys even the greatest sins.
But he who bathes in moonlight with milk using this aforementioned mantra remains as long as the earth endures, his body sprinkled by the uninterrupted stream of mantras.
That very same one, whether timid or wise, goes to the abode of the Moon, the supreme state.
To its southern direction, at a distance of four *dhanus*, || 19 ||
That sacred ford named Mānasa destroys all sins;
one should perform a ritual bath there during the bright fortnight of the month of Kārttika.
O Supreme Goddess, by means of this mantra one attains the world of Viṣṇu;
therefore, there is no doubt that this holy site (tīrtha) bestows satisfaction upon Viṣṇu.
O Lord of Rivers, grant satisfaction and the arghya for the attainment of the knowledge of yoga;
to its south, at a distance of twenty-eight dhanus, [is the place].
Having bathed there at the lake called Ayuta, one shall go to the station of Ayuta;
he who performs the ritual bath there during the four months of the rainy season [attains the same]. (23)
O Daughter of Śaṅkara, if he performs his bath with the mantra and offers the *arghya* (water of respect) at midday, that practitioner goes to the abode of Brahmā.
The great mass known as Amṛta, a perfection venerated by the gods, which is the abode of nectar for all and superior to the sins of living beings. (25)
To the south of that is the lake Ṛṇamocanaka, measuring ten dhanus;
having bathed there, one is liberated from the three debts, and the bond of worldly existence no longer arises. (26)
Having bathed there on the Lalitā-saptamī in the month of Bhādrapada, one shall go to heaven;
and having bathed on the fourteenth day of the month of Māgha, one attains liberation.
All people seized by debt are bound by three types of actions through various karmas.

Having been liberated from the three debts at the end, one is released from the three debts at the Lake of Debt-Liberation (Ṛṇamocanaka-saras), located to the south of Aśvakrānta, slightly in the direction of Agni. (28)
At a distance of one bow-length from there is the lake named Aśvakrānta;
and from the world of the Nāgas has arisen Janārdana, the God of gods, in the form of Kalki.
Having bathed right there at Virajā, he established the Aśvatīrtha;
one should take up residence there on the northern path, or indeed offer the water of honor (arghya) there.
One should diligently worship with scented water—and indeed with both scented water and milk—using this mantra with effort:
"O you who are frequented by Brahmā, meritorious, and superior even to a fraction of Vārāṇasī! (31)
"Accept this water offering (arghya) along with your wife; I shall provide you with the means for that."
Homage to you, who cause the falling away from the sins accumulated through the manner of horses; homage to you, the Horse-Treaded, the source of ten thousand [virtues]. (33)
By bathing with this mantra, one obtains the fruit of sacrifice;
through the mere act of the *mausala* bath, one gains the merit of the horse-sacrifice (*aśvamedha*) and other such rites. (34)
By merely bathing according to the prescribed rite, one obtains the fruit of the Rājasūya sacrifice;
likewise, one's gifts become inexhaustible, as does the libation offered to the ancestors.
When the sun is situated in Viśākhā and the full moon is in Kṛttikā, that conjunction is named Padmaka; it is very difficult to encounter during Aśvakrānta.

Those who shall perform their ablutions here at the Devatīrtha in the intermediate space, at the Aśvakrānta Devatīrtha, and then at the auspicious Paitāmaha Tīrtha, for them there will be worlds of great prosperity.
O Maheśānī, they have no longing for the merit that has been performed, nor for that which has been done improperly; this which has been declared is the truth. (38)
Among all sacred fords in this world—indeed, among those found in the three worlds—the Kārttikī is the supreme ford; it is especially meritorious and the highest remover of all sins. (39)
Whatever duty is accomplished by the twice-born through mantras, gifts, and austerities, that is achieved merely by bathing with auspicious and well-concentrated [intentions]. (40)
O beloved, through this vision, those who have committed great sins and are associated with minor offenses emerge well-delivered; seeking liberation, they go forth by themselves. (41)
O Daughter of Śaṅkara, a man who observes a fast there quickly obtains the fruit of the Puṇḍarīka sacrifice with very little effort.

He who bathes in the month of Māgha and offers sesame seeds to the twice-born, giving according to his ability and with devotion, shall dwell as a sovereign in the world [with joy in the realm of Viṣṇu]. || 43 ||
p. 158) In that regard, the man who performs fasting, bathing, giving gifts, and likewise consuming products of the cow, shall attain heaven upon death. || 44 ||
Those who dwell nearby that place, whether they be of the letter-born classes or of the human classes (or the kṣatriya classes), they too, by its power, go to heaven; of this there is no doubt. (45)
Those who bestow wealth upon a righteous twice-born man for the sake of Vedic tranquility,
having died, ascend to heaven with four arms and seated upon lotuses.
Those best of men who perform the fast unto death there attain union with Brahmā and are not born again. (47)
Those men go to heaven by means of a swan-vehicle, free from fear from any quarter;
their ancestors dance, and their grandfathers are indeed satisfied. 48.

Through libations, they obtain satisfaction; through offerings for their ancestors, they attain heaven. Having touched that place, even sinners are liberated from the bondage of worldly existence. (49)
By suppressing [the senses] and by giving gifts there, he always becomes an attendant of Brahmā;
having reached the place trodden by horses, he performs the ritual bath— [for the mind is not purified by mere bathing anywhere]—
as long as he remains untiring.
Whether one has eaten or not, whether by day or by night,
that sacred ford is considered the foremost abode among all holy places; it is proclaimed as the destroyer of sins and the generator of merit for all living beings.
Furthermore, those of purified souls who, having bathed there, [worship] Janārdana—
Those who worship according to their ability go to the celestial realm;
Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Rudra—these three—are eternally present there.
O Maheśānī, at Aśvatīrtha there is nothing more meritorious on earth;
its stainless water, free from passion (viraja), is renowned throughout the three worlds. (54)
Blessed are those who behold the holy site of the Brahma-world,
even those who maintain the sacred fire-offering for more than a hundred years.
In Kārttika, at that singular sacred site in Vāsudeśa— [for that single sacred site in Vāsudeśa is indeed equal to all others]—
those who partake in liberation obtain a fruit equal to the merit of all sacrifices and bestow the fruit of all sacred sites. || 56 ||

And the completion of all the Vedas was indeed achieved by those who, having bowed down at Aśvakrānta, have performed the twilight devotions (sandhyā)— [those by whom the three twilights were performed at the sacred ford of Aśvakrānta]. || 57 ||
O Daughter of Śaṅkara, [one should offer] with the water from one's own wife's hand, or with water from the hands of those who have trodden upon a horse,
using either a golden pitcher, a skull-cup, or even one made of clay.
Having brought that meritorious water, the wise man, at the conclusion of the twilight rites,
should concentrate his mind through meditative absorption (samādhi), preceded by breath control (prāṇāyāma).
O fair-faced one, hear now the merit that arises when this is performed;
by it, the twilight prayer becomes as if perfectly saluted for twelve years. (50)
By bathing there, one obtains the fruit of an Aśvamedha sacrifice; by drinking [the water], ten times that;
and by fasting as well, one attains an infinite and most great fruit.
He who would give ten million cows according to the prescribed rites at another sacred ford shall obtain that same fruit of merit by staying for a single day at this sacred ford.
He who gives gold measuring half a *pāda* obtains the full fruit of the gift of gold; there is no doubt about this. Therefore, one should give him more than that.
When the stream touches Candraśaila, it is proclaimed as the Jāhnavī;
when the stream touches Aśvatīrtha during immersions, it is designated as such [one would attain heaven].
When the stream touches Indraśaila, it is to be known as the Sarasvatī.
"In that place trodden by horses, the wise man who immerses himself enjoys the fruit of infinity. [This additional reading is found in manuscript *kha*.
Furthermore, a confluence is observed during the rainy season. || 65 ||
One should know that to be Prayāga, especially during the month of Kārtika;
whoever performs the tonsure there at Prayāga obtains the full fruit of the tonsure.
Even today, O Goddess, the Dvidhāraka [spring] is seen at Gayākunda;
for one who is poor in this world, or perhaps one whose kingdom has been lost— (67)
Having gone to water that has been stepped upon by horses, one should daily recite the Vaiṣṇava mantra;
and having performed the offering of worship to the gods and the libation for the ancestors, [one should proceed]. 68.
Having performed the offering of a funeral ball (piṇḍa), he shall soon be freed from rebirth and become a sovereign monarch, a Cakravartin with a single wheel; this is the truth, there is no doubt.
In this life, good fortune, wealth, grain, and excellent women—
these various things belong to those by whom the pilgrimage was performed during the month of Kārttika.
Whoever performs this ritual for the journey, causes it to be performed, or even hears of it, is liberated from all sins whatsoever. (71)
The man who performs the pilgrimage knows by whom the arrival of Agastya was brought about, and he knows by whom the approach to the unapproachable was made;
through the attainment of the Brahma-rite— [the Brahma-rite performed for many hundreds of years]— he attains it.
And after many hundreds of years. || 72 ||
One should likewise perform the Caitrī festival procession; in this way, one attains consecration.
What is the use of saying much more here? It has been declared that there is nothing else [to be done]. (73)
By reaching it, one attains whatever is to be attained, whether it be merit or where one perceives evil;
it is equal to the fruit of all sacrifices and bestows the fruit of all sacred fords.
Indeed, satisfaction was thereby brought to all the gods by those who went to the Aśvatīrtha and bathed there once, according to the prescribed rite. (75)
Together with sons, grandsons, daughters-in-law, or daughters, they shall remain united in their lineage, filled with wealth;
for those who give young women as brides along with a mountain-peak (śikhariṇī), there is no doubt of this. || 76 ||
Indeed, all his limbs rejoice when they are completely fulfilled by residing in Kāśī for eight yugas, which is equal to a single day spent in Puruṣottama. || 77 ||
That same merit multiplied ten million times is obtained by beholding the face of Virajā;
one should know that a merit equal to that is acquired at every single moment at Aśvatīrtha.
For by the sight of him, the Rājasūya shines forth; indeed, bathing in his water is said to be ten times more meritorious than the Vājapeya sacrifice,
and even a single mouthful of it is worthy of the Aśvamedha.
Even more than all sacrifices combined, it is the ocean of existence. || 79 ||
Thus ends the third chapter in the second part of the upper [section] of the twenty-two thousand [verse] *Yoginītantra*, the great king of tantras, in the section concerning Kāmarūpa.
Chapter Four.
The Goddess said:

"O Lord, if you are pleased with me, then tell me this, O Master: if I am worthy of such a boon from you, then, O God, let it be told to me—by what name among the lords of the gods and others should one designate me, and in what manner?"
And in what place do you reside? || 1 ||
In which various fire-offerings (homas) do the twice-born always behold you? And by what name does which place shine upon the surface of the earth?
The Blessed One said:
"I am Sureśāna at Puṣkara, Sukṣemada at Gayā, Vedagarbha at Kānyakubja, and Pitāmaha at Bhṛgukaccha. (3)
In Kauveryā he is the Creator, in Nandipurī he is Bṛhaspati,
in Prabhāsa he is the Lotus-born, and in Svarganadī he is the Beloved of the Gods.
In Dvāravatī he is Vāgdeva; in every drama he is Nāṭakeśvara;
on Mount Nīla he is Kāmeśa; and on Hastiparvata he is Piṅgala.
Vijaya is at Kuśāvarta, Jayanta on Mount Puṣkara;
Bhayānanda is on Bhasmācala, and Mādhava is on Candrakūṭa.
Within the inner chamber is Padmahasta; in Maṅgalā is Tryambaka;
on the divine Bhadrapīṭha is Divyeśa; and in Aśvakrānta is Janārdana.
At Ahicchatra he is Tulyānanda; at Śrīśaila, Jagatpriya;
at Padmapāṇi, Kuśahasta; and at Mānaśaila, Munīśvara. || 8 ||
In Śrīkaṇṭha I am Śrīnivāsa, and in Kāmpilya I am the bestower of success—listen, O beloved of my life! In Kanyāśrama I am Rudra, and on Maināka I am Viśvanādaka. (9)
Nāgeśa is at Ekāmra, Maheśvara at Virajā, Viṣṇu at the place called Mūlika, and likewise Bhārgava at Mahendra.
Likewise, Bodhi is at Kauśikī; Bhārgava is at Ayodhyā;
Hayagrīva is at Maṇikūṭa; and Varāha is on Mount Vindu.
Jaṭādhara is at Godanta; Jāṅgaleśvara is at Gomanta; Parameṣṭhin is at Brahmaputra; and Gahvara is at Viśvaśaila. || 12 ||
Citreśa is on Citraśaila, Caturbhuja is in Devikā,
Padmapāṇi is in Vṛndāvana, and Kuśahasta is in Naimiṣa.
And at Mandara was Mahābodhi; Gopīndra was on Mount Hanu;
Padmagarbha was on the Bhāgīrathī; and Kanakapriya was in Kāmpilla. (14)
In Karaṇa he is Kāmīra; in Kapota he is Havyavāhana; in Arbuda he is Vasiṣṭha; and in the Śvetanadī he is Manobhava. || 15 ||
Pinākin was born in Dhavalā, Trivikrama in Picchilā;
Yajñagarbha in Āgastyā, and Madhusūdana in Urvaśī. (16)
Hari himself is Rukmiṇīśa at Paitrika, as well as Ruci;
he is Vāyana on Mount Gomanta, and is called Viśveśvara in Kāśī. || 17 ||
Prajāpati is at Prayāga, and Dvijapriya is in Vidarbha; Gaṅgādhara is at Madrapīṭha, and Tryambaka is indeed at Mātaṅga. || 18 ||
Tripurāri is on Mount Nandaśaila; Trilocana is on Mount Pāṇḍuśaila; Trilokeśa is at Gaṅgāhrada; and Divākara is in Bhittipurī. || 19 ||
At Vamaṭa is Miṅgilanātha; at Dāsaśṛṅga is Kalānidhi;
at Dāsavana is Mahāliṅga; and at Aśoka is Vināśaka. || 20 ||
Harisena is in Cullukā, Anantaka in Parṇāṭa;
Mārkaṇḍeya is in Vaṭa, and Divākara is at Ikṣudvāra. || 21 ||
At Gokarṇa is the one named Vikarṇa, and at Mandāra is Madhusūdana;
thus, one hundred and eight sacred sites have been proclaimed by me to you.
O lady of virtuous vows, my presence shall indeed be eternal wherever these exist;
and whatever devoted man should behold even one of them, [he too shall attain me]. || 23 ||
Having attained freedom from passion through bathing, he rejoices for eternal years; whatever evil has been committed mentally, verbally, or physically [is thereby purified]. (24)
All that indeed comes to rest; there is no need for deliberation here.
Whatever sacred fords (tīrthas) there may be, having gone to all of them, a man beholds me;
he becomes one on the path to liberation wherever I am established. || 25 ||
O Supreme Goddess, through offerings of flowers, incense, and the gratification of Brahmins, as well as through steady meditation, one shall quickly attain [the goal]. || 26 ||
To the north of Aśvakrānta and to the west of Ṛṇamocana,
there is a field measuring twenty-two dhanus in extent, which is exceedingly difficult to attain.
The sacred field named Dvipañcaka is saluted by all the gods;
having worshipped Rudra there, one obtains the fruit of the luminous void.
O Goddess of the Gods, having dwelt there for six months with restricted food, established in celibacy and meditative concentration, one shall attain the supreme state. (29)
In the Kṛta age, Puṣkara is [the preeminent place]; in the Tretā age, Naimiṣa is considered so;
in the Dvāpara age, Kurukṣetra; and in the Kali age, Aśvatīrtha. (30)
Therefore, on its northern bank, one should accomplish whatever is desired by the mind;
in the Dvāpara age, however, Kurukṣetra bestows the fruit of all merit [wherein the fruit of giving is inexhaustible]. || 31 ||

Giving at Pañcaka is difficult to perform; [it bestows the fruit of all accomplishments] and all that is difficult to achieve. Whatever sin has been committed elsewhere becomes lightened at this sacred ford (tīrtha). || 32 ||

Sin committed at that sacred ford (*tīrtha*) does not perish anywhere else; however, sin committed elsewhere is indeed removed by staying there for twelve days, ten days, half a month, or even a full month. (33)
Seated upon half of Rudra’s throne on the summit of Mount Meru,
the illustrious goddess then bowed to Mahādeva and questioned him.
The Goddess said:
"O Śaṅkara, tell me how that sin which has been accumulated previously over thousands of births comes to its destruction. (35)
The Blessed One said:
"Listen, O Goddess, I shall proclaim that which is more secret than the secret, unsurpassed, renowned among all sacred fords (tīrthas), and beyond even Aśvakrānta. (36)
To the north of that, however, is the field called Vimuktaka which has been described by me;
this alone is supreme knowledge, and this alone is supreme austerity.
This alone is the supreme Brahman; this alone is the supreme state.
Just as Nārāyaṇa, the Supreme Person, is the most excellent among the gods. || 38 ||
(166) Just as Giriśa is the foremost among lords, so is this place the highest among all locations;
whatever is given, chanted, offered in sacrifice, the remainder, penance performed, or whatever else is done [here], [is most efficacious]. 39.
Meditation, study, and knowledge—all these become inexhaustible.
In Aśvakrānta lies the supreme yoga; in Aśvakrānta lies the supreme goal. (40)
Beyond Aśvakrānta there is no higher liberation; there is no other holy place like it.
Even a heap of sin as vast as the mountains Meru and Mandara [is destroyed] entirely by it.
Having encountered that which is trodden by horses, everything goes to destruction;
for even the dust-particles, though meritorious, are driven away by the wind once they have been trodden upon by horses.
If those who have committed evil deeds were to attain the supreme destination,
that destination could not be found even at Kurukṣetra, Gayādvāra, or Puṣkara.
The destiny ordained for those men who dwell in Aśvakrānta cannot be attained by gifts, nor by austerities, nor by sacrifices, nor even by sacred knowledge.
Indeed, at Aśvatīrtha, an exalted state is attained;
through association there, liberation occurs, whereas from the acceptance of the false comes another state [and from the acceptance of the true, the supreme goal].
Even compared to Agastya or Agni and the others, this very place is greater.
Even a slayer of a Brahmin may at some time approach the place trodden by a horse.
Through the greatness of Aśvakṣetra, the sin of killing a Brahmin is averted;
for him, no return to this world is ever seen. (47)
One should consider either the northern or the southern meritorious gate;
O fair-faced one, every time is auspicious for him when he has stepped upon the horse.
Whatever fruit a man obtains through a great gift, he obtains that same inexhaustible fruit by giving even a single cowrie at Aśvatīrtha. || 49 ||
O my beloved, he who observes a fast for even a single day here, being devoted to me, obtains the fruit of a thousand years. (50)
Whoever duly gives ten million cows at another sacred site and stays here for a single day—the fruit of those two acts shall be equal. (51)
Whatever fruit is obtained by bathing properly at Prayāga during the month of Māgha,
that fruit is multiplied ten millionfold at Aśvatīrtha at every single moment.
O Daughter of Śaṅkara, by performing worship at midday and in the afternoon for thousands of millions and hundreds of millions of creations, [one attains the goal].
Indeed, a heap of evil as vast as Mount Meru or Mandara is entirely destroyed once it encounters the Horse-tread. || 54 ||
Insects, moths, mosquitoes, and whatever living beings move upon trees, in water, or on land—
even frogs and fish— attain Śiva by casting off their bodies at Aśvatīrtha in due course.
He who would dwell constantly in the Pañcaka shall go to the supreme goal;
it stands above all worlds, situated in the world of Brahmā. || 56 ||
If one desires to go to that state, one must dwell here in what is difficult to perform,
just as Madhusūdana is the primordial source of all the gods.
In the same way, the first pentad of all the fields is taught through both direct and reverse order, as well as individually and collectively. || 58 ||
O lady of beautiful countenance, whatever merit is gained by bathing at Pañcaka and at Aśvatīrtha,
one obtains that very same fruit by bathing likewise in Uttaramāraṇya.
Whatever fruit is obtained by visiting all sacred fords according to the prescribed rules, a person attains that very fruit simply by beholding the five [deities] at the proper times. (50)
Indeed, ten thousand times ten million sacred fords (tīrthas) on the surface of the earth are present at Aśvatīrtha, near the gateway to liberation.
As long as the mountains endure and as long as the oceans endure,
for that long the one who has died [while observing] the Pañcaka is honored in the world of Brahmā.
O Daughter of Śaṅkara, by bathing even once, one may burn away all sins committed throughout thousands of other births, from birth until the end of death.
The man who remains steadfast in the practice of yoga for three full years attains liberation through a single birth; indeed, he finds both yoga and mokṣa.
O Goddess of gods, that which ends with the Liberation from Debt (Ṛṇamocana) is remembered as the Pentad on all sides;
O auspicious lady, the Abode of Brahmā is likewise praised everywhere as the bestower of liberation for living beings. (65)

O Maheśānī, it is traditionally taught that bathing, recitation, fire-offerings, ancestral rites, giving gifts, and so forth— each one performed individually— purifies the seventh generation of one's lineage.
To the west of Aśvatīrtha,
at a distance of eight bow-lengths, that which is here called Siddhakuṇḍa is situated.

Having bathed here and drunk the water, one is liberated from all sins. Whether fasting for three nights or fasting for a single night, the service of these sacred bathing places (tīrthas) has been described here for the twice-born.
He who restrains his breath with the moon and keeps his hands and feet controlled—such a celibate student, free from sin, shall obtain the fruit of all sacred fords. (69)
O Siddhakuṇḍa, which provides great enjoyment and is well-consecrated by the deities;
purify me from all sins, O best of holy fords, salutations be unto you!
By means of this mantra, however, on the thirteenth day of the dark fortnight of the month of Vaiśākha, merely by bathing, one purifies both lineages.
To the west of that sacred ford, in a somewhat arid region [or in the region of Vāyu],
there is a sacred ford measuring sixty-four dhanus, known as Brahmasaras.
Having bathed there and offered libations to the ancestors with devotion according to the prescribed rite, one delivers even those ancestors who have committed sins; of this there is no doubt.
Having bathed properly, the twice-born man then attains the state of being consecrated;
this was indeed created by Brahmā himself out of a desire to do what is pleasing to the Lord.
"Since Brahmā himself has bathed, therefore destroy my sin"—having performed the bath according to the rules with this mantra, [one should purify oneself from evil]. 75.
Especially on the fourteenth day of the bright fortnight in the month of Māgha,
by giving gifts according to the prescribed rite, one is glorified in the world of Brahmā.
O beloved, one should know that the field of Rāma is located at Indrakūṭa in the north, measuring eighty bows; its pool is in Kula.
Having bathed at the Bindu-kuṇḍa and having worshipped the ancestors as well,
one is liberated from all sins and is glorified in the world of Viṣṇu. O lady of beautiful countenance, Rāmatīrtha is the supreme holy place among all holy places.
Having honored the Brāhmaṇas, one is glorified in the world of Brahmā;
[this was established] on your bank, O highly fortunate one, by the high-souled Śrī Rāma. (79)
"All the ancestors have been gratified; O best of holy places, salutations be unto you!"—with this mantra, during the dark fortnight of the month of Vaiśākha, [one should offer libations].
Having worshipped Mahādeva there, one obtains the fruit of giving a thousand cows.
To the east of that, O lady of beautiful countenance, is the Sītātīrtha extending nine dhanus.
Having bathed there, the twice-born go to heaven with their physical bodies.
Furthermore, at the great śrāddha at Krauñca, it is declared to be inexhaustible;
this supreme tīrtha was established by Sītā and Rāmabhadra.
Therefore, O Goddess worshipped by the gods, purify me from sin and grant me liberation;
having observed silence on the thirteenth lunar day and bathed there, one obtains great fruit.
Having bathed with this mantra, one should cause the arghya offering to be presented with the jewel;
one is liberated from all sins and, upon death, shall dwell in the world of Brahmā.
And to the south of Sītā, at a distance of ten dhanus, by merely performing an ablution there, one shall always be victorious. (86)
There is a most splendid holy place among all holy places named Vijaya;
there stands the famous Liṅga of Maheśa known as Vijaya.
Having lived there for six months with restricted food, practicing celibacy,
and having completed his stay, O Goddess of Gods, he is liberated from all sins.
The supreme among all holy places (tīrthas), renowned as the Yoga-tīrtha,
which removes all sins, is the abode of Śambhu, the Supreme Lord.
Having beheld the Linga of the God renowned by the name Yogīśa, one obtains all desired objects and becomes beloved of Rudra. (90)
Know that the Mukti-tīrtha measures twenty-two *dhanus*.
Having bathed with the mantra to be recited hereafter, one should present the *arghya* offering. (91)
O Yogakuṇḍa, O highly fortunate one, worshipped by the immortals, may you— who are saluted day and night by the disciplined seekers of liberation and constantly honored— purify me. 92.
There, at a great distance from the world, is the unsurpassed Kuṇḍa;
having bathed there as well according to the rules and having satiated the ancestors and the deities, || 93 ||
Then, having bestowed various gifts upon the Brahmins,
one should bathe and offer the arghya with the Kaula seed-syllable according to its true essence.
Afterwards, having beheld Kauleśvara, one is liberated from the bondage of worldly existence.
The sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa), frequented by gods and gandharvas, measures fifteen cubits.
On the third lunar day of the bright fortnight at Kuṇḍa, one shall obtain a village, grain, and wealth;
and by bowing at Indraśaila during the watch (yāma) of the night, one obtains twelve bows' length of land.
Known as Sūryatīrtha, it is the most excellent of all sacred fords (tīrthas).
There, the Lord, whose form is invisible and who is borne by a chariot drawn by seven horses, is impelled by the seven charioteers.
He himself, all-pervading and possessing a body of yoga, remains for the sake of the welfare of the world,
since Hara and Mahāhara have made this their eternal abode here.
All the deities have gathered right there for the purpose of serving him.
Having bathed with the seed-syllable of the Sun (Bhānu), one should offer the water of honor (arghya) with the Tāra mantra. || 99 ||
Then the practitioner, whose mind is intent on success, should go to Rāmakṣetra;
there stand two wells named Durga and Kūpa, as well as the Brahma-yūpa.
Having drunk the water from a well in a fortress on the fourteenth lunar day of the month of Māgha, she shall,
through devotion, become pregnant with one who is Rāma himself.
Reciting the mantras ten thousand times. || 101 ||
Whoever performs a śrāddha ceremony after circumambulating the sacrificial post (yūpa) shall deliver his ancestors; by that act, he is glorified in the world of Brahmā. || 102 ||
One should place a kākini, as well as gold and silver, into the pit;
one should purify whatever wealth belonged to whichever friend [the deceased] possessed in a previous birth. 103.
From there, one should go toward Indraśaila facing south;
then one should behold Maṇīśvara, and one is liberated from hell.
Even one who is bound by fetters and shackles, or even one joined with minor sins (upapātaka),
having seen Maṇinātha situated on Indrakūṭa, [is liberated] by that Wind-god.
O Goddess, one is liberated in an instant; there is no need for deliberation here.
At the western end of Lomatīrtha, measuring five dhanus, || 106 ||
From that, Nāgatīrtha was born and attained renown upon the earth;
for having bathed in the Nāgakuṇḍa, Vaikuṇṭha should worship the Nāgas [or summon them]. 107.
That merit, which destroys the poison of serpents, belongs to all holy fords;
those mortals who perform their ablutions with devotion on the fifth day of the month of Śrāvaṇa [attain it].
In the family of those men on earth who shall perform the ancestral *śrāddha* ceremony there, the serpents will never cause them any affliction. (109)
Brahmā, being pleased, will grant the supreme abode; there is no doubt about this.
To the north of Candra is a mountain measuring sixty-four [yojanas]. || 110 ||
In that water is the Gayākuṇḍa; the sacred field is said to be on its bank.
Gayāśīrṣa is located in the eastern part, measuring twenty-two bow-lengths. (111)
Extending as far as the Lauhitya river in the north lies the Brahmayonika [region],
the supreme secret Gayātīrtha, which is exceedingly dear to the ancestors.
Having indeed offered the funeral ball (piṇḍa), a man is not born again.

O beloved, one should offer the funeral cake (piṇḍa) at this Āgastya-tīrtha, at Gayā, and likewise on the auspicious Nīlācala; and specifically at Gayā, it should be offered even once during each distinct pilgrimage.
His ancestors grieve here that his exertion has been in vain; it is a delusion born of a curse.
The ancestors sing this song, and the great seers proclaim it. (114)
"Whoever shall go to Gayā will deliver us;
one should desire many sons who are virtuous and endowed with good qualities. (115)
If even one among those who are assembled together should go to Gayā, then, for that reason, a Brāhmaṇa especially should do so with every possible effort. (116)
He who, having gone to Gayā with a concentrated mind, offers the funeral cakes (piṇḍas) according to the prescribed rule—blessed indeed are those mortals who offer the cakes at Gayā! (117)

The deliverance of seven generations on both sides of their families shall be attained; furthermore, he should indeed offer the funeral cakes (piṇḍas) with milk-rice (pāyasa), even for those who are strangers by name.
That which is prescribed by the sages should be performed with oil-cake and ghee;
it should always be offered with sesame oil-cake by men who are full of devotion.
However, the śrāddha ceremony should be performed there, excluding the offering of water (arghya) and the invocation (āvāhana);
for mice, vultures, and crows do not move about while being observed. 120.
(174) The *śrāddha* performed at that sacred site (*tīrtha*) is declared to be supremely gratifying to the ancestors;
one should strive to perform it there, for the consumption [of the offerings] is indeed the cause [of their satisfaction]. (121)
Through the enjoyment [of the offerings], the ancestors are satisfied; being satisfied, they grant all desires. They bestow long life, sons, wealth, grain, and other desired objects.
When Rudra has been propitiated with devotion, the ancestors are pleased with men; therefore, the Śrāddha at Gayā should always be performed by men, whether out of season or in season. (123)

And having reached that very place, one should always perform the libation for the ancestors and the offering of funeral cakes (piṇḍa); by that, it is attained, which is exceedingly dear to the ancestors. || 124 ||
For the ancestors, having arrived in the sky, gaze [upon him] with supreme hope and devotion; one should fulfill their hope. 125.
No delay should be made, nor should one create obstacles;
their lineage shall remain uninterrupted at all times. 126.

The ancestors are the givers of sons and are desirous of the *vṛddhi-śrāddha*; therefore, one should offer it to them according to the prescribed injunctions. By that, all those ancestors shall indeed be satisfied for all time. (127)
Therefore, the Śrāddha was proclaimed of old by Svayambhū himself;
it must be performed promptly by those twice-born who are devoted to their ancestors.
At a sacred ford, in a holy field, or even in one's own home;
on the occasion of a solar transit, or during an eclipse; likewise at the equinoxes, or when one is afflicted by the birth asterism. (129)
"These indeed are the times for the Śrāddha ceremony," Svāyambhuva declared of old; "when the Śrāddha is performed, physical affliction arises for men. (130)
In this world or the next, one abandons all evil deeds committed;
there shall be no suffering from Yama, nor from planets, thieves, kings, and the like. [Fear of death, affliction from planets, and likewise fear of enemies and kings. (131)
All evil deeds are destroyed, and one obtains an auspicious rebirth in the next world;
there is no doubt about this, just as in the case of Prajāpati-vara. 132.
In the month of Kārttika, one should worship Kāmeśvara, the knower of all Vedas, and Aśvakrānta; likewise, one should worship Kāmeśvarī, Saptaveda, and Aśvakrānta.
The principal rite for the Mother-goddesses is the Śrāddha at Gayā, while the principal rite for the ancestors is performed elsewhere. || 133 ||
The wise one should offer the sixteenth *piṇḍa* and cause the *bahula* rite to be performed;
he should pour streams of milk and ascend the mountain of the Moon.
May the gods Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara be my witnesses;
having reached Mahāgayā, a wise person should perform the śrāddha rite, even if the three classes of ancestors have not been invited. 135.
Then, to the sound of kettledrums and other instruments, the man should ascend the palanquin;
having gone home, he should worship the household deity according to the prescribed rite. (136)
Afterwards, he should feed the Brahmins and offer the inexhaustible (akṣayya) water;
he should associate with the Brahmins and bestow the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā). || 137 ||
By the offering of funeral cakes here at Āgastya, at the Virajas, at Daśāśvamedhika, and likewise at the Viṣṇupadas; || 138 ||
If someone who has offered a funeral ball (piṇḍa) at one place should again perform a śrāddha rite elsewhere, a curse falls upon his head after he has been drawn back once more. 139.
One should cause the funeral cake (piṇḍa) to be offered for three days, especially at Gayā;
then one should offer it for even a single day at Mātṛgayā, and one should offer it for three days at Āgastya and Virajā. (140)
Thus ends the fourth chapter in the second part of the section on Kāmarūpa [the section on the Kāmarūpa Pīṭha], within the *Yoginītantra*, the great king of tantras in twenty-two thousand verses.
Chapter Five.
The Blessed One said:
Then, at the clear dawn, the practitioner, whose mind was intent on success,
[should go] to the northeast of Somaśaila, at a distance of merely a glance, O Dear One.
Then, having gone to Mānaśaila, one should proceed to the lake of Vārāṇasī,
located slightly to the east of the northeast of Maṇīśvara.
At a distance of seven bows away is the Vārāṇasīya Kuṇḍa,
twenty-two bows in length, and it is frequented by all the gods.
There are the goddess Tripathagā, the Gomatī, and the Sarasvatī;
the Karatoyā, the divine river Lohitya, and then the Gharghara.
The Sarayū that washes away sins, the great river Narmadā, the Dṛṣadvatī, the Devikā, and likewise the river Carmaṇvatī; || 5 ||
The Kṛṣṇaveṇī, likewise the meritorious Śoṇa, the Śyena, the Mahānada, the Kāverī, the Yamunā, and whatever others have not been mentioned; (6)
For the sake of my pleasure, they come to the Kuṇḍa of Vārāṇasī:
the ocean, the abyss, and likewise the milk-ocean with its waters.
And there is the ocean of clarified butter, the ocean of wine, and the ocean of curds;
as well as lakes, rivers, and various sacred fords (tīrthas).
On the fourteenth day of the month of Madhu, they arrive without a doubt;
on the third day of Vaiśākha, O slender-waisted one, they arrive.
Having bathed there, they go to heaven until the dissolution of all beings—O you who are the illusion of the world, the seed of the world, and the destroyer of the world's sins! || 10 ||
"O Kuṇḍa of Vārāṇasī, grant me nectar;
salutations be unto you!"—with this mantra, one should offer the arghya with another [mantra]. || 11 ||
To the south of that, at a distance of five bows,
is the pit named Maṇikarṇikā, measuring twenty-two bows in size.
A holy site equal to Maṇikarṇa has never existed, nor will it ever exist;
this is the truth, the truth, again the truth—this is most certainly the truth alone. (13)
O Maheśvarī, there is no sacred site equal to Maṇikarṇa within the sphere of the universe; [this applies] at the beginnings of the Yugas, during the transit of the sun, and during eclipses.
One should perform a bath at midday, which destroys even the greatest sins, at Maṇikarṇa, O best of goddesses, O Maṇīśvarī, O beloved of Maṇi! (15)
"O Hara, O Kṛttivāsa, O Maṇikarṇa [this is the abode made by Hara, O Maṇikarṇa], salutations be unto you!
Having bathed with this mantra, one should prostrate and worship [or dismiss] [Him]. || 16 ||
In the northeast of Maṇiśaila is the river named Maṅgalā;
carrying water upon water, purify me from the multitude of my sins. (17)
Having bathed with the mantra, O Goddess of gods, one should prostrate and seek grace;
then, having gone to Maṇīśvara, one should wash it while reciting the Kāma-mantra [or praying while reciting the mantra]. 18.
Having performed the bath with the first [verse], with a mind purified and restrained,
one should touch [the deity] with the second and worship with the third.
The Siddhakṣetra is said here to consist of two parts of a kalā and a hand. || 19 ||
The swan has ascended the seat of honor and is seated upon a drop of light, composed in meditation;
this is the mantra of the God of gods, proclaimed by the sage Garga.
The meter is Anuṣṭubh, the deity is Bhava (Rudra); one should employ this for the fulfillment of desired aims. || 21 ||
That God of gods indeed bears a pure crown with its front portion raised; clad in a tiger skin, he holds a trident,
the gesture of fearlessness, a boon-granting hand, and a thunderbolt— red, three-eyed, supreme, and mounted upon a deer.
In the center, one should worship the god Kṛttivāsas; in front of him, the formidable god Hara;
behind him, the god Bhava, who is the primordial Śakra and known as Bhaveśāna-Śakra; and to the west, the god Vāmana, known as Kāla.
One should worship the Śaktis upon lotus petals, and the goddesses Vārāṇasī and Kīrti in front of those two.
One should indeed worship Śrīkaṇṭha and the others outside of that; afterwards, the planets in front of them, and the lords of the directions (Dikpālas).
Ananta is worshipped on the left, Pinākin on the right side, and Kamalā everywhere.
And in front of the one called Siddheśa, the [Siddhas and Sādhyas] are to be worshipped with their respective mantras as prescribed in their own ritual manuals. || 25 ||
Maṇinātha, Ādiliṅga, and the imperishable Brahmapāṣāṇa;
O Goddess Maṅgalā, these are situated in the northeast, O beloved, and constitute the most excellent [group] among them. (26)
O Goddess worshipped by the gods, this sacred field extends for three krośas and has a jeweled pedestal;
Kāmeśī is in the southern face, while Hayagrīva is in the west.
In the north is the lotus-liṅga, the source of Uttarā;
and in the eastern face is Virajā, from which Kauśalā originated.
Elsewhere, indeed, there are two crores; everything else originates from the left.
Five hundred and one hundred *kuṇḍas* have arisen from Ramaṇā. (29)
Likewise, O beloved, in the Kali age there are one and a half crores of liṅgas on the earth,
thirty lakhs situated within the ground, and one hundred and fifty thousand in the water.
Two hundred thousand on a mountain, five hundred thousand in caves, seven hundred thousand on a ground-pīṭha, and one hundred thousand at the root of a tree. || 31 ||
Know that the Linga situated in the center of the Kuṇḍa extends for half a hundred thousand [yojanas];
the Sandhyā and Sandhyāṃśaka are indeed the purifying Lauhitya Kuṇḍa.
O Goddess of the gods, when nine hundred and ten years have passed, everything will indeed be known;
and when a third part of the twilight period remains, a Śūdra shall become king. (33)
Then the goddess Kāmeśvarī manifested in the middle portion;
at the end, Śākeśvarī likewise manifested in the middle portion.
And in the final portion, Śākadevī was clearly manifest while Urvaśī was then unmanifest;
O beloved, in the Bhūśāka [portion], Mādhava was manifest, while Virajā was in the Sudhāṃśa [portion].

O beloved, the fruit that is obtained from worshiping and bowing before Vāyu on Mount Mānasaila is the same as that which is gained from the Rājasūya sacrifice; there, on the mountain named Varāha, || 36 ||
There, the god Nārāyaṇa always makes his dwelling;
and to its southeast is the lake of Nara and Nārāyaṇa. (37)
Having bathed there and drunk the water, one is glorified in the world of Viṣṇu.
And on its western bank is the supreme Liṅga Someśvara [Hara]. || 38 ||

The sacred ford named Prabhāsa (Prabhāsākhya) bestows the fruit of liberation upon those who have died there; by visiting it and offering funeral cakes, it conquers the sins of men and grants their desires. || 39 ||
There, in the northwest, at a distance of eight bows, is the Vaināyaka Tīrtha;
the excellent Prabhāsa Tīrtha extends for one hundred bows.
O Goddess of the gods, to the northwest of that place, at a distance of twelve hundred bow-lengths,
is the meritorious Bindusaras Tīrtha, which destroys all sins through bathing.
From Maṇi to Somācala, the bow measures five thousand [yojanas];
at Bhūliṅga it is ten million, and beyond that is Sarasvatī.
Śambhu, the archer-cuckoo, is proclaimed as Lakṣakāli;
to the east of the Nāṭaka mountain, however, is the mountain named Mataṅga.
From the fire up to Hayācala is known as the inner sanctum (antargṛha) of Śiva;
those who die within this inner sanctum go to the eternal Brahman.
Whatever is performed there is honored and becomes inexhaustible;
those who reside on the Jewel Mountain and those who have died there are no longer subject to rebirth. (45)
In that place, a gift is equal to one made at Kurukṣetra, and not otherwise;
it is declared that the limit extends as far as Brahmā, situated between Aśvatīrtha and Indratīrtha.
Having seen water in the mouth of the Boar, Matsyodarī then [arose] during the rains in the month of Āṣāḍha, when Viṣṇu’s belly becomes that of a fish. (47)
Then, my dear, one should perform a bath with every effort and with a concentrated mind;
the sin committed during a hundred lifetimes is certainly destroyed by that bath. 48.
In the months of Bhādrapada or Śrāvaṇa, one obtains half of that half [of the fruit];
in Kārttika, some fruit is seen, increased tenfold. (49)
To the east of Hastācala, slightly in the direction of the northeast,
one should gaze at the firm Bhasmācala while reciting the Kāma-mantra.
In that part of the *kīlaka* which is not yet occupied by the final *kalikā*, one should cast the thread;
that is, one should cast it in the northern part of that field, measuring twelve *dhanus*. (51)
She is celebrated as Urvaśī, the destroyer of all sins;
one who is composed should [worship her] on the twelfth day of the bright fortnight in the month of Māgha. || 52 ||
By bathing at the transitions of the sun (saṅkramas), one obtains the merit born of an Aśvamedha sacrifice;
however, one should never bathe during the end of a day (dina-kṣaya) or during an eclipse.
O Supreme Goddess, there is also the destruction of the eldest son and of wealth;
Tāra is devoid of Śravaṇa, and Vārāha is situated with Śikhī.
This is proclaimed as the infinite [mantra] ending with the wife of Agni (svāhā).
Whatever holy places exist on earth, including the oceans and lakes— || 55 ||
"O destroyer of all sins ending with Urvaśī, salutations be unto you!
Having bathed according to the prescribed rite with this mantra, facing the northern direction— || 56 ||
One should offer the *arghya* with the Vāruṇa mantra for the sake of prosperity;
having performed ablutions facing the eastern direction, Mahālakṣmī becomes firmly established [and one is liberated]. (57)
Wealth, grain, and the increase of progeny result from immersion in the Kuvera-āśā;
likewise,
to its east lies Sūryatīrtha, renowned as difficult even for the gods to attain, extending for ten thousand parts (or a ten-thousandth part) of the length of the sun’s bow.
The sages, the Siddhas, the Gandharvas, the sacred fords, and the lakes.
O Śāṅkarī, the majesty of that Sūryakuṇḍa is incomparable;
O Goddess, its expanse reaches to the sky at the edge of Bhṛgu, where the sage Bhṛgu is the mantra leading to heaven.
One should employ the arghya offering during bathing, worship, and recitation of hymns;
specifically on the seventh lunar day of the month of Caitra (or Māgha), and on a Sunday in the month of Māgha.
Having bathed, one attains heaven and finds the world of the Sun;
O Raktāṃśa, born from the twenty [tithis], you are the destroyer of great sins.
O highly fortunate one, whose nature is Hari, remove my sin; salutations be unto you!
To the east of that is indeed a lake named Kāmākhyā, measuring five dhanus.
Having bathed there on the thirteenth lunar day, one shall attain all desires;
and whoever performs the ritual bath while placing an emblic myrobalan fruit in his mouth [shall likewise attain them]. (64)
One without a son obtains a son, and a king becomes a lord of the earth;
by bathing on the thirteenth day of the bright fortnight of Caitra, one also attains sovereignty. 65.
One should offer the *arghya* with longing, using the mantra to be recited hereafter:
"O Kāmakuṇḍa, O highly fortunate one, you who grant the fruits of all desires, you who are consecrated by the goddesses yourself... (66)
"O beautiful lady, grant all desires and protect me from every sin—he who offers the *arghya* oblation at Sūryatīrtha. (67)
Whether one hundred and eight, a thousand, ten thousand,
or likewise twelve or eight times, one shall obtain the fruit of an Ashvamedha sacrifice.
In the month of Māgha or Phālguna, having offered *svāhā* and *arghya* on the seventh day, a leper who bathes at the time of sunrise is liberated from sin. (69)
O Supreme Goddess, if a woman has not yet menstruated twenty days after [her period], she shall become fertile by worshipping there with the offering of arghya. || 70 ||
O Daughter of Śaṅkara, he who offers arghya to Āditya with a vessel made of clay shall not be born into poverty for seven births; upon death, she is likewise reborn [into a noble state].
And a woman whose children have died, having worshipped the Sun during the day with *karavīra*, *vārka*, and likewise with the fruit of the *dhātrī* tree, [attains her desire]. (72)
By offering a hundred *karavīra* flowers, a woman is never born without sons; she shall become possessed of sons.
In the absence of *karavīra*, one should offer even its leaves. (73)
O Goddess, red *rudrākṣa* beads, as well as red *karavīra* flowers, are likewise praised for the worship of the Sun because of their redness. (74)
Of all flowers indeed, the karavīra is the most excellent;
even a single karavīra is equal to a thousand red lotuses. || 75 ||
For every flower, the fruit of an Ashvamedha sacrifice is perfectly produced;
therefore, one should worship with Karavira flowers with every effort.
In the absence of a *karavīra* flower, one who is restrained in speech should remember [the deity] three times;
the merit of uttering "Karavīra" is not attained even by ten million recitations otherwise.

There may be joy from the *karavīra* flower, yet the Sun does not travel [so swiftly] as he does during the single weekly observance of the seventh lunar day (*saptamī-vrata*) in the midst of the year. (78)
Having performed it even once at Sūryatīrtha, one purifies the seventh generation of one's lineage. O Supreme Goddess, know that the afternoon is the supreme time for this vow. || 79 ||
O Goddess of gods, if there is deficiency or excess, success does not arise on this earth;
therefore, one should avoid ghee that has been cooked twice or that which is "kalāpaka. (80)
One should not eat kaśeru, ginger, salt, astringent, sour, or bitter food, nor anything that has become spoiled. || 81 ||
One should eat from a stone bowl, or occasionally from one made of silver or copper;
on the right side of the Madana [vessel], there should be a bow measuring five finger-breadths.
There is a sacred ford named Gaṅgāsaras; by bathing there, one obtains great fruit.
Having bathed on the bank of the Gaṅgā, a man should offer libations to the ancestors and the gods.
One attains the world of Brahmā during an eclipse at the sun's transit;
O Gaṅgā, who flows through the three paths and whose waters are born from the dust of Viṣṇu’s feet! 84.
O giver of Dharma, O best among those who are green, protect me from all sins!
O beautiful lady, [this should be done] on the eighth day of the bright fortnight during the months of Tulā and Makara.
By merely bathing there, that man is glorified in the world of Viṣṇu.
To the south of that place, at a distance of eight bow-lengths, || 86 ||
The supreme sacred site of Agastya bestows enjoyment and liberation upon those who have died there;
the mortal who, having heard of it, bathes therein shall attain omniscience. (87)
The Lord Mahādeva Viṣṇu himself is established there at the excellent Agastya-kuṇḍa for the sake of sporting with Kāmākhyā.
It removes all sins, is pure, and is attended by Viṣṇu, Brahmā, and others;
it is praised by gods, dānavas, and vidyādharas [and gandharvas], and grants all desires. (89)
Covered with various jewels and the like, the steps were most enchanting;
this pond was created by Śalya for the pleasure of the Great Goddess.
O fair-faced one, by merely bathing on the tenth day of the bright fortnight in both the months of Māgha and Kārttika, one obtains the fruit of Puṣkara.
Sin committed over a hundred lifetimes perishes at that very moment;
sin born of a thousand lifetimes perishes during the equinox and at the end of the day.
O Maheśvarī, O Goddess, one should avoid bathing on the eighth day of the dark fortnight in the months of Pauṣa and Karkaṭaka,
for it will certainly result in the loss of one's wife.
Just as Vārāṇasī is meritorious, so too is this undoubtedly meritorious;
it is a supreme secret sacred site, O Goddess—there is no need for deliberation on this matter. (94)
This is the most secret of sacred fields, this is the supreme and most secret;
having gone there, a person is immediately liberated from all sins. 95.
Wherein dwells the god Mahādeva, wherein dwells the goddess Sarasvatī,
and all the rivers beginning with the Gaṅgā, as well as the seven oceans themselves.

O lotus-eyed one, where there are rivers such as the Śoṇa and others, as well as sacred fords and lakes— what need is there to speak at length of that supreme pool of Parameṣṭhin situated to the left? It is impossible for me to describe it in detail.
Just as it would swiftly illuminate the entire three worlds, including all that is moving and unmoving. || 98 ||
"O best of holy places, protect me thus forever; salutations be unto you! To the south-east of that sacred field, slightly within its western range... (99)
There is a sacred bathing place named Vāsava, measuring twenty-one dhanus; having bathed at that supreme Vāsava tīrtha and having worshipped Vāsava, [one attains merit].
O Goddess of the gods, by means of the seed-syllable of Śakra, one shall go to the abode of the desired deity;
with the mantra to be spoken hereafter, one should offer arghya to Dharaṇī [and Indra]. 101.
There is a great sacred ford named Vāsava, which destroys all sins;
having immersed yourself there in the water, become one who bestows the fruits as described.
To the west of that, O Goddess, situated not very far away at a distance of seven bow-lengths, is Rambhātīrtha, O Maheśvarī. (103)
Having bathed at Rambhātīrtha, a man is born endowed with beauty;
and that woman who, being devoted to her husband, dies along with him through knowledge, [attains the same].
He attains the world of Rambhā and thereafter, at the end of that, he goes to the abode of Hari;
there is no doubt about this, especially on the day of Śeṣa and on Thursday.
O auspicious one, arisen from the ritual of Brahmā, bestower of all desires, O Kāmadraviṇī, salutations be unto you; protect me from the ocean of worldly existence. 106.
Having bathed with this [mantra], one should offer the arghya to Rambhā with the mantra;
[this should be done] on the western side of the sacred field (kṣetra), at a distance of thirty dhanus.
Having bathed right there in the Rukmiṇī-kuṇḍa, whether a woman or even a man, one should wash one's face and proceed to Brahmapura.
One is born handsome in the next world; of this there is no doubt.
Now hear the mantra for bathing and the mantra for washing with the seed-syllable of Kandarpa.
Your face has been washed by Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśāna;
you possess the beauty of the two Aśvins—by the power of truth, grant it to me. (110)
To the northwest of that sacred field, at a distance of eight bows, is the supreme tīrtha of the ancestors; by bathing there, one attains the highest state.
O highly fortunate one, you who are yourself honored by the eight gods as the sacred ford of the ancestors;
for the sake of my satisfaction, O blessed one, purify me from the Aghora [mantra].
Having bathed here with the mantra, one obtains the fruit of the Pitṛmedha sacrifice;
and having gone to the south of Agastya, having bathed and offered libations, [one attains the same].
The lake known as Gavākṣāyatī is indeed the standard for the science of archery (dhanurveda);
having gone there on the seventh lunar day, one becomes free from debt to the ancestors.
The Gayā-tīrtha is a great sacred site; there is nothing equal to it for the ancestors.
Purifying among all holy places, may it cleanse me from sin. (115)

Having performed his bath with this [mantra] and having emerged [from the water], he should put on two washed garments, apply the *tilaka*, and perform the circumambulation of the sacred field (*kṣetra*). || 116 ||
Having performed [the rites] at Daśāśvamedha-kṣetra, one should offer the funeral cake (piṇḍa) with a concentrated mind;
there, O Goddess, at Ṣoḍaśaka, the wise man should worship the ancestors.
With milk, with honey, and by the removal of the foot,
one should perform four hand-washings here, each in sequence starting from the right.
There are sixteen altars there; one should worship at each altar.
Having bathed in the Gayākūpa and beheld the Lord Umāpati, a man [attains the fruit]. || 119 ||
One shall immediately deliver oneself, as well as ten ancestors and ten descendants;
[for] Viṣṇu, Brahmā, Rudra, Agastya, and Śatakratu [are pleased]. 120.
Gaṇeśa, Krauñca, Kumāra, Prajāpati, Cyavana, Kaśyapa, and Pulastya, in their respective order. (121)
Just as [the ancestors] dwell in Aśvakrānta through prosperity, so too do they dwell in Āgastya on the day of immortality (Amāvāsyā) through prosperity alone.
Here, the mother receives a separate piṇḍa; elsewhere, she is together with her husband. 122.
Whoever offers a funeral cake (piṇḍa) at Daśāśvamedha by [the name of] those [ancestors],
those dwelling in heaven go to the celestial realm, and those already in heaven attain liberation.

Those ancestors in our lineage for whom the rites of the rice-ball (piṇḍa) and water-libation have been omitted, those whose tonsure ceremony has not been performed, and those who died while still in the womb; || 124 ||
May those whose wives were sold, those who had no wives, and likewise others who were consumed by fire,
be satisfied by what is offered upon the earth; being satisfied, may they go to the supreme goal.
The father, the maternal grandfather, and likewise the paternal grandfather;
the mother, the maternal grandmother, and likewise the paternal grandmother. (126)
Just as [the maternal grandfathers and others, and whoever else of one's lineage has died]: "The maternal grandfather and the great-grandfather,
and those who were struck down by lions, tigers, and serpents, or struck down by others."
And those who have been slain. || 127 ||
I offer this funeral cake to those who have been consumed by fire, as well as to those others who have not been consumed by fire, and to those who possess fangs or horns.
I offer this funeral cake for those who have been struck by lightning or killed by thieves, and for those who have entered the womb of animals as birds, insects, or reptiles. (129)
Or else, I offer this funeral cake (piṇḍa) to those who have tree-bodies,
and to those who, having lived as countless beings, were led under the command of Yama.
For the sake of their deliverance, I offer this *piṇḍa*; wandering through thousands of other births by virtue of their own karma, [I offer this]. (Yajurvedins use the neuter form *idam*. 131.
To those included among humans for whom hundreds of torments have been brought, and to those to whom I offer this ball of rice,
as well as to others dwelling in the world of pretas in places of torment— [may it reach them]. (132)
For the sake of their deliverance, I offer this ball of rice (piṇḍa);
to those who were kinsmen or non-kinsmen, and to those who were kinsmen in another birth.
May they all always attain satisfaction through the offering of funeral cakes (piṇḍa)—those who are born in the paternal lineage as well as in the maternal lineage. (134)

Those who have died among one's gurus, fathers-in-law, and kinsmen, as well as others who were relatives; those in the family for whom the funeral rice-balls (piṇḍas) have been discontinued, and those deprived of sons and wives—[for all these, one should perform the rites]. || 135 ||
And those who have failed in their religious duties, those born blind or lame,
those who are deformed or pregnant, and those who are born into my family— [may they all be purified].
"May this ball of rice offered by me reach them and remain inexhaustible. (136)
Those who were born in the paternal lineage and likewise in the maternal lineage,
those who were slaves in both families, and those who were indeed servants;

For the sake of uplifting my friends, companions, the wicked, and those who have done me harm, I offer this funeral ball (piṇḍa). Those kinsmen born of my father’s lineage, as well as those born from my mother’s family and so forth— [for them I offer this].
Those in both families who have been my servants, as well as those who served the nectar, likewise [attained immortality]. || 137 ||
To my friends, companions, and close associates; to the trees, both sacred and harmful;
to those who have rendered me service;
and to those who were my slaves and servants in other births—to all of them I offer this funeral cake (piṇḍa).
Located in the north-west of Sūryakuṇḍa, within the distance of one bow-length, stands the god Gadādhara; having prostrated there, one should cause [the gift] to be given. (139)
May those who are witnesses—the gods, the Brāhmaṇas, and likewise the Vasus—bear witness that, having reached Gayā, I have performed the rite of expiation for my ancestors. 140.
"O Lord Gadādhara, I have come to Gayā for the sake of the ancestral rites;
you alone, O Blessed One, are my witness that I am now free from the three debts. (141)
One should offer sixteen rice-balls in the middle of the ancestral rice-ball;
one should make the rice-ball round and cause a stream of milk to fall upon it.
O Śāṅkarī, not far to the left of Gadādhara is Mātṛgayā; O Goddess, to its south is Sutīrthaka.
Likewise, by bowing with great effort to that god Gadādhara, the bestower of liberation, Keśava, the Supreme Person (Puruṣottama), a man is not born again.
Having beheld the high-souled Maunāditya, and especially Kanakārka,
with silence, the brahmin sage shall become a follower of the ancestors.
And by worshipping Brahmā, one shall attain the world of Brahmā.
On the southern bank of the Urvaśī is a stone with the luster of gold. (146)
She is to be known as Gāyatrī; one should worship her with perfumes and sandalwood.
Having risen early in the morning and approached Gāyatrī with a concentrated mind, one should approach her by name. || 147 ||
By performing the twilight devotion (saṃdhyā) with diligence, one obtains the fruit of all the Vedas;
and by beholding the Sāvitrī at midday, one obtains the fruit of sacrifice. || 148 ||
At Daśāśvamedha, Dhanada is the God of Gods, Janārdana;
there, by the offering of funeral cakes (piṇḍa), eternal satisfaction is attained. (149)
At Gayā, Janārdana, the God of gods, exists in the form of the ancestors;
by beholding that lotus-eyed one, one is indeed liberated from the three debts.
Having beheld the divine Grandfather (Brahmā) during the month of Makara, or during an eclipse of the moon or sun, one is liberated from all sins.

In the three worlds, it is rare to find one who casts a funeral ball (*piṇḍa*) at the well of Agastya; likewise, whether it be one's own son or another, by performing this at the Aśvamedhika well of Gayā, there is no further rebirth.
By uttering whose name one should cast the rice-ball (piṇḍa), that person is led to eternal Brahman;
O Brahmins, that place is fashioned by Brahman, for you Brahmins are fashioned by Brahman. (153)

All the deities, together with the ancestors, are honored by those who have been honored; one should satisfy the Brahmins at Gayā according to the rites for offerings to the gods (havya) and the ancestors (kavya).
Indeed, at Gayā, giving is not merely a matter of renunciation;
rather, whoever performs a great gift or whoever performs the rite of releasing a bull [attains the highest merit]. || 155 ||

O lady of excellent vows, sixty-four bow-lengths in measurement is said to be the sacred field of Agastya; at that Daśāśvamedhika Tīrtha, which bestows liberation, sixty tīrthas are situated there for that man.
Fifty-five holy sites have been described, O slender-waisted one;
and likewise Urvaśī, Sūrya, Kāma, and Vāsava as a son [are among them]. (157)
Āgastya, Aśvamedha, Tīrthasāra, and Gayāvila; those who died by hanging and those who died by a noose around the neck. (158)
For a woman who has been corrupted by her husband or who has fallen from her caste, no religious rites are prescribed;
there is no funeral sacrifice, no cremation, and no period of ritual impurity prescribed for them. (159)
One should perform the ritual for three nights at Agastyatīrtha and at Gayā;
beginning on the new moon day, one should indeed perform it for three nights.
Furthermore, that evil-minded person who performs any ritual action on their behalf finds that those actions become fruitless; he must instead perform the Cāndrāyaṇa vow.
From there one attains purification; otherwise, one becomes a sinner. Sin committed at other holy sites is destroyed at Gayā. (162)
Whatever sin has been committed at Gayā is destroyed in Rāmakṣetra;
whatever sin has been committed in Rāmakṣetra is destroyed at Maṇikūṭa. || 163 ||
Sin committed at Maṇikūṭa is destroyed at Nīlaśaila; sin committed at Nīlaśaila is destroyed at Antargṛha. || 164 ||
Sin committed within the inner apartment is destroyed at Somatīrtha; sin committed at Somatīrtha is dispelled at Maṅgalā;
and sin committed at Maṅgalā is destroyed at Āgastya. (165)
Whatever sin has been committed at Āgastya perishes at Mandara;
whatever sin has been committed at Mandara perishes at Vajralepa. || 166 ||
Whatever sin is destroyed by the Vajralepa [rite] at Aśvakrānta, that very sin committed at Aśvakrānta is removed at Urvaśī. || 167 ||
O Maheśānī, one should spend the day by listening to the greatness [of the Lord] and indeed by listening to the Saṃhitā; at night, one should contemplate Viṣṇu.
Having made your dwelling right here, you must not remain awake at night;
then, on the following day at dawn, O Brahmin, you should perform your bath in the Agastya [tīrtha]. (169)
Touching Bhasmācala, that stream is to be known as Sarasvatī;
there, O Maheśānī, one obtains the fruit of the Agniṣṭoma sacrifice by offering Svāhā.
O auspicious one, O beloved of Makaranda, O beautiful one residing on the chest of Viṣṇu!
O Supreme Goddess, take away my sin accumulated through birth after birth. 171.
One should bathe with this mantra, especially during the month of Kārttika; for there stands a beautiful step-well on the eastern side of the deity. (172)
Having drunk its clear water, one is not subject to rebirth.
It is located in the Āgneya direction from Bhasmaśaila, at a distance of eight dhanus. || 173 ||
O auspicious lady, there is a supreme and most holy sacred site named Piśācamocana;
at the Piśācamocana tīrtha, he worshipped the wielder of the trident (Śūlin).
This is that supreme Liṅga of the God, Kapardīśvara, located to the northwest of Bhasmakūṭa and to the north of Dhanurmadana. || 175 ||
The sacred ford named Kapālamocana is the most excellent among all holy sites;
it should be worshipped with diligence and praised with various hymns.
O beautiful one, my skull fell into that very bath;
O lady of excellent limbs, one who has bathed therein dispels even the sin of killing a Brahmin. 177.
Lord Kapāleśvara is established in this sacred ford (tīrtha). To its north, O Śivā, there is a place five bow-lengths away known as Kapilā. 178.
Having bathed there, O lady of excellent hips, one is liberated from the bondage of worldly existence;
having bathed in this Kapilāhṛda-tīrtha with a restrained mind, [one attains liberation]. (179)
Upon seeing Śiva, whose banner bears the bull, one obtains the fruit of all sacrifices;
facing the eastern direction, one should ascend the mound of ashes.
Having worshipped with the mantra that will be spoken, one is praised:
"O Vṛṣācala, salutations to you, O abode of Dharma and heaven!"
I cause you to ascend the peak of the heap of ashes; salutations be to you! || 181 ||
If anyone should ascend a mountain facing westward, the merit accumulated over ten lifetimes perishes at that very moment. (182)
But he who faces north, or even he who faces northeast—at that very moment, his wealth, sons, and wife are all destroyed. || 183 ||
Now I shall proclaim another auspicious matter, more secret than the secret;
O Goddess of beautiful countenance, listen to the majesty of the Bull-bannered Lord. 184.
If the new moon day (amāvāsyā) should coincide with Monday,
then one should go to Bhasmācala and worship the Lord with diligent effort.
Having extracted the twenty-first lineage, he shall go to the supreme state;
one should bathe the Liṅga with perfumes and other offerings, and with most beautiful lotuses.
One should smear the Great Soul with the five nectars, water, and sandalwood paste; then, at the end of each month and on every sacred festival day, one should perform this rite.
Having worshipped with a bilva leaf, one should bathe [the deity] with water containing jewels;
one should worship with the Rudrapuṣpa using the Prasāda mantra. || 188 ||

By means of the *bandhuka*, *jayanta*, and especially the *mālūra* flower, the God of gods, the wielder of the Pināka bow, should be meditated upon with joy. Rudra, whose limbs are adorned with ashes, directly removes the entire flood of sins; he is the one who bears the third eye, which blazes with flickering sparks of ash.
He who is the fourfold God of Gods. || 189 ||
Wearing a tiger-skin garment and possessing a bright body as lovely as the moon, he—
his own body dark blue— became utterly intoxicated, touching the goddess’s limbs and her face with his hand.
One should worship these deities of Parameṣṭhin upon the leaves:
Dhāman, Dharma, as well as Sūkṣma, Viṣṇu, Nārāyaṇa, and Hara.
One should worship Vijaya, Virajā, and Viśvā, starting from the center;
and one should also worship the Śaktis, beginning with Rāmā, who possess the characteristics previously described.

One should worship Śrīkaṇṭha and the others with devotion on the exterior, and likewise outside of that, one should worship the Lords of the Seats (pīṭheśas); furthermore, one should worship the Lords of the Seats in front.
