One should worship Kamalā with the Traiyambaka mantra, excluding [the other deities];
then one should worship Nandīśa, the crown, and the guardians of the directions in their proper sequence.
Having thus worshipped the Lord of Gods with offerings, a devoted man, having prostrated before the Supreme Lord, should recite this hymn of praise. (195)
Oṃ, homage to the one of universal color, to the golden one, and indeed to the one of golden hue;
to the one with golden ears, to the one with a crest fashioned of gold, and to the Lord of Gold, homage! 196.
Obeisance to you, Harikeśa, born from the vajra of Īśāna;
obeisance to him who has the color of the rising sun and who bears a blazing form. || 197 ||
Homage to the impure and the pure, to the fortunate and the imperishable;
homage indeed to him whose hair is cast off from the limbs of existence, to the one with disheveled hair. || 198 ||
Salutations to him who is pleased by the six rites and devoted to the three duties, who causes the specific activities of the castes and stages of life to proceed according to rule. (199)
Homage to the one who purifies and is purified, to the one who is being cleansed, and to the instrument and the cause;
homage to the one with ringing ornaments, and to the one whose eyes are white and tawny, and whose mouth and gaze are black. || 200 ||
Salutation to the one who grants dharma, action, wealth, and liberation, and who removes all sins; salutation indeed to the one who holds a trident in his hand, the beloved of Umā. 201.
O Harikeśa, born from the face of Īśāna, homage be to you! Be gracious, O beloved of Pārvatī; indeed, homage to the one who brings joy to Umā. 202.
Then, having received permission, Karahastaka, with palms joined in reverence, bowed down, made offerings, and should recite this mantra: || 203 ||
O Umānanda, salutations to you, who increase the joy of Pārvatī!
May my accomplishment be free from obstacles, since today my worship has been performed before you. (204)
O Lord of Gods, by the grace of Jagannātha and by your command, I shall today worship the glorious Kāmeśvara Śiva, the Great Lord.
Having worshipped Viṣvaksena Janārdana in the east of that [temple],
one should worship the deity named Mātaṅga in the western part of the sacred site.
By residing there for a distance of twenty-two bows, one does not grieve;
whatever sin has been committed there becomes equal to the murder of a Brahmin—or rather, it is as expiable as the murder of a Brahmin. || 207 ||
Whatever merit one may have performed there, one shall obtain the fruit of the Agniṣṭoma sacrifice; a devoted person should worship Mātaṅga there with offerings such as water from the Gaṅgā.
O Goddess of the Gods, being well-composed through the state of mind associated with the seed-syllable of Māyā, one situated there should behold the temple while facing the south. (209)
Having uplifted his entire lineage, he is glorified in the world of Brahmā.
Homage to the Creator, who is the form of Viṣṇu and the Mandara mountain. || 210 ||
Having seen you, may he who dwells in heaven cast off his sin;
thereafter, he should look toward the Sunset Mountain (Sandhyācala) and recite this mantra: || 211 ||
O elephant, O witness, may whatever sin has been accumulated over thousands of millions of aeons be destroyed by the sword-like tusks of the elephant-faced one.
Then one should offer the *arghya* to the Sun, accompanied by sesame seeds, water, and *kuśa* grass.
Having risen, one should offer water for sipping with a prostration,
especially during the offering of the *arghya* as part of the ritual observance (*vrata*) dedicated to the Sun.
Then, having sat down, he should offer [the water]; rising from another [position], he should cause it to be given.
Having placed the arghya vessel face-down at the conclusion of the arghya, the wise one should then offer the arghya.
And there, having prostrated before Caṇḍeśvara Sūrya, one should bid him farewell. O beautiful one, [this is] my western Daśāśvamedha in the south.
And as for the Kaliparvata situated at a distance of an arrow-shot,
by merely ascending it, one's merit perishes.
One who is suffering is stained; strife touches him, and not otherwise.
Whatever stream of water strife touches, that stream becomes my army.
One should likewise avoid this entire sacred ford (tīrtha) which is defiled by the impurity of the Kali age; for it is situated sixteen dhanus to the northeast of Mount Mandara.
Cakratīrtha is a great sacred ford that destroys all sins,
as well as the multitude of transgressions born from the afflictions of the planets and whatever other evil has been committed.
Having seen a lion or a half-moon on the fourth lunar day of either the dark or the bright fortnight, whatever sin exists from that defect is entirely destroyed by bathing. (220)
O my beloved, O Goddess, he who causes bones to fall for seven nights shall become marked with the discus; there is no need for deliberation on this matter. (221)
Whatever being dies at Cakratīrtha obtains the fruit of even holding sandalwood; becoming radiant, upon death, that creature shall go to the city of Hari.
O King of Tīrthas, arisen from the ocean of existence for the twice-born at Dvārakā, salutations be unto you; protect me from the bonds of worldly existence. || 223 ||
Having bathed with this mantra, one should offer an arghya oblation to Savitṛ;
and that man who, having bathed at Cakratīrtha, worships the Creator (Brahmā).
By touching the mountain Cakratīrtha, the mountain named Nandana, one delivers ten ancestors, ten descendants, and oneself as well. (225)
And sixty-two *dhanus* to the west, O beautiful one,
is Janārdana, the Lord of Gods, who in the Kali age takes the form of a Buddha.
Having seen that [place], one is liberated from most terrible and extremely dreadful sins;
it is the harsh Pauṇḍravardhana, which has emerged as a stone discus.
And to the west of Mandara, on the auspicious mountain that is to be,
the emblem and form of Janārdana are proclaimed.
To the north of that mountain, in the northeast, is Virajā;
to the south of Gajaśaila, in the west, is the Śaubhraliṅga.
This Gayā, known as Āgastya, is indeed the most excellent field among these;
thus, this field is remembered as consisting of one hundred [sub-fields], beginning with Asambhava.
One should know that this is the field of hope; anything else is called "red. By offering a ball of rice (*piṇḍa*) there, the ancestors attain the supreme goal. || 231 ||
And one should offer the *piṇḍa* with the utterance "Svadhā" [or "Svāhā"] into the hand of Janārdana:
"O Janārdana, this *piṇḍa* has been given by me into your hand. (232)
"For one who has gone to the next world, you shall indeed be my giver; for the remainder of the Kali age [in this Kali age], however, it shall be measured at eight bow-lengths from the east. (233)
That stone serves for the liberation of the ancestors from the state of a preta;
by offering funeral cakes (piṇḍa) there, one is never born again as a preta anywhere.
To the southeast of Cakratīrtha, at a distance of two bows, is the supreme Laula Liṅga; one should propitiate it with sesame seeds and milk.
Then, by beholding Janārdana at the junction of the Kali and Dvāpara ages, one is indeed released from the three debts; [this occurs] at a distance of half a bow's length.
The Liṅga established by Śukra is known by the name Śukreśa.
Having beheld the god Śukreśvara, one is liberated from the bondage of worldly existence; who indeed would not be released from bondage? (237)
Then, having seen Goleśvara (Golokeśa), one is liberated from the sin of killing a Brahmin;
likewise by seeing Aṅgāreśa, Siddheśa, Gayāditya, and Gaja. || 238 ||
Having beheld Mārkaṇḍeyeśvara, one becomes free from debt to the ancestors;
having beheld Gayāgoleśvara and bathed Janārdana [there]. || 239 ||
Together with the ancestors, it protects twenty-one generations of men.
Is this not sufficient as a cause for the purification of men?
Here, twenty-one generations of men go to the world of Brahmā. || 240 ||
Whatever holy sites exist on earth, including the oceans and lakes, shall visit Cakratīrtha once every single day. (241)
On earth, Gayā is meritorious; likewise, there is Kūpaka at Gayā.
O Goddess, Kūpa is eight times more meritorious than that, but O auspicious one, Mātṛgayā is the most excellent.
A son becomes free from debt to his mother in an instant by going on a pilgrimage to Gayā;
by offering funeral cakes (piṇḍas) at Gayā, he becomes free from debt to his ancestors.
The offering of funeral cakes (piṇḍadāna) ends at Gayā; the sacred ford (tīrtha) itself ends at Gayā;
Kāmarūpa ends at Pañcaka; and the auspicious river ends at Picchilā. (244)
A man should offer his own funeral ball (piṇḍa) into the hand of Janārdana,
and likewise at Viraja, at Aśva, at Karṇī, and at Somaka.
By offering a funeral ball (piṇḍa) for one who is still living, a man is born with a short lifespan;
however, he who offers his own piṇḍa at the great sacred field of Agastya [is exempt from this]. || 246 ||
The lifespan increases by one year and two months in succession for him who performs the rite of releasing a bull (vṛṣotsarga) as a funeral ceremony (aurdhvadaihika) with his own hand. || 247 ||
O Queen, that [merit] is also remembered as inexhaustible even when one has gone to the other world;
yet, while one's parents are still living, a son should not perform the funeral rites for them. (248)
O Maheśvarī, [this applies] when there are many sons, or a single son, or a son who practices yoga;
or when the son has reached the waning dark fortnight, or when there are three sons.
O Goddess, for forty days at most, one should personally perform the rites for oneself;
one should indeed perform acts of charity and the release of a bull, but never the ten-day [mourning] observance.
While both husband and wife are alive, one should always perform two *vṛṣotsarga* rites;
one should carry out the *vṛṣotsarga* separately within a single mandala and a single sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*).

If performed for one who is dead, it yields a single-fold result; if for one who is living, the fruit is eight-fold. And if performed for one of another lineage, one obtains only a very slight result. || 252 ||

Having performed the *śrāddha* rite according to the rules, one who is intent on going to Gayā should visit Karkaṭikeśa, converse with his own kinsmen, and perform the circumambulation of the village. (253)
Then, having gone to another village and eaten the remains of the *śrāddha* offering,
she should circumambulate [the village] and depart, avoiding the acceptance of gifts.
And from the house, for a distance of one cubit toward the place where Agastya went, there is a staircase for ascending to heaven at every step for the ancestors. || 255 ||
One should perform the śrāddha ceremony at Agastyatīrtha every day, both by day and night;
likewise, the śrāddha performed at Aśvatīrtha, Nīlakūṭa, and Pañcaka [yields great merit]. || 256 ||
At Sobhakūṭa in Rāmāśrama, one who performs a śrāddha ceremony leads his ancestors to heaven;
and at Ārustya, having performed a tonsure and beheld the Lord Janārdana, [one attains the same]. || 257 ||
Having ascended Mount Mandara, one purifies the seventh generation of one's lineage;
likewise, a Śrāddha performed at Gayā for a year, a Pārvaṇa Śrāddha on every lunar festival (parvan),
a Śrāddha performed without meat, and similarly [at the two equinoxes].
In the two equinoxes. || 258 ||
His ancestors depart forever from that funeral offering (piṇḍa) disappointed;
in the case of an *āma-śrāddha*, one should offer raw meat without hesitation. || 259 ||
O my beloved, the ancestors remain with their faces turned downwards;
however, he who eats the śrāddha food without meat after it has been prepared with meat [is blessed]. (260)
One shall go to the Tāmisra hell along with one's ancestors; it cannot be otherwise.
O Śāṅkarī, having taken [the thread], one should fashion it from long threads there.
O my beloved, one should perform my vow in this manner even without the practice of *śrāddha*.
He by whom it has been made meatless should perform the *śrāddha* without meat. (262)
The liberated one eats that which is free from worldly attachment, never that which is tainted by it;
a wise man should invite [guests] immediately for a Śrāddha and perform the rite.
O Śāṅkari, when a Brāhmaṇa is censured by a Śūdra during a śrāddha, a sacrifice, or a rite for the gods, he who feeds that Brāhmaṇa eats excrement. 264.
The meat of the buffalo, the large goat, the deer, and likewise the yak;
the meat of the monitor lizard, the tortoise, the porcupine, the hare, and likewise the boar. || 265 ||
The meat of the boar and likewise the meat of the deer should be given in every way at a śrāddha;
however, the knower of reality [should avoid] the meat of cows and the dog in the Kali age.
One should avoid the meat of animals with defective organs and of goats that have not been used for plowing;
furthermore, one who would satisfy the ancestors with the meat of a black goat [commits a fault]. 267.
The ancestors depart disappointed, having uttered a most terrible curse, against one who gratifies them with the meat of goats that are deficient in their senses. (268)
It is declared to cause great fear; therefore, one should avoid it.
With the flesh of a buffalo, satisfaction lasts for twelve years and is eternal. (269)

O Pārvatī, by means of a goat one gains [the fruit] for a year; by means of chāgas or śaileyas, for six years; by means of a yak-tail fan (cāmara), for a hundred years; and by means of a cow or a goat, O beloved, for a thousand years.
O lady of excellent hips, by means of boar meat one attains [the fruit] for six months, and by tortoise meat for only one month [or three months];
by the meat of the *śālū* fish [or by boar meat] for six months, and by hare meat for nine months indeed. (271)
For twenty-two months in the case of the small boar, and for one hundred years (or six years) in the case of the yak, one should avoid its coarse flesh. (272)
That which is to be avoided by four or even six men is declared by the ancient sages to be "excessively thick" (atisthūla). || 273 ||
O my beloved, the meat of a buffalo, or that of a cow, or even that of a boar, as well as that of a large deer or a thick-bodied animal, is indeed recommended for me. (274)

O my beloved, one should avoid eating the meat of the rhinoceros (khāḍga), even if it is among the five-clawed animals permitted for consumption; likewise, one should avoid the four-clawed animals and those born in water when they are associated with the rhinoceros.
A wise man should avoid the lizard, the golden rhinoceros, and the black yak-tail; he should also avoid the tortoise if it is marked with a wheel.
The siṃhaśuṇḍa, the rohita, the rājīva, the citraka, as well as the mahāśalka, the prauṣṭhika, and the mountain-dwelling (pārvatīyaka) fish. || 277 ||
One should diligently employ the bṛhadrohitamatsya, the bṛhatprauṣṭhika, the bṛhacchālka, and the citra fish at a śrāddha ceremony.
One should avoid fish that lack scales and those shaped like serpents;
however, for a scaleless fish, two pieces of meat should be offered from its middle.

One should avoid those with the form of a hungry ghost (preta) and others, as well as those with deformed shapes, those with mouths like serpents, those who are excessively corpulent, and those who are dark-complexioned. || 280 ||
One should carefully avoid jīvāṃśa, śeluka, padmaka, kuṅkuma, svarṇaka, and granthivarṇa in a śrāddha ceremony.
One should avoid smoky-colored *pañcakadala* mixed with sugar and insects, as well as buffalo ghee; one should carefully avoid milk and ghee [of such quality] at a *śrāddha* ceremony. (282)
One should carefully avoid coconut, palm fruit, dates, and pineapples, as well as milk that has not been processed with buttermilk or clarified butter. (283)
One should avoid a lamp with a defective wick, as well as visible oil, safflower, nālikā greens, and likewise the mālatī flower. (284)
In a Vṛddhi-śrāddha, one should avoid the lotus and the karavīra;
one should not offer the Gāṅgeya (white water lily) nor the red water-born lotus.
O Goddess of the Gods, a śrāddha performed without clothing, without the sacred thread, without sesame seeds, and without products of the cow is fruitless. (286)
In the absence of a garment, one should offer kuśa grass and a garland;
in the absence of a sacrificial thread (yajñasūtra), one should instead place two strands of thread.

In a Śrāddha for a Śūdra and in a Śrāddha for a woman, one should avoid the sacrificial thread (yajñasūtra). O Consort of Śaṅkara, a Śrāddha performed without betel-leaf and without the lime-paste is deficient.
In its absence, one should give jīvaka with milk-rice mixed with honey;
being composed, one should offer the food in a vessel made of a single type of metal. || 289 ||
One should first present the portion for the deities and offer it into the vessel for the ancestors;
however, one must never at any time cause food remaining from the ancestors' portion to be given to the deities. (290)
In an *āma-śrāddha* performed for one who has no sacred fire, one should never wash the food;
however, in the case of a *vṛddhi-śrāddha*, during a solar transit (*saṃkrānti*), and during eclipses, one should wash the food.
One should offer food to a Brahmin measured by eight handfuls, provided it is not from a single source. || 292 ||
Therefore, one should give neither more nor less in the rite of Śrāddha;
he who performs the very beautiful Śrāddha upon a lotus leaf— || 293 ||

O Goddess, daughter of Śaṅkara, for one hundred years his father remains satisfied; for a full hundred years he experiences satisfaction, and not otherwise— when [the offering is made] under the shade of the Aśvattha tree upon the Brahma-vessel.
Satisfaction for six months is produced by [offering] on a banyan leaf;
for one month on a copper vessel, and for a year on a golden vessel.
It is said that on a silver vessel it is tenfold, and on a sword-blade vessel it is more than a hundredfold.
However, at the Śrāddha rite on the anniversary of death, as well as in the Pārvaṇa and Vṛddhi rites, one should employ separate vessels for those belonging to different castes. || 296 ||
One should employ rice for that duration of one year;
however, one should avoid rice that grows in the rainy season when performing a Śrāddha for a deceased person.

One should avoid grain produced during the rainy season, as well as sesame, barley, and chickpeas, when used for sacrifices and the like, or for ancestral rites (śrāddha), if they have been boiled twice. || 298 ||
Ṣaṣṭidhānya, rājadhānya, bṛhaddhānya, ballabha, somadhānya, śiśnadhānya, vaṅga, and raktaśāli. (299)
The ketakī, the kalaviṅka, the dhānya, the nārāyaṇa, as well as the mādhava, the pradīpa, the viṣṇudhānya, and the ballabha. || 300 ||
One should employ in the Vedas grains suitable for sacrificial offerings (śrāddha), such as bhogya, dhānya, aśoka, nāgākṣa, and likewise pañcaka. || 301 ||
O Maheśvarī, one should offer wheat, barley, cakes,
wild rice (nīvāra), and likewise other excellent divine grains in the Śrāddha rite.
Grain sown in the spring should be avoided with great care;
by eating it here, sin is transferred to men. (303)
By eating the food of the Śrāvaṇa month, one is born poor;
by eating Soma-grain, one should perform the Cāndrāyaṇa vow.
It is said that by eating *vṛddhadhānya*, one indeed attains prosperity;
by eating *rājadhānya* or *śiśnadhānya*, one becomes a partaker of the world of Viṣṇu.
Having eaten red śāli rice, one shall obtain the glory of victory;
O beautiful lady, [one obtains] the enjoyment of Nārāyaṇa and Mādhava, as well as mine. 306.
By eating grain and fodder, a man shall attain renown;
however, if he should exclude an invited Brāhmaṇa from a Śrāddha ceremony, [he incurs sin]. (307)
If a Brahmin, having been invited to a house, should somehow eat there [without first offering], he would go to a terrible hell until the dissolution of all beings. (308)
He shall go to the Kālasūtra hell and enter the womb of a sow, especially if he is one who has been invited while observing a vow or is a celibate student (brahmacārī). || 309 ||
One should not bypass that śrāddha; there is no fault in eating honey, fresh ghee, grain, meat, and likewise oil. (310)

O Goddess, there is no fault in consuming food while observing a vow during a sacrifice for the ancestors (pitṛyajña), nor in a śrāddha at Gayā, nor during the fortnight of the departed (pretapakṣa), nor when following a husband in death (anumaraṇa), O Beloved. (311)
O beloved, she should never smell the funeral ball (piṇḍa) during the ritual of grasping [the hand] or at a śrāddha performed at a sacred ford;
except at the ford of liberation, a brahmin woman should not follow her own husband [in death].
One should never follow a separate funeral pyre on the paths to liberation at any time;
the ritual should be performed within ten days, whereas otherwise it is a hindrance. (313)
Likewise, [if one touches] one who has died by hanging, or a corpse in water, or a corpse that has been left overnight, or likewise a corpse afflicted with consumption or leprosy; || 314 ||
O beloved, a Brāhmaṇa should not follow [the corpse] except at a sacred bathing place (muktitīrtha);
likewise, a woman with many sons, one who is pregnant, and one who is in her menses [should not follow]. 315.
One who has fallen from her caste, an unchaste woman, and an unfaithful wife should never follow [the corpse].
Therefore, for the sake of following it, one should keep the corpse for one day.
If she follows [the husband] on the following day, no fault arises in that regard;
likewise, whatever property belongs to the husband who has died in a foreign land [she may take]. || 317 ||
Keeping that object in her heart, she should follow after the Kṣatriya and others;
or else, being a virtuous Śūdra woman who is either veiled by her devotion or impassioned by love, she may at some time follow him.
This is the prescribed rule for the Vaiśya woman as well regarding her following him in death.
If the husband dies on the third day, she may follow him even on the fourth. || 319 ||

On the anniversary of her husband's death, the wise man should perform the rite for her during that year; O Goddess, when two have died together, one should offer the funeral rice-ball (piṇḍa) at a single location.
One should perform the śrāddha simultaneously; one should not perform them sequentially, nor should one perform separate śrāddhas.
Furthermore, a man should fashion the rice-ball (piṇḍa) for the husband and wife as a single circle. || 321 ||
One should cover [the vessel] with a cloth and pour in honey and milk;
one should never offer milk together with the rice-ball (piṇḍa), nor ever dried mango.
(208) Neither ghee nor buffalo clarified butter, nor the *dhātrī* fruit, nor the *lakuca*, nor the pomegranate, nor the citron, nor likewise the cucumber fruit [should be offered]. || 323 ||
One should avoid the rose-apple fruit, lotus seeds, plantain, and rāmaka;
as well as kaśeru, yugānañja, and the milk of a tawny-eyed cow.
Likewise, ripe jambu fruit should be diligently offered at a śrāddha;
however, unripe fruit, honey-milk [as praised by Brahmā], radish, and karamarda that is infested with insects must be avoided. || 325 ||
One should offer bilva, tinduka, madhuka, madhurī, jambū fruit, padmākṣa, and jīvantī. || 326 ||

Brahmins, Kṣatriyas, and Vaiśyas should perform the Śrāddha as proclaimed by the well-spoken word [of the sages], having first obtained the consent of their family traditions; it should be given accompanied by the sacred mantras. || 327 ||
The three castes, including the Śūdras, should give according to the instruction of the Brahmins;
this should be done according to the rule, excluding mantras and without the cooking of fire. || 328 ||
O Śāṅkarī, [one should perform this] at sacred fords such as Puṣkara, in holy sanctuaries,
on the peaks of the great mountains, and in auspicious regions.
In sacred waters, in rivers, and in streams;
in the confluences of rivers and in the seven oceans.
In a temple of the gods, in a cow-pen, at the root of a nurse-tree, at the roots of divine trees, and in the midst of *tulasī* plants; || 331 ||
In the Daśārṇas, the Kumāryas, the Magadhas, and the Kuśas,
on the northern bank of the Virajā and the southern bank of the Lauhitya.
To the south of the Narmadā and to the south of Agastya’s [hermitage], and to the east of the Karatoyā—it is said that a śrāddha should not be offered in these regions. (333)
They say here that the śrāddha should be offered month after month at the waning of the moon;
and on the full-moon days, the śrāddha must be performed while the sun is within the range of sight.
The daily *śrāddha* is always sung of by humans;
the occasional (*naimittika*) is together with the gods, as is both the daily and the occasional. || 335 ||
The optional Śrāddhas which are performed by the twice-born every year,
as well as the Vṛddhi-Śrāddha, should be performed on occasions such as rites and the commencement of new undertakings.
In that regard, O Daughter of Śaṅkara, know that the bath preceded by the worship of the Mothers should indeed be performed when the sun has entered Virgo for fifteen days. (337)
A wise person should perform the Śrāddha according to the Pārvaṇa rite;
he who gives sesame seeds mixed with jaggery during the Śrāddha ceremony [attains great merit]. || 338 ||
By worshipping the ancestors with honey and offerings mixed with honey on the Kṛttikā constellation according to the rite prescribed by Manu, a person attains liberation. || 339 ||
One desiring offspring should perform it under Rohiṇī; under Saumya (Mṛgaśiras), one obtains brilliance;
under Maghās, progeny; and under Phālgunīs, prosperity and good fortune.
It may also be performed according to one's own preference under other lunar mansions as well;
even for those whose ancestors died by the sword in battle. (341)
Therefore, one who desires their satisfaction should perform the rite on the fourteenth day;
when the fifteenth-day śrāddha is to be performed out of a desire for specific results.
The Śrāddha is prescribed as being performed on the fourteenth day and the sixteenth;
it may also begin from the tenth day or even from the fifth day.
Then, one should perform rites for the gods on the fourteenth lunar day (tithi), which is to be avoided [for other purposes];
and one should perform the śrāddha on the new moon (amāvāsyā) every month, or occasionally at that time. (344)
He attains all desires, and upon death, that man enjoys heaven;
likewise through the daily śrāddha, the libation, the worship of the gods, and the daily ritual service.

And for the feeding of Brahmins, no sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) is prescribed. O beloved, if one is unable to perform the Śrāddha, one should feed Brahmins during the fortnight of the deceased (pretapakṣa). || 346 ||
O Goddess, one should offer water to the gods here and likewise present it as an offering;
even while one's parents are living, this should be done at sacrifices and on the day of a śrāddha.
One should feed [the guests] with various kinds of foods, both solid and soft, as well as fruits;
for if they are not fed, the sacrifice is ruined and the śrāddha becomes ruined as well. (348)
O Maheśvarī, one should avoid the daily śrāddha (nityaśrāddha) during the śrāddha for prosperity (vṛddhiśrāddha), the pārvaṇa śrāddha, and when feeding many Brāhmaṇas.
If one desires to attain that difficult-to-reach state through the Rājasūya or Aśvamedha sacrifices,
one should then go to Gayā and the Gaṅgā and perform the Śrāddha according to the prescribed rules.
Even with barley-meal mixed with water, vegetables, roots, and black pepper,
the city of the ancestors remains empty until the awakening of Viṣṇu.
When their awakening has passed and they have been overcome by their father or by the deities,
they depart with a sigh, having uttered a most difficult curse.
O Goddess of the gods, one whose father is still living should avoid the Śrāddha at Gayā, the ritual bath at Gayā, as well as the libation with sesame seeds, and the use of a sword-shaped vessel.
On a Monday coinciding with the new moon, one should avoid observing silence and bathing.
O Goddess, he whose mother has died should also go on a pilgrimage to his mother’s [shrine], O Beloved.

O Queen, if the deceased father is the eldest, or even if it is a paternal uncle who has died while the mother and father are still living, one should deliberate before going to Gayā; [in such cases], one should never go to Gayā. || 355 ||
One should offer the funeral cake (piṇḍa) for the father, and then also for the grandfather;
one should likewise offer the cake for the great-grandfather—this is the settled rule in the scriptures regarding the cakes. (356)
When they have died, a funeral ball (piṇḍa) should be offered and Brāhmaṇas should also be fed;
however, the Sapiṇḍīkaraṇa rite does not exist for them, nor is the Pārvaṇa rite prescribed. || 357 ||
The fulfillment of the sacrificial fee is accomplished; it is secluded and possesses auspicious characteristics.
One should smear with cow dung a pure and secluded spot. || 358 ||
One should offer the rice-ball (*piṇḍa*) for the ancestors on a spot of ground purified by fire; one should never offer it otherwise.
O Goddess, when the *śamanīya* graha is present, one should avoid the house of evil. (359)
A mendicant and a celibate student who have arrived for the sake of food should be honored, even if they are filled with desire, once the guests of the śrāddha have been seated. (360)

The performance of the rite together with the proper place and time, and the excellence of the materials and the Brahmins—these five destroy the efficacy of that [rite] upon the body; such is the detailed explanation of the cause.
Alternatively, one should indeed feed a Brāhmaṇa who has mastered the Vedas;
or whoever performs that rite for the further satisfaction of the gods. (362)
That śrāddha should not be performed for the sake of a specific desire; one may conclude it even by means of a tantra.
Furthermore, at the commencement of the Vaiśvadeva rite, one should avoid that śrāddha.
In the construction of a palace, on a journey, or during domestic work, [these activities] do not exist during the dark fortnight; therefore, one should avoid bathing at that time.
Thus ends the fifth chapter in the second part of the section on Kāmarūpa, within the twenty-two-thousand-verse *Yoginītantra*, the great king of tantras.
The sixth chapter.
The Blessed One said:
O Goddess Pārvatī, listen to what must be done on the second day [and so on, every day]:
having bathed at Cakratīrtha, a man is liberated from all sins. || 1 ||
Having gone to the south of the Lauhitya [river], Kolaparvata is situated in the northwest;
on its western side is the mighty Pāṇḍunābha.
To the north-west of that [place], there is a lake twelve bows in length,
renowned as Brahmakuṇḍa, which destroys all sins.
What is the use of recitations, what use are austerities, what use are gifts, or even sacrifices?
By bathing in Brahmakuṇḍa, a man attains perfection at that very moment.
By the command of Īśvara, the gods and dānavas formerly dwelt there with Brahmā; now they hasten to that tīrtha for the purpose of bathing. (5)
O beautiful one, the sages, Siddhas, Gandharvas, sacred fords,
and lakes [constitute] the supreme circle of majesty belonging to that Brahmakuṇḍa.
Having bathed quickly on the bank according to the rules, one should give gifts in accordance with the prescribed ritual,
such as jewels, gold, and gems, according to one's own means.
If such an opportunity arises, he who out of delusion does not bathe is the lowest of men;
he is cooked in a terrible hell for as long as the reigns of fourteen Indras endure.
To its south, at a distance of five bow-lengths, is that sacred ford named Lauhitya; by bathing there, sin is destroyed.
Likewise, through bathing in the king of sacred fords, there is the total destruction of all evil.
The lake of the King of Tīrthas is meritorious and bestows the fruit of all holy places.
Whatever sacred sites, rivers, and lakes there are among all living beings—all those holy places certainly enter the King of Holy Places. 11.
Just as the ocean, the lord of rivers, is the king of all holy fords (tīrthas), so too is this [place] the most excellent among all holy fords, granting all desires. || 12 ||
O beloved, just as darkness is destroyed when the sun has risen,
so too is there the destruction of all sins through bathing in the King of Tīrthas.
p. 214) There has never been, nor will there ever be, a sacred ford equal to this king of tīrthas, where indeed the Lord Nārāyaṇa is eternally present as its presiding deity. (14)
O my beloved, who is able to describe the virtues of the King of Tīrthas,
wherein there truly exist ninety-three crores of sacred sites?
Therefore, O beloved, whatever merit is performed— whether bathing, giving gifts, burnt offerings, recitation of mantras, or worship of the gods— it becomes inexhaustible.
Salutations to you, O son of Brahmā; salutations to the son of Śāntanu.
O Lauhitya, always remove whatever sin has been committed in the three births.
Having bathed with this mantra, one should present the *arghya* offering;
O noble lady, one should worship with supreme devotion using this mantra. (18)
The best among the kings of sacred fords, the supreme and most excellent Haṃsa joined with the left eye;
the teaching, the heart of Fire, the beloved, the body of Dhruva, and the lake. 19.
Situated on its southern side, not very far away,
extending as far as the Dhānvantara family, is what is known as Viṣṇukuṇḍa.
Having bathed in Viṣṇukuṇḍa, a man should behold Pāṇḍu Śaunaka,
who stands before him in the form of a beautiful stone, accompanied by Mañju.
A human being obtains the fruit of five horse-sacrifices;
[he understands] that he is the vital breath residing in all beings and the source of the lord of rivers.
"O Viṣṇukuṇḍa, salutations to you; protect me from all sins [one is liberated, O beloved].
Having bathed here on the eleventh day of the month of Phālguna, O lady of excellent hips," || 23 ||
Completely liberated from all evil, entirely freed from all suffering, he was called Vṛndāraka [equal to the gods], illustrious, and proud of his beauty and youth. (24)
Having uplifted twenty-one generations of his lineage by means of that which is stainless, sun-colored, and frequented by divine gandharvas, he goes to the world of Viṣṇu. || 25 ||
In its southern chamber, slightly toward the region of Nairṛta,
there is what is known as the Śiva-kuṇḍa, measuring eleven dhanus.
By merely performing an ablution there on the fourteenth day of every month at Śivakuṇḍa, O my beloved, he goes to the world of Rudra.
Having bathed at the time of dawn, one is not born as a ghost on earth;
the supreme among all holy places is that which arises from the bathing of Viṣṇu.
"O Lord of Rivers, salutations to you; protect me, for you are dear to Śiva.
Having bathed with this mantra, one should offer the arghya with the *haṃsa* [mantra].
Thence one should go to Pāṇḍuśaila and bathe it with scented water;
one should worship it with white lotuses and auspicious white karavīra flowers.

Having addressed the word "Viṣṇave" (to Viṣṇu) and the true word "Pāṇḍunāthāya" (to the Lord of the Pāṇḍus), one should then utter "Natiḥ" (salutation) for those beginning with Janaka, who are rich in speed and rich in worship.
That which consists of fourteen syllables and is proclaimed as ending with the *śikhā* [mantra] has Nārada as its seer (*ṛṣi*), the *gāyatrī* as its meter (*chandas*), and Hari as its deity.
And its application is for all purposes, especially in rites performed for specific desires;
one should meditate on Viṣṇu as white-complexioned, two-armed, with hands adorned by the discus and the conch.

Having performed meditation, the wise one should worship the Giver of Boons— who is served by gods and gandharvas, who is the Lord of all worlds, the Giver of Boons, and the eternal Grantor of Desires— beginning from the eastern vessel and proceeding in due order. (34)
Lakṣmī, Sarasvatī, Gaṅgā, Yamunā, Narmadā, Śivā, Bālā, Kamalā, and likewise Saṅkarṣaṇa and the others.
One should worship the guardians of the quarters, the planets, and Viṣvaksena;
having bathed according to the rules at Lauhitya, one should worship Pāṇḍunātha.
Completely liberated from all sins, he is glorified in the world of Viṣṇu for the duration of a full Manvantara, free from old age and death.
Having returned here from the exhaustion of his merit, he is born into a family endowed with all virtues; yet,
having taken up birth like a preta, he does not become righteous and indeed does not attain the state of Viṣṇu.
Having recited the mantra, one should worship the deity; one should perform the adoration with the chosen mantra:
"O Pāṇḍunātha, salutations to you; salutations to you, the bestower of liberation. (39)
Save me, O Lord of all worlds, O you who have the form of Viṣṇu; salutations be unto you!
O you who resemble the stainless cloud (or the stainless sun), salutations to you, O Puruṣottama! 40.
Salutations to you, O lotus-eyed one; O Lord of Pāṇḍu, let there be salutation to you!
Salutations to you who shine like the interior of gold; salutations to you whose banner bears Garuḍa.
O you whose form is Brahman, salutations be to you; O Nārāyaṇa, salutations be to you!
Salutations to you who resemble collyrium; salutations to you, O lover of your devotees! || 42 ||
O Lord Pāṇḍu, salutations be unto you; protect me, protect me, salutations be unto you!
Salutations to you, O abode of the wise; salutations to you, O beloved of the wise. || 43 ||
O Nārāyaṇa, salutations to you; protect me who have come to you for refuge.
Salutations to you, O best of the wise; salutations to you, O lotus-born one. (44)
O four-faced one, abode of the world, white-hued one, salutations be unto you! Salutations to you who resemble a dark blue cloud; salutations to you, worshipped by the thirty gods.
Save me, O Viṣṇu, Lord of the World; O you who take the form of Pāṇḍura, homage be to you!
O Narasiṃha of great heroism, O you with blazing eyes, save me! 46.
O you who possess the form of Viṣṇu, salutations be to you; O Lord of Pāṇḍu, salutations be to you!
Five bow-lengths to the southwest of the deity [is the site]. || 47 ||
Know that the field marked by the Aśvattha tree is the Field of Dharma (Dharmakṣetra).
There one should recite the Saṃhitā and chant the Gītaśāstra. || 48 ||
By reciting the mantra four times during a yuga-cycle, one obtains that very fruit;
there is no doubt in this matter regarding the thousand repetitions in a single cycle.
O Goddess, by ascending this sacred field (kṣetra), one obtains the fruit of Kurukṣetra;
it extends for the distance of one bowshot on the eastern side of the deity. || 50 ||
That beautiful stone of translucent form is proclaimed to be Lakṣmī;
having worshipped her with the seed-syllable of Śrī, one should sacrifice with *mālatī* flowers.
Then, having bathed in Viṣṇukuṇḍa and recited the Lakṣmī-mantra according to the prescribed rite on the full moon day when the sun is in Libra, Lakṣmī becomes pleased with him.
O Śāṅkarī, know that not very far to the south of that place is the Kolakṣetra, measuring eight bows in extent. || 53 ||
Having seen the Lord of Gods at the foot of the Aśvattha tree, made of beautiful black stone and appearing restless, he who worships Him with devotion goes to the world of Viṣṇu. || 54 ||
To the north of Brahmakūṭa is a lake named Śrīkuṇḍa, measuring two bows in extent; by bathing there, one obtains prosperity. (55)
Having bathed with the mantra at the Śrītīrtha on the tenth day of the bright fortnight of Caitra, or on the auspicious eleventh day of the bright fortnight, one attains the unsurpassed goal.
May there be prosperity! O most excellent Lord, bestower of health and victory, grant me fortune, grant me glory, and take away my sin; salutations unto You! 57.
To its east, at a distance of exactly twenty-two bows in measurement,
is declared the Kanakhala Tīrtha, which destroys even the greatest of sins.
Especially on the third day of the bright fortnight of Vaiśākha, one who bathes with the mantra of Dakṣiṇāmūrti is glorified in heaven. (59)
O best of rivers, O highly fortunate one, served by gods and gandharvas;
O holy ford, remove the sin accumulated over ten births; salutations be unto you! (60)
On its southern side, on a beautiful mountain,
one should worship Campakeśa, who is the embodiment of the science of archery (Dhanurveda).
Having touched the waters at Kanakhala while endowed with a state of purity,
one is liberated from all sins and proceeds to the world of Brahmā.
To its east, O auspicious goddess, is a holy site (tīrtha) seven bows in measure, renowned throughout the three worlds, belonging to Brahmā Parameṣṭhin.
O Maheśvarī, he who even mentally remembers Puṣkara—which destroys all sins and bestows the world of Brahmā upon those who have died—[attains that goal]. (64)
He is liberated from all sins and rejoices together with Śakra.
There, the gods dwell along with the Gandharvas, Yakṣas, Uragas, and Rākṣasas. (65)
The hosts of Siddhas worship Brahmā, who is born from the lotus;
having bathed there, one becomes liberated and beholds Brahmā, the Supreme Lord.
Having indeed worshipped the boon-granting Brahmā,
he then beheld the irreproachable Puruhūta, the Lord of Gods, having approached him.
A mortal is born in his true nature and enjoys his desires;
O lotus-faced one, O Puṣkara, O highly fortunate one, salutations to you, O Tripuṣkara! 68.
*Hu*, *hū*, *hauṃ*. O Lord of Rivers, O Puṣkara, take away my sin!
One should perform the ritual bath with this [mantra], and one should offer the *arghya* with this. (69)
And to the southwest of Puṣkara, slightly to my left, O beloved,
is the sacred site of Badarikāśrama, measuring twenty-eight dhanus.
Having gone there, one should worship the god Nārāyaṇa, who is free from ailment;
by bathing and worshipping on the day of Hari, the fruit of giving a thousand cows is obtained.
Whoever performs the Rohiṇī vow in the hermitage of Nārāyaṇa shall obtain the fruit of one hundred times ten million such vows.
There, the Linga of Maheśa is known as Vibhāṇḍaka;
by worshipping it with a temple, one attains the state of Rudra. (73)
The supreme holy site of Pañcagodāvara is frequented by Brahmā and the other gods;
having worshipped Rudra, the gracious Supreme Lord, there— (74)
He propitiated Hara, who is devoted to the five-syllabled mantra;
having worshipped him, one should offer salutations and obtain the fruit of [giving] a hundred cows. (75)
To the east of Puṣkara, however, is the lake named Kumāra;
he who bathes at the Kumāra-tīrtha attains the status of a leader of the Gaṇas.
To the southeast of Kumāratīrtha, O Goddess, is the Naramāraṇyaka tīrtha, fifty dhanus in length, surrounded by hosts of all the gods.
Dwelling in Kumāreśapura, devoted to the welfare and pleasure of Viṣṇu:
Oṃ oṃ īṃ hūṃ! O Youth who pervades the universe, remove my sin! 78.
Having performed his ablutions with this, one should present the *arghya* offering to the Lord of the Gods;
there, the Great God is designated as Sthāṇu. (79)
Upon seeing it, a person is instantly liberated from all sins.
To the north of Campakeśa, at a distance of sixty-two bows,
is that forest named Campaka, which is worshipped by Siddhas and Brahmanical sages.
There lies the meritorious abode of Viṣṇu, where Puruṣottama resides within the midst of the five stones of Brahmakūṭa in the region of Dhanada.
Indeed, by bathing at Durgākūpa— the great well that has openings on all sides—
with the ten-syllable mantra, one shall attain all desires.
Having bathed in the Durgā-well on the eighth lunar day while muttering the Kāma-mantra three or five times with black Vijaya flowers, [one attains success].
Having worshipped the supreme deity, a person shall become a possessor of the sacred scriptures.
Even a woman who is barren like a crow, or one whose children have died, attains that same destination, especially during the autumn season. (85)
If one worships the goddess Kāmeśvarī there with Bandhūka flowers, O Queen of Gods, or with Bilva leaves, one shall attain eternal perfection. 86.
One shall accomplish one's desired wishes and attain perfection there;
[the deities are] Kaula, Viṣṇuśaila, Śaṅkara, and Parameśvara. || 87 ||
Īśa, Pārijāta, Kumāra, and Gaṇeśvara,
as well as Nīla and Śveta, are situated immovably on the northern part of the earth.
In the middle are Viṣṇu, Sthāṇu, and likewise Dharmabala;
as well as Kamala, Śikhā, Kapota, and Marutācala. || 89 ||

In the southeast, O Goddess, are the mountains Cācala, Hastikarṇa, and Vikarṇaka; while in the south are Amācala, Maruvaka, and Prajeśvara. [Note: An additional reading found prior to this states: "Previously, in the southeast, the mountain Pānakūpa and others have been proclaimed."]
Dyumant, Kanaka, Vāyavya, and Nīlalohita. || 90 ||
Mānaśaila, Vahni called Kāma, Indra the performer of a hundred sacrifices (Śatakratu), Lohita, Kamala, and likewise Nirṛti in the southwest (Nairṛta). || 91 ||
Gandharva, Lakṣaṇa, Piśāca, Vihagācala, Brahmayūpa, Hayamedha, and Girīśvara are located in the west. || 92 ||
Uttara, Uttaraśca, and likewise Uttarapāṇḍuka;
Āditya is in the northwest (vāyukoṇa), while Vāyu and Bhallātaka are likewise [there].
Dhanada, Mahīdhra, Janaka, and likewise Nala; in the northeast, Maṇḍala, Aśvakrānta, and Candraka. (94)
Yama, Citravāha, and Graha follow in due order;
from there, O Supreme Goddess, one should proceed to Nīlaśaila at midday.
On the eighth, the thirteenth, or even the fourteenth lunar day;
or during the equinoxes, the solstices, or likewise at the transit of the sun.
If one goes to the eastern gate, one shall obtain abundant wealth;
if desiring liberation, one should go to the north; and if desiring a kingdom, to the west. || 97 ||
When one ascends the Blue Peak by way of the southern path, the king shall be deprived of his kingdom, and the destruction of others shall occur. || 98 ||
If one goes toward the northeast at that time, one shall obtain abundant prosperity;
however, in the northwest and the southwest, it will bring about great fear. || 99 ||
One should visualize [the deity] as blue, with ten arms, peaceful, adorned with jeweled earrings, wearing a necklace and upper garment of serpents, and seated upon a bull. 100.
One should worship [the mountain] with the seed-syllable of fire (RAṂ) after paying homage according to the prescribed rite;
by ascending the mountain while reciting the mantra, one obtains the fruit of an Aśvamedha sacrifice.
At the eastern gate of the very house, one should ascend Mount Nīla;
for this Nīla, O mighty-armed one, bestows dharma, kāma, artha, and mokṣa.
"I cause you to ascend the peak; O remover of evil, be gracious to me!
At Durgākūpa, in the east, is the deity Āmnātakeśvara. (103)
O Goddess, one should worship [the deity] beginning with Keśava at a distance of three *dhanus*;
O Beloved, to the south of that deity, however, it is at a distance of eight *dhanus*.
One should worship Gaṇanāyaka, who has the form of an elephant and is black in color;
to his very east stands Trivikrama, holding a bow.
By bowing to it with devotion, a person shall obtain all their desires;
its length, measured by the bow, extends to five parts.
O Goddess of the Suras, that pleasure-pool named Saubhāgya, belonging to Kāmākhyā, measures forty cubits.
Formerly, Prajāpati was worshipped there by Śakra along with the gods;
having bathed at its western bank, one should perform the maṇḍala there.
Having performed the ritual procedure correctly, one should observe the fast;
then, when the fifth day arrives, one should bathe in water according to the prescribed rite.
Whoever goes to the Krīḍāpuṣpa-kariṇī and worships Kāmeśī quickly delivers his ancestors and rejoices in the world of the Goddess. || 110 ||
O you who possess auspicious fortune, O whirlpool of rivers, O stainless one, O beloved of Lake Mānasa!
Homage to Oṃkāra, Vaṣaṭ, and Svāhā; take away my sin; homage be to you!
Having performed the immersion with the mantra, one should offer the arghya with the Kāma-mantra. To the northeast of that sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) is indeed the lake named Lohitya.
O Goddess of the gods, having bathed at Dhruva, one is liberated from the bondage of worldly existence;
there is the fire-pit Kālahasta and the lake named Yāmala. (113)
Having bathed there, one becomes handsome on earth;
O Supreme Goddess, five cubits to the southwest is the place for good fortune.
One should know that the Gaṅgāsaras contains water originating from all sacred fords (tīrtha). The pool situated within the enclosure of the pillar is celebrated as Saubhāgya. (115)
Three crores and a half-crore [of beings] in heaven, on earth, and in the intermediate space—all those [lost their] good fortune when the sun grew dim. (116)

Therefore, one should perform the bath when the sun is in Capricorn; for he who performs the bath at the equinox of Libra or during the transit [of the sun] into Libra [attains great merit]. || 117 ||
One without a wife obtains a wife and rejoices in the world of the gods.
O Supreme Goddess, the five-fold Hasta [mudrā] is in the southwest;
one should know it as Gaṅgāsaras, and having bathed there, one shall go to the city of Viṣṇu. || 118 ||
O Dear One, one should know that the stone which is both manifest and unmanifest, having the form of a lizard, is named Ananta; above it is the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa).
Ananta is on the western side, and that which is the black stone is on the eastern side;
one should know that to be Varāha, whose water originates from all sacred fords (tīrtha). One obtains [the fruit of] visiting them even without a wife.
One who is childless shall become possessed of a son through his wife. || 120 ||
Or during the month of Tulā, or especially on the eighth day of the bright fortnight in the month of Kanyā,
one who bathes and beholds the Goddess shall obtain the fruit of the Agniṣṭoma sacrifice.
One should satisfy the ancestors and the gods, and one may also satisfy other deities associated with specific desires;
however, O Goddess of Gods, one should not perform rites for specific desires at any of the sacred bathing places (tīrthas).
In this Kuṇḍa, at Aśvakrānta, Āgastya, and Prayāga;
likewise in the lake of Vārāṇasī, at Bhārgava, and at Meru-puṣkara. (123)
One should meditate at the Gaṅgā-hrada, the Brahmasaras, and the Durgā-well;
[thereby one obtains] that fruit which has been proclaimed by the great seers for circumambulating the earth. (124)
That fruit is obtained simply by circumambulating that very pool;
it is situated in the south-eastern part of the pool, at a distance from the Tulā.
Having beheld Śiva known as Kambala, one is liberated from the bondage of worldly existence;
one should worship him with the mantra "Smara," endowed with the proper resonance and ending with "Namaḥ. (126)
Salutations, salutations to you, O Lord of Gods, adorned as if with mantras!
O Beloved of Lakṣmī, salutations to you, O Infinite One, O Supreme Person! 127.
Worshipped by the lotus-feet of gods, dānavas, and gandharvas, the auspicious one; homage to the boon-granting liṅga, homage again and again to Kamala. 128.
O my beloved, having bowed down to the form of Kṛṣṇa, which is the very form of Viṣṇu,
and having praised and circumambulated him, one should then proceed to the temple of the Goddess.
Having gone to the corpse-seat and performed recitation, O Śāṅkarī, one should gaze with the Tāra mantra;
then one should bathe it with the five nectars, with water, and with very auspicious waters.
One should purify that deity with that vessel using the root mantra;
O my beloved, one should write the Kāmatantra [or Kāmamantra] with *kuśīta* on the right side.
Having drawn Kāma on the left, one should perform worship there;
likewise on the body of the Goddess, on a painting, on the Puṣṭimaṇi gem, and on a sword, O Śāṅkarī.
In a cremation ground, at a great liṅga, in an image, or likewise in water; in a yantra, in a tantra, or in a śālagrāma—one should dismiss the maṇḍala.
In a great *homa*, one may incur the sin of a major transgression (*mahāpātaka*) regarding the mandala;
and he does not accept that worship, but having abandoned his station, he goes to the city of Viṣṇu. (134)
Nor [should one do so] when situated in another birthplace or to the east of a cremation ground;
rather, having established the great maṇḍala of the Goddess there, one should perform worship. || 135 ||
The stone, red as the blood of a Rakṣasa, measures eighty-seven dhanus;
the Liṅga, endowed with horripilation, is eight cubits in height and possesses fifty thousand [marks].
The field in the west is equal to four cubits; it is the maṇḍala of the womb (yonimaṇḍala), measuring many mātras, and twelve finger-breadths in its extent.
There, within the center of the womb, the waters reach down to the netherworld (Āpātāla);
there flow the Urvaśī, Yamunā, Dhārā, Kāverī, and Sarasvatī. (138)
That which arises from the Brahma-pool and is stainless at Maṇikūṭa goes [to the supreme state] for one who worships Viṣṇu with the heart; of this there is no doubt. (139)
O beloved, after flooding the mandala of the goddess, the Brahma-lake becomes clearly visible;
after sixty-three months, the bala-plant becomes dry.
For two months up to three days, it certainly remains free from obstacles; however, after six months, it causes misfortune.
(O Goddess, when it remains stable for six months, it is remembered as bringing great fortune.)
When the stream in the channel is dry, one should indicate that the excrement and urine have been discharged outside;
when the stream in the channel is dry, one should declare the feces and urine to be external. || 141 ||
O Śaṅkarī, whenever a dry stream occurs year after year, there will undoubtedly be famine in that region. || 142 ||
If the interior is dry, there is loss of sovereignty; listen to the result when everything is dry:
the king shall be deprived of his kingdom and enter another's realm. (143)
In this very way, O fair-faced one, many kinds of defects may arise;
therefore, one should perform a pacification rite according to the prescribed rules in order to quell those defects. One should perform the pacification rite in that case where a defect has occurred.
The wise practitioner should perform two hundred thousand oblations with *karavīra* flowers soaked in ghee, or two hundred thousand oblations with milk-rice, red lotuses, or *śrīphala* fruits.
Or else, O auspicious lady, one should offer two hundred thousand oblations of *karavīra* flowers mixed with ghee, along with the "three honeys" and the meat of a monitor lizard. 144.
O Goddess of the gods, the wise one should offer either a red lotus, or milk-rice, or a bilva fruit, or even the meat of a monitor lizard, smeared with the three sweets. (145)
Sugar, honey, and ghee—this combination of the three sweets is proclaimed as "trimadhu.
One should perform the oblation with boiled milk mixed with clarified butter. 146.
And to the west of Ananta stands the river named Asi.
And to the west of that is the stream which is the river named Varuṇā. || 148 ||
Having drunk its pure water, one is never born again anywhere;
[there are] Siddheśvara, Koṭiliṅga, Hemaka, and Muktimaṇḍala.
It should be known that Vārāṇasī is the field, Dhārā is the Śamī-field, and the inner chamber of the Goddess is renowned.
O Maheśvarī, she resides in the liṅga, in the book, in the image, and on the sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila).
One should worship the Goddess in her sandals, on a painted cloth, as well as in a sword, in fire, in water, in a book, and in images. 150.
On a sacrificial mound, on sandals, in a painting, on a sword, in fire, and in waters;
likewise in the Lauhitya river, in the Gaṅgā, in the ocean, and at the confluence of sacred fords (tīrtha). || 151 ||
O Śaṅkarī, one should worship the Goddess situated in the liṅga at each pedestal— at the root of the *bilva* tree and at the mouth of the *bilva*—
and wherever there is the *kāmaśilā*, that is the *maṇipūraka* pedestal. (152)
The inner house is the great seat (mahāpīṭha); that very same [place] is called the jewel-seat (maṇipīṭhaka).
It is on a rock, at its summit, and likewise in a mountain cave. (153)
A person endowed with devotion and faith should worship the Goddess daily;
just as worship at Vārāṇasī yields full fruit, so too at Puruṣottama, worship bestows twice the full fruit. 154.
Twice that merit is said to be obtained in the presence of Puruṣottama;
in all sacred fields and holy fords, worship performed with a desire for the Kāmaśilā yields fruit equal to that of Kālagiri.
At Saumāra it is said to be eightfold, and at Cauhāra it is equal to that.
In Āryāvarta, in Madhyadeśa, and likewise in Brahmāvarta [and Śrīhaṭṭaka]. || 156 ||
O Goddess, like Maṇipūra, she bestows fruits when worshipped; O Maheśvarī, she is the giver of fruits at Śrīhrada.
(At Āgastya and at Aśvamedhika, the fruit shall be fourfold.)
Then, O Goddess, it is certain that [the merit] at Jalpeśvara is four times greater than that; this has been declared in the presence of Jalpīśvara.
Where the Yoni shines, the fruit is remembered as tenfold; from where the Yoni is located...
It is said to be tenfold. || 157 ||
p. 229) Thereafter, O Goddess, Supreme Sovereign, it is fourfold at Ekāmra;
at Maṇikūṭa it is a hundredfold, and at Maṇiśaila it is a thousandfold.
It is said that at Aśvatīrtha, whether in water or on land, the fruit is tenfold;
and at Kāmarūpa, whether in water or on land, the fruit from worship is equal. Thus it has been declared, O Supreme Goddess, regarding Ekāmra.
Therefore, O auspicious one, O Maheśvarī, it is a hundredfold more [meritorious] at Maṇikūṭa.
Therefore, O Maheśvarī, it is ten times more [efficacious] at Maṇiśaila;
from that, it is said to be ten times more so in the water and on the land at Aśvatīrtha.
Equal to that [in Kāmarūpa] is [the worship] everywhere, both in water and on land.

Just as Viṣṇu is the most excellent among the gods and Lakṣmī Maheśvarī is the most excellent, so too is the Goddess in Kāmarūpa; thus, I consider her worship to be supreme everywhere. As is Viṣṇu, so is Lakṣmī.
Just as [she] is the most excellent of all. || 160 ||
O my beloved, the worship of the Goddess is likewise praised in Kāmarūpa;
there exists no other field of the Goddess equal to Kāmarūpa [nowhere else is there anything equal to it]. 161.
Elsewhere the goddess is rare, but in Kāmarūpa she is in every house.

In Kāmākhyā is Mahāmāyā; the man who worships Mahāmāyā, having attained all desires in this world, shall become Śiva in the next world. He who has performed worship even once here obtains his desires in this life and the nature of Śiva in the hereafter. 163.
There is nothing else created that is equal to it;
having obtained one's desired object here, one is born with long life. Indeed, no other deed like that exists elsewhere on earth.
Having obtained the boon of his desired object, he will certainly become long-lived. || 164 ||
At the time of bathing, at midnight, and at the conclusion of the great worship (*mahāpūjā*), there is no presence (*sānnidhya*) of Mahāmāyā; one should neither go near nor touch her.
On the eighth day of the month of Kumāra, during the night and at the end of the day, one may indeed touch her.
One whose mind is intent on attaining accomplishment should not go to Mahāmāyā. || 165 ||
On the night of the Mahāṣṭamī, at the end of the day,
and at the beginning of the Yugas, during the month of Kārttika, a man should not look upon the Goddess, nor indeed should he gaze at her in the presence of the Kumāras.

O Goddess, if a Śūdra beholds our King or Dhyānarti, he shall become handsome, O Goddess, and will certainly attain a good rebirth. And whatever Brahmin widow always beholds Mahāmāyā— [and always beholds her].
One should cause [the disciple] to look [at the deity] after bathing. || 167 ||

At the time of bathing at midday, during the dismissal of the offering flowers (nirmālya), women—and especially young women—should not look upon the Goddess; nor should a woman ever touch the Goddess, especially a young woman. (168)
On the eighth and ninth days of the month of Pauṣa, and likewise on the thirteenth day.
One should not go to the house of Pārvatī for three days starting from the first day of Karkaṭa;
during these times, if one touches her, a curse will be incurred and there will be a loss of life. One must not go to the house of Pārvatī at the beginning of Karkaṭa.
If one touches [the image], one utters a curse; if one looks at it, there shall be a loss of life.
Only by one who is initiated [is worship permitted]; indeed, not by one who is uninitiated, even upon hearing of the worship of the initiated.
For this very reason, one seeking initiation should likewise not wear red garments.
Adorned with red sandalwood paste and applying forehead marks made from the products of serpents,
he sits upon a deer skin and receives initiation with devotion— neither without such feeling nor by one who is uninitiated. (170)
Clad in red garments and adorned with red sandalwood paste, he should apply a tilaka made from the products of snakes and lie down upon a deer skin. (171)
Supreme knowledge is bestowed and the bondage of the fetters is destroyed;
therefore, O Mistress of the Gods, it is called "initiation" (dīkṣā) by those who contemplate reality. 172.
Whatever evil has been accumulated through mind, action, or speech—
having destroyed that entirely, this *viśeṣakaraṇī* shall bestow supreme knowledge.
Because she bestows the supreme knowledge. || 173 ||
Therefore, it is for this reason that initiation (*dīkṣā*) is proclaimed in this world by those learned in the scriptures;
it alone bestows the fruit of higher knowledge (*vijñāna*), while the second [type] effects dissolution (*laya*).
The third is indeed the bestower of liberation; therefore it is called *dīkṣā*.
According to the rules for the accomplishment of *dīkṣā*, it is both with support (*sādhārā*) and without support (*nirādhārā*). || 175 ||
Whether it be the daily, the occasional, or the optional rite, for whomever there is eligibility, initiation is twofold: with support and likewise without support.
That which is without support—[it is called] "without foundation" (nirālambā)—should be understood as that which bestows liberation. 176.
And that [initiation] should be known as stainless, so it is said by those who contemplate reality.
Having prepared the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) and the mandala, [the initiation] is bestowed upon worthy recipients;
thus the initiation becomes fruitful, otherwise it would be fruitless. In this regard, it is fruitful.
Preceded by the construction of the sacrificial pit and the mandala, it is certainly held to be devoid of efficacy through mere mental activity alone. || 177 ||

One who is childless, one whose children have died, a *kuṇḍa*, as well as a dwarf; one with deformed nails, one with black teeth, one with an extra limb, and likewise one who is conquered by his wife. (178)
O Goddess, O Mistress of the Gods, one should never at any time avoid such a teacher; he is indeed one who is thus perfected—
one of excellent form, of noble lineage, and endowed with the qualities of knowledge and right conduct.

At that time, the wise teacher, being himself conversant with the conduct of the observances, should bestow the mantra; and likewise, the initiation should be granted by one who knows the conduct of the observances. || 179 ||
"O Goddess, one should not receive initiation; I tell you this as the truth, the very truth.
A man should not receive the mantra from his father, nor should he receive the mantra from his maternal grandfather or his father, nor likewise from his maternal grandfather."
And that which is obtained in a dream or given by a woman is purified by the rite of consecration alone. || 180 ||
And for the sake of attaining mantra-siddhi through what is obtained in a dream, one should cause the life-force (prāṇa) of the Guru to enter the flask;
likewise, having written [the mantra] on a banyan leaf with saffron, there should be its formal reception.
Thereby one attains purity; otherwise, it would be fruitless. || 181 ||

O Goddess of the Gods, [this should be done] during the solstices, the equinoxes, during the eclipses of the moon and the sun, on the day of the sun's passage into a new zodiac sign (saṃkrānti), and on the first days of the Yugas.
On the lunar days belonging to the Manvantaras, on the fourteenth and eighth days, on the day of the Great Worship, or on the days for the purification of the disciple. (183)
A person who is devoted to the worship of the Goddess, being purified and endowed with devotion and faith, should receive [it] during the ritual procedure for the worship of the Goddess. (184)
Only such a person is to be initiated, and no other, for he is entirely devoted to the meaning of all the scriptures.
Initiation in the month of Caitra leads to suffering, whereas in Vaiśākha it bestows all perfections.
In the month of Jyeṣṭha it bestows death; in Āṣāḍha it brings many calves;
in Śrāvaṇa there will be great loss; and in Bhādrapada it is considered to be a giver of suffering. (186)
In Āśvina, she leads to all accomplishments; in Kārtika, she bestows the increase of knowledge;
in Mārgaśīrṣa, she brings about auspiciousness; and in Pauṣa, she destroys knowledge. (187)
In the month of Māgha there shall be an increase in intelligence, and in Phālguna it brings forth all kinds of crops;
during an eclipse at a great holy site (tīrtha), there is no fixed restriction regarding the time.
At Gayā, in the field of Bhāskara, at Virajā, on Mount Candra, in Koṅkaṇa, at Mataṅga, and likewise in the hermitages of Kanyā; || 189 ||
Therefore, O Pārvatī, one should not receive initiation at these sacred sites;
rather, the disciples who have been initiated must carry out the supreme instruction of the Guru.
He who is devoted to the worship of the Guru in the heart of the deity should perform the preparatory rite (puraścaraṇa), being pure in soul and having conquered his senses. || 191 ||
Even though he thought, "I have attained the mantras, yantras, Purāṇas, and the [sacred] speech at Gayā and other such places," he was constantly instructed by the Guru.
O Maheśvarī, a disciple must not commit violence against women;
likewise, [he must avoid] the *sayava*, the *cakravāka*, the *krauñca*, and the *pārāvata* bird. (193)
A mountain of blue stone and the like shall always be dear to him;
thus, the day should be spent by the initiate in this very manner. (194)
Having eaten at night, the wise man should likewise meditate with effort and perform worship;
on that day as well as the preceding one, he should consume sacrificial food (haviṣya) or meatless food.
Having eaten, on the following day one should partake of sacrificial food (haviṣya) and betel;
having cooked the caru oblation, one should offer half a portion to the deity. || 196 ||
One should give half of that to the Guru, while the full amount should indeed be kept by oneself;
having eaten together with the Guru, this is the procedure for all initiations.
If the Guru, having imparted the mantra, should remain fasting, he becomes a worm in the hell of the darkness of delusion; it is not otherwise. (198)
If, after performing the initiation, the practitioner of mantra should observe a fast, the deity will always be enraged; having uttered a curse, he shall return to his own city.
Thus ends the sixth chapter in the second part of the *Kāmarūpādhikāra* within the *Yoginītantra*, the great king of tantras in twenty-two thousand [verses].
The Seventh Chapter. The Blessed One said:
"In a beautiful, secluded place, within a hidden and auspicious maṇḍala..."
In a place crowded with flower-walls, perfumed with fragrant flowers and other scents.
In a place devoid of the third [gender] and free from the sight of cattle, the practitioner of mantra should then extract the mantra there from a crystal or similar material. (2)
Without the extraction of the mantra, it is considered to yield very little fruit;
one should extract the mantra within the yantra, whether it be concise or fully expanded.
One should not scratch the mantra on the ground, nor should one write it in a book; one should write it properly.
A book should not be placed on the ground, for from that, a ḍākinī might carry it off.
O Goddess of gods, during an earthquake or an eclipse, if the syllable or the book remains on the ground, there shall be ignorance birth after birth.
Then it happens, O Goddess of Gods; therefore, one should avoid him.
One should not even mention his name in one's lineage; his downfall will certainly occur.
For by means of a copper needle, prosperity arises and there shall be no decline;
indeed, with a rod of gold, one bestows great fortune.
O Goddess, by means of a needle or by [the worship of] Vṛhannala, an increase of intelligence arises; likewise, through Agni, there is the acquisition of sons, grandsons, and wealth. (8)
With silver there is abundant prosperity; with bell-metal, death may occur.
[The vessel] should be eight finger-breadths in measure, or perhaps ten finger-breadths.

Whoever should write a *prastha* [of this text] on an auspicious day with a needle four fingers long, for that person, a lifespan equal in number to the syllables [written] passes away in a single day. (10)
(236) O Goddess, listen as I describe in brief the dimensions of the book.
One obtains the fruit even by [using it for] a month; if there is no measurement, prosperity is destroyed. (11)
Having invoked [the deity] into a space measuring one cubit, or a fist, or twelve fingers, or ten fingers, or likewise eight; one should not make it smaller than that.
O Maheśānī, there are two types of piercing (*vedha*): the ancient one located at the fist and the hand, and the one at the length of the forearm;
O Great Goddess, the binding of form (*rūpabandhana*) occurs at equal intervals starting from the hand. (13)
Having set aside eight finger-breadths, one should cause a piercing to be made in the middle;
the piercing should be at the distance of a span (prādeśa) or one should perform it at two finger-breadths.
Furthermore, whoever should cause a piercing at the beginning or end of a book will quickly suffer the loss of a wife or the depletion of wealth. (15)

O beloved Mistress of the Gods, one should have a book made on birch bark, or on *tejapatra*, or likewise on palm leaf; or, O beloved, one should have a book made on a board of *agaru* wood that is not too short. 16.
O Śaṅkarī, it may be written on a leaf of gold, a leaf of copper, O Goddess, or on the bark of another tree, as well as on a ketaki leaf. (17)
O fair-faced one, having written it on a clay plate, a copper plate, a silver plate, a banyan leaf, or on any other multi-petaled leaf, whoever should practice it; || 18 ||
He falls into an evil rebirth, and the loss of wealth will certainly occur.
Having written the scripture on scorched paper, he who recites it becomes a killer of a Brahmin.
Or, if the book remains in the house, he will certainly attain the Vajrayāna. [Additional reading]
There would be suffering; it should be circular to be auspicious. || 19 ||
In a quadrangle there is ruin, but in a triangle death shall occur.
Śambhu, the trident-bearer with three eyes, is established in the syllable *satya*. (20)
In the Dvāpara age Prajāpati is the deity, and in the Tretā age it is Sūrya;
in the Kṛta age it is Pinākī, and in the Kali age it is Hari in the form of written letters.
At both the beginning and the conclusion, one should worship the written text and Śrī Hari with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings, as well as with very beautiful garments. (22)
O Śaṅkarī, for as many thousands of yugas as there are syllables counted in the gift of a vessel, one shall dwell for a long time in the heavenly world.
And if one does not accept the fee after having written it in a book, he shall burn in hell for as many years as there are syllables in that text. (24)
One should know the great seed-syllable as that which has ascended to the place of the consonant and is joined with the moon of the left eye; through its recitation, one attains liberation. (25)

I shall explain the Praṇava within the Praṇava, and the two syllables "ṭha" at the end of "vaṣaṭ. One should personally utter the word "namaḥ" at the end of the vowel, which consists of the essence of the heart.
For a householder, the Praṇava alone is present at the beginning of all mantras;
it resides at the beginning and end of every syllable for the sake of increasing self-knowledge.
But in the division of mantra and vidyā, O beloved, two types arise:
mantras are said to be male deities, and vidyās are remembered as female deities. (28)
Mantras for males should end in *huṃ* and *phaṭ*; those for females are considered to end in *svāhā*; and mantras for neuters should end in *namaḥ*. Thus, mantras are considered to be of three types.
A mantra that lacks these [suffixes] is a *vidyā*, as proclaimed by Mahāśaṅkara.
Parameṣṭhin is declared to be the seer (ṛṣi) and Gāyatrī the metre (chandas). || 29 ||
The deity is declared to be Tripurā; one should employ her for all purposes.
O Dear One, one should first install the Goddess with water according to the prescribed rite. (30)
Having performed the washing of the face, one should again perform a bath;
O Goddess, rising after two days or after eight days.
One should perform anointment with oil and dry the skin thoroughly with a decoction;
at the end of a fortnight and at the end of a month, one should perform the great ablution (mahāsnāna).
O Goddess of gods, O beloved, one should perform [the rite] with the root seed-syllable, or with the substance-mantra,
or with a Vedic mantra, or with the Māyā-syllable.
Thereafter, one should bathe [the deity] with water-pots; immediately following that bath, the *arghya* offering is made.
Having performed the *arghya* bath, one performs the bath once again. (34)
There will be a fall from the world of the goddesses, and loss of wealth will arise.
First, a bath with water [should be taken], and immediately after that, one with milk. (35)
One should bathe [the deity] with curd, ghee, two balls of food, sugar, jaggery, honey,
sesame and milk, and curd and sesame, using honey and milk.
Warm water, fruit-water, as well as kuśa-grass water, scented water, water with jewels, and flower-water. || 37 ||
Water with *vilva* leaves and seven-leafed plants, as well as water with red flowers, and likewise water in a golden conch, followed by that in a copper vessel. (38)

One should perform the ritual bath with water from a jar and *kuśa* grass as an offering (*arghya*); likewise, one should bathe the Goddess with the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*), as well as with milk and *kuśa* water. (39)
One should bathe [the deity] with various mantras; for that is known as the Brahma-bath, performed with the five products of a tawny cow (pañcagavya) as well as with milk.

Bathing is said to be a hundredfold more meritorious when performed with sugarcane juice; likewise, he who bathes [the deity] with milk, endowed with faith and devotion, [attains a hundredfold merit]. (41)
O Goddess, O Beloved, by worshipping Kāmākhyā according to the prescribed rite with ghee for anointing the limbs of the deity, one is honored in the world of Indra.
Having specifically rescued ten ancestors, ten descendants, and himself from the ocean of worldly existence, he is glorified in the world of Durgā. (43)
He who bathes [the deity] according to the rules with curd, dūrvā grass, and unbroken rice grains is honored in the world of Śiva by means of a silver celestial chariot. || 44 ||
He who bathes Kāmākhyā with fresh sugarcane juice rejoices together with Viṣṇu upon the Garuḍa-vimāna.
Having cleansed Durgā with water scented with sandalwood,
a man, pure as the rays of the moon and endowed with glory, is honored in the world of the Moon.
Having bathed [someone] somewhere with fragrant flowers and water, a person reaches the world of the nāgas and sports there together with the serpents. 47.
Having bathed Kāmeśī with faith using golden water,
one ascends a golden vehicle and rejoices together with the Vasus.
Droṇa leaves, bilva leaves, karavīra, and utpala lotuses should be employed at the time of bathing; they bring great pleasure to the Goddess. (49)
Having performed any one of these ablutions, a man endowed with faith and devotion is honored in the world of Viṣṇu by the Blessed Lady.
The man who bathes the Goddess with camphor water goes to the supreme abode where Kāmeśvarī resides. (51)
Listen to the meritorious fruit of him who, with devotion and according to the prescribed rite, bathes the Goddess with milk or honey for the sake of his ancestors. || 52 ||
His ancestors remain satisfied for two hundred years by each of the five nectars (pañcāmṛta) and by each of the hundred fruits. || 53 ||
One should employ one hundred jars of water for the great bath (mahāsnāna),
along with exactly one hundred jars of water and three palas of oil.
The wise declare that the *mahiṣṭha* (greatest) great bath is thus;
the middling bath is prescribed as being half of that. (55)
Half of that should be the smallest size; one should not make it smaller than this.
Any man who should ever perform the ritual bath in this manner [attains the fruit]. (56)
Sin committed over seven lifetimes is destroyed at that very moment;
as are lifespan, strength, fame, splendor, good fortune, and nourishment. (57)
Having snapped [the fingers] with both hands, one obtains [the fruit]; there is no doubt in this matter.
Thus, the devoted man who performs the great ablution (mahāsnāna) in this manner— || 58 ||
One obtains bodily health, long life, and supreme prosperity by means of ten *tolika* measures of each of the various substances. (59)
Alternatively, when the bath is performed without the four-legged stand,
its opening is eight finger-breadths wide and its belly is twenty-one finger-breadths deep.
A water-jar (*maṇikumbha*) is said to have a height of one *arali*;
where this solar ray exists, it is indeed like a line (*lekhikā*) within the path of the sun that is the size of a window-lattice. (61)
Eight *lekhikās* make one *dhūlī*, and eight *dhūlīs* make one *sarṣapa*.
Four *sarṣapas* are designated as one *raktikā*. (62)
Twenty *raktikās* are proclaimed to be one *pādaka*;
and a *tolikā* consists of four *pādas*, that is, four *tolas*, measured by the *prasṛti*.
Two *prasṛtis* and one *karṣa* [make one *karṣa*]; two *karṣas* shall be one *pala*. Half a *pala* shall be a *mukti*, and two *muktis* are considered a *guḍaka*.
Having thus performed his bath, the wise man should then cleanse his body;
the wise man should apply fragrant sandalwood and fashion a tilaka mark. (65)
One should offer a waist-thread, a garment, and a sacrificial thread;
[and one] whose beautiful hair is glossy and resembles the feathers of a peacock. (66)
She was large, with lips like red bimba fruit and blood-red eyes, appearing utterly astonished; her mouth was indeed crimson, possessing the luster of well-applied red collyrium.
"O Tripureśī, the supreme abode of the three worlds has been fully described; it is the unsurpassed eastern face, which was formerly enjoyed by Narakeśa.
O Maheśānī, one who desires prosperity should meditate upon it within the clay."
That mouth which is indeed formidable, black, and situated on the right side; || 68 ||
It is renowned as Kāmākhyā, endowed with divine vision;
