it bestows all spiritual perfections (siddhis) and accomplishes every purpose. || 69 ||
To the right of the god, one should contemplate the yellow face;
and that auspicious dark-blue face which is the abode of the north. (70)
O Mistress of the World, it is wondrous, to be known through its hundred-fold limbs;
it is unmanifest, beautiful, divine, and possesses a supreme face like that of a key.
Those desiring victory should meditate upon him who is enjoyed by Narakeśa [or Śambhu], who resembles pure crystal and is endowed with all jewels. (72)
The object of knowledge, consisting of all-knowledge, is the mouth of Kālavāgīśvarī; it is like a mass of honey constantly drunk by the bee whose mark is the bull. 73.
O beloved, the eastern face of the Goddess, which possesses the radiance of thousands of millions of suns, should be meditated upon by those seeking all forms of forgiveness. 74.
Likewise, O auspicious lady, the seat Kāmeśvarī should be known as the supreme and great;
it is the face of the highest light, kissed by Narakeśa.
For the destruction of the evil of worldly existence, one should meditate solely upon that;
for this deity Tripurā, the Mother of the Gaṇas of Kāmākhya, these goddesses are established within the mandala, endowed with their respective powers (śakti). || 76 ||
Kāmākhyā, who wears a lion’s skin as an upper garment, has a large belly;
she is clothed in a tiger’s skin, bestows all accomplishments, and is auspicious, with a belly like that of a boar. 77.
Born of supreme bliss, accompanied by loud laughter and great festivities,
she is Sunandā, the delight of the eyes, manifesting eighteen eyes.

Adorned with a pair of earrings filled with beautiful rubies, she is the Great Sovereign, the Fierce One who bestows all goals; she is terrifying through her wrathful forms, yet she is Raudrī, wearing a garland together with a swarm of bees. (79)
She wears a crown whose crest is joined with the radiance of lotuses by the white rays of its jewels,
and she bears a neck-ornament studded with various clusters of gems.
She is smooth with arms as tender as lotus stalks, joined by twelve divine arms adorned with jewels and unsteady ornaments, and marked by the mud of lotuses and bees.

With his six arms—those on the left and right—he holds [the following], which shine with the splendor of the thunderbolt, the lotus, the thread, and the wheel at his ears: listen to those held by the right arms. (82)
She holds a bow, a severed head, a skull-topped staff (khaṭvāṅga), a lotus stalk, and a lotus;
she wears a skull-cup, a book, and a bell, and is adorned with a garland of heads as her sacred thread.
She stands upon the tips of a balance scale, resting upon a multitude of lotus feet;
she is reclined upon a lion throne, having made her seat upon a corpse.
The supreme goddess Kāmākhyā is embraced by Śiva, the Supreme Lord, who possesses matted hair and is the source of all existence, through the manifestation of the radiance of his jewel.
In this manner, O Goddess, the meditator should perform the meditation; the Goddess should install the Mātṛkā, the Supreme Sovereign,
together with one's own name and birth star, preceded by the installation of Śrīkaṇṭha.

One should perform the placement of the digits (kalānyāsa), the placement of the seats (pīṭhanyāsa), and the placement of the mantras (mantranyāsa); having established [the deity] tenfold within the yantra and having consecrated it according to the prescribed rule.
One should scatter unbroken grains (akṣata) there and perform the worship of the pedestal (pīṭhapūjā),
beginning from the east in due order, [worshipping] Gaṇeśa and the Lord of the Gaṇas.
One should worship Gaṇanātha, who sports with his hosts, and Manu, the refuge of heaven;
first one should worship Śrī, and immediately after that, Gopada.
One should worship with a long *manvantara* joined with the letter *tā*;
the *krīḍāsaras* is to the south, while *mandara* has the "left eye" (*vāmanetraka*). (89)
In the west, one should worship Lohajaṅgha, who is joined with the *raśmibindu*, using the seed-syllable of Nārasiṃha as the lord of the field (*kṣetreśa*). || 90 ||
In the north, one should worship Bhūtanātha together with Mandara,
as well as Gaurīputra, Vaṭuka, and Samayaputraka.
Having meditated upon the Wisdom-Son and the Samaya-Son in the eastern and other directions respectively with this mantra, "Haṃsa," one should worship them with red [offerings].
The gatekeeper of the peaceful [deities] is likewise the supreme *bindu-kalā*;
after that is the *nivṛtti-kalā*, and then the *pratiṣṭhā-kalā*.
With the seed-syllable of Māyā, one should indeed place Hetukā and the others there, starting from the east.
Hetuka, Tripuraghna, and likewise Agnivetālaka; then Kāla and Karālaka, following the sequence beginning with Vāma. 95.
Likewise, Ekapāda, Bhīma, Gagana, Manu, and Asitāṅga and the others are endowed with the perfections (siddhis) beginning with Brāhmī. || 96 ||
One should worship the ten Carcikās in the six corners, starting from the yoni;
and at the front of the hexagon, one should worship Madana and Ratiputrī on either side.
Likewise, one should worship the five arrows, as well as the planets and the lords of the directions, upon the seat, each positioned higher than the one below.
Having meditated thus, one should invoke the Goddess and recite this mantra:
"Come, come, O Supreme Sovereign! Be present here in this mandala. (99)

O Mother of the worlds, O you who ferry beings across the ocean of saṃsāra, O you who abide within the forest of great lotuses, O you whose form is the bliss of the ultimate cause—act [for our welfare]. 100.
"O Kāmeśvarī, who consists of the Brahman of sound and who are pure, be gracious to me!
O Śāṅkarī, one should perform the invocation of Kāmākṣī with this mantra. (101)
Salutations to Bhava, to Sarva, to Rudra, and to the Giver of Boons; salutations to the Lord of Creatures and to the one who is eternally the soul of all bliss. 102.

Salutation indeed to the one with three matted locks, the three-headed, the eternal wielder of the trident, the three-eyed, the one who exists in the three times, and the destroyer of Tripura. || 103 ||
Salutation to Caṇḍa, to Muṇḍa, and to the wielder of the staff of the universe;
salutation indeed to the red one, to the smoky-colored one, and to the blue-throated one. || 104 ||
Salutations to the one whose form is Tripura, salutations again and again to the multiformed one;
salutations indeed to Sūrya, the Lord of Sūryā, and the Master of Siddhis. || 105 ||
Therefore, not very far to the north of Aruṇī, there stands the stone of Godhikā, which is entirely white yet black in color. (106)
Know that Śiva is at its western end, and Gayātīrtha is proclaimed to be in its belly, toward the north. 107.
Gayāśiras is at the head according to the measurement of the four divisions;
Rāmagayā is on the side of the head, and Rāmapiṇḍa is to the south.
At the tail is the Mānasa tīrtha, and at the right side is the Mahānadī;
there one should perform a bath according to the prescribed ritual procedure.
To the north of that, O beloved, within the very range of an arrow-shot, is the sacred ford named Pretaśilā; performing a śrāddha there leads one's ancestors to heaven. (110)
By performing a śrāddha at the Mahānadī, one obtains inexhaustible fruit;
likewise, by performing a śrāddha at Akṣayavaṭa, the performer leads his ancestors to the world of Brahmā.
Having bathed at Gayātīrtha, a man is liberated from all sins;
O Maheśānī, at Gayā, even without sesame seeds, one is purified in the Self-born [place]. (112)
A person should also perform the offering of the funeral rice-balls (piṇḍa) and the remaining rites at the western [site] of Vāsudeva, within a distance of eighteen bows.
The northern [lake] is long in shape, five-cornered, and consecrated by the Sage;
a man who performs a śrāddha at Uttaramānasa is not born again.
To the south of Koṭiliṅga is the quadrangular Śiva;
that is indeed Dakṣiṇamānasa, which destroys all sins.
One who performs a śrāddha at Dakṣiṇamānasa leads his ancestors to the world of Brahmā;
when a śrāddha is performed at Mahānadī, he leads his ancestors to the world of Brahmā.
O Goddess, a person faithful to the ancestral rites (śrāddha) at Rāmahrada leads his ancestors to the world of Brahmā;
as it is with the offering of funeral cakes (piṇḍa) at Gayāśiras, so it is at the northern tail-end (uttara-puccha).
One should cause the funeral ball (piṇḍa) to be offered for three days and thus uplift one's entire lineage;
for ancestors, terrified by the fear of hell, long for sons.
"If anyone among you goes to Gayā, he shall deliver us;
[it is] situated seven dhanvantaras to the west of Kāmanātha. (119)
Having beheld the goddess Dīrgheshvarī, who bestows the fruits of all desires,
one rejoices on earth for sixty thousand years like a god.
O Goddess of the gods, one should worship with the seed-syllable of Māyā on the eighth lunar day; one obtains all knowledge and becomes the foremost among the assemblies (or inhabitants). 121.
Then, having gone to the wish-fulfilling tree known as Tintiḍī, one should perform three circumambulations and worship it with this mantra: || 122 ||
Oṃ, salutations to the one of manifest form, who is praised by all the gods, whose nature is the abode of Śiva, and who takes the form of the tamarind tree. || 123 ||
It is praised in all mantras, for rites of desire, for liberation, and in the right-hand path;
likewise, it is used for touching with the left hand and for holding the rosary.
O Goddess, when one who has entered the earth is touched by others within the interval of a year,
one should consecrate a garland and place it in a copper vessel.

Having first sprinkled [the site] with the Gāyatrī mantra, and immediately thereafter with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), one should subsequently perform the oblation with that very same mantra: "HŪṂ, obeisance to Siddhi."
Thereafter, having established [the deity] with scented water, various kinds of fragrant flowers,
and three jars, one should worship with red flowers.
(Having offered an oblation of barley-alkali, one should establish the life-force of the deity.
Then, having brought it, one should touch the rosary and place it in the intermediate spaces. 127.
Having brought it, one should then place the rosary upon a seat at night,
having offered scented sandalwood paste as well as dūrvā grass and unbroken grains of rice.
Furthermore, one should place [the deity] upon the pedestal of the Lord during that night;
[reciting] a hundred, a thousand, ten thousand, and likewise a million [times].
The measure for recitation and fire-offerings is one hundred thousand (lakṣa) or ten million (koṭi);
at the image, it should be eight cubits, and one should perform the recitation on every festival day.
Alternatively, one should also apply three [mantras] there using eight seed-syllables:
"O Mālā! O Mālā! O Mahāmālā! O you who are present everywhere in your own essential form! (131)
The fourfold group has been entrusted to you; therefore, O Māle, be the bestower of success! You are Puṣkarī, the seed-syllable of the Friend (sakhibīja), subtle and likewise endowed with subtlety.
Joined with the power of space (ākāśa-śakti), this five-syllable mantra, known as the Heart, is proclaimed for the sake of accomplishment; it is celebrated as the mantra of the rosary. || 133 ||
One should employ [the mantra] in the acts of grasping, establishing, and worshiping;
having assigned Śiva at the beginning of the recitation, one should recite the hymn of praise at the conclusion of the recitation.
Then one should perform the offering of the sacrificial victim (balidāna) and give away one's own wealth;
one should worship with the root mantra in both direct and reverse order.
With the mantra "Ambe Ambike" and likewise with the Puranic one:
"Victory, O Kāmeśī Cāmuṇḍā! Victory, O remover of spirits! (136)
Victory to you, O omnipresent Goddess, O Kāmeśvarī; homage be unto you!
O you whose form is the universe, auspicious one, pure one, O Virūpākṣī, O three-eyed one! 137.
O you of terrifying form, O Śivā, O Vidyā, O Kāmeśvarī, salutations be to you!
O Mālājapā, O Jayā, O Jamme, O Bhūtākṣi, O Kṣudhitā, O Akṣayā, O Mahāmāyā, O Maheśānī, O Kāmeśvarī, salutations be to you! 138.
O goddess with terrifying eyes, O fearsome one, O goddess who causes the destruction of all beings, O Karālī, O Vikarālī, O Kāmeśvarī, homage be to you! 139.
O Kālī, Karālī, O valiant one, O Kāmeśvarī, beloved of Hara!
O Goddess who wields all weapons [who slays all enemies; who bears all weapons], O Kāmeśvarī, salutations be to you! || 140 ||
O you who illuminate Kāmarūpa, who dwell on Mount Nīla, who crush Śumbha and Niśumbha, O Kāmeśvarī, homage be to you! 141.
O Kāmeśvarī, who resides in Kāmākhyā, who dwells in Kāmarūpa, beloved of Hara!
Grant me desires eternally; O Kāmeśvarī, salutations be unto you. (142)
O Mistress of the Three Worlds, you who were intent on drinking the wine of blood;
O Goddess Kāmeśvarī, salutations be unto you for the slaying of the demon Mahiṣāsura! 143.
O you who are satisfied by goats, O greatly formidable one, O Kāmākhyā, O bestower of happiness!
Victory to you, O fulfiller of desires; O satisfied Kāmeśvarī, salutations be unto you! 144.
If a king who has been deprived of his kingdom, being self-controlled and pure, fasts on the eighth, the ninth, and the fourteenth [lunar days], he becomes the best of men. || 145 ||
Within a year, he shall again obtain a kingdom free from all thorns. || 146 ||
O Goddess, whoever hears this account of your origin with devotion, being liberated from all sins, attains supreme nirvāṇa. || 147 ||

Obeisance to the Goddess Kāmeśvarī, who possesses the splendor of gods and demons, who is restrained within the manifested lotus, and who is intent on the skillful mastery of the abode of Brahmā, the enemy of the gods.
And I bow to you, O Goddess, who consist of the three Vedas. || 148 ||
I bow to her whose forms are manifested as white and black, red and tawny; she in whose hand and skull-bowl the auspicious and inauspicious are envisioned. (149)
O you who have arisen from Kāmarūpa, the ornament of the seat of desire (Kāmapīṭha), the support of the universe, the great illusion—O Kāmeśvarī, salutations be to you! 150.

O Goddess Kāmeśvarī, obeisance be to you, who possess an unmanifest form, who are weary yet continuous, who can assume any form at will, who are accessible through time, and who are the supreme peace.
I bow to her who resides within the interior of the Suṣumnā, who is contemplated as having the form of light;
I am prostrate before the supreme Heroine—O Kāmeśvarī, homage be to you! (152)
O Goddess, whose face is formidable with fangs, adorned with a garland of skulls, who pervades all things and goes everywhere—O Kāmeśvarī, salutations be to you! 153.
At the time of bathing, at dawn, during meals, while cleaning the teeth, and likewise when one is naked, one should not look [at her], nor should one touch her. || 154 ||
On the thirteenth or fourteenth day of the month of Madhu (Caitra), as well as on the day of Vṛṣa (the Bull),
one should never touch the Goddess, and on those days one should avoid seeing her.
One should know that seeing him brings fear and a curse falls upon one's head;
thus, on the eighth day of the bright fortnight of Jyeṣṭha, Kumāra must not be looked upon. 156.
The practitioner, even when accompanied by beautiful maidens, should never touch a woman at night, nor should he ever offer a sacrificial oblation (bali) while touching one. 157.
One should never approach the Great Goddess when she resides in her phallic form (liṅga).
For the Brahmins, there should be offerings of milk, rice-balls, or alternatively, boiled rice with milk (pāyasa). || 158 ||
One should offer him a chewable fruit soaked in ghee and a flower accompanied by ghee;
one should also present milk, milk-rice, or cooked rice. || 159 ||

Rice of the *śāli* variety, or likewise milk-rice with *madhuka*, and sugar-candied balls (*khaṇḍamodaka*)—for kings, animals are indeed prescribed as offerings, and for Vaiśyas, *vrīhi* rice is likewise [prescribed]. (160)
For those of the Śūdra caste, one should offer honey; or else, all animals may be offered—such as a red-beaked bird, a human, or a buffalo.
One should offer a boar, or else a pair of goats, a goat, a yak, and likewise Varuṇa;
furthermore, one should present a ram, a boar, and a monitor lizard. || 162 ||
Ten chowries are surpassed by a single goat; ten goats are praised as being equal to a single tortoise. (163)
Even with a hundred tortoises, a single hare excels;
and a boar excels even thousands of hares. (164)
A buffalo is said to be worth two thousand times a boar;
a rhinoceros excels a wild ox by two thousand. (165)
From a thousand rhinoceroses, however, there is incomparable human fruit;
two thousand humans are praised as being equal to a single red-beaked [bird]. (166)
Two hundred Śoṇatuṇḍas are excelled by one Śvetagrīva;
even a hundred Śvetagrīvas are considered inferior to a single Godhikā. (167)
O Goddess, a hundred lizards, a young boy, and even cattle shall become an offering after six months. (168)
If a black or white goat is more than two years old, it is pure as guggulu; likewise, a jackal known as "red" (śoṇa) is pure. || 169 ||
Likewise, [a dog], as well as a musk deer, a mountain goat, a mouse, a *karāla*, and even a small cat; || 170 ||
The kolila, the kālaviṅka, the rājahaṃsa, and the śārika; the parrot, the vulture, the kākolaka, the peacock, and likewise the citraka. || 171 ||
The horse, the bamboo-backed [bird], the black pigeon, as well as the large dove and likewise the wagtail; || 172 ||
One should diligently avoid both the crane and the heron by offering them oblations; however, one need not deliberate over a woman. 173.
O beloved, no fault arises when [the gift] is given during the month of Mithuna;
one should offer a buffalo in a cremation ground in the presence of Devaka.
He goes to the world of Brahmā and rejoices on earth like Śiva;
and for those who die within the inner sanctum, he attains eternal Brahman.
Even today, O beloved, that Brahman which is seen to the south falls [there];
of this there is no doubt—that Sadāśiva is the giver of knowledge.
By her right ear, a man indeed falls to the ground, even if he is burdened with great sins (mahāpātaka) or joined with minor offenses (upapātaka). || 177 ||
By offering an oblation in the cremation ground, one who is liberated shall go to the abode of Śiva;
whether free from desire or possessed of desire, he indeed casts off his life-breaths there.
Even if he has abandoned his own country, Gaṇeśvara himself attends [to him];
or else, having offered a sacrifice (bali) after acquiring wealth in a foreign land, the king [attends to him]. || 179 ||
One should not, with any effort, employ a perpetrator of a mortal sin, a thief, a fool, a solitary hero, one conquered by women, or a hater of Brahmins.
Whatever gems, pearls, and gold have been offered to the deity do not become *nirmālya* for twelve days; the same applies to the copper vessel.
O Maheśvarī, by the mere offering of a silk cloth, a cotton garment, and sweetmeats along with rice-and-pulse porridge for six months, [the fruit is attained] within half a watch.

Silk cloth is prescribed for three months, and the sacred thread (*yajñasūtra*) is remembered as being for one day; likewise, food should be served while it is still warm, as should the finest rice-milk (*paramānna*). (183)
O Pārvatī, with half a watch (muhūrta) one obtains a head and blood;
O Śāṅkarī, with a watch (yāma) one obtains curds, milk, and clarified butter. 184.
Karavīra for one day and night, as well as bilva leaves, javā, and a garland of bandhūka, [are effective] along with faded garlands (nirmālya) for half a month. 185.
O Maheśānī, by merely offering a garland of Karavīra, Padma, and Bilva flowers, along with betel leaf, for half a month, [the desired fruit is attained]. || 186 ||
Dates, jackfruit, grapes, citron, and young shoots;
plantains, oranges, and likewise rose-apple fruits. || 187 ||
One should diligently offer the śālūka and madhuka, as well as the bilva fruit, the pomegranate, the jayantī, and likewise the karkatī. (188)
Trapusa, vārtākī, and those things that bring pleasure to the Goddess;
likewise, O beloved, one should not offer flower remains (nirmālya), nor pomegranate, nor bilva fruit.
One should diligently employ the *saugandhika* and the plantain;
one should offer the plantain, the citron, milk, and ripe fruit. (190)
Kandupakva, kaśeru, and jambūbāla are pleasing;
likewise, ginger, salt, jīvaka, and long pepper [are beneficial]. (191)
The *jātī* bud, the *tinduka*, and the great fruit most dear to the Goddess; the fruit of the *rāmarambhā*, the flower, and the face heated by smoke. (192)
A mortal should not offer the seed of the blue lotus to Mahādevī; he should avoid grains harvested in Śrāvaṇa and those that have been double-boiled. 193.
One should offer a golden-colored coconut and a coconut from the left side to Mahādevī; its water, in particular, [should be offered]. (194)
One should avoid the coconut and the bhāṇḍīra fruit at rites for the gods or at a śrāddha; likewise, one should avoid the ripe fruit of the bakula and the fruit of the lotus.
One should employ them for the Great Goddess, and one shall obtain the fruit of the Cāndrāyaṇa vow.
Listen, O Goddess, I shall explain the chapter on flowers in brief. (196)
With flowers produced in their proper season, such as mallikā and jāti blossoms, as well as white and red flowers, and pale blue lotuses; 197.
With *kiṃśuka*, *tagara*, *javā*, *kanaka*, and *campaka* flowers; with *kiṃśuka*, *tagara*, *vakula*, and *mandāra* flowers as well. (198)
And with [flowers] joined with saffron and musk, those originating from the bandhūka and agastya, with madana and sindhuvāra flowers, and with the very tender sprouts of dūrvā grass. (199)
Whoever offers thousands of Tulasī leaves, very tender Bilva leaves, Karavīra flowers, and Māhī [or Kuṇḍa] flowers,
having attained all desired objects, is glorified in the world of the Goddess. || 200 ||
One should never offer flowers growing in the forest without first discarding two thousand karavīra flowers and two thousand lotuses.
Indeed, even when they exert themselves, the gods are unable to draw out even a single flower, because ten yakṣas guard each one. || 202 ||
Likewise, five yakṣa maidens are perfectly arrayed on all sides;
having taken flowers from them, one should offer them to the gods and the ancestors as well.
One should construct it; having constructed a flower-house there, one offers it to her who is called Kāmā.
O Śāṅkarī, by offering that flower-house above [the image of] Kāmā, one attains desires in this world and is glorified in the world of Durgā. (204)
Whoever worships the consort of Śaṅkara with *karavīra* flowers, or with those of the same species (*sajāti*),
having obtained the fruit of the Agniṣṭoma sacrifice, is glorified in the world of the Sun. || 205 ||
Having worshipped Caṇḍikā with devotion using a garland of lotuses,
a man attains the fruit of the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice and is glorified in the world of the Sun.
By offering *vaka* flowers of their own kind, as well as by the recitation of the *Rudra* hymns (*rudrajapa*), one obtains the fruit of the *Vājapeya* sacrifice; it is not otherwise. || 207 ||
Of all flowers, the blue lotus is the most excellent;
he who offers a garland made of a thousand blue lotuses— || 208 ||
O Goddess, hear now the fruit of his merit for having worshipped Durgā according to the prescribed rites:
for thousands of crores of years and hundreds of crores of years.
Having become an attendant of the Goddess, he is glorified in the world of Rudra;
as is one who [offers] that which arises from curved grain, as well as that which arises from fine grain. || 210 ||
And likewise, that which arises from royal grain and that which arises from red grain.
Unhusked rice is recommended in a quantity of seven, eight, or nine grains.
One should offer [the food] together with dūrvā sprouts to the Blessed Lady;
on the eighth or the ninth lunar day, he shall obtain the fruit of an Aśvamedha sacrifice.
Having offered fragrant unguents, one obtains the fruit of the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice;
having anointed [the image] with saffron and offering the arghya, one obtains the fruit of giving a thousand cows. || 213 ||
One who worships Durgā, who has been anointed with sandalwood, agallochum, camphor, white flowers, and saffron, shall obtain the fruit of the Vahniṣṭoma sacrifice.
The leaf of the neem tree, the madhuka flower, the leaf of the tamāla and the āmalakī, the kahlāra lily, the tulasī, and the lotus—the most excellent of flowers. || 215 ||
O Śāṅkarī, this [flower] does not become stale, nor does any other that is in bud; and even if it is cut or broken, the jasmine flower does not become defiled.
The lotus, the dūrvā sprout, and the tulasī leaf do not become stale;
nor does that flower [become stale], O Śāṅkarī, when it is together with tulasī, O Śāṅkarī. (217)
One should not worship with *jhiṇṭī* flowers, nor with yellow *tagara*, nor with white or black *vijaya*. || 218 ||
One should recite the mantra three hundred thousand times for the sake of accomplishing the preliminary rite (puraścaraṇa);
one should also perform the ritual placement (nyāsa), libation (tarpaṇa), fire-oblation (homa), and eight rows [of offerings].
O Maheśānī, one who has conquered the senses shall obtain the fruit of the Agniṣṭoma sacrifice by worshipping the Supreme Goddess on the eighth or ninth day of the bright fortnight.
O my beloved, he who worships me three times a day on the fourteenth lunar day goes to the supreme abode where the Goddess resides.
Having played for a long time, he becomes a king upon the earth by means of bathing,
fasting, observances, worship, keeping vigil, and purification.
He who worships Kāmeśī at all times and in all places, having ascended a most excellent celestial chariot adorned with rows of banners, [shall proceed]. || 223 ||
A person goes to the world of Brahmā and rejoices there for eternal years,
having always been devoted to devotion through various forms of service and by means of extensive displays of wealth.
One should constantly worship Durgā with the desire for the fruit of great merit, O beloved, especially during the solstices, the equinoxes, and at the commencement of the six aśītis.
O Goddess, one obtains that same fruit on the ninth day of the month of Kārttika which is gained by worshipping Caṇḍikā according to the prescribed rites for four months.
Listen to the meritorious fruit of him who worships the Goddess Maheśvarī on the ninth day of the bright fortnight in the month of Āśvayuja. || 227 ||
One obtains the fruit of a thousand horse-sacrifices and a hundred Vājapeya sacrifices; one should reflect that nothing else need be sought here. (228)
To the north of Hanumān, at a distance of twenty-one dhanus,
is the place named Muktimaṇḍapikā, which is extremely difficult to attain.
One should recite [the mantra] while remaining established therein and shall attain the supreme goal;
then, with palms joined in reverence, one should propitiate the Goddess by forming the mudrā. || 230 ||
Salutations to you, O Sovereign of all goddesses, who removes the fear of devotees;
O Supreme Goddess, protect me who am submerged in the ocean of worldly existence. 231.
Having thus propitiated that goddess and prostrated before her like a staff,
one should then worship the Guru with devotion using flowers, perfumes, and ointments.
p. 258) One should feed a young maiden there and cause a vigil to be kept at night;
one should also have the majesty of the Great Goddess recited and songs performed. || 233 ||
Meditating and offering praise to the supreme goddess, the wise man should impel the Night;
he should do so month after month, especially on the eighth and fourteenth lunar days.
At the time of *godhūli*, one should lead the Goddess to the temple of Kāmeśvara,
having seen her there at some point either in a chariot or in a palanquin.
Completely liberated from all sins, he is glorified in the world of the Goddess;
for he who, having led [the devotee] to the Pavilion of Liberation, worships the Consort of Śaṅkara.
One obtains the merit that is found at Daśāśvamedha; of this there is no doubt.
One should not undertake the journey by day, nor by night, nor during the dead of night.
On the seventh day of the autumn season, O Maheśānī, one should lead [the image] to the south of the city during the evening; thus one shall obtain the fruit of all sacrifices. || 238 ||
Having worshipped on the eighth day, whoever bathes the Goddess in flowing water on the ninth day is not defiled by that day.
Then, by touching the Goddess upon the chariot, no sorrow arises on earth;
he who carries the Goddess upon his shoulder earns the merit of an Ashvamedha sacrifice at every step.
Therefore, having exerted effort, one should have a large palanquin constructed;
meanwhile, for the sake of the Goddess's bath, [one should prepare] the mountain in that same manner. || 241 ||
One should behold the god Kāmeśvara situated on the ground-pīṭha;
to its north is the Lake of Desire (Kāmasaras), measuring one cubit in extent. || 242 ||
There, having recited the Kāmāsava mantra at the Kāmāsana and bathed, one shall obtain all desires.
A man who, having bathed in the Kāmakuṇḍa, beholds the Lord Kāma, [shall likewise attain his wishes]. || 243 ||
He shall not return again; he is glorified in the world of Rudra [as one] with four arms, holding a trident, a khaṭvāṅga staff, and granting the boons of protection and fearlessness. (244)
One should worship the God seated upon a lotus, who destroys all sins;
one should fill [the vessel] and propitiate him by means of the Dakṣiṇāmūrti yantra. || 245 ||
Oṃ, salutations to Śiva, who is that which is beyond the night [of ignorance]; salutations to Śiva, who is worshipped by Śivā;
salutations to you, who are devoted to compassion; salutations to the one who has no abode within the house of Māyā. || 246 ||
Homage be to Śoṣa, the Great Darkness; homage to the one worthy of refuge, the protector of those who have come for shelter; homage to the Gaṇa!
Homage be to you, the follower of the formidable Gaṇas; homage be to the creator of various worlds and all else! || 247 ||
Having snapped [the flowers], one should worship with ghee, honey, perfumes, and lamps,
as well as with gold, bilva leaves, and red rudrākṣa beads.
On the thirteenth day of the bright fortnight in the month of Caitra, one should worship the Lord Kāma with shouts of victory, hymns of praise, and various offerings of food.
Those who behold the best of gods go to the supreme state;
on the eighth lunar day, during the portion of the night, one should lead [the deity] to the abode of Kāmeśvarī.
There, one should especially worship the God together with the Goddess;
from that, one obtains the fruit of the Agniṣṭoma sacrifice—of this there is no doubt. || 251 ||
One obtains the fruit from the mere sight [of her], for by seeing Kāmeśvarī thereafter, whatever one prays for in that place, that very thing is attained; of this there is no doubt. (252)
And at the watch of Kambala, where the goddess is united with the god—O auspicious one, in the space between Dhanu and Aṇṭā, one should worship the supreme Koṭīśvarī. (253)
And having seen her, if one who desires a son should never touch the goddess, he is liberated from all sins and is glorified in the world of Rudra. || 254 ||

Thus ends the seventh chapter, and [begins] the eighth chapter, in the second part of the section on Kāmarūpa within the *Yoginītantra*, the great king of tantras consisting of twenty-two thousand verses.
The Blessed One said:
"Therefore, O Goddess, on this very day,
one should set out for the celestial river known as Lokacakṣus, which removes all sins and is auspicious."
To the south of the Goddess, at a distance of two arrow-shots, three streams are seen there; the middle stream is Sarasvatī.
To the south is the stream of Varuṇā, and to the north is the Yamunā;
one who has performed his ablutions in the Yamunā is liberated from terrible sin.
Having performed his ablutions at the Sarasvatī, one is glorified in the world of Viṣṇu;
having performed his ablutions at the Varuṇā, one attains unsurpassed liberation.
Where the confluence of three streams is seen as infinite,
that goddess is the Ākāśagaṅgā, the destroyer of great sins.
Salutations to the goddess who possesses a thousand eyes, who destroys the bonds of worldly existence;
O auspicious Jāhnavī, dwelling upon the blue mountain, take away my sin.

Having performed his ablutions with this [mantra], he should worship her with the seed-syllable of sound (śabda-bīja), situated not too far from her in the direction of the quarter of Kubera (the north). (7)
Vāsudeva is proclaimed to be white in form and beautiful in appearance;
one should worship his liṅga with the god of love (Kāma) using perfumes and other offerings, as well as milk-rice (pāyasa).
On the twelfth day of the month of Kārttika, by beholding [the deity], one attains liberation;
by keeping a vigil here at night, one is released from all sins.
And situated exactly four dhanvantaras to the south of the Gaṅgā,
the Blessed One sports with hosts of women in the great cremation ground.
There, the gods along with the Gandharvas, and the sages together with the Cāraṇas,
constantly come with great reverence for the purpose of propitiating the Lord.
There, having propitiated Mahādeva, the Lord of the Gaṇas, with hearts purified by devotion,
he indeed attained the status of a leader of the Gaṇas, which is difficult even for the gods to obtain.
Even today, a great wonder is seen there every day:
having cast down human bones, Prajāpati is reduced to ashes.
Having gone there, the man who worships Mahādeva attains the divine world after his body has perished; of this there is no doubt.
Especially on the fourteenth day of the bright fortnight in the month of Kārttika,
one should worship there the Lord of Gods, the Grandfather (Brahmā), who is dear to all.
To that extent, through devotion, one becomes a follower of Rudra among them all;
and therein, the northern limb of Hara is seen as a third part, according to the sacred tradition.
The western limb is Heruka, the imperishable one in the form of Viṣṇu;
Bhairava is the southern portion, and he is designated as Tripura. (17)
By worshipping the Supreme Lord with the *prāsāda* mantra, one obtains the supreme fruit of the horse sacrifice (*vājimedha*). || 18 ||
A devoted person should worship with the three sacrificial pits (tri-kuṇḍa) beginning with the Kulādi;
he attains the Great Vidyā from the mandala—of this there is no doubt. (19)
By means of the twelve-syllable mantra, one attains Heruka in the form of Vāsudeva;
becoming a lord of all worlds, he passes away and is born into a superior caste.
One should worship the Supreme Goddess with blood, meat, and wine;
however, one should never offer tortoise flesh at night.

One should carefully avoid the *cāmara*, the *madgura*, and the fish. Having eaten *ciñcā* or *nīlaśaiva* by mistake, or having touched a cremation ground (*śmaśāna*) or oil-cake (*piṇyāka*), one should know that it brings great terror; it bestows a curse.
O beloved Kāmeśvarī, one should not touch the leafy vegetable (śāka) against the left heart for seven nights.

By performing three *cāndrāyaṇa* penances, purification will then occur. O Goddess, having eaten lotus, turmeric, or vegetables grown from cow-dung out of negligence, one should likewise swiftly perform this same vow. (24)
One should avoid from afar the jujube mixed with sugar, as well as the daṇḍa-śāka vegetable, and the mountain-grown pumpkin (kūṣmāṇḍa). || 25 ||
Especially on the eighth, the ninth, and the thirteenth [lunar days],
[the rite should be performed] with twenty-one threads and likewise with those tripled.
p. 263) By the single application of the term "consisting of the three qualities" (triguṇa), thirty [units] are considered for the position [of the garland].
In the absence of a silk thread from a treasury, one should place a red [thread]. || 27 ||
One should show the garland with the other hand and not touch it with the left hand;
this applies likewise to the forest-dweller, the ascetic, and the student of sacred knowledge, O beloved. (28)
O beloved, during the recitation of the Viṣṇu-mantra, as well as that of the mantra itself,
one should then hold it in the left hand, O beloved, between the seven seed-syllables.
O fair-faced one, he should mutter [the mantra] with his right hand for each seed-syllable:
"Homage to Tintiḍīkā, the giver of boons, who has arrived at the door of the house. (30)
One is liberated from a thousand sins like a snake shedding its worn-out skin;
[this applies] from the back of Kāmeśvara as far as Siddheśvara is situated. || 31 ||
And in the section contained therein, Chāyārudra is proclaimed;
like that of a living being, his shadow never leaves him, and here the casting off of the body as well as the shadow is ordained.
O fair-faced one, he who performs the rite of releasing a bull in that sacred field obtains the merit of a hundred Agniṣṭoma sacrifices; of this there is no doubt. || 33 ||
O Maheśānī, in the month of Māgha, at Chāyārudra, by performing the offering of rice-balls (piṇḍa) without sesame seeds, one becomes free from debt to one's mothers.
Then, having gone to the Vindhya mountain, there is a stone that is black and red;
she is known as Vindhyeśī, and one should worship her with lotuses and other offerings.
O Parameśvarī, O beloved Pārvatī, she should be worshipped with the mantra of Kāmeśvarī;
the fruit that one obtains there by the gift of ten thousand cows, O dear one, [is obtained here]. (36)
One truly obtains that fruit by beholding the Goddess of Vindhya;
she is located in the north-eastern region of that place, at a distance of more than a hundred arrow-shots.
The stone known as Suradīrghikā, which serves as a mark for the Ākāśagaṅgā, is situated slightly to the south of it and stands somewhat elevated. (38)
She who is celebrated as Lalitā and Kāntā, the remover of the sin of killing a Brahmin;
at the root is the Aśvattha tree in the form of Nandin, and the stone has the shape of a tortoise.
A man, having seen that deity, never again sees him due to his sins.
There, within the womb, is a *liṅga* measuring four cubits;
it has the form of a lamp for the path and is the destroyer of all evil. (40)
Having seen the god Vyāseśvara there, a man removes his sin;
having bathed at Vyāsatīrtha, he who worships Lalitā [attains the same]. (41)
One obtains the great fruit of a thousand horse-sacrifices at Viṃśaddhanvantara, which is marked by the Saira [and] distinguished by Vanadāsa in the east. || 42 ||
The leaf has the shape of a lotus petal and is marked with resin;
at its base resides the Goddess in the form of a tall elephant.
By the mere worship of her, one is not tainted by the defects of the planets;
and by touching the tree situated there, a barren woman becomes a bearer of offspring. (44)
A man with a severed hand shall obtain gold [or a jewel], and at the proper time, a man with joined hands shall obtain a nāga; it is established not too far to the east of the pomegranate tree. (45)
One should worship that god Bhuvaneśvara within a cavity measuring nine cubits using the Kāma-bīja; such a man becomes victorious. || 46 ||
To the north-west of that, in the auspicious hermitage of Agastya,
one should worship the Lord Gadādhara there with flowers and other offerings.
Not far from the Lord, there is a white and radiant stone;
one should worship that great liṅga, Jalpīśa, while reciting [the mantra]. 48.
O my beloved, he who bathes according to the prescribed rite during the Saubhāgya festival and worships Jalpīśa shall obtain the fruit of the Agniṣṭoma sacrifice.
To its west, on the twenty-first portion of the ground, Sadāśiva resides, marked by the insignia of the Lord of the Pātāla realm.
Having bowed with devotion to that deity at the sacred site of Kālahastaka on the earth, a person is never born again anywhere.
On the delightful Govinda mountain, one should recognize that white-colored stone as Govinda himself and worship it on the day of Hari.
To its east, at a distance of nine dhanus, there is a stone resembling the color of blood;
it is known as Śaraśeṇī, which destroys great sins.
On the lofty Śivācala mountain, there is the supreme Śivā known as Prakara;
by worshipping her with diligent effort, one shall attain great prosperity. || 54 ||
To the north of the Vindhya mountain, at a distance of nine arrow-shots, Mahālakṣmī resides; there one should worship her with white flowers. (54)
O Maheśānī, one should perform a bath at Śrīkuṇḍa on Śrīparvata;
having bathed in the Kuṇḍa named Dhruva on the full moon day of the month of Āśvina.

Having seen [the deity], one should worship him with devotion; he shall become a lord of the earth. Having gone to the hermitage of Gautama and having worshipped the bull-bannered Lord (Śiva), [one attains the same]. || 56 ||
A person shall not go to hell, and there shall be the destruction of their sins,
as far as from the west to the north, reaching as far as Dakṣiṇamānasa.
O Śāṅkarī, having gone to that field situated within it, not very far away, and having worshipped there, one shall attain the world of Brahmā. || 58 ||
Right there on the shore of that very lake is the unsurpassed Haṃsatīrtha;
by worshipping the Twelve Ādityas there, one shall attain supreme radiance.
Having worshipped Revanta, one then attains the unsurpassed goal;
by honoring Indra, one obtains great sovereignty and the good fortune of Gaurī.
By worshipping Puruṣottama, one obtains all desires;
by worshipping Nārāyaṇa, one becomes a lord of men.
Having seen and bowed to Nārasiṃha, one shall be victorious in battle;
and having worshipped Varāha, one shall obtain the sovereignty of the earth.
Having worshipped Somanātha, one is glorified in the world of Rudra.
That stream which belongs to Pāṇḍukūṭa is the river Narmadā.
Having bathed in it on the fourteenth day, one obtains the merit of a horse sacrifice;
it is the source that has issued forth, situated between Śiva and Viṣṇu.
O Supreme Goddess, that stream between the hips and the breasts should be known as the Great River, which destroys all sins. 65.
That stream named Maṅgalā brings about all auspiciousness;
and that stream which is at the edge of Bilvaśrīparvata is Sarasvatī. (66)
By drinking its clear water, one becomes the foremost among poets;
and that which is the stream of Mataṅga is proclaimed to be the Narmadā, without a doubt. (67)
The stream of Kāmakuṇḍa is called the Kāmagaṅgā;
and the stream of Kāmākhyā is celebrated as the Gaṅgā. || 68 ||
The stream of Nandikuṇḍa should be known as Madhusravā,
and the stream of Kāmadhenu should be understood as Sudharmiṇī.
The stream of Padmaśaila is known as Gaṅgā-Urvaśī;
the stream of Nīlakuṇḍa is celebrated as Subhadrā. || 70 ||
The stream of Vyāsakuṇḍa is known as Candrabhāgā;
the stream of Śakraśaila is called Urvaśī. (71)
The stream from the Somakuṇḍa is the river Vaitaraṇī,
and the stream from Yamaśaila is known as the Godāvarī.
Having bathed in the stream of Bhaṇḍīśa, drunk its water, and bowed down,
one obtains the supreme fruit of even a hundred Agniṣṭoma sacrifices.
Then, having gone to Dharmāraṇya and bathed in the beloved Rāmahrada, one should behold the Koṭiliṅga; thereby, one shall attain an immortal body.
O beloved, he who beholds Koṭiliṅga, located thirty dhanvantaras to the north of Kāma, shall obtain the fruit of the Vājapeya sacrifice. (75)
Salutations to you, the eternal one who inflicts punishment upon the vital breaths, and to the Red One;
salutations to the thousand-headed one, and let there be salutation to you, the one with ten million forms.
Salutations always to the Lord of the Mountain, and to him who is fond of mountains and trees;
salutations to the Sovereign of Sacrifice, O Koṭiliṅga, may there be salutations unto you.
Having worshipped with this [mantra], one should worship further with hibiscus flowers;
having offered milk-rice as an oblation, and having praised and recited [the mantra], one should dismiss [the deity]. || 78 ||
To its right is the rock joined to the side;
there is that Vetāla Mahādeva, and on the left is Viṣṇu Dvikarṇaka.

Having taken up a handful of flowers, one should recite the mantra with undistracted mind for the sake of dharma, desire, wealth, and liberation, as well as for the purpose of speaking harsh words. (80)
Salutations again and again to Sāṃkhya, the foremost of the Sāṃkhyas, and to Vetāla;
to him who has a black antelope skin as an upper garment and who wears yellow robes;
you alone are Brahmā, O Lord of the Universe, O you whose form is Brahman—salutations be to you! 81.
Standing before it, having gone out from the Brahma-yoni while reciting the mantra that is difficult for others to withstand,
he who enters the Brahma-yoni shall not enter a womb again. 82.
One shall not go to the womb of an animal, but shall enter the station of Brahmā;
indeed, in the land beloved by Śiva, which blocks the path to liberation [for others], [one attains it]. 83.
"O Lord of the gods of gods, be gracious and protect me from this peril of birth!
Having emerged from the womb of Brahmā, he should worship Gaṇeśa at the doorway.
The practitioner [should fashion] a large body carved from stone with this mantra:
"Homage to the excellent Lambodara, the bestower of desired boons to the gods! (85)
O Lord, O Protector named Akhila, I bow to you;
[save me from the peril of the womb]. Then one should go upon the path of liberation, if one is facing Śakra as if with a face turned toward him. (86)
On the left and right sides are the two ages, the Tretā and the Dvāpara, while above is the Kṛta age; on the sides are the Tretā and the Dvāpara, born of Truth.
The Liṅga situated in the mouth of Bali is named Gupta-Bhuvaneśvara;
by bowing to it with devotion, a person shall attain the state of the Lord.
Having paid homage to the Four Yugas and touched the god Kapardin,
one is not born again in a womb and is not defiled by the defects of the ages.
For he is indeed the lord of the ages, who assumes the very nature of the world's births;
O Supreme Lord, protect me from whatever sin has been committed in that age! 90.

O Lord of men, may that sin born of the earth which was committed in the Kṛta age, in the Tretā age, or in the Yuga of the Lord of the Age (Śiva), be dispelled by you who are fully endowed with the accumulation of merit. 91.
O You whose essence is the means of truth, O You who are known as Truth and consist of Nara and Nārāyaṇa, O Satyadharma, the cause of the Kṛta age and the others, homage be to You! 92.
O Lord of the powerful wheel of the Yugas, whose command prevails at the beginning of the victory [of the aeon], I bow to you constantly with devotion; O remover of sin, salutations be unto you! 93.
One should worship Kapardin with the five-syllable mantra;
that man shall obtain the fruit of the Rājasūya and Aśvamedha sacrifices. (94)
Then, having seen the Kāmadhenu, one shall obtain all desires;
after worshipping her and paying homage, one should then feed the Brāhmaṇas.
Salutations to you, O daughter of Surabhi; O you who fulfill desires and move at will!
May that Goddess, in the form of a cow, dispel my sin. (96)
And it was declared: "The fruit which is proclaimed to result from the gift of a man's weight in gold at Puṣkara and Kurukṣetra when the sun is eclipsed by Rāhu," || 97 ||
One obtains that same fruit by beholding the Kāmadhenu;
one should give a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to the preceptor and offer the respectful water-offering (arghya) to Savitṛ.
Having performed the rite of peace (*śānti*), O Goddess, one should then practice meditation with undistracted mind;
having arisen and gazed at the sun, O Beloved, one should recite the two mantras. (99)
Salutation be to Kālī, to Girijā; salutation be to you, O Kāmeśvarī!
Salutation be to the Goddess born of the Mountain; salutation! 100.
Salutation be to Gaurī, the ender of afflictions;
this is the truth, O Lord of the Gods, regarding her playful power.
Salutations again and again to Vyāsa and others who are devoted to sacred sites, even though they are themselves beyond the need for such sites.
Salutations again and again to the elephants and to the Kṣatriyas who are their protectors. || 101 ||
O Poṇḍravighna, salutations be unto you; salutations to you, O Kāmabhairava!
Salutations to you, O Dakṣiṇāmūrti; salutations be unto you, O Daṇḍapāṇi! || 102 ||
Going to a sacred ford, fasting, faith in the act of recitation,
and the conviction that "I shall perform it"— these are the characteristics of success.
The Illustrious Goddess said:
"If a man who constantly commits sinful deeds in this sacred field—even terrible sins such as the drinking of liquor—will he attain liberation? (104)
Īśvara said:
A man who, though situated in a holy field, is always devoted to sinful acts, shall enter a womb and dwell there for ten thousand years. (Or he shall wander [through various births]). 105.
In that very city he shall obtain the supreme state, and there knowledge is perfected for the virtuous one;
he too shall go to liberation—this is my secret, O beloved. (106)
The Lauhitya is easily accessible elsewhere, but it is difficult to find at five locations:
at the Tīrtha of Agastya, at Maṇikarṇa, and likewise at the Hrada.
In the Moon-Pond (Candrakuṇḍa) of the state beyond rebirth, five locations are proclaimed;
specifically by means of unbroken [grains], there are hundreds and thousands of paths.
There is no distinction whatsoever between those who stand outside the field and those who are empty;
[these include] the one called Kāla, Raṇabhadra, and the very powerful Saurabha.
Vetāla and Vikaṇṭaka—these are the Gaṇas stationed in the east; as well as Ekajaṅgha, Anala, and Kardamāliptavigraha. || 109 ||
Ghaṇṭākarṇa and [the one] above him are stationed on the right side;
Balanāśa and Bhīṣaṇa are established in the west.
The fifth is Lohitākṣa, and Nandana is likewise considered [the sixth];
Keśava and Cakrapāṇi are the northern hosts of Dhanada.
Madhura, Madhuka, and Jayanta, who is fond of honey—these three, stationed as Kāmeśvarīs, protect [the world] without distinction. (112)
Gaṇeśa, Kāladaṇḍa, Vikarṇa,
and Kapidhvaja guard the entire entrance, while Hara himself guards the pavilion.
Kandarpa, Makaranda, Prabala, Gadadhara, Soma, and Vipula— these are the Gaṇas stationed at Aśvatīrtha.
A hundred thousand yakṣiṇīs guard the gateway to liberation. || 114 ||
And with ten thousand [attendants], he guards the inner apartments;
thereafter, he protects Kubjatīrtha with eighteen thousand.
Indeed, obstacles dwell at sacred fords, in the construction of temples, especially in the undertaking of dharma, and at the commencement of vows and sacrifices.
One should first worship them with offerings such as sweetmeats (modaka) and the like;
otherwise, an obstacle arises—know this from me, O beloved. (117)
Moreover, O beloved, there are indeed other obstacles residing within the body that destroy knowledge; hear about them from me. 119.
O Goddess, some are obstructive while others are conducive; they may be near or far, at a distance of a thousand or even a hundred thousand [yojanas]. (119)
Furthermore, recollecting past sins and even indolence are defects;
they cause grief, delusion, old age, disease, and the loss of youth and wealth. (120)
Quarreling with his wife, facing famine and domestic distress, yet filled with various vows and thinking in his mind, "I am a righteous man. (121)
But for one who has incurred grief on account of dharma, though it be a minor offense, [the remedy is] a leaf of the Tulasī tree, as well as the fruit of the Dhātrī tree. || 122 ||
A fragment of a Śālagrāma stone, likewise an image made of wood, a human being, a Brāhmaṇa, and a self-manifested (svayambhū) circular Śiva-liṅga. (123)
The distinction between a conch and a snail, the origin of the flesh of a rhinoceros,
the human-like perception toward one's guru, and likewise the water in the waters of a sacred ford—
upon seeing all this, everything indeed becomes so, as does the water born of the sacred fords. || 124 ||
Whether it be the Ganges in the form of a river or a sacred field as the ground—these obstacles arise again and again. (125)
The mind alone always prevails; the mind alone is the cause here.
The mind alone is the cause of bondage and liberation for human beings.
That [mind] is fixed upon it, that has become its supreme [object], and that is the primary cause of suffering;
the mind, when corrupted within, cannot be restrained by bathing at sacred fords.
Whoever recites this or even hears it shall attain devotion and liberation;
one desiring a son obtains a son, and one desiring fame attains fame. (128)
One seeking knowledge obtains knowledge; one seeking victory obtains victory;
and one shall attain purification from sins such as the killing of a Brahmin.
Even a barren woman obtains a son, and a maiden finds a virtuous husband;
one seeking liberation attains liberation, and one seeking enjoyment obtains enjoyment; one desiring poetic skill gains the power of poetry, and even the worthless attains the essence. (130)
One who seeks knowledge attains knowledge that destroys all saṃsāra;
this is the auspicious and blessed Tantra of the Yoginīs. 131.
There shall be no untimely death for him who recites even a single verse;
by reciting even half a verse of this, the destruction of malevolent planets shall occur. (132)
Thus ends the eighth chapter [and begins the ninth] in the second part of the section on Kāmarūpa, within the *Yoginītantra*, the great king of tantras in twenty-two thousand verses.
The Blessed Lord said: Listen, O Goddess, I shall proclaim that which is stainless and rare upon earth;
I have created a hundred and eight auspicious Liṅgas equal to Harikṣetra.
The sacred field of Viṣṇupushkaraka is endowed with one hundred and eight holy fords;
it is crowded with joyful and well-nourished people, and filled with men and women.
Abounding in hosts of learned men, endowed with wealth, grain, and other riches,
it was delightful before the houses and adorned with courtyards upon the earth.
It was strewn with various clusters of jewels, adorned with various gems, crowded with various archways, and beautifully decorated with streets. || 4 ||
It was adorned with white palaces resembling royal swans,
yet it was constantly washed by waters as if it were an impure vessel for liquor.
If he dwells for long in a cave on a mountain peak,
or if he dwells in the three regions [holding the triple staff or wearing the covering of ashes].
And at a distance from its side. || 6 ||
If one recites the Purāṇa, which contains the essential truth of the Vedic doctrine, yet the heart is impure, all of this is in contradiction—especially so. (7)
Neither sacred fords, nor gifts, nor vows,
nor stages of life can save one whose intention is corrupt, whose delight is in evil, and whose senses have lost their clarity.
Having brought the senses under control, wherever a man may dwell,
that place for him is Kurukṣetra, Prayāga, Puṣkara, and Gayā.
One should not transgress the laws of drinking, nor should one transgress the laws of the country;
whatever custom prevails on a particular seat, that custom is recorded as the prescribed rule.
O lady of excellent complexion, in Oḍra, at the sacred field of Puruṣottama and at the Pīṭha, one should not defile food; there, a Brāhmaṇa must subsist by it as his livelihood.
In that case, the defect of touching or not touching the womb (the marriage bed) and the defect of drinking [wine] are not taken into account;
nor is the reversal of marriage orders, such as the elder brother marrying after the younger, considered a fault.
Sleeping upon Śeṣa, conversing with women in secret, and dwelling together with women—
O Maheśānī, at the Jālandhara stone-tīrtha, one should not defile oneself with fish or meat.
One should avoid eating fish and meat. || 13 ||
The offering of sandals and their purification, bright buttermilk, and the condemned [food];
the full twilight according to one's own dharma—therein the law of time (death) does not exist. || 14 ||
In Siddhakṣetra, the seat (pīṭha) of all yoginīs, the Dharma is considered to be that born of the Kirātas;
in Kāmarūpa, O Dear One, there is neither renunciation nor the long vow. 15.
O Goddess, one should not abandon the vow of celibacy while still possessed of worldly desires, nor should one resort to the duties of women through the sin of social contact. (16)
One who always eats betel-leaf should not look upon the private parts of women; nor should one eat the flesh of swans, pigeons, tortoises, or boars. (17)
By abandoning [his duties] in Kāmarūpa, a miserable rebirth may occur for him;
he becomes one of base conduct, eating all things and selling all things in Soma.
There the women are always contented, and there the king is highly meritorious;
in Kolvapīṭha, one should follow the duties of the *kola* caste as prescribed for one's own birth.
Through the investigation of dharma and adharma, he perceived his own form and its defining characteristics; he was a great lord, a yogi, a knower of Brahman, and possessed of supreme intelligence.
The vast drinking-hall at Śrīhaṭṭa and the preparation of food—
this which you have just asked has all been fully explained.
It must not be given to one who is not a disciple, nor to one who reviles the gods or Brahmins;
it must not be given to a slanderer, nor to one who is devoid of devotion to the Vedas. || 22 ||
It should be given to one endowed with devotion and devoted to his own duty;
it is adorned with various beautiful palaces— blue, red,
and white— and protected by multitudes of weapons and embellished with moats.
With white, red, yellow, black, and other colors as well. || 24 ||
Adorned with smoky breezes, fumes, and banners,
it was a place of constant festival, full of joy, and resounding with the sounds of various musical instruments.
Adorned with lutes, flutes, and drums, as well as with slings, it was graced by divine temples embellished with walls and gardens. (26)
Adorned on all sides with offerings arranged in various ways, slender-waisted women were seen there, filled with joy. (27)
With their necks adorned with garlands of flowers, their eyes as broad as lotus petals, their pairs of breasts full and elevated, and their faces like the full moon; || 28 ||
They were firm in nature, possessed beautiful cheeks, and resounded with the tinkling of waist-bands and anklets;
they had well-formed, lovely hips and eyes reaching as far as their ears.
And there were other various reservoirs adorned with hundreds of lotus ponds,
as well as charming lakes with abundant waters.
With white water-lilies, lotuses, and beautiful blue lotuses;
with kadamba trees, ruddy geese, and likewise water-fowls. || 31 ||
It was filled with flocks of *kāraṇḍava* ducks, swans, and other water-birds,
as well as various kinds of trees and diverse sounds.
Adorned and endowed with various other reservoirs of water, the Lord Janārdana himself resides there as Hayagrīva. (33)
Whatever sacred fords, rivers, lakes, lotus ponds, tanks, wells, pools, and oceans exist upon the earth— || 34 ||
Having previously collected waters from each of them individually,
Rudra, together with the hosts of Soma, acted for the sake of the welfare of all the worlds.

"In that field, O fair-faced one, he established a sacred ford named Apunarbhava; because [he attained] non-rebirth there together with those who were full of desire, it is therefore remembered as Apunarbhava.
And in this vast field, O my beloved, during the month of Māgha—"
He who performs a pilgrimage there, being pure in soul and having conquered his senses, [attains purification]. || 36 ||
Having bathed in the lake according to the prescribed rules, he should then, endowed with faith,
offer libations to the gods, the sages, human beings, and the ancestors.
Having bathed there according to the rules with water mixed with sesame seeds, following the prescribed method for the name and lineage, he shall obtain the fruit of an Ashvamedha sacrifice. || 38 ||
During an eclipse of the planets, at the equinoxes, at the solstices, likewise at the beginning of the Yugas, at the Ṣaḍaśīti, and on other auspicious lunar days. || 39 ||
Those who bestow gifts such as wealth and other goods upon Brahmins there always obtain a fruit that is a hundred times greater than at any other sacred site. || 40 ||
There, on the bank of the lake, they offer funeral cakes (piṇḍa) to the ancestors;
that provides inexhaustible satisfaction to the ancestors, of this there is no doubt. || 41 ||
The measurement of the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) is proclaimed to be eight bow-lengths;
that holy site (tīrtha) situated between Varāha and Kāma grants all desires.
Because one does not return to existence there, that lake is called Apunarbhava;
having bathed there, a person goes toward the abode of the Sun.
"A living being is not born again because of immersion in you;
therefore, O great holy ford, I bathe here—remove my sin, salutations be to you!
With this [mantra], one should perform the ritual bath and behold the three-eyed Lord. (44)
Gokarṇa, Vikarṇa, and Yogīśa, the granter of all desires;
Gokarṇa has the form of a bull, and Vikarṇa has the appearance of a man.
Below the yogas, there is the knowledge of yoga;
beyond that, on the northern bank of the lake, on the Bhadrakāśaka mountain. (46)
O beloved, that stone which is Pauṇḍravittā, and where the Śoṇa flows in the middle,
extending for five dhanvantaras, is the sacred field known as Varavīthī.
Having duly and devotedly prepared the three deities upon their respective portions of that Śiva-stone with various kinds of perfumes and flowers, (verse 48).
And one who dies on the fourteenth day under the sign of Gemini shall attain liberation,
[by offering to Him] who holds a trident and the gesture of fearlessness in His hands and who bears a mass of matted locks.
Salutations again and again to the god who has the bull as his emblem, to Gokarṇa;
salutations to the god who embodies the ages, to Viṣṇu who holds the moon in his hand.
Salutations again and again to him who holds a mace and a bow in his hands, to Vikarṇa;
salutations to Maheśa, who dwells upon the bull, whose form is knowledge, and who is the possessor of wisdom.
Salutations be to you, the knower of Dharma, whose nature is the Self, the Lord of Yogins; salutations to him who preceded the state of no-more-rebirth and who consists of nine Dhanvantaris.
O Maheśānī, for as far as seven dhanvantaras lies the Kuṇḍa of Vārāṇasī; having bathed there, one who dies shall attain liberation.
On the thirteenth day of the month of Caitra, by means of this mantra and with diligent effort,
one who is completely liberated from all sins shall go to the abode of Brahmā.
Whatever merit is gained by bathing in all sacred fords even for a hundred years, one obtains that same fruit instantly by bathing just once in the pool at Vārāṇasī. (55)
O Śāṅkarī, its eastern bow measures five [yojanas] in length;
having bathed there at the lake named Mārkaṇḍeyahrada, one shall go to Śiva. (56)
To the north, on the bank of the lake, those who bathe in the Māheśvara pool and then behold the one known as Mārkaṇḍeśvara; || 57 ||
Having worshipped the Sun there— the three-eyed God of gods—
they, liberated from all sins, ascended an excellent celestial chariot.
Being sung of by Gandharvas, they indeed go to the world of Śiva;
there they remain joyful for one kalpa, O fair-faced one. (49)

The great-minded Mārkaṇḍeya, the best of sages, performed austerities here; known as the excellent lake named Mārkaṇḍeyahrada, may you always take away my sin. (O Hara, take away my sin! Indeed, this famous and superior lake is truly renowned.
Having performed an immersion with this [mantra], one should perform the tonsure of the shaven-headed;
one should perform the śrāddha rite with diligence and observe a fast.
Then, at the clear dawn, having now completed her daily rites,
O Maheśvarī, she stayed not far from the god Gokarṇa (also known as Vikarṇa).
There is a pool named Brahma-saras, measuring twenty-one [yojanas] in extent;
having bathed there, one dispels fatigue and shall no longer point toward rebirth.
O highly fortunate Brahmakuṇḍa, created by Brahmā in ancient times for the liberation from all sins, protect me from the ocean of worldly existence! (64)
Having bathed with this mantra at the western side of that lake,
there is one known by the name Kṛṣṇa, who is in the form of a mountain and is called Varāha by name.
Having bowed with devotion to Him, a person rejoices in the world of Viṣṇu.

Salutations to the Great Boar (Mahāvarāha), whose lofty body is bristling with tawny hair, who supports the earth with the tips of His tusks, and whose form is that of the charming Blue Mountain (Nīlācala)— salutations to Him whose very limbs and body are the Blue Mountain.
Salutations to you, the bestower of liberation; salutations, salutations to you!
Then, having gone to the delightful Madana mountain, located three arrow-shots away to the northeast of Gokarṇa, one shall behold Śaṅkara.
Having beheld with faith and a well-composed mind that imperishable Liṅga, the Great God named Kedāra, who is saluted by all the gods; || 68 ||
Having worshipped him with devotion by means of fragrances, charming flowers, incense, lamps, food offerings, prostrations, and likewise hymns of praise; || 69 ||
By prostrating like a staff and likewise by means of dance, song, and other arts,
a man who worships him according to the prescribed rite shall go to the world of Śiva.
O Madana, best of oceans, bestower of happiness and good fortune!
I ascend your peak; remove my sins, homage be to you! (71)
Facing the eastern direction, one should go and perform a circumambulation;
by merely lifting [the image] for a moment, one goes to the world of Śiva.
Śiva is white in color, mounted upon a white bull, and seated upon a lotus throne.
He has a white serpent as his sacred thread, his hands display the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness, and his eyes are the moon, the sun, and fire.
He wears a crown of matted hair with the moon as its crest-ornament, and his body is smeared with white ashes. (73)
The Ardhanārīśvara form has five faces and three eyes;
on his left side are Tatpuruṣa, Aghora, and Īśāna.
Below and to the west is Vāmadeva, who holds a hand-drum (ḍamaru), a sword (khaḍga), and other implements;
his color is like that of a sword or cow's milk. 75.
[He saw] the supreme Lord Tatpuruṣa, the bearer of the conch and discus, possessing the luster of molten gold,
and holding a mace and a lotus.
The southern face, Aghora, has the luster of pure vermilion;
it possesses fierce, tawny-colored fangs and resembles a dark blue cloud or collyrium.
Having thus meditated upon Śiva known as Kedāra according to the procedure taught in the Śivatantra,
and having worshipped him, one should take a handful of flowers and worship with the individual mantra for each image. || 78 ||
Salutations to the one who has the crescent moon as his crest-jewel; salutations to the bearer of the khaṭvāṅga staff;
salutations be to the trident-handed one; repeated salutations to Kedāra.
I bow to the Lord of all worlds, the divine, the imperishable cause of liberation,
the partless, supreme, and ancient God.
Salutations to you, the imperishable Śambhu, the protector of all beings.
"I bow to Śambhu, the imperishable, who transcends sound and transcends the qualities.
Having thus performed this act of propitiation to the west of Kedāra, [he remained there]. (82)
Having gone to the excellent Brahma-tree, a man should fix his attention upon it; he should fix his attention upon it without any gaps.
Then, having paid homage to Kedāra and the Kalpa-tree once again, (he should proceed). || 83 ||
The sin accumulated over ten lifetimes perishes at that very moment.
Salutations to the one whose nature is unmanifest, who dwells upon the great Malaya mountain! 84.
Salutations again and again to Nyagrodha, who dwells above Mahendra;
and to Kedāra in the region of Kuvēra, at a distance of three arrow-shots away.
In the city of Pauṣpaka, at the sacred site, one should worship Kamalākṣahara, who [rescues] one submerged in the ocean of worldly existence, seized by sin, and devoid of consciousness. 86.
Save me, O destroyer of Bhaga’s eyes! O enemy of Tripura, homage be to you!
O enemy of Tripura, homage be to you! O Lord of Kamalā, homage be to you! (87)
O beloved, to the south of the Kalpavṛkṣa, at a distance of one arrow-shot,
that mountain which is Chatrakora is the mountain Paripātraka.
Merely by ascending it, one is not born again on earth.
On this mountain, there are sixty-eight peaks, and in its center is the lofty mountain.
Having gone to that mountain named Mandara,
Hari, the enemy of Madhu, remained there composed in meditation on the eastern side of the mountain.
By the sight of that deity, one may deliver a hundred generations of one's lineage;
if one drinks the water of Kedāra and touches the Kāmadhenu, [the same result follows].
One who worships Keśava with devotion is never born again anywhere.
O beloved, the Mandāraka mountain is the most excellent of all sacred fields.
Having seen Kakudeśvarahara, he goes to the supreme goal;
and Brahmeśvara is established right there in the midst of the sacrificial fire-offering (homa). || 93 ||
Having paid homage to Brahmeśvara, one shall obtain the knowledge of Brahman;
and having beheld Bhāvabhūteśvara and performed a circumambulation of him, [one attains the same]. (94)
He is liberated from the multitude of sins and is glorified in the world of Śiva—he who worships Śiva on Mandāra, the mountain of the sacred field. (95)
The sin accumulated over a lifetime goes to complete destruction by the mere sight [of this place];
it is the same fruit that a man obtains by bathing at the confluence at Prayāga. || 96 ||
He indeed obtains that foremost fruit multiplied a thousandfold;
for the well of the god Dharmeśvara stands right before him.
There, O Goddess of gods, by bathing and by the offering of funeral cakes (piṇḍa), one duly obtains the fruit of giving a thousand cows, O lady of beautiful countenance. (98)
To the north of Pāripātra, at a distance of twenty bows, O beloved, one should behold Kapileśvara in the delightful hermitage of Kapila;
by worshipping him with devotion, a person is glorified in the world of Viṣṇu. || 99 ||
For those who behold the God stationed on Mount Pāripātra, the destroyer of all sins and fears, there is no fear whatsoever in the terrible ocean of saṃsāra. || 100 ||
To the east of that is the sacred ford named Piśācamocana;
at a distance of eleven dhanus from there, Kālabhairava resides in that very place.
O beloved, at the Piśācamocana Tīrtha, she worshipped the wielder of the trident (Śūlin), who had gone to the eastern region in the form of a white bull and was dark-complexioned.
Thus, this supreme Liṅga of the God, Kapardīśvara, should be worshipped with diligence and praised with various hymns. (103)
(285) O lady of excellent complexion, to the south of the god Vyāghreśvara, there is indeed a self-manifested (*svayambhū*) linga which is difficult even for the gods to obtain. (104)
That linga facing east is declared to be the most excellent place;
having reached Kṛttivāseśvara, those free from the fever of saṃsāra [attain liberation]. 105.
Freed from the fear of saṃsāra and devoid of all evil, they attain liberation with ease, according to their respective merit. || 106 ||
To the northeast of Vyāghreśvara, at a distance of ten dhanus,
one reaches Kṛttivāseśvara, established upon the source of the Liṅga.
The god Kṛttivāseśvara should be beheld again and again, if one desires the saving knowledge and the eternal, immortal state. (108)
All this should be performed by one who desires his own happiness,
at a distance of three arrow-shots to the northeast of Mount Madana.
Vāṇeśvara is renowned as the piercer of the seven netherworlds;
Vatsahata is the most excellent among all the liṅgas. (110)
Having bowed to that with devotion, a man is reborn as a man after a year.
To the northwest of that deity is a stone of various colors.
A man should worship the great liṅga named Garuḍa, even without [the presence of] Garuḍa.
By the sight of that deity, one obtains the fruit of [giving] a hundred cows. || 112 ||
Salutations to you, O Lord of the kings of birds, who are devoted to the welfare of Vāsudeva;
O Lord of birds, grant me permission regarding this vision of him.
Having prostrated, one should recite the mantra within the great western enclosure;
having reached the abode of Viṣṇu, there is the auspicious water of Śiva.
Having bathed and performed the tonsure, and having meditated upon Viṣṇu, one should pass the night.
Then, O Goddess of Devas, at dawn, to the north of Maṇikūṭa— (115)
There is a meritorious river named Ballabhā that liberates one from all sins;
having bathed there on the fourteenth day of either the month of Māgha or Phālguna, [one attains the highest goal]. || 116 ||
O Goddess of gods, at Ballabhā there is the destruction of great sins;
having bathed at Ballabhā and beheld Nīlakaṇṭha, a man [attains this]. (117)
Sins committed even over seven lifetimes do not touch him who, having bathed in that sacred ford, beholds Mādhava with reverence. (118)
Wherever one may stand, even within saṃsāra, one shall not enter it again;
and for those fallen into saṃsāra, the Gaṅgā shall be their savior. || 119 ||
Having seen the boar’s cave, a man should go to the Mahānadī river, which arises from the stainless Aśoka tree and issues forth from the trunk of a *kola* tree. 120.
Nandinī, Paṅkajā, and the supreme river Madhumatī all flow together at Maṇikūṭa; for one who goes there, the fruit is exceedingly great.
Homage be to you, O one of meritorious waters; homage to you who flow to the ocean!
Homage to you, O stainless cleanser of sins; homage to you, O Goddess of noble form, the bestower of auspiciousness! 122.
Having bathed in the waters of Apunarbhava, one should enter the presence of Lord Gokarṇa;
and at that very place, Svargadvāra, one should utter this mantra: || 123 ||
Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and likewise Rudra have been designated by all the gods as the gateway to heaven; one should ascend this most meritorious and very difficult place to attain.
O Maṇikūṭa, best of mountains, yellow-hued, three-eyed!
I offer this water of honor (arghya) to Dharma, who is endowed with the ten characteristics, who possesses four feet, who is beautiful, and who dwells at the gate of heaven. (125)
Having gone there, one should untiringly pay homage at Pañcahasta [or Yugmahasta],
as well as at the lake of Vārāṇasī and the Mārkaṇḍeya lake.
Having bathed and seen Kāmahara (Kāmeśvara), one should then bow to the Kalpavṛkṣa;
after bathing again at Durlabhā, one should then proceed to the temple of Hari.
He who, with his senses restrained, performs worship at a sacred ford according to the prescribed rules,
uplifts twenty-one generations of his lineage and goes to the world of Viṣṇu.
O Maheśvarī, not far to the east of Maṇikūṭa,
there is a place named Viṣṇupuṣkaraka, whose water originates from all sacred fords (tīrthas).
Having bathed there, O lady of excellent hips, one obtains abundant prosperity;
for he remains upon the surface of the earth, having assumed the form of a lotus. (130)
"O Puṣkara, for the sake of the welfare of the mortal world, take away my sin.
Having bathed there with this mantra, one should mutter the Vāruṇa mantra.
One should offer the respectful water (arghya) according to the rules and may even ascend Mount Maṇikūṭa;
for on Mount Maṇikūṭa, Viṣṇu dwells, assuming the form of Hayagrīva.
O Goddess, one should ascend the eight thousand immovable [pillars] measuring a hundred cubits by means of the mantra, and worship them with yellow flowers. || 133 ||
Then he should propitiate Viṣṇudeha and Dvārika, saying:
"O mighty-armed one with staff in hand, O destroyer of the Kāla demon! (134)
O Gatekeeper, homage be to you; grant me the door-panel always.
He is yellow, two-armed, peaceful, and adorned with jeweled earrings. (135)
Homage to you, who hold a wheel and arrows, who are white and surrounded by a halo;
you who are endowed with all auspicious marks, who possess a mountain of jewels, and who have three eyes.
Having meditated upon that, one should then ascend the peak of the mantra upon its pedestal:
"O Maṇikūṭa, best of mountains, yellow-colored, three-eyed one! (137)
Having ascended onto you, I shall likewise behold the temple,
facing either toward the east or toward the north.
One should ascend Maṇiśaila and avoid facing any other direction;
having gone to the Vindhya mountain, one should then perform a circumambulation of it three times.
Having entered, becoming self-restrained, wearing clean garments, and having conquered his senses,
he should bathe the deity with the root mantra using auspicious, fragrant waters.
With fragrant flowers and other offerings, moistened with camphor and made smooth, as well as sandalwood, agallochum, lotuses, and whatever else is desirable; 141.
Having drawn the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) for the rites,
one should perform a bath in its water with pure white water as well as with lukewarm water.
With warm water and likewise with the five nectars (pañcāmṛta) in succession, with the three sweets, the three fragrances, and the three waters, O my beloved. (143)
O Goddess, for the sake of pleasing that deity, one should perform a ritual bath;
sandalwood, lotus, and uśīra are proclaimed as the three white substances. 144.
p. 289) Sandalwood paste from the Malaya mountains, which is eternal for mortals, fragrant with the three scents and most enchanting;
likewise, water from sacred bathing places, scented water, and water infused with camphor. || 142 ||
O Maheśānī, one should sprinkle the three-fold water at intervals;
having bathed [the deity] according to the prescribed method, one should likewise perform the bathing again.
Then, O Supreme Goddess, one who knows the ritual procedure should perform the half-bath according to the rules,
using jars fashioned of gold, numbering one thousand and eight.
One should perform a bath with rice mixed with camphor and other substances;
however, O beautiful goddess, one who is unable to do so should perform it ten times a hundred times.
One should perform the bath with vessels made of copper or silver, or if those are unavailable, with earthen pots; however, one who is incapable may perform it in this manner.
O Maheśānī, before the bath, one who knows the ritual procedure should go to the sacred bathing place (tīrtha) that has been proclaimed;
having fetched water from there and placed it in a pitcher along with a flower, he should do so according to the prescribed rite. || 147 ||
Then, having offered incense and flowers, one should again recite the mantra;
one should perform the rite of nectarization (amṛtīkaraṇa) and display the mudrā there.
One should perform the placement of the six limbs (ṣaḍaṅga) there, and after consecrating it, one should worship it;
then, having performed a great festival, [one should prepare] for the bath to the right of the deity.
One should bathe [the deity], and with the thought that it is the Divine, one should apply the remnants of the bath to one's own body.
Rubbing with unguents (udvartana) should be performed every day or on alternate days. 150.
Whether within three days or at any time, especially,
