O my beloved, with fragrant oil produced from sesame seeds— (151)
With effort, using one pala, half a pala, or even half of that, along with unctuous substances, dyes, and treatments such as rice-paste rubs; || 152 ||
O Śāṅkarī, O beloved, having installed the Lord of the gods upon a bilva leaf (or, O Śāṅkarī, upon a bilva leaf),
one should rub his body with the leaves or the roots of the apāmārga plant.
O Maheśvarī, one should prepare a brush from the fibers of the *nalapuṣpa* flower; furthermore, it may be made with *kuśa* grass, a yak-tail whisk, or especially with cow-hair. 154.
By offering uśīra grass as a brush, one is liberated from all sins;
by offering a brush made of cow-hair, one casts off all evil. || 155 ||
And having given a chowrie and a brush, one attains unsurpassed prosperity;
never by the hair of a boar, nor ever by bamboo. (156)
One should likewise avoid the hair on the body of a gavaya or a horse, whether on a linga, an image, or a śālagrāma stone. (157)
One should not comb every day; rather, O beautiful one, one should comb me every five days, or seven, or at the end of a month, or at the end of a fortnight. 158.
One should not perform an oil bath during the solstices, at the equinoxes, on Tuesdays, on the day of the new moon, on the twelfth lunar day, or when Rāhu eclipses the sun or moon. || 159 ||
O Goddess, one should certainly not scratch that on the excellent limbs, nor on the face, nor then on the tip of the nose, nor likewise on the secret parts, the penis, or the pores of the skin. (160)
O Goddess, one should wipe [the deity] with a cloth made of cotton or with sandalwood paste;
however, by using red garments, one becomes afflicted with leprosy and shall incur the disease of jaundice. || 161 ||

By means of cotton cloths one incurs agitation, and by those dyed with indigo one goes to ruin; likewise, having caused a garment to be worn, it brings about the destruction of heaven [and similarly, two gold threads].
One should give him a waistband and various ornaments such as gems; having thus covered his lower garment, the man who performs the bath [in this manner]. (163)
At the time of worship, during meals, and especially while bathing, he too meets with destruction, as well as the loss of wealth. (164)
With the fragrance of malayaja sandalwood, or with cow-pen sandalwood (gopīcandana), or else with wood originating from the bilva tree, or with wood from the tulasī plant. || 165 ||
Having applied a tilaka— the most excellent mark— with either padmaka, tamāla, or gorocanā, using one or another of these.
O Goddess of the Gods, having smeared the body here with the fourfold equal, the exceedingly equal, and the twofold equal [pigments], one should then dismiss it with this [mantra].
Furthermore, on a cold night, having bathed and anointed oneself with fragrant substances,
one should especially apply them to the forehead, but never to the head.
O Goddess of the Suras, one should not apply an ointment that is equal in four parts, three parts, or two parts to the feet, the back, or the eyes.
(292) Fortune is destroyed when [the moon] is in the fourth ascendant; glories are destroyed when it is in the face-ascendant (the first);
one becomes impoverished when it is in the hand-ascendant (the second), and there is loss of wealth when it is in the foot-ascendant (the seventh). || 170 ||
O beloved, one should not apply sandalwood paste to the tip of the *liṅga* after it has been covered with horripilation;
likewise, one should not use lotus petals, *bilva* leaves, or *karavīra* petals.
There, one should apply sandalwood paste to the linga, and furthermore, O Goddess, when possible, one should especially anoint the eyes with collyrium.
O Goddess, one should heat *mālatī* leaves with sesame oil in an iron vessel; that which falls [from them] is proclaimed as *kajjala*. (173)
O lady of excellent complexion, he who performs worship with the rite of lustration (nīrājana) shall attain immortality both in this world and in the next. || 174 ||
Furthermore, he who does not provide water for purification during the worship of the deity becomes a fool or a sick man, or he shall quickly meet his destruction. (175)
O my beloved, first of all, one should cleanse the yantra with water at either a linga or an image, having performed a circumambulation.
O blessed lady, let them touch the image and me in the form of the *liṅga*, those wise ones who utter "Oṃ namo nārāyaṇāya. (177)
What is the use of many efforts that cause the mind to wander?
The mantra "Oṃ namo nārāyaṇāya" is the accomplisher of all aims.
Sacrificing with that very mantra, or with the Puruṣa-sūkta,
one should worship with the twelve-syllable seed-mantra or the Kṛṣṇa-bīja.
One should contemplate there the mandalas of the Sun, Moon, and Fire, both individually and collectively, in direct and reverse order.
Then, having meditated upon the heart as the syllable Oṃ in the form of light, seated upon the pericarp, whose very nature is the form of light; (181)
Then they proclaim the eight-syllable mantra in due order;
having first established the city of Keśava and the others, one should install the twelve-syllable mantra.
Having meditated upon the Great Being with four arms, possessing a radiance equal to ten million suns, and then upon the eternal yoga in the form of light; 183.
Then, with a mind purified through the sequential stages, one should invoke the mantra—whether in the form of a Fish, a Boar, or again as a Man-lion. (184)
May the boon-granting Lord Nārāyaṇa come before me;
let there be a lotus-prepared seat upon the footstool of Mount Sumeru. || 185 ||
"O Madhusūdana, remain for the sake of the welfare of all beings!
Homage to the Lord of the lords of the three worlds, and homage to the God of gods!
This is the *arghya* offering for Viṣṇu, Hṛṣīkeśa; [thus the *arghya* for Viṣṇu: homage!"
Thus [is the offering of] arghya.
"O eternal Lord Padmanābha, O Viṣṇu, lotus-petal-eyed Madhusūdana, accept this water for washing Your feet. (187)
"Thus, O Mahādeva, this water for the feet and this honey-mixture (madhuparka), prepared by Brahmā and the other gods and offered by me with devotion, accept it, O Puruṣottama. (188)
Thus, let this Madhuparka be for you; let the water of the Mandākinī be your drink, which removes all inauspiciousness. Accept this Ācamanīya offered by me with devotion. (189)
Thus, [the water for] sipping:
(p. 294) "O Waters, you are indeed the Earth, and you are indeed Light, the Fire itself.
By means of this water, through the mere consciousness of the world, I bathe myself. (190)
Thus,
O Keśava, these two garments of yours, joined with a fine cloth and adorned with the splendor of a sacrifice, possess a golden radiance in their distinct hues.
"Thus, O Keśava, I anoint your garment and your body; let your own movements be as they are.
Accepting the perfumes offered by me, please anoint yourself. (192)
Thus, the unblemished sacred thread (*upavīta*), purified by Brahmā with mantras from the *Ṛgveda* and other Vedas, and tied with the *Sāvitrī* knot, is used as an ointment.
Thus [is the sacred thread]:
You alone are the sun, the moon, and the lightning; likewise, you are the fire.
O God, you alone are the light of all lights; may this lamp be accepted. (194)
Thus, O Keśava, this lamp, food of five kinds endowed with the six tastes, and this offering have been presented by me with devotion unto you. (195)
Thus, one should place the food offering on the eastern petal; one should place the god Saṃkarṣaṇa on the southern [petal];
Pradyumna on the western, and likewise Trivikrama on the northeastern [petal]. (196)
And likewise, one should place Garuḍa in front of Vāsudeva;
similarly, one should place the great mace (mahāgadā) to the right of the deity. (197)
Then, one should place the bow along with the Veda to the left of the deity;
to the right, one should place the goddess Vasudhā and there install the Vāṅmaya.
One should place Śrī to the south, and Puṣṭi one should install to one's own north;
then the garland of forest flowers in front, and thereafter the Śrīvatsa and Kaustubha.
One should assign the heart-mantra and the others, and one should also assign them in the four directions;
however, one must not assign them in the corners of the God of Gods.
One should worship the Lord of the Pīṭha and his Śaktis as well on the outside;
one should also present the planets, the lords of the directions, and three offerings of flowers and oblations.
Having thus worshipped Janārdana, the Lord of Gods, who resides within the maṇḍala (or the sacrificial mound), a man shall obtain his desired objects; of this there is no doubt. || 202 ||
Whoever beholds Hayānana, situated within the pavilion, worshipped according to this very procedure, shall see neither obstacle nor the imperishable Viṣṇu.
By whomsoever Keśava is worshipped even once according to this rite,
he shall transcend birth and death and attain the abode of Viṣṇu.
For one who constantly remembers Hayagrīva with devotion and without sloth,
Śvetadvīpa is prepared for him every day at both twilights.
The name of each reality (tattva), preceded by the syllable Oṃ and concluded with a salutation (namas), is designated as its mantra. (206)
O Goddess of gods, he who worships Hayānana situated in the pavilion according to this very procedure should offer perfumes and flowers. (207)
Thus one should perform this according to the sequence specified;
then one should bind the mudrā according to the application of the stated sequence. (208)
The knower of mantras should perform the recitation (japa) using the root-mantra (mūlayantra),
either twenty-eight times, eight times, or one hundred and eight times.

And in rites for desired objects, O beloved, one should perform it even more extensively—by the hundreds of thousands and tens of millions—[depicting] the lotus, the conch, the Śrīvatsa, the mace, and Garuḍa. (210)
The moon, the conch, and the spotted deer—these eight are proclaimed as the mudrās;
yet they do not know the mantras of Hari as they have been declared, which are to be worshipped.
One should worship the Supreme Lord with the Hiraṇyagarbha mantra;
one should honor the Supreme Lord with the mantra that is about to be described.

Oṃ, salutation be to Ananta, whose mind is pure; salutation to the one whose nature is light, who possesses a thousand arms, the creator who is the most excellent of the thousand-rayed suns; salutation, salutation to you in the form of Hayagrīva! 213.
Salutations to the one of vast body, whose actions are pure, who removes the suffering of the entire universe, and who is Śambhu;
salutations to the one with the sharp brilliance of the sun and fire, who has the form of a horse-headed being; salutations, salutations to you!
O beginningless one, [Devācala], O Lord of Gods, whose splendor is the crest-jewel;
homage to you, O All-pervading One, Lord of Beings, Maheśvara!
O Lord of the Maruts, Lord of All, Lord of the World!
O Lord of Ramā, O Lord of the World, salutations always! || 215 ||
O Lord of the waters, Nārāyaṇa, benefactor of the universe, Sovereign of the earth, Lord of the universe, whose eyes are the universe— to You,
whose cosmic form is as vast as the moon and the sun!
Salutation, salutation to you who have the form of Hayāsya. || 216 ||
To the white one, the giver of the Puṣpaka lake,
who possesses four arms with the eyes of knowledge as his assistants, and who has made his dwelling in the Lauhitya; To the one who has established his residence in the creation of the Lauhitya.
Salutations, salutations to you, the horse-faced one! || 217 ||
To Śukra, whose palace is a mountain of radiant jewels,
who grants liberation to the yellow-syllabled Rākṣasa folk,
and who bestows honor upon his devotees; I am a devotee of the book-bearer.
He too shall uplift the host of ancestors; salutations to You! He grants all desired wealth;
O Hari, he too shall uplift the host of ancestors; salutations to You! 218.

Salutations, salutations to you, who are pure, liberated, and adorned with jewels; whose arms hang down long and who sits upon a lotus throne; who is the destroyer of sins and the shatterer of the cities [of the demons]; and who assumes forms such as that of a horse—homage to you! 219.
Victorious is the Bestower of Boons, who holds a book in one hand and a white lotus in the other;
he bears the form of the moon, bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation, and grants all enjoyments.
Murāri, whose face is like that of a horse, [is the one] to whom gods and men bow down. || 220 ||
O Iḍāsura, Hayagrīva, Murāri, Madhusūdana!
O lotus-eyed one who has made Maṇikūṭa your dwelling, homage be to you! (221)
The sin committed over ten million lifetimes and even for hundreds of millions of eons—
all of it perishes in that very instant simply by the sight of Hayagrīva. 222.
O Goddess, one whose self is purified should perform this recitation of praise consisting of seven hymns;
he should perform three circumambulations in the form of a lotus and then pay homage.
Having gone from south to north of the deity, O Maheśvarī, one should then,
with devotion and palms joined in reverence (*kṛtāñjali*), circumambulate and thereafter bow down.
O Goddess, one should bow down to each [deity] individually and prostrate like a staff;
if one were to circumambulate them without bowing, that would then be an offense.
Whoever performs a salutation with unjoined palms—having failed to join them—is cooked in the hell of the darkness of delusion; of this there is no doubt. || 226 ||
One should bow with the head toward another vessel and not let it touch the ground;
for the deities curse him, and his recitation is declared to be fruitless.
O beloved Maheśānī, listen to the fruit of the merit of one who offers salutation to the God of gods, however many forms of His may exist within his own body. || 228 ||
As many particles of dust as there are in that [stūpa] and for as long as it remains,
for so many thousands of eons is he honored in the world of Brahmā.
The Goddess said:
"Speak to me, O Lord of the gods, my beloved, Lord of the universe!
By whom indeed was this Viṣṇu established in Maṇikūṭa in the past? (230)
The Blessed One said:
"Listen, O highly fortunate goddess, to this tradition which is equal to the Vedas;
I shall relate the ancient account of the origin of the image."
And while the great sacrifice was underway in the temple built by the gods, the king, distressed by his desire for the [divine] form, sought the image day and night. (232)
By what means, O Lord of Gods, may I behold the Supreme Person—the Lord of the gods, the creator of the world everywhere, and the author of its creation, maintenance, and end? || 233 ||
The king, consisting of the suffering of anxiety, neither sleeps nor eats day or night; he enjoys no various pleasures, nor does he bathe or adorn himself. (234)
Whether it be a mountain peak or a tree standing upon the earth that is auspicious, it is fit for an image of Viṣṇu if it is endowed with all the required characteristics. || 235 ||
"By these very means alone, my lord, I shall perform that beloved worship of the gods;
by what other way shall I do so? May the Lord command me. [O Lord] 236.
Having spread out kusha grass and lain down upon it, the mighty Indradyumna, having become intent on meditation upon Hari, slept soundly with his senses restrained. (237)
While that king was asleep, Vāsudeva, the teacher of the world, revealed himself to him; and the wielder of the discus remained hidden from him.
He beheld Viṣṇu, the god of gods and teacher of the world;
the wielder of the discus revealed himself to him while he was asleep. (239)
That king beheld the God of gods, the Teacher of the world—
the Lord bearing the conch and the discus, with mace and lotus held in his formidable hands;
possessing a luster like the sun at the end of an eon, resembling blue lapis lazuli.
Seated upon his golden back, auspicious with eight arms, [O King,
you have attained this] through this sacrifice, through this gift, through wisdom, and through excellent devotion.
"I am pleased with you, O protector of the earth; why do you grieve? For here, O King, is the eternal image, worthy of worship by the entire world. (242)
O wise one, you shall establish it; therefore, I shall tell you the means for that:
at the edge of the ocean's waters, adorned with various trees. (243)
But even when struck by the waves, that tree does not yield;
and having taken an axe in his hand, he then proceeds toward the surging wave.
"O King, while dwelling alone, you see the tree as real";
reflecting on these words, he cut it down without hesitation. (245)
"O King, in the morning, having cut down that tree in the western quarter—which presents a wondrous sight—with an axe, and having applied oil-essence to it, bring that tree here. (246)
"Carve that divine image; abandon this deluding anxiety.
Having spoken thus, the mighty-armed Hari vanished from sight.
Having reflected upon that dream, he was filled with great wonder;
gazing toward that very direction, he remained there with his mind fixed upon it.
Having recited the Vaiṣṇava mantra, which is declared to be identical with Him, when the night has turned to dawn, he whose mind is constantly and exclusively focused [on the Lord]— (249)
Having bathed in the delightful ocean according to the prescribed rites,
he beheld that great tree, which was like a tree of radiant splendor.
It brings an end to delusion, is difficult to ascend, meritorious, and yields fruit;
it is of great height and massive body, and lies asleep near the water. (251)
Having seen that tree of Viṣṇu, which possessed the luster of the finest color of blue gems and was devoid of name and genus, the king of men was filled with joy.
With the axe, he indeed felled it by means of its very sharpness;
that king of trees fell upon the surface of the earth in seven pieces.
The omnipresent Lord fashioned the root portion in the land of Oḍra,
and the upper section in Kāśmīra in the form of a headless trunk.
One should know that Āditya was established there by Rāma in ancient times;
and above that, O beloved, Śoṇāditya was established by Śukra. 255.
Then, O Great Goddess, the preceptor installed a stone image;
two parts were placed in Kāmarūpa and one part on the Malaya mountain.
Half of that [measure] was indeed established by Varuṇa at Maṇikūṭa;
in the east is Nāndī, and in the northeast is the Mādhava named Matsyākṣa. (257)
Made of stone and wood, it was established by Kubera himself;
it is named Mahāvarāha and is endowed with eighteen arms. || 258 ||
The one named Hayākhya is established at Maṇikūṭa, and the one named Mādhava is likewise situated there.
O Goddess, the origin has been told; now hear, O Pārvatī, about the attainment.
Iṅgudī fruits, bilvas, jujubes, and āmalakas; dates, jackfruit, and likewise palm fruits. (260)
One should diligently employ pomegranate and plantain, as well as breadfruit, licorice, and betel nuts. (261)
One should offer sweet citron and jujube fruits,
as well as the leafy vegetables of radish and likewise of turnip.
O my beloved, the leafy vegetable that grows from that which has a vast fruit is the *vāstūka*, and the leafy vegetable of the *pālaṅga* is likewise [to be known]. (263)
Indeed, *vilaya* fruits, as well as *tintiḍī* fruit, *kuṣmāṇḍa*, mountain-grown [vegetables], and those produced in the forest; 264.
One should likewise avoid plantain, citron, romaka, pautraka, untimely jackfruit, and whatever else is similar. || 265 ||
O Śāṅkarī, I shall now declare the uses of grains;
O Śāṅkarī, with a concentrated mind, listen to the method of their preparation. 266.
Somadhānya, bṛhaddhānya, and raktaśālika, as well as rājadhānya, ṣaṣṭika, and devaballabhaka. || 267 ||
O beautiful one, you must avoid chickpeas and kodrava grain; likewise, avoid alkaline substances, black milk, and vessels made of clay. (268)
I shall now describe the salt produced from the eastern [ocean] as well as that arising from the northern, and also the [meat] of domestic animals and those dwelling in the wild. (269)
O Goddess, whatever products of the cow are suitable—milk and ghee—as well as [the meat of] the deer, the fish, the goat, the śarabha, and likewise the hare; (p. 303) 270.
With these, one should present an offering that is dear to Viṣṇu;
one should avoid buffalo meat, as well as milk, curd, and ghee. (271)
And I shall declare the birds that are to be employed, O my beloved:
the partridge, the peacock, the nāraka, and likewise the quail. (272)
Kapila, cāṣa, crow, cock, and two types of insects [on the head], as well as the wild cock, the sarāri bird, and the pigeon. || 273 ||
The bilvaka, the kulika, the red-tailed ṭiṭṭibha, and the one that eats black fish—these are distinguished among winged creatures. || 274 ||
Meat that is unfit for consumption, and that of any five-toed animal, as well as the variegated fish, the Rohita, the Madgura, and the Kabika; || 275 ||
One should give the mahāśūla, the rājīva, and likewise the siṃhartuka;
these fish are to be given, but one should avoid the vibhālī.
And web-footed mongooses, as well as vevi-vārāṭṭakas, safflower greens, oil-cake, and red-footed kesaras. (277)
The best of practitioners should avoid *śobhāñjana*, red *śelu*, *kemuka*, *ninduka*, as well as *pūtika* and *kānaka*. (278)
As it has been said: "The yogi, devoted to meditation, should accomplish the mantra;
he should avoid all that is unfit for consumption during the practice of meditating upon the deity. (279)
Eating sacrificial food, having become pure, and being proficient in the mantras and tantras, one should recite the vidyā day and night with an inner self absorbed in that. (280)
He shall become a son of Kālikā and shall be fearless everywhere;
O Goddess, this supreme secret has been revealed out of affection for you. 281.

Thus ends the ninth chapter, and [begins] the tenth chapter, in the second part of the section on Kāmarūpa within the *Yoginītantra*, the great king of tantras consisting of twenty-two thousand verses.
The Blessed Lord said:
When the Mahājyaiṣṭhī occurs through the conjunction of a zodiac sign and a lunar mansion, then mortals should visit Puruṣottama with great effort. || 1 ||
On the earth, at all sacred fords (tīrtha), in the temples of Hari, on mountains containing holy sites, and in rivers and lakes; || 2 ||
Having observed that the entire fruit which is obtained from bathing and giving gifts when the sun is eclipsed by Rāhu is attained on Mahājyaiṣṭhī, a person should speak [of this merit]. || 3 ||
Therefore, O Great Goddess, those who desire the fruit of all their wishes must go to Puruṣottama with every effort on the day of Mahājyaiṣṭhī.
Having seen Kṛṣṇa standing upon his chariot, as well as Lakṣmī and Sarasvatī there,
a man goes to the world of Viṣṇu, having uplifted his esteemed lineage.
Having enjoyed excellent pleasures there until the dissolution of all beings,
he returns here upon the exhaustion of his merit and becomes a twice-born master of the four Vedas.

Devoted to his own duty, with a tranquil mind, a devotee of Viṣṇu who has conquered his senses, having reached the world of Viṣṇu, shall attain that world. (7) (Note: The phrase *svāntaḥ śrāntaḥ* is found in some versions; however, as indicated by the note in the source text, this line is absent from one palm-leaf manuscript.)
And every month on the twelfth lunar day, he should lead [the deity] to the Kedāraka house;
there, at the foot of the Kalpa tree, he should worship with yellow sandalwood.
Having performed the pilgrimage according to the prescribed rite, and having beheld Kṛṣṇa and bowed down to him, one should offer milk-rice, sugar, and flour-cakes prepared with ghee.
One attains the world of Viṣṇu for as long as the reign of fourteen Indras.
For as long as a man performs the pilgrimage in the month of Jyeṣṭha according to the prescribed rites, for that long he enjoys happiness in the world of Viṣṇu; of this there is no doubt.
On the full moon day of Phālguna, there is a pilgrimage toward Mandāraka;
having seen [the deity] there, a certain man is glorified in the world of Viṣṇu.
O Maheśvarī, at the time of a procession, whether on a chariot or in a palanquin, one should not touch the deity; likewise, one should not touch him upon the ground. (13)
Having undertaken a journey to Kṛṣṇa, or having performed it while restraining his senses, a man who is childless obtains sons, and one who is destitute obtains wealth. 14.
The sick person is liberated from disease, and the maiden obtains a virtuous husband;
[one gains] longevity, fame, renown, intelligence, wealth, knowledge, fortitude, and cattle.
A man attains a good rebirth, youth, and perfection of form;
whatever enjoyments he desires, he obtains upon beholding that Supreme Person.
Whether a man or a woman, one undoubtedly attains those various [goals], just as the letter 'A' is among all letters and the Gāyatrī is among the meters. || 17 ||
Likewise, O Maheśvarī, Puruṣottama is the most excellent of all sacred fords (tīrthas), just as the head is the best among all the limbs. (18)
Likewise, Puruṣottama is the most excellent among all holy places (tīrthas), just as Varuṇa is among aquatic beings and Yama is among those who exercise restraint. || 19 ||
Likewise, Puruṣottama is the most excellent among all sacred fords (tīrthas),
just as the Ocean of Milk is the best among oceans and the lord of rivers.
Likewise, Puruṣottama is the most excellent among all sacred fords;
O Goddess of the Gods, I do not see anyone on earth who is his equal.
Moreover, what is the use of speaking much or saying it again and again?
Truly, truly, and once more truly, that field is supreme and great. (22)
Having enjoyed various and manifold pleasures accompanied by celestial nymphs, he goes to the supreme abode where Hari, the Lord of Yoga, resides.
O Goddess, at the end of the kalpa, having returned once more to the mortal world, that best of men is born as a yogi; he becomes a knower of wisdom and is born as a householder.
Having attained the Vaiṣṇava yoga, he is born into a preeminent family;
facing the south, he beholds the southern ocean.
Having bowed down to that Mandāra tree, one is glorified in the world of Brahmā. || 26 ||
O Kirīṭin, Lokavāsa, and most excellent son of the Brahmaputra river!
You who are seen stationed at Maṇikūṭa, be the bestower of all fruits. (27) [Stationed at Maṇikūṭa, may you be the bestower of the fruits as described to me.]
O tiger among the mountains of Mandara, O Maheśvarī in the form of Viṣṇu!
O lord of mountains, O you who possess the form of Viṣṇu, salutations to you simply by the sight of you. (28)
Having paid homage to Mādhava and remembered Maṇikūṭa even once, he shall realize the knowledge of Brahman and no longer experience dwelling in a womb [he does not see it]. || 29 ||
Having fasted for a full year, or even for just one month, at the place of Hari known as Dakṣa-sannihita and at Nārasiṃhaka; || 30 ||
By him alone was the desired goal achieved; by him alone was it accomplished; and by him alone was great austerity performed here.
To the north of Mandāra is the region called Āmilā, which resembles blood in color.
She is remembered as Kālarātri by the mark of the Ākāśagaṅgā;
she, who bestows dharma, artha, and kāma, is to be worshipped with the kavaca.
Furthermore, in the six cities of Puṇḍrarājya (Padmarāśi), there resides Kṣauṇī within the Viśva-antarāla,
as well as Jayā, Vijayā, Bhadrakālī, and Kapālinī.
One should worship Mahāmāyā and Tārā within the six enclosures;
in the center, one should offer sacrifice to Bhavānī, Kālī, and Kālarātri.
On the preceding petals, one should perform meditation upon Brahmā and the others, as well as the Bhairavas beginning with Aliṅga; listen to this meditation from me, O my beloved. (35)
Standing in the *pratyālīḍha* posture upon a mountain, resembling a dark-blue peak and possessing the splendor of a mass of clouds;
holding a sword, a flaying knife, a skull-cup, a bow, and likewise armor;
moon-faced, illuminating [the world] with her eyes; resembling a white lotus and adorned with a garland of severed heads.
I worship Kālarātri, who destroys hundreds of evils with her terrible, loud, and echoing laughter. || 36 ||
Then, having performed the assignment of the six limbs, one should worship with each verse:
"O Viśvamūrti, auspicious, pure, Virūpākṣī, three-eyed one! (37)
O Śivā of terrifying form, O Vidyā, O Kālarātri, homage be to you!
O Mahārātri of variegated limbs, O auspicious one who delights in secret dance! 38.
O Kālarātri, you who hold a noose in hand and a staff in hand, homage be to you!
O Cāmuṇḍā, whose mouth is garlanded with severed heads, who have sharp fangs, [O Great Knowledge], O Great Power! || 39 ||
O Goddess, abiding in the abode of corpses, O Kālarātri, salutations be to you! O Kālī, O Karālā, O Vikrāntā, O Kālī with the terrifying face, you who are saluted by all the gods! || 40 ||
"O Goddess who removes all sins, O Kālarātri, obeisance be to you!
Having thus worshipped that goddess, one should perform the vow with a concentrated mind. (41)
One should begin it in the month of Māgha, or Kārttika, or Jyeṣṭha-Āṣāḍha;
or for a year, or even for a fortnight thereafter.
One should observe the vow for three months, neither less nor more;
while doing so, one should not eat fish or meat, nor should one eat at night.
One should eat food harvested out of season and subsist on a single meal a day;
one should worship the Goddess in every limb with fragrant flowers and unyielding devotion. 44.

O Goddess of the gods, at the conclusion of the vow, one should perform a grand feast according to the rules with the five types of offerings, including meat, milk-rice, and sweetmeats on the new moon day.
Having placed a water-pot upon the sacrificial ground, one should wrap it with a triple-stranded thread that is blue and red, and adorn it with the five types of sprouts.
One should worship the Supreme Goddess during the night and at the time of twilight;
one should offer double the quantity of food offerings (naivedya) and likewise triple the sacrificial oblation (bali).
Having cooked the *caru* oblation, one should afterwards present that *arghya* to the Goddess;
then, amidst great festivities of dance and song, one should personally receive the *arghya*.
O Maheśānī, one should pass the night by listening to songs and other such [devotional] sounds.
One should likewise avoid the leaves of the tamarind tree (*ciñcā*), the *nālikā* vegetable, peas (*kalāya*), and the *niṅkuca*. (49)
During the vow, one should avoid plantains, coconuts, and pumpkin;
as well as the kaṅkāra flower, the jhindī, the kunda, and the mandāra.
One should avoid the *droṇa* flower, the *śirīṣa*, and the *munipuṣpa*.
O Maheśānī, having worshipped [with these], the place of worship is not seen again.
O lady of excellent vows, one should neither accept nor touch my flower-offering;
it should then be given to a Brāhmaṇa, and never to a Śūdra.
Whoever should bring it forth, listen to it with devotion, or maintain it in their home, for them there shall be no terrible fear from snakes, thieves, and the like. 53.
And whoever worships this with devotion by means of animals, sweetmeats, and other offerings, that wise person, together with his sons and grandsons, attains prosperity. (54)
When a king who has been deprived of his kingdom observes the vow on the eighth lunar day, being self-controlled and pure,
that monarch shall, within a year, regain a kingdom free from all thorns.
And to the west of Varāha, on Mount Bhadrakāma, one should worship the Kāmeśvara Liṅga, whose emblem is the bull. (56)
To the east of Hayagrīva, there is a stone resembling white [in color], adorned with a skull, fragrant substances, and an extensive array of great riches. (57)
That goddess Mahālakṣmī is the bestower of worldly enjoyment and liberation;
whatever fruit is proclaimed for bathing and giving gifts at all sacred fords, [she grants it]. (58)
A man obtains that fruit by beholding and bowing down to Lakṣmī,
as well as to Tulasī, Mandāra, Kalhāra, and Tamālaka.
One should not worship Mahālakṣmī with materials grown from *kuśa* or *kāśa* grass;
and that which is her right vulva is to be known as Sarasvatī.
By worshipping her, the Goddess purifies both lineages;
whatever fruit is proclaimed for dwelling in the forest and for the stage of the forest-dweller (vānaprastha), [that she bestows]. || 61 ||
A man obtains that fruit by worshipping Sarasvatī;
and in the opening to her east, there is a stone in the shape of the five remaining [syllables].
Having either established [the image] yourself or performed worship according to the prescribed rite,
O beautiful one, you should observe a fast on the twelfth day of the bright fortnight for my sake.
The wise practitioner, with senses restrained and mind concentrated, should indeed recite [the mantra] one hundred thousand times;
freed from minor offenses and those arising from the great sins, O Goddess, the practitioner shall certainly be liberated—of this there is no doubt. (64)
Having performed a circumambulation there, one should worship Narasiṃha with perfumes, flowers, and incense, bowing one’s head to the Lord. (65)
One should place jasmine flowers anointed with camphor and sandalwood upon the head;
by placing them there at the base of the head, accomplishment (siddhi) arises.
O Supreme Goddess, the stream that flows forth from that lake of saffron-colored water,
which was held by him out of desire—
that stream is called Ūrdhvabhadra (or Turaṅgabhadrā). Having bathed in it, one shall go to heaven.
The stream of Mandara that rests upon the northern quarter is known as the Kāverī; by bathing in it, one's sin is destroyed.
The stream belonging to Subhadra is considered to be the Tāmraparṇī;
by bathing in it on the fourteenth lunar day, the destruction of sins occurs.
The wise know that the stream of the Hayamedha sacrifice is the Kauśikī;
having bathed in the Kauśikī according to the prescribed rites, one is liberated from all sins. (70)
The stream of Gokarṇa is known as the Śiprā stream;
by merely bathing in the Śiprā, even a poor man becomes wealthy. (71)
The stream of the Boar is indeed remembered as the Karatoyā;
by touching the waters of the Karatoyā, one is glorified in the world of Viṣṇu.
The stream that flows from Maṇikūṭa is indeed Sarasvatī;
by drinking its clear water, a man is not born again.
O noble lady, he who bathes in the waters of the Sarasvatī and beholds Puruṣottama obtains the fruit of thousands of horse-sacrifices.
Whatever fruit is proclaimed for renunciation as described,
and whatever fruit is proclaimed for various kinds of severe austerities—
a man attains that fruit simply by seeing Kṛṣṇa and bowing down to him. (75)
Furthermore, O beautiful one, what is the use of saying more regarding his majesty?
Having seen Kṛṣṇa and having bowed down to him, a man attains liberation, which is difficult to obtain. (76)
Freed from sins arising from tens of millions of kalpas, his soul purified, endowed with supreme splendor, and delighted by all virtuous qualities. || 77 ||
Honored by the gods, he shall travel in a celestial chariot (vimāna) that fulfills all desires;
having uplifted twenty-one generations of his lineage, he shall at last go to the city of Viṣṇu.
There, having enjoyed captivating pleasures for as long as a hundred kalpas together with Gandharvas and Apsarases, he was like the four-armed Viṣṇu.
Having passed away from there, he comes here to be born into a family preeminent among brahmins;
he becomes all-knowing, truthful in speech, and free from envy.
Devoted to his own duty, tranquil, and intent on the welfare of his dependents, having attained Vaiṣṇava knowledge, he shall thereafter obtain liberation. || 81 ||
Whatever merit one might gain by remaining without food on Kurukṣetra for seven years, standing on one foot with senses conquered and anger subdued; || 82 ||
Having observed a fast and beheld Puruṣottama even once on the twelfth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Jyeṣṭha, one obtains a fruit far greater than that.
Therefore, O Great Goddess, O Supreme Sovereign, one should visit [the shrine] during the month of Jyeṣṭha;
having reached the world of Viṣṇu, they never fall again.
Then, having performed the eightfold pilgrimage (aṣṭatīrtha), Puruṣottama should be beheld;
even from a great distance, one who recites the name of Puruṣottama with devotion [attains the goal].
Day after day, that pure-souled person who, with concentration and faith, performs the pilgrimage of Kṛṣṇa, shall go to the city of Viṣṇu. (86)
Upon seeing from afar the banner of Hari situated atop the temple, a man shall be liberated from all sins and go to the world of Viṣṇu. (87)
A man who, with devotion, bows down to him and dwells at Viṣṇupuṣkara for the four months of the rainy season, is instantly liberated from sin. (88)
Those wise ones who dwell right there at all times obtain the full fruit of a third pilgrimage and even more. (89)
One who has conquered the senses and conquered anger obtains the fruit of austerity;
even if a man performs penance at other sacred sites for ten thousand years, [he does not attain it here]. (90)
Whatever one obtains by means of austerity, celibacy, and the renunciation of attachment during the month of Puruṣottama, that same fruit one obtains then. 91.
The wise constantly obtain that fruit there—the merit which is proclaimed to result from bathing and giving gifts at all sacred fords (tīrthas). || 92 ||
Whatever has been declared regarding the fruit of perfect, variegated giving, as well as through vows and observances, he obtains that fruit there daily, being self-restrained and pure. 93.

Whatever fruit a man obtains through various kinds of sacrifices, he obtains that very fruit and attains liberation; there is no doubt about this. [He obtains that fruit which is difficult to attain and they reach liberation; there is no doubt.]
One who has restrained the senses obtains that fruit there every single day. || 94 ||
(Additional reading, p. 314): Those persons who cast off their bodies in the sacred field of Viṣṇupuṣkara, having reached the Kalpavṛkṣa tree, are liberated; of this there is no doubt.
Those who cast off their physical frame at the foot of the Vaṭa tree until the arrival of Vallabha...
They attain supreme liberation, which is difficult to obtain; of this there is no doubt.
Even that man who gives up his life there against his will, being liberated from suffering, goes to that liberation which is hard to attain. (95)
Even those who belong to the animal realm, such as worms, insects, and fish, having cast off their bodies there, attain the supreme goal. (96)
He who was formerly proclaimed as the Supreme Self (Paramātman) in the Purāṇas and Vedānta—that Puruṣottama remains here for the sake of fulfilling desires and providing assistance. || 97 ||
Whether on a path, in a cremation ground, in a house pavilion, in a forest region, or in a place called Vārāṇasī—
wherever on earth a person casts off the body, whether wishing for it or not, they attain liberation. (98)
Those who delight in Kṛṣṇa, who remember Kṛṣṇa at night, and who again remember Kṛṣṇa upon waking,
enter Kṛṣṇa when their bodies are dissolved, just as an oblation consecrated by mantras enters the sacrificial fire.
Then, having meditated upon Gaṇapati, one should worship him with sweetmeats such as *laḍḍukas* and so forth;
one should honor him with red *karavīra* and *bandhūka* flowers.
Having performed circumambulation, one should then propitiate him with the mantra. || 100 ||
To the pot-bellied one, the pure one, the elephant-faced one,
the lofty one, adorned with sweetmeats and a goad—
he who bears both celebrated qualities.
Salutation be to that Puruṣa, the Lord of the Gaṇas. || 101 ||
At the beginning and the end of the pilgrimage, one should also worship Gaṇeśa.
Then, having gone to Maṇikūṭa, one shall attain the desired state. (102)
Therefore, one should propitiate that God, the Supreme Person, with devotion:
"Salutations to you, O Lord of all worlds, the bestower of fearlessness upon your devotees. (103)
O Supreme Person, save me who am submerged in the ocean of saṃsāra!
O Lord of the World, whatever worship has been performed by me at Maṇikūṭa, [may it be accepted]. (104)
"O Govinda, by your grace, may those [desires] of mine be fulfilled.
Having thus propitiated that god and prostrated himself like a staff, he [spoke]. || 105 ||
Then, having worshipped the preceptor with devotion using gold, garments, and ointments,
one should offer the arghya to the Sun and thereafter feed the Brahmins.
Whoever should read it, or even hear it, or cause it to be heard with a concentrated mind,
shall go to the eternal world of Viṣṇu, cleansed of all impurities.

This [teaching] is auspicious, a destroyer of sins, bestowing both worldly enjoyment and liberation; it is secret, highly difficult to obtain, and meritorious. It should not be given to just anyone—not to an atheist, nor to a fool, nor to an ungrateful person, nor to one who is arrogant. (108)

I have described this most excellent sacred seat (pīṭha) of Puruṣottama, known by the name Kāmākhyā, which is the cause for destroying all sins, bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation, and grants the fruit of every desire.
Thus ends the tenth chapter in the second part of the section on Kāmarūpa, within the *Yoginītantra*, the great king of tantras in twenty-two thousand [verses].
The eleventh chapter.
The Blessed Lord said:
In the land of Bhārata, situated to the south of the southern ocean, there is a place renowned as Kāmarūpa, which bestows both heaven and liberation. || 1 ||
From the Lohita river in the north up to Viśveśvara in the east,
this region is inhabited by those of virtuous character and adorned with every excellence.
Those Brāhmaṇas born in that region who have their senses restrained, and who are devoted to austerity and the study of the Vedas, are always worthy of salutation and worship. (3)
At the time of ancestral rites, at weddings, at sacrifices, and at festivals—
in all such undertakings, the twice-born born in that region are highly commended.
There, the Brahmins were devoted to the six duties, masters of the Vedas, knowers of the Itihāsas, and knowers of the meaning of the Purāṇas. || 5 ||
They were skilled in the meaning of all the scriptures, performers of sacrifices, free from envy,
detached from the pursuit of sons and wives, generous givers, and speakers of truth.
The other three castes—the Kṣatriyas and the rest—who are well-restrained, devoted to their own duties, peaceful, and righteous, remain there in those worlds. || 7 ||
In the portion of Venus, the portion of Mercury, and the portion of Mars, all manifestations [arose]:
Āgastya, Śaunaka, Bhāradvāja, and Kapiñjala. (8)
Ātreya, Vātsa, Sāvarṇi, Dhṛta, Kauśika, Jāmadagnya, Vasiṣṭha, Ātreya, and Parāśara. || 9 ||
Kamaṇḍalu, Garga, Śaunaka, and likewise Śaunika;
Śāṇḍilya, and another, as well as Cyavana and Aṅgiras. || 10 ||
These lineages of Brāhmaṇas were established in Kāmarūpa in ancient times;
therefore, O Śāṅkarī, listen to those who are to be honored and saluted, and those who are to be avoided. 11.
And those who reside in the region purified by the Lauhitya [river] to the south, O Dear One, they—starting from the sacred seats (pīṭhas) up to Sauvarcala—are to be avoided. (12)
O Maheśānī, listen with a focused mind as I describe those twice-born ones who reside in Ādityāṃśa and Kāmarūpa during the Kali Yuga. (13)
Bhāradvāja, Raghu, Śaunaka, and Keśava are remembered; likewise Kapiñjala, Agastya, Mādhava, and Dharādhara. || 14 ||
He too, having reached Vārāṇasī and bathed, delivered his ancestors from their lineage;
and from Ātreyī were born Dharma, Bhānu, and Dhanañjaya. (15)
And the high-souled ones who have conquered their senses—Sambhava, Damayantī, Vatsa, Narasiṃha, Dāmodara, and Mahīdhara. (16)
Śubhānta, Patita, Capala, Satyadharman, Sāvarṇa, Śaṅkara, Bhānu, Madhu, and Madhusūdana [are the Manus]. || 17 ||
Sauri, Dhanañjaya, Viṣṇu, Kāmadeva, Hari,
Bhāskara, Bhūdhara, and Rāma— all these remaining ones were possessed of great luster.

Kauśika, Viṣṇu Mādhava who is devoted to dharma, Jamadagnya, Manu, Brahmā, Soma, Bhānu, Purandara—and Bhānu the handsome—as well as all the learned, meritorious, and virtuous ones who have conquered their senses; (p. 318) [all these were present].
Rāma was born from Bhāradvāja; he is remembered as a twice-born man within the inner apartments.
O Goddess, he becomes a sinner; therefore, one should avoid him.
Vasiṣṭha, Damana, Krama, and Trivikrama—[these are the names]. || 21 ||
From Pārāśara, however, Ātreyī gave birth to Bhānu, who is remembered as the one clad in yellow garments (Pītāmbara).
From Kamaṇḍalu, the Prajāpati, two brothers devoted to righteousness were born.
Both Ugra and Dhaneśa—[namely Ugreśvara and Dhaneśvara]—were devoted to the hermitage;
O Maheśvarī, he himself became Gaṅgānīlāmbara, so it is said.
From Śaunaka came Balabhadra, and from Madana came Gadādhara;
from Kauśika came Vāsudeva, and his son was Mahīdhara.
Nārāyaṇa, Dhruva, Acyuta, and Viṣṇu—
these were born from Vasiṣṭha and likewise emerged while staying in their hermitages.
From Śāṇḍilya were born Manmatha, Soma, Kṛṣṇa, and Divākara; and from Cyavana were born Rāma as well as Dhanañjaya. || 26 ||
Lakṣmīpati, Śrīpati, Bhava, and Śubhāśaya;
Aparastha, Bradhya, Narasiṃha, and Mahīdhara—[these are the names]. (27)
Baladeva, Bhānu, Purandara, and Dharādhara—these were born from the serpent [Karkoṭaka], having taken up the burden of the earth. || 28 ||
From Cyavana, Bhūdhara was born, who is celebrated as having fallen [from heaven];
and from Āṅgirasa came Lakṣaṇa, who was righteous and possessed of true valor.
O beloved, he who belongs to the Śāṇḍilya and Madhyaga lineages is also most worthy of worship;
O my dear, Bhīma, Dāmodara, Vatsa, and Vedagargha are likewise dear to me.
p. 319) Those who were born in the portion of Śukra, two by two in each lineage, and one of these being preeminent—thousands of such Vrātyas have been born. || 31 ||
Furthermore, O beautiful one, those vrātyas mentioned in the supreme tantra were brought down by Śāmba himself;
the Sun, stationed in the field of the earth, was likewise descended. (32)
Sāmbāditya is thus renowned, famous throughout the three worlds;
extending for a full *krośa* in every direction, he bestows the fruits of both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
There the divine Sun himself, the thousand-rayed maker of day, dwells,
having conquered his senses, on every fifth [or seventh] day of the bright fortnight of each month.
O Goddess of gods, having observed a fast and bathed when the sun is in Capricorn,
one should bathe according to the rules in the Lauhitya river and worship with a concentrated mind.
Having gratified the gods, sages, humans, and ancestors, remaining restrained in speech,
he should emerge from the water and put on two freshly washed, perfectly clean garments.
Having sipped water and become pure on the lower bank of the Lauhitya,
he should sit facing east at the time of sunrise, likewise toward the sun.
Having drawn an eight-petalled lotus with red sandalwood water, including its filaments and so forth— a circular design with a white pericarp at the top— the wise one [should proceed]. (38)
And having placed sesame seeds, rice, water, red sandalwood paste,
a red flower, and *darbha* grass into a copper vessel, (verse 39).
In the absence of copper, however, O Great Goddess, having placed sesame-water in a cup of *arka* wood and covering it, one should set that vessel down within another vessel. (40)
Having performed the ritual placement of the limbs and the body (*karāṅganyāsavinyāsa*) by means of the *aṅga*, *hṛdaya*, and other mantras,
and having meditated upon oneself as the Sun with perfect faith, [in some versions...]
[There is not] || 41 ||

The wise one should worship the Root in the center, at the tooth of Agni, at the tooth of Nairṛti and Vāyu, and likewise in the sphere of Kāma and so forth; indeed, one should worship the Root in the center.

Having worshipped the abundant, stainless, and essential [deity], one should indeed propitiate the bliss of the mind; having fully honored the lotus and commenced [the rite], one should invoke the sun there from the sky. (43)
Having established [the deity] upon the pericarp, one should then display the mudrās;
having performed all the worship and so forth, one should remain concentrated, meditating upon him. (44)
Upon a red lotus, well-established is one of red splendor [the sun-disk situated in the center];
he has tawny eyes and a massive body, with a lotus in his hand and reddish garments. 45.
Endowed with all the primary marks, adorned with every ornament,
his own form bestows strength, peaceful, and graced by a halo of light.
Seeing the rising sun, which resembled thick vermilion,
he then took that vessel and knelt upon the ground with his knees.
Having placed that vessel upon his head, with a one-pointed mind and restrained speech,
he should offer the *arghya* to the Sun with the three-syllabled mantra.
Even if he is uninitiated, one who is devoted to worship should honor him as well, until he beholds Viṣṇu, Śaṅkara, or Maheśvara (Sureśvara). (49)
Therefore, exerting effort, one should offer the arghya water day after day;
having bathed and become pure, one who offers it to Āditya shall obtain his desired fruit.
Having entered and performed three circumambulations,
the wise man should worship the Sun with both Tantric and Vedic mantras dedicated to him.
O Supreme Goddess, having bathed in the Kapotakuṇḍa, one should worship Āditya with supreme devotion and ascend the Mountain of Sunrise.
There, O Queen of the Gods, by worshipping the Sun, one obtains the desired fruit;
having bathed according to the rules on a Sunday when the Sun is in Aries. (53)
A person obtains the fruit of ten horse-sacrifices,
O Pārvatī, having uplifted seven generations of descendants and seven generations of ancestors.
Being sung to by Gandharvas, he goes to the world of the Sun in a celestial chariot that has the brilliance of the sun, moves at will, and is full of splendor.
The man who performs the Madanabhañjikā procession during the bright fortnight of the month of Caitra shall obtain everything previously mentioned. || 56 ||
O Maheśvarī, [this applies] at the rising from sleep, as well as at the passage of the sun (saṅkrānti) and the solstices (ayana), on the day of the week and the lunar date, and indeed at all times.
Those who perform a pilgrimage there with faith and with their senses restrained go to the world of the Sun by means of a celestial chariot with the brilliance of the sun. (58)
There resides Mahādeva to the south of that deity, renowned as Rāmeśvara, the bestower of the fruits of all desires. (59)
Those who behold him performing austerities after bathing in the Karaṇapāyasa at Kāmādi—whether they be men or women—shall obtain the fruit of all desires. || 60 ||

To its east is the Navadhanuḥ-kuṇḍa; within the interval of nine dhanus—meaning with a distance of nine dhanus between them—is this hundred-cubit kuṇḍa, which originated from the rays of the sun. (61)
There stands a lake whose waters arise from all sacred fords (tīrthas);
having bathed in the waters of all those tīrthas and having sprinkled water upon his head with kuśa grass, [he remains there].
A man liberated from all sins goes to heaven;
it is located to the east of Dharmāraṇya, extending for seven dhanus.
Having bathed there in the lake called Kapota, one shall go to the state of immortality [or the purified state]. O lord of rivers, you who are named Kapota and are born from the rays of the sun! 64.
"Remove the sin committed by me over ten lifetimes; salutations be unto you today!
O Daughter of Śaṅkara, having offered the arghya with the *tāra* mantra, one should then bathe while reciting the mantra. (65)
The sin committed over ten lifetimes perishes in that very instant.
To the west of that [place], extending for a distance of ten bows (dhanus), [is the site].
Having bathed there in the lake known as Karaṇa, one shall go to heaven from that place.
I pay homage, O Lord of Beings, O Master worshipped by Brahmā!
Hūṃ gāṃ guṃ! Homage to you, O Amṛta of Karaṇa, within the paths of smoke. [The verse is left incomplete.]
By bathing with this mantra, one shall go to the abode of Brahmā.
One should perform the bath on the seventh lunar day in either the month of Phālguna or Māgha. (67)
Especially during the bright fortnight, one is glorified in the world of the Sun;
and at the western side of Kapota is the bow measuring eleven [units]. (68)
There is a lake named Vasiṣṭha there; by bathing on the fifth day of the month of Kārtika with the Vāruṇa mantra, one shall attain the world of Varuṇa.
Likewise, on the eighth day of the month of Mārgaśīrṣa, having bathed and worshipped Janārdana,
one should worship Him with great devotion through fasting at midnight [or throughout the day and night].
And on the eleventh day, O Goddess of Gods, one is glorified in the world of Viṣṇu;
one should perform the śrāddha rite, the shaving of the head, and give gifts according to the prescribed rule.
Having ascended that immovable mountain, one is not born again on earth;
the Śiva-yūpa is to the west of Nakṣatrakūṭa in the north-western direction.
To the south is the Nārmada mountain, to the north is the Harakūpaka, and to the east is the Nāga mountain; O beloved, that [place] is the most excellent in the center.
O beloved, Mahīkṣetra is a great field, superior even to Kurukṣetra;
bathing, giving gifts, austerity, and fire-offerings—all these yield inexhaustible merit there.
To the east of Bhasmācala, extending for as many as a thousand bow-lengths, is that auspicious field named Candana, which is equal to Vārāṇasī. (75)
Therein lies the Vārāṇasī-pool, measuring five bow-lengths;
having bathed there according to the prescribed rite, a man attains absolute liberation.
In that very place, on the eastern side, there is a Vāyu-kuṇḍa measuring three dhanus;
having bathed there on the ninth lunar day, a person is glorified in the upper world [properly,
in the heavenly world].
Having bathed there on the ninth day, one [resides] in the heavenly world. || 77 ||
And by dying in that sacred field, one is not born again anywhere;
having attained the Pāśupata knowledge, one shall thereafter obtain liberation. || 78 ||
Situated in the northwestern quarter of the sacred seat (pīṭha), at a distance of merely a glance, is the mountain Vṛṣākāra, also known as Somagiri and Vṛṣabhācala. || 79 ||
To the south of that pool is the lake known as Nandikuṇḍa;
by bathing there during an eclipse of the moon or sun, a person shall attain liberation.
There stands a Śiva-liṅga named Nandīśvara;
by worshipping it, O Goddess, one is liberated from all sins. (81)
Having become free from disease in this world and attained supreme happiness,
and having reached the abode of Brahmā in the end, one shall thereafter attain liberation.
Having bathed at Nandikaṇḍa, a man should likewise observe a fast during the night;
then, on the following day, he should proceed toward Bhasmācala.
Situated at a mere glance's distance to the northwest of Vṛṣācala,
one who has conquered his senses should worship the Liṅga there named Ratna.
One whose self is purified of all sins is glorified in the world of Śiva. To the northeast of the mountain, there is indeed a lake named Kānnaka. (85)
Having bathed at a distance of eight bow-lengths, one is glorified in the world;
to its northeast are the two caves of Śiva and Viṣṇu.
Having bathed there, a man or a woman is liberated from the bondage of worldly existence.
Right there is Gaṅgākuṇḍa, measuring sixteen dhanus.
Having bathed and drunk there, one casts off the sin of killing a Brahmin;
facing that direction, eating sacrificial food and self-restrained, one should spend the day there.
Then, when another day has arrived, one should go to Nakṣatraparvata.
She is situated to the south of Rasakūṭa, not very far away. || 90 ||
In the midst of the great earth, that river which flows toward the north is known as the Puṣpanadī; it liberates one from all sins.
Having bathed there on the Mahāmāghī day, a person goes to the abode of the gods;
having bathed throughout the entire month of Māgha, one shall go to Viṣṇupurī.
Having bathed on the ninth day of the bright fortnight of Caitra, one's sin is destroyed;
that Gaṅgā of the Dvāpara age originates from Viṣṇukūṭa.
O Great Goddess, having bathed there in the Mātṛyoni (or Mahāyoni), a noble-souled person is not born again.
One should perform the tonsure at that holy site while staying together with the Mahīkṣetra.
Having worshipped the Nāga at that very place [on Nāgakūṭa], it is said that the fruit is twofold.
There, bathing, recitation, and fire-offerings—all these shall become inexhaustible. (95)
Having bathed on the seventh lunar day falling on a Sunday with a restrained mind,
one shall indeed be free from disease in this world, and in the end, go to the city of Śiva.
In the western part of the field, that stream which flows toward the north should be known as the Maladhārā; one who bathes there becomes free from sin.
Therefore, one should not touch its water, nor should one dwell upon its bank;
if one has touched it through negligence, one should perform the *pauṣpaka* bath merely by means of bathing.
Alternatively, one may touch the Sun at a holy pilgrimage site;
this is the merit-bestowing field of the high-souled Bhārgava. 99.
Having known this, a person goes toward the abode of Śaṅkara;
and to the east of that sacred field is the meritorious river Candrikā.
O Great Goddess, having bathed in that [tirtha] within the Yamāntara, one shall go to heaven;
in its north-eastern quarter is indeed the Kṛttivāsas Liṅga. (101)
Having worshipped that [liṅga] with diligence, one rejoices in heaven like Śiva;
likewise, a man who bathes in the Candrikā and worships Kṛttivāsas [attains the same]. || 102 ||
On the fourth day of the bright fortnight of Bhādrapada, a man shall become free from blemish;
O Maheśānī, she is situated within a krośa to the east.
The meritorious river Phenalā (also known as Kalilā) originates from the Gaṅgā mountains;
having bathed in the Phenilā, especially during the month of Phālguna at Karatāla, a man [attains great merit]. || 104 ||

On the thirteenth day of the dark fortnight of Āṣāḍha, during the excellent transit [of the sun], there stands the meritorious river that destroys sin, where the water is pure and the arghya-offering has been well-prepared. (105)
O Śāṅkarī, the goddess named Madanā emerges from the fire of desire;
by bathing according to the rules in Caitra or on the full moon day of Caitra, one obtains the fruit of bathing in the Gaṅgā. || 106 ||
Having frequently ascended the mountain and bathed in the waters of Madana,
one should worship Maheśvara on the fourth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Māgha.
Having attained all his desires, he goes to the world of Śiva;
and there the river Trisrotas is situated on the right side.
There, two Śiva-liṅgas eternally assume the form of Bhairava;
Kṣīroda and Maheśa are situated within the cave.
Endowed with faith, one should worship with the *dhruva* mantra alone, using side-mantras as well, along with perfumes, flowers, incense, food offerings, and even according to one's means. (110)
In the cave-forest dwell the exceedingly powerful monkeys;
having approached Śaṅkara while he is being served there, one should propitiate him. || 111 ||
Upon seeing the monkeys, fearlessness arises on earth;
there is abundance of sons and grandsons, as well as wealth, grain, and excellent women. (112)
One obtains one's desired objects within six months; of this there is no doubt.
To the east of Kāmākhyā is the river Kṣīrodā, which flows for six [yojanas].
Having bathed there according to the prescribed rites, one is liberated from all sins;
on the mountain Amarakaṇṭaka (or Śarakaṇṭaka), in the eastern part of the Kṣīroda [ocean].
There, the Śoṇeśvara Liṅga is made of beautiful stone from the Guru mountain;
by worshipping it with diligence, a person does not experience sorrow. (115)
There, O Maheśvarī, to the south is the Ghaṭeśvara Liṅga;
having beheld that most formidable Liṅga with faith and a well-composed mind, [one attains the fruit]. || 116 ||
Having bathed him with devotion using delightful perfumes and flowers,
and having performed this on the fourteenth or the eighth day of the bright fortnight,
he rescues his lineage of five generations and goes to the world of Śiva.
O Great Goddess, in the southeast is the Gandhamādana mountain. || 118 ||
In the western and eastern corners of that [place], there are two caves;
by bathing there, one obtains the fruit of the Aśvamedha sacrifice. || 119 ||
On the eastern part of the mountain, at Lauhitya, there is a holy site named Vilvasaras extending for eight bow-lengths; by bathing there, one's sin is destroyed.
On the northern side of the lake, having worshipped the two feet of Bhṛṅgīśa (or Bhṛṅgeśa),
and then worshipping Bhṛṅga, one shall attain the status of a Gaṇapati.
There, by the offering of funeral cakes (piṇḍa), one becomes free from debt to the ancestors.
To the south of that mountain is a mountain named Nivedha. || 122 ||
In its north-eastern part are two caves of Manmatha;
having bathed there, a man or a woman shall attain the world of Brahmā.
Not far from that mountain, however, is a mountain named Niṣadha;
to its north, in the Lauhitya region, it extends for a measure of seven bows.
The sacred ford named Piśācamocana is extremely difficult to attain;
having bathed there with the Tāra mantra, one certainly does not fall into the state of a preta. (125)
O Goddess, O Supreme Sovereign, by climbing a mountain on the southern shore of the Red Sea, one incurs the sin of killing a Brahmin.
The excellent river named Caṇḍikā always flows toward the south;
O lady of beautiful hips, bathing there destroys even the most heinous sins. (127)

On the seventh day of the bright fortnight of Māgha and on the fifteenth day of Phālguna, a woman who has suffered the death of her children should bathe and drink milk; thus she shall never again lose her offspring.
Having performed a bath according to the prescribed rite, one obtains the fruit of the Rājasūya sacrifice;
merely by performing the Mausala bath, one obtains the fruit of the Rājasūya sacrifice and attains the Aśvamedha.
O Maheśvarī, in the north-eastern part of that place, on the Bhūmipīṭha...
Know that the sacred field named Paṅkaja extends for one krośa;
there, one intent on devotion should worship Śaṅkara as Bhṛṅgīśa.
Then, having bathed at Caṇḍikā and performed a circumambulation of the sacred field, one should worship Śaṅkara with devotion; such a person is glorified in the world of Brahmā.
Having worshipped throughout the entire month of Vaiśākha, that best of men,
having reached the world of Viṣṇu, shall thereafter attain liberation.
Four-armed, white in color, seated upon a lotus, radiant with a crown, wearing bright earrings, and adorned with a necklace of serpents. || 133 ||
Holding a trident and a drum, esteemed for granting boons and fearlessness, endowed with all auspicious marks, and adorned with a crown of matted hair. (134)
Having meditated, one should worship with the Aghora mantra and the Śiva-tantra;
taking a handful of flowers, one should worship with the individual mantras. || 135 ||
One should offer blood and worship Rudrajaṭa with Dhuttūra flowers, [saying]:
"Salutations to you, O Blessed One, O God, O Guardian of the World, O Lord of the Universe. (136)
I bow down to the Lord Bhṛṅgīśa (also known as Ghṛṅgarīśa), the unborn Viśveśvara, the imperishable sustainer of the universe and the creator of all worlds. 137.
Having gone north from Lohita, one should ascend Mount Darpaṭa (Karkaṭa).
There, one should worship Kubera, who is white in form and identical with Brahmā. || 138 ||
In its north-eastern part are two caves of Kubera;
having bathed in that pool, a man is glorified in the world of Viṣṇu.
To its southeast is Rohiṇa, the best of mountains, which has the appearance of rising;
upon it, iron and other metals, when touched, instantly attain the state of gold [or become golden-hued].
In the Kali age, one should offer an oblation to Kubera at the location on the ground known as the dvādaśānta, ensuring it is not empty by including a side dish.
O Śāṅkarī, in the Kali age, during the portion belonging to Āditya,
the river named Kūrpaṭa, which indeed issued from the mouth of Maheśa, becomes manifest.
Having bathed there on the fourteenth day, one shall attain the world of Varuṇa;
he remains upon the surface of the earth, having assumed the form of a Rohita fish.
"O Dhanadeśvara, for the sake of the welfare of the mortal world, take away my sinful *kūrpaṭa*.
Having bathed with this mantra, [one should worship] Dhanadeśvara. (144)
Having worshipped according to the rules with devotion, one is glorified in the world of Soma;
having bathed according to the rules at Lauhitya, one should ascend the Vahni mountain.
Having worshipped the fire right there in the fire-pile within the circle of fire, one attains the world of Viṣṇu and rejoices together with Viṣṇu. || 146 ||
To the east of Vahnikūṭa is the mountain named Kamala;
right there is the Vāruṇa Liṅga and the pool called Vāruṇa.
Having bathed there and worshipped Varuṇa, one shall become wealthy.
Not very far to the east of that place is a mountain named Kāliṅga.

One endowed with faith should worship the Liṅga named Yameśvara on the new moon day of the dark fortnight of the month of Māgha; the world of Yama perishes for him, and Śamana does not behold him. (149)
To its northeast is a stone image of Pāṇḍu in the form of Kṛṣṇa;
having seen and touched it with devotion, one is never born again anywhere. (150)
To its northwest is Dhanu, measuring one *rudra* [five] in extent;
it is the great *tīrtha* Gaṅgātīrtha, where sin is destroyed by bathing. (151)
To its east are Navadhana and Sumadrā; having bathed at the two caves there and touched the Pāṇḍuśilā stone with the Kāmabīja mantra, one should proceed from there.
Having worshipped the Lord of Drama (Nāṭakeśa), one is glorified in the world of Indra;
[to the deity] who holds a book and the gesture of fearlessness in his hands, and who bears a rosary. || 153 ||
Homage to him who resides on the *parkaṭa* tree, homage indeed to Pāṇḍunātha;
then one should propitiate the deity within the range of vision of a mortal [to the north]. (154)
On that well-situated mountain, which has the form of a palace, one should resort to that mountain with each of the seven seers individually. || 155 ||

Having bathed in the Gaṅgā-kuṇḍa and worshipped, a man should ascend Ṛṣiparvata; there, on the Seven Mountains, he should worship the Seven Sages in order, starting from the center and proceeding eastward. || 156 ||
Having prostrated before the Lord of Mountains, one should worship him with perfumes and flowers;
for such a person, there is no fear in his lineage, and he becomes a meritorious man on earth. || 157 ||
Being sung of by Gandharvas, they indeed go to the world of Śiva.
To the north of that is the great tree, the Kalpa-tree, which is a Bilva tree.
Having gone there and worshipped with the root-mantra, O Goddess Śāṅkarī, one rejoices upon the vault of heaven by virtue of worshipping trees with their leaves. (159)
One should not worship with its leaf; this rule is prescribed for all cases.
To the northwest of it is the mountain Dhanadapuraskāraka.
One should worship Nāṭakeśa, who stands in the middle of the great cavity;
to the right of that deity is the abode of Vāsava together with his three weapons.
By bathing in its eastern [pool], a person becomes free from disease at that very moment; and by bathing in the central pool, one who is poor becomes wealthy—this is not otherwise.
Having first bathed at Dhatrika in the Kuṇḍa, one is not tainted by the defects of the planets;
O Goddess, wherever a man may be situated, he is freed from such afflictions by bathing in the waters of this lake.
Afterwards, [one should worship] the god Virūpākṣa, the goddess Śivā Siddheśvarī, Gaṇa Caṇḍa, Kārttikeya, Gaṇeśa, and likewise the Bull. (164)
One goes to the Kalpadruma, Sāvitrī, and the world of Śiva;
[this occurs] in the middle part to the north of that, near the inner chamber. || 165 ||
On the delightful Bhūṣaṇḍa mountain, to the north of Vāsudeva,
there is the Yoni of Siddheśvarī, measuring two cubits in size.
O Śāṅkarī, having honored her with a yak-tail whisk while reciting the Tārā mantra,
one should worship her on the eighth lunar day and observe a fast.
By offering meat, milk-rice, vegetables, and other such foods, one becomes possessed of sons and prosperity.
To the east of that [shrine], on the peak of Vilva, one should worship Virūpākṣa.
To the west of Siddheśvarī, on the mountain Sumadāha, there is a mountain in the form of an elephant, possessing a high current and black-colored. || 169 ||
Having worshipped the god Gaṇapati, there shall be no obstacle in the family;
and one should worship Candra and Kārttikeya in the two eastern caves.
Likewise, within the midst of the Aṅgaja stone, there is another [stone] in the form of mud,
marked by the celestial Gaṅgā, red-protecting, and golden.
O Goddess, Siddheśī, who always grants all desires, is established at Śrīkūṭa.
The water has reached the end of the triangle; there is an enclosure around those [elements] from the hexagon.
The field measures five cubits; the wish-fulfilling tree is a *campaka*;
it is born from a bull, white in color, and shaped like a bull on the shore of a lake. (173)
To the south of Bhavakuṇḍa is Sāvitrī, and likewise to the north;
he who, with his senses restrained, performs the ritual at those sacred fords according to the rules, [attains the fruit]. (174)
Having rescued seven generations of his lineage, he goes to the world of the goddesses after seeing Mount Nīlācala to the east of Nāṭaka. (175)
That field named Kambana, as well as Harikṣetra and others, are the fruits [of practice];
there, in the accomplishment of mantras, one shall obtain the desired fruit. (176)
Upon ascending the mountain, one should release the stone-position;
on the right side, one should perform the slaying, which is delightful from the southern part. || 177 ||
One should perform attraction in the east and eradication in the west;
Subhadrā is in the southeast, situated at a distance of merely a glance. (178)
Situated upon the surface of the earth by the Kāmottara mountain, there is the Dīrgheshvarī-yoni in the form of a red stone. || 179 ||
On the eighth lunar day, with his senses restrained, he should worship with supreme devotion using various kinds of perfumes and flowers, employing the seed-syllable of Māyā and the syllable of Kāma.
On the fourteenth day of the month of Māgha, one obtains abundant desires;
[therein resides] the four-armed goddess Umā, with full and elevated breasts. (181)
Resembling a mass of vermilion, she holds a curved knife and a skull-cup with her right and left hands, bestowing fearlessness and the gesture of granting boons.
Her head is adorned with matted locks, and she stands upon a red *preta*. || 182 ||
O Supreme Goddess, she should be worshipped with the mantra of Kāmākhyā;
having done this, the heroic man is not born again in a womb.
Twenty bows' length to its east stands a beautiful corpse;
and Durgā is also right there, where by bathing, one's sin is destroyed. || 184 ||
On Mount Umā, Umā is to be worshipped in the form of the Yoni-mudrā;
one should worship her with the Śrī-bīja, and never shall misfortune arise. 185.
There, the Māheśvara Liṅga is situated within the cave;
by worshipping it on the fourteenth day [of the lunar fortnight], one is glorified in the world of Śiva. (186)
To its east, on a mark made by the earth, is the mountain named Kūrma;
and indeed, on the Lauhitya [river], there is a mountain in the form of a tortoise. || 187 ||
Endowed with faith, one should worship with the mantra known as Kūrma;
and below, in Lauhitya, it extends for twenty-two dhanus.
The great sacred ford named Prabhāga destroys sin through bathing;
having bathed there even once, one is glorified in the world of Brahmā.
Whoever shall cause funeral cakes (piṇḍas) to be offered on that beautiful bank of the lake, having uplifted twenty-one generations of his lineage, shall be glorified in the world of Viṣṇu. || 190 ||
To the east of that, at a distance of two arrow-shots,
situated within the Śiva-forest on the delightful Madgura mountain, there is the Madgura Liṅga.
Having duly worshipped the Liṅga, which bestows the fruit of the Rājasūya sacrifice,
[one should do so] in the north-east of the God, within a cave in the Vilva forest.
There, one should worship the Lord Śvetākṣa while uttering his name;
from that very place, on its eastern side, a river flows forth from the best of mountains.
The river known as Maṅgalā, which issued from the mouth of the Kāmadhenu,
flows for only a yāma’s distance toward the western direction and then turns back.
Having left the daughter of the Himalaya mountain, she reached the abode of Kubera;
that sacred field is difficult to attain in the world, having gone to which one no longer grieves.
There, by the offering of funeral cakes (piṇḍa), one becomes free from debt to the ancestors;
at the end of the three watches of the night, the White Gaṅgā and the Water-Mountain arrived there. 196.
In former times, two sisters were encountered there by the great seer Cyavana;
therefore, a wise person should dwell for even a moment in that most excellent and meritorious sacred field. (197)
One obtains the supreme fruit of the Rājasūya sacrifice at that place where Hara always sports in the water together with the Daughter of the Mountain. 198.
And there, O Goddess, it always remains adorned with golden lotuses;
having bathed there on the great full-moon day, it bestows fruit like the Gaṅgā herself. (199)
Whether one performs the immersion in the west or likewise in the east, for such a person there is the destruction of all sins; no further expiation is required. || 200 ||
Where there are indeed auspicious fragrances, where the waters are thick and destroy diseases, that holy place, rich in ascetic merit, is a land of purity where no expiation is required. || 201 ||
Salutations to you, O Auspicious One, O Blessed One, O Destroyer of all sins!
You are the venerable, stainless Rudrā; remove my sin, salutations be to you. (202)
Having performed the bath with this mantra, one should worship the peaceful *satramantra*, the *mata*, as well as *vijaya* and *ambaram*. (203)
One should offer worship and respectful oblations with the *tejasya*, *samaṅga*, and *sasaṅga* mantras as they are recited;
whether one has died in water, in the air, or on land. || 204 ||
Having attained the knowledge of Brahman, he shall go to the eternal Brahman;
liberated from all sins, he shall proceed to the abode of Brahman. || 205 ||
That man who performs the ritual bath throughout the entire month of Māgha [destroys] thousands of killings of Brahmins and various other sins. (206)
O Goddess, at that very moment [the sin] perishes when the sun is situated in Capricorn;
for the wise person who performs a ritual bath on the thirteenth day while the sun is in Pisces or Aries, [the merit is immeasurable]. (207)
Having rescued seven generations of his lineage, he is glorified in the world of Brahmā,
provided that he has bathed according to the rules on the full moon day of Phālguna and beheld the Bull-bannered Lord (Śiva).
Having attained the state of a Gandharva, one is glorified in the world of Śiva;
[this is the place] to the northwest of which, at a distance of two arrow-shots, [is situated].
Having bathed in that very Kapila-kuṇḍa, one should worship the deity;
especially when the new moon day (amāvāsyā) coincides with a Monday.
Then, having gone to Kapileśvara and performed his ablutions according to the prescribed rite,
he shall uplift twenty-one generations of his lineage and go to the supreme state.
O Śāṅkarī, on the ground-pedestal in the eastern part of Maṅgalā, one who beholds the god Keśava there shall go to the city of Viṣṇu. || 212 ||
But those who, having fasted on the new moon day, behold Keśava, become lords of Śvetadvīpa and are glorified in the world of Viṣṇu. || 213 ||
O Supreme Goddess, that stream of hers which flows toward the northeast should be known as the "Blood Stream" (Raktadhārā); one should avoid bathing in it. || 214 ||
To the east of that, O Maheśānī, is the river named Tāpikā;
having bathed in it according to the prescribed rites, one shall attain great fame—or rather, the great goal.
To the northeast of that deity is a supreme river of flowing milk;
having bathed in it according to the prescribed rites during an eclipse of the moon or the sun, [one attains the fruit]. || 216 ||
Having obtained the fruit of a hundred cows, one is honored in the world of Śakra.
O Maheśānī, further to the east of that is the supreme river Vetravatī.
Having bathed in that [river], a person shall obtain the fruit of bathing in the Gaṅgā.
Therefore, in the northeastern quarter, there is a river flowing toward the north. (218)
Therefore, the pool of nectar is indeed honored by the name Tripurā;
having bathed in Tripurā on the twelfth day of the bright fortnight, a man [attains merit]. (219)
Having worshipped the liṅga of Viṣṇu, one shall not enter the peril of the womb;
adorned with that very body, he goes to the abode of Viṣṇu, O wise one.
One should worship with supreme devotion using perfumes, flowers, incense, and unsurpassed offerings, as well as various presentations of food oblations. || 221 ||
At the end of one krośa to the east of that city, the river Dīpavatī is situated;
this river, known as Mandarā, destroys the darkness as effectively as a lamp.
Therefore, among gods and humans, there is the auspicious river Dīpavatī;
having bathed in it according to the prescribed rites, one obtains the fruit of all sacrifices. || 223 ||
O Maheśānī, there is a most rare river born from Padmamānasa called Durvārā; having bathed there, one shall go to heaven. 224.
Having bathed at the Durvāra Viṣuva, or especially on the full moon day of Kārttika, || 225 ||
Completely liberated from all sins, he shall attain the state of Brahman. There is a supreme river of auspicious waters originating from Pañcamānasa. || 226 ||
Having bathed there, O Maheśvarī, a man or a woman shall not enter into rebirth;
[there is] the great liṅga Someśvara to the south.
Having worshipped that [liṅga], O Maheśānī, one rejoices upon the surface of heaven;
nearby it, not too far away, is another supreme river named Padmā.
Born from Padmamānasa, she is celebrated as Uttarasravā. || 229 ||
And having bathed there according to the prescribed rites, one obtains the fruit of an Ashvamedha sacrifice.
In the Kali age, O beloved, that place in my Bilva-kshetra is renowned as Panchanadi.
Somavatī, Yajñadhārā, Kanakābhā, Nadī, and [Nadīvatī], Padmāvatī, and Pañcadhārā—these are known as the five rivers and are remembered as the Pañcanadī. || 231 ||
And having bathed there according to the prescribed rules, especially on the eighth and fourteenth days of the month of Caitra, one is glorified in the world of Śiva.
To its east is the auspicious and famous Varaṇadī, known as Campāvatī;
it flows from the Kadamba-bila and merges into that river which carries the Yāma.
And having bathed there according to the prescribed rites, one obtains the merit of an Ashvamedha sacrifice;
for she, born from the Mānasa lake of Kadamba, bestows fruits like the Gaṅgā herself. || 236 ||
