O Gomaheśānī of manifold forms, destroy my sin; salutations be unto you!
Having bathed in the waters of Campāvatī and especially having beheld Śambhu, [one attains liberation]. || 237 ||
Having beheld Gaurī, the Queen of the Gods, one is not born again in a womb;
for there the Blessed Lord Śambhu is established in the form of a Liṅga. || 238 ||
Viṣṇu, assuming the form of a stone and bearing the form of the Brahma-linga, is situated on its western bank, not very far away. (239)
One krośa to the east of it is known as Divyaputranada;
by bathing there on the new moon day, one obtains the fruit of all sacred fords (tīrthas). || 240 ||
O Supreme Goddess, he who bathes throughout the entire month of Kārttika obtains the supreme fruit of a thousand horse-sacrifices.
In the divine city, there is a supreme river that destroys all sins;
having bathed there with the mantra, men go to heaven, fully purified. (242)
Having performed his bath with this [mantra] on the bank, he should present the arghya offering;
having bathed in the waters of the divine city and beheld the three-eyed Lord.
Having rescued the entire world, he is glorified in the heavenly realm;
he who, having crossed the river Campāvatī, performs his ablutions elsewhere [is likewise blessed]. || 244 ||
It bestows fruit in the north, the west, and indeed the south;
having bathed there once while observing silence, to the south of Madhukūṭa.
Having bathed duly in the Mānasa lake, one should worship Kapardin;
one obtains the desired fruit of the Rājasūya sacrifice. || 246 ||
By the sight of her, a mortal purifies his lineage up to the seventh generation;
indeed, by seeing that goddess even once, having worshipped and prostrated before her with devotion. || 247 ||
A man who has himself extracted [the soul] does not go to the world of Yama;
other stainless Mothers of the World remain there.
All these goddesses are removers of sin, bestowers of boons, and affectionate toward their devotees;
there stands the supreme Vaitaraṇī Tīrtha, which removes all sins.
Having bathed there, an excellent man is liberated from all sins.
Not far to the east of the Goddess is the Vaitaraṇīya pool.
It is twenty *dhanus* in length, with eight *dhanus* in the middle;
there, Hari himself dwells in person in the form of a boar.
Having seen and bowed with devotion to him, a person shall go to the city of Viṣṇu;
[so too shall one go there by visiting] Kapilā-gogṛha and Somatīrtha at the place known as Lobha.
At Mṛtyuñjaya, Siddhatīrtha, Vāsuki, and Siddhakeśvara—at these sacred sites and fields of pilgrimage—the wise man, with his senses restrained, [should perform worship] at Viraja. (253)
Having duly performed the consecration of the sacred site, bathed, and bowed to the deity,
a man who himself bathes there goes to the world of the immortals.
And whoever goes to Virajā and performs the offering of funeral cakes (piṇḍa), he provides inexhaustible satisfaction for the ancestors; there is no doubt about this. || 255 ||
O Maheśānī, those men who cast off their bodies at Āgastya and Virajā indeed attain liberation. || 256 ||
Having worshipped the Supreme Goddess with the Tārā mantra and its ritual manual,
using animal products, milk, and perfumes, along with extensive displays of great opulence.
To its east, O Maheśānī, is the mountain shaped like an umbrella; there, within the center of the liṅga, is the womb named Maṅgalā Candrikā.
One should worship according to the rules with devotion and is thereby liberated from the bondage of existence [the bondage of karma].
The Vāgbhava, the middle seed-syllable, and the Śrī-bīja should be placed at the front. (259)
Alternatively, another seed-syllable consisting of two letters or a mantra of three syllables has been proclaimed;
its seer (ṛṣi) is Nārada, and its meter (chandas) is celebrated as Gāyatrī. || 260 ||
And Śambhu shall be the deity, while the application (viniyoga) lies in the practice;
O lady of excellent vows, may he unite me with virtue, wealth, desire, and liberation. 261.
Having established there the lotus with three rows of petals, the earth-pavilion to be sung three times, one should perform the worship of the pitcher along with the ancillary rites.
Measuring sixteen finger-breadths, it is charming and two mātrās long;
one should release the *camaka* by sounding it, beginning with the *praṇava*.
One should offer the bali-offering for birds, but one must never present broken foodstuffs; likewise, one should offer plantain, *śamī* leaves, the *dhatrī* fruit, and *tulasī*. (264)
One should not offer *karkaṭī* (crab), nor should one worship it; likewise, one should never offer *varālī* or fish at an improper time. || 265 ||
On a Tuesday, one should perform an extensive worship with abundant offerings;
one should likewise worship on the eighth, the fourteenth, and the thirteenth lunar days. (266)

One should never worship the Goddess at night after bathing in water; likewise, one who has anointed himself with *ciñcā* oil, or one who has asked [for instruction], or even one who has five tufts of hair on his head [should not do so]. 267.
Having eaten garlic or leeks, one should not perform worship for a full month;
one should not worship the Goddess with forbidden foods, nor should one offer anything dyed with indigo.
One should not offer a yak-tail whisk, nor a monitor lizard, nor a wild boar, nor a human being to Mahādevī; however, one may offer a swan and a goat.
A rabbit, a svastika, a rhinoceros, and the vehicle of Yama;
a hibiscus flower, saffron, and a tender bilva leaf. (270)
One should give the midday offering, a horse, an enemy, a victory, red objects, silver, as well as water-born items and those produced in the proper season.
Likewise, there is the red Dantapuṣpa and Viṣṇukrāntā;
and the goddess, two-armed and yellow, wearing golden bracelets. (272)

One should worship her who is in the supreme posture, with hands granting boons and fearlessness, either on a large scale or likewise upon a hide or a woolen blanket, with the pollen of flowers. (273)
Having sat down, one should mutter the mantra; one should perform three hundred thousand recitations as the preliminary rite (*puraścaraṇa*).
On a black antelope skin, there is the attainment of knowledge; on a tiger skin, prosperity and liberation.
On a cloth seat there is liberation from disease; on wool, the release of wealth.
On a leather seat one will be poor; on stone, there is fear born of illness. (275)
On the ground, there is an abundance of wealth; on a wooden seat, misfortune; on a seat of grass, loss of fame; and on a seat of leaves, the loss of riches. (276)
"Know from me, O beloved, that there is always a loss of ascetic merit in the Yantrāsana;
one should worship Vārāhī right there in the western part. (277)
By means of the seed-syllable of the Sun and with fragrant substances, especially on the eighth lunar day, one obtains the supreme fruit of the horse sacrifice (Aśvamedha). || 278 ||
On a rag, one should worship the Liṅga named Yameśa Śaṅkara;
one should worship it thoroughly with the five-petaled *dhruva* flower, perfumes, and other offerings.
And in the west, at Lauhitya, one should know that Rambhātīrtha extends for the measure of a bow; by bathing there, all fear is destroyed. || 280 ||
O Maheśānī, on that mountain, below Mādhava,
there are two lakes measuring sixty-four dhanus in extent.
Having bathed in it, one quickly purifies twenty-one generations of one’s lineage.
To the east of that, on the mountain named Kañjana (or Kajjala), are the two feet of Viṣṇu;
in the Kali age, one should ascend them when they are hidden during the period of renunciation and worship them.
One should never ascend that mountain there known as Cañcala.
The merit accumulated over seven lifetimes perishes at that very moment at the confluence of the Kapilā and the Kajjalī in the western region.
O Daughter of Śaṅkara, bathing according to the prescribed rites at Lauhitya bestows the fruit of an Aśvamedha sacrifice; this extends from Mṛnmūrti up to the confluence of the Kapilā. (285)
O lady of beautiful countenance, the river Piśaṅginī, which resembles the Gaṅgā,
flows at the end of the third watch of the night on the southern side within the Raivata mountain range.
From the middle [line] of the Piśaṅginī, there is the mention of both sides;
now hear indeed of the deities of that sacred site (tīrtha) belonging to the nine-fold pedestal (navapīṭha). || 287 ||
Due to the curse of Vasiṣṭha, having gone to one place, he remained concentrated there;
he established a sacred bathing place (tīrtha) in one spot and likewise installed deities in another.
O Goddess, having bathed according to the prescribed rites, the pilgrimage in the month of Caitra is especially distinguished;
one should worship with supreme devotion and obtain the fruit of every sacred seat (pīṭha). || 289 ||
Situated at a distance of one *yāma* to the southeast of that seat is the great sacred field of Kurukṣetra, where the lake of Brahmā is said to be located.
Having bathed there according to the prescribed rites, one should behold the Grandfather (Brahmā);
one shall obtain the merit born of ten horse-sacrifices—of this there is no doubt. || 291 ||
In its southeastern part, where the Prācī Sarasvatī flows,
one who bathes there according to the prescribed rules is cleansed of the sin of killing a Brahmin.
And Udumbarīvajjātā is considered to have gone for a distance of one yojana;
Udakāpsarā is in the first [quarter], while Paścimāpsarā is in the second. (293)
She was born as Vilā and Kavilā; therefore, she is known as Kavilā.
Having bathed in the Kavilā while the sun is situated in Capricorn, a man [attains merit]. || 294 ||
Having attained all desires, one goes to the world of Śiva;
this [path], created by Brahmā in ancient times, leads to liberation from all sins. (295)
"O Kaśyapa, having bathed in the Nirmala [tirtha], save me from the ocean of worldly existence!
Having performed the bath with this [mantra], one should offer the arghya for the sake of prosperity. (296)
Having seen kuśa grass, sandalwood, and dūrvā grass, together with sesame seeds and unbroken rice, as well as milk and water, the arghya offering is then declared.
Kañjana, Śūnyasambhūta, Vāgara, Vijaya, and likewise Mahāsena, [followed by] Vahnijāyā; this is the six-syllable mantra for the arghya offering. || 298 ||
Having bathed on the eighth day of the bright fortnight in the month of Caitra, or on the full moon day, O Maheśānī, one shall go to heaven; indeed, one shall go to the abode of Śiva.
O Daughter of Śaṅkara, he who bathes throughout the entire month of Kārttika shall be free from disease in this world and shall attain supreme happiness.
In the remainder, having reached the abode of Brahmā, one shall thereafter attain liberation;
and when Kuśāvarta and Daivata have arrived together at Kubjikāmukha. || 301 ||
This [Sarasvatī] is fruitless and difficult to find elsewhere, but she is fruitful at Kuśāvarta;
likewise are the Kubjadhārā and the Prācīdhārā Sarasvatī at Mānasa.
Where there is the confluence of three streams, that place is called Kuśāvarta;
there, for embodied beings, worship, recitation, and fire-offerings become truly efficacious.
All that is given as a śrāddha there at that time becomes inexhaustible, yielding infinite fruit for those whose souls are devoted to the liberation of Brahman.
That supreme and great sacred field extends for a thousand bow-lengths;
at its upper portion, during the half-watch of the night, there is the confluence of only one [river]. || 305 ||
That stream flowing to the south is the great river Kubjī;
having bathed in it, O Cāruvān, one becomes free from disease—this is not otherwise.
The stream of the northern [face], however, is known by the name Mānasa; and that which is proclaimed as the stream of the eastern [face] is Sarasvatī. (307)
Where there is a confluence of the three places, that is proclaimed as Prayāga;
it is located in the north-eastern field at a distance of one bow's length. || 308 ||
Having bathed there at the great holy site known as Kubjī, one shall go to heaven;
upon seeing a son who has reached Kubjī, one becomes free from debt to the ancestors.
Having gone there and sipped water, whether it be a woman or a man who has bathed, one is released from the sin of killing a Brahmin through the grace of Kubjikā. (310)
Where Kālī is present in the form of a quadrangle, there men who offer funeral cakes (piṇḍa) all go to heaven by means of celestial chariots drawn by swans. || 311 ||
On the bank, extending for a hundred bow-lengths as far as the lake of Rāma,
one should go to that sacred field of Bhadrakālī and worship Kālikā.
During the junction between the Kali and Dvāpara ages, Sarasvatī was Guptakālī, [worshipped] with animal products, milk, curd, perfumes, and the like, as well as with meats and offerings.
Therefore, having worshipped the Goddess there in the water at that sacred field (kṣetra), one should perform worship;
by ascending to that field, O Goddess, one obtains abundant prosperity.
Then, having bathed at Kubjikā, whoever should go to Kālīkṣetra, the sin committed throughout their entire life perishes at that very moment. (315)
Whoever performs a libation there, it shall yield infinite fruit;
their ancestors dance and their grandfathers are truly satisfied. (316)
Through libations they obtain satisfaction, and through the offering of funeral cakes they attain heaven.
The great liṅga Ādīśvara is established in the eastern quarter. (317)
Likewise, Āditīrtha bestows liberation even by its mere sight;
having touched Mānasa there, one is released from the bondage of worldly existence.
By immersing oneself in the Brahman, one always attains the supreme state;
moreover, those who have purified their souls, having bathed there, [worship] Janārdana.
Those who worship according to their ability go to the celestial realm;
for among all riches, gold is supreme, and among all purifiers, the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) is supreme. || 320 ||
Likewise, Kubjitīrtha is proclaimed to be the most excellent among all holy fords (tīrthas), just as the Aśvamedha is celebrated as the best among sacrifices. || 321 ||
Likewise, among all sacred fords (tīrthas), Kujvitīrtha is the most excellent;
just as Nārada is the best among the celestial sages (devarṣis), O lady of virtuous vows, so is it for me. (322)
Likewise, among all holy places, Kubjitīrtha is the most excellent;
to the north of the Kālikṣetra is Janārdana, the God of gods.
In the Kali age, he exists in the form of a *liṅga*, hidden and invisible;
there on that shore, one should drink milk with devotion (and effort) using the *nāra* mantra (or the *sāma* mantra).
One is liberated from the sins committed throughout ten lifetimes at that very moment, situated at a distance of only one *krośa* to the west of Kuśāvarta. (325)
Having approached the deity known as Kāla-liṅga,
one should worship it on the fourteenth day, as well as on the eighth, the eleventh, and on festival days.
Having bathed there at Kavilā, he who beholds Kapardin obtains the merit of an Aśvamedha sacrifice, or if service is performed there. (327)
The sacred site extends as far as the Liṅga at Kurukṣetra; to the north is the Kapilā River, and to the south is the Kalpavṛkṣa tree; the middle area measures one krośa. || 328 ||
The sacred field named Daśāśvamedhaka is extremely difficult to attain;
whatever gift is given here yields fruit greater than that of Kurukṣetra.
Whoever accepts [a gift] here shall go to an inexhaustible hell;
but by bathing at Prayāga or at Kubjītīrtha, one shall not be born again.
In Aśvakrānta and Picchilā, the fruit of shaving the head is supreme. || 331 ||
As many hairs as there are on his body, whether he be moving in water or on land,
for that many hundreds of kalpas he shines in the world of Brahmā.
There is a river known as the Vaguḍā, which arises from the Anarghācala mountain;
by bathing in it on the fourteenth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Bhādrapada, one shall go to heaven.
There is also the one known by the name Toyadā, which flows from the Piñjācala mountain;
having bathed there on the Mahāmāghī day, one purifies one's lineage up to the seventh generation.
And to the south, O Supreme Goddess, is the Dvārakeśvara Liṅga;
there were Brāhmī, Vārāhī, and Lakṣmī in the middle.
Having bathed at the Sarasvatī-tīrtha and having worshipped the God of gods, the Lord of Umā, on the thirteenth lunar day, one is liberated from the bondage of worldly existence.
Here, in the northwestern corner, is the meritorious Svarṇanadī belonging to Śaṅkara;
on the third day of the month of Bhādrapada, no sorrow arises anywhere.
Having bathed in the waters of Vājavāri, one is liberated from terrible sin;
having bathed in the waters of Viṣṇudhārā, one rejoices on the back of the sky [in the heavenly world]. (338)
Having bathed in the waters of Gurudhārā, one obtains the merit of an Aśvamedha sacrifice;
having bathed in the waters of Kālidhārā, one shall attain all desires. || 339 ||
Situated five bow-lengths to the west of Tṛṇaśaila is the field named Śṛṅgāṭaka; one should avoid Kardama there. (340)
O Maheśvarī, having bathed in the Maṅgalā river,
a man should ascend the Śṛṅgāṭaka and worship Kapardin.
With his body radiant and his soul purified, having obtained incomparable desires here,
he goes at the end to the abode of Bharga and from there attains liberation.
To its western side is the famous river Kālanarā, celebrated as the White Symbol (śvetasaṅketakīrtitā), which liberates one from all sins.
O Great Goddess, one should worship the Lord of Pārvatī on the twelfth day of the bright fortnight in the month of Māgha, or on the ninth day.
He goes to the abode of Viṣṇu, resplendent in his body;
salutations to you, O Sarvatobhadra, bestower of heaven and liberation!
O you who have arisen from Viṣṇukūṭa, O remover of sin, salutations be unto you! || 345 ||
With this mantra, one should perform the bath and perform worship;
[the seed-syllable] vam, joined with the ten syllables and adorned with a ray and a bindu. (346)

Having made the *śūnya* [syllable] conjoined with the moon (*candra*), and likewise the heart and the crest (*śikhā*), he who has conquered his senses should recite this during worship and the offering of the *arghya*. || 347 ||
Patantī, Suparṇā, Māgadhī, Yamunā, Parā [Palanāparā], Kallolā, Śikhaṇḍī [Śikhinī], Śatarudrā, and Ghṛtārcikā. || 348 ||
Wherever that best of rivers, the Puṇyadhārā, has its eight streams,
one who bathes there on the fourteenth day is not defiled by the afflictions of the planets.
Having bathed at the confluence of the Ghṛtācī, one obtains the fruit born of bathing at Prayāga;
having bathed at the confluence of the Kallola, one casts off even the sin of killing a Brahmin.
The goddess who carries sixty yāmas, having emerged from Viṣṇukūṭa,
bathed Vāsava as she issued forth from the mouth of Varāha.
Upon the abandonment of the body there, one is not born again in a womb;
a funeral rite (śrāddha) performed on that bank yields fruit equal to Kurukṣetra. || 352 ||
Bathing, giving gifts, austerity, and fire-offerings—all these shall become inexhaustible.
Blessed are those men born who dwell in the northern region, O beloved. (353)
Those who dwell in the western part would attain a difficult rebirth; those who dwell there would fall into an evil destiny.
It is one *krośa* to the east of that place and to the west of Maṅgalā. (354)
And at the end of a krośa, O Maheśānī, is the great river named Kaluṣā;
by bathing in it, O Maheśānī, one becomes a sinner at that very moment.
Emerging from Somakuṇḍa, the Sarasvatī flows for fourteen yojanas;
she originates from Gautama’s hermitage and flows forth from that mountain.
The length is approximately three hundred and sixty *dhanus*; the *āśrama* is situated slightly less than that.
To its east stands the Saura-śilā in the eastern part. (357)
Cursed by Gautama in the past, she shall not touch water for as long as three births and oceans, until she becomes a goddess worthy of worship as Tārā. || 358 ||

The stream of the Sarasvatī is meritorious; having bathed there at Śāṅkarī, one obtains the fruit of a thousand cows and is glorified in the world of the gods (nākapṛṣṭhe). That best of rivers with holy waters, which rises from the field of Gautama for the sake of the higher realms, flows upward. || 359 ||
O lady, during the turbid night of the third watch, when the moon has arisen,
you should not dwell on the bank of a river while traveling by boat, nor should you ever touch its water.
They declare that water extending up to ten cubits is [suitable];
and the man who performs his bath with that water which has been drawn out [from the river]. || 361 ||
For that purity may come about through another life; therefore, having bathed, one should perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance.

Alternatively, one should perform the auspicious ritual bath, observe the Ekādaśī vow, or, being composed, bathe in the waters of the white Gaṅgā or at the time of the appearance of the star Agastya. 362.
Thus ends the eleventh chapter in the second part of the section on Kāmarūpa, within the *Yoginītantra*, the great king of tantras in twenty-two thousand [verses].
The twelfth chapter.
The Blessed Lord said: Listen, O Goddess, I shall explain correctly and in brief that meritorious seat (pīṭha), which removes all sins and is most difficult to attain. || 1 ||
Endowed with twelve lingas, it possesses the excellent fruit of Vārāṇasī;
it is renowned as Bhadrapīṭha and is graced by a hundred holy bathing places (tīrthas). || 2 ||
It was endowed with families of learned men [and abounded in hosts of scholars], possessed wealth, grain, and other such riches;
it was equipped with house-towers and adorned with great crossroads. || 3 ||
Therein is the Divyeśvara Liṅga, which destroys great sins;
its temple stands in the center of Jaya, and this mantra has been proclaimed for it. || 4 ||
The seer is Nārada, the metre is Anuṣṭubh, and the deity is Hara;
O lady of virtuous vows, its application for me is for the sake of dharma and desire. || 5 ||
A nine-limbed mandala should be constructed; one should delineate the nine tantras.
First, a svastika should be placed, provided with eight petals. (6)
Thereafter, one should provide the three qualities (guṇatraya), followed by the leaf of the Kalā;
one should fashion the abode of Dharaṇī (the Earth) as red, in accordance with the fundamental qualities.

Then one should know the sixteen [syllables], and one should purify the *svastika* and the maker of the *svastika*. In the east, one should likewise place the seed-syllable of desire (*kāma*), the seed-syllable of Śrī, the *prāsāda*, and the *praṇava*.
One should place the peaceful [letter] with its nasal bindu on the eastern petal and so forth, starting from Indra’s direction;
and one should remember the [letter] joined with a ray and a bindu on the outer covering.
Having drawn Nṛsiṃha in each corner with chalk, or with cool ashes, or with red ochre, or with saffron and gorocanā. (10)
And one should draw the great yantra; one should draw it in some place with sandalwood paste, using [the resin] from a *nāga* tree together with its flowers, and never with *kuśa* grass.
Having written Śambhu there together with Umā, one should indeed worship him;
a wise person should never effect a separation of Śambhu from Gaurī.
But if the worship is performed during separation [from the deity], it becomes fruitless for him.
The vessel for the *arghya* offering should be made of gold, or fashioned from bilva wood or a skull-bowl. || 13 ||
Having fashioned it either out of copper, measuring twelve finger-breadths in size,
with one finger-breadth being the measure for the arrow-hole (śarakāsa).
One should avoid conch shells, silver, and stone vessels;
those made of bhadradāru wood, mango wood, and *apattrā* are recommended. (15)
Now I shall describe meditation, which destroys all sins;
[one should visualize the deity] with four arms and three eyes, and holding a trident in the right hand. (16)
In his left hand, O Dear One, he holds a ḍamaruka drum as well as the gestures of fearlessness and boon;
he is white, clad in white garments, and adorned with a crown of matted locks.
Endowed with three serpent necklaces, adorned with the jewels upon their hoods,
possessing all auspicious marks, and graced by beauty attended by the cowherds.
The god who removes all sins, praised by Brahmā and the others, worshipped by gods, dānavas, and gandharvas, and truly enchanting. (19)
One should worship Virūpākṣa, Hara, Viṣṇu, and Maheśa in one's own presence;
then Asitāṅga and the others on the petals, and Śrīkaṇṭha and the others outside of that.
Outside, one should worship the sixteen *kalās* joined with the powers (*śaktis*) beginning with Brāhmī, as well as the two treasures, Śaṅkha and Padma, and Brahmā at the front. (21)
Furthermore, Kandarpa, Hara, Bhīma, Nandīśa, and Vṛṣabha,
as well as Rāma and the others, are to be worshipped on all sides, along with the planets and the guardians of the directions.
One should worship with ritual offerings and, immediately thereafter, with verses for each stanza;
one should also present food offerings, drinking water, and the *śrīphala* fruit. (23)
Dates, palmyra fruit, pomegranate, and likewise jackfruit;
sweetmeats, milk-rice, and winter grain as well. || 24 ||
One should avoid sesame seeds, black gram, green gram, and chickpeas; likewise, one should avoid those lacking a voice, *nārāra*, bottle gourd, and round lentils (*masūra*),
as well as the mango bud.
And also grain, such as wild rice (*nīvāra*) and the like. || 25 ||
And likewise the vārtākī, the white variety, the potikā, and the kalambikā;
the śimbī, the karkī, the māna, the kavīra, and the madhukas. (26)
One should avoid siddhārtha, kālaśāka, and somaśāka;
as well as candra-śāka, candrabimba, agravaktra, and prarohaka. (27)
Know these to be vegetables; now hear, O beloved, the varieties of meat:
the vādhrīṇasa, the eṇa deer, the hare, and likewise the porcupine.
The flesh of the iguana is highly praised; one should offer it for consumption, as well as the flesh of the boar, the tortoise, and likewise the black goat. (29)
One should carefully avoid the meat of an elephant, as well as that of a black antelope, a black deer, a buffalo, and a rhinoceros. (30)
The *suloṅka* (or *suloḍa*), the partridge, the *śāma*, the *caunika*, the *sarārī*, the dove, and likewise the white pigeon; || 31 ||
The bird Vradhrianasa, the Vandaki, the village swan, the Tittibha, the red-tailed one, the Harita, and the woodcock (Kāṣṭhakukkuṭa). || 32 ||
Likewise, a fresh citrabaka, a vartaka, and a red-beaked bird. || 33 ||
These meats are declared [by the wise]; listen now to those which you must avoid. (34)
The vṛhat-kāpotaka, the cakora, the crane, as well as the peacock, the gallinule, and the domestic cock. || 35 ||
One should avoid the kalaviṅka, the śārikā, the koyaṣṭi, and other pecking birds;
likewise, one should avoid fish, the vaiḍālika, the rājīva, and the madgura.
O Dear One, one should diligently employ the *prauṣṭika*, the *hairuka*, the *candra*,
the *kuvaṅkuṭa*, the *jālapāda*, and likewise the *citrabaka*.
One should diligently feed fish, buttermilk, as well as the Śoṇa, Hārīta, and Citraka [birds]; listen, O beloved, to what they are by Śambhu. (38)
One should avoid mārīca, raktaka, pālaṅga, and mānaka; likewise, one should avoid śastaka, vikira, varvāśāka, and vṛtraka.
Punarnavā, rājīva, lakala, and likewise panasa;
vṛtrikā, pucumarda, and likewise hinamocikā.
O Daughter of Śaṅkara, one should offer these vegetables which are highly commended; as for the flowers, I shall now describe those which are to be offered and those which are to be avoided.
Listen to them in brief, O giver of joy to the heart: water-born flowers should be offered, and one should cause *karavīra* flowers to be given. (42)
One should offer leaves of the *tamāla* and *āmalakī*, two types of *tulasī*,
as well as the *droṇa* flower, the lotus stalk, the *javā*, and likewise the *siṃhāsya*.
One should offer two *rudrajaṭā* flowers and two *mālatī* flowers; likewise, one should present *mallikā*, *campaka*, *aśoka*, *punnāga*, and *nāgakeśara*.
One should offer the *sandhyāvaktra*, the *kapuṣpa*, and the *munipuṣpa*;
likewise, the *ketakī*, *vandhujīva*, *śirīṣa*, and *bakula*.
One should avoid the white kāñcanaka, the white sindhuka, the sahakāra, the madhya, the white aśoka, and the karṇikāra.
One should offer a garland made of a thousand flowers smeared with sandalwood paste;
thus, a garland for Śiva is presented with one thousand and eight flowers.

One should avoid a rosary made of knots from the side [of the stem], which is considered by me to be a knot of the heart; one should avoid it among all deities, and one should especially avoid that which has three colors. 48.
One should not give anything entirely red, nor should one cause anything entirely white to be given; O lady of excellent vows, nothing entirely black or entirely yellow should be offered to me. (49)
At the edge of the white [square], one should place red and yellow, and red, yellow, and black;
however, one should not give red and black at the white [edge], nor should one cause yellow to be placed there.
A neck-garland (*kaṇṭhamālā*) is proclaimed to be two cubits (*bāhumātra*) in length;
a *śivamālā* is one cubit long and is approved for those of four *aṅgulas*.
O Great Goddess, one should offer a necklace for the neck measuring ten finger-breadths;
however, one should avoid including aquatic flowers in the garland as appropriate.
When a garland is made with bilva leaves, there is no fixed number of leaves;
one should make it measuring one cubit, or four cubits for the most excellent. (53)
One hundred and eight cubits is the eighth; twenty-five is the next;
ten cubits is the smallest, as well as sixteen cubits.
One should make it the length of an arm, or even less than that; one should not make it smaller.
As for other petals, there is no fault in their number.
One should make it only as high as the armpit; one should not create a mixture of leaves.
A garland made of five leaves dedicated to Śaṅkara does not incur any fault.
That which consists of aquatic flowers is proclaimed as the garland of Śaṅkara;
likewise, the leaves of tulasī, bilva, kahlāra, dhātrī, and tamālaka [are also suitable].
With a concentrated mind, one should fashion a garland from these five flowers and offer it to Śiva on the fourteenth day or at night. (58)
O beloved, one obtains the full fruit of the fourteenth day [of the lunar fortnight] correctly and not otherwise;
never with wood, nor with bamboo, nor ever with hair.
On the fourteenth and likewise on the eighth lunar day, one should offer a garland of bilva fruits;
by offering one measuring a hundred cubits, one shall obtain royal fortune.
By giving a [shrine] measuring ten cubits, one obtains one's own moving fortune;
and with a Tulasī [shrine] measuring one hundred cubits, one should offer it to Śiva.
The sin committed over ten lifetimes perishes at that very moment;
one who is composed should offer a garland of red karavīra flowers.
By giving a lotus measuring one cubit, one shall obtain all desires and attain the supreme fruit of the Rājasūya sacrifice. || 63 ||
With a concentrated mind, one should diligently offer a garland of *mālatī* flowers that are entirely white.
A garland made of *jātī* and *yūthī* flowers is also considered excellent when they are entirely white. (64)
One should offer sandalwood produced from the *bilva* tree to Śiva,
or else that which is produced on the Malaya mountain or is infused with *bhṛgu*.
One should apply an effortful ointment for the primary [limb], or one consisting of four ingredients;
however, one should apply that consisting of two ingredients, but never that which consists of only one.
Malayaja, somaka, agaru, and mṛgamada are likewise declared; there is also catuḥsama, dvisama, and kalāgaru.
Sandalwood, uśīra, and agaru are considered equal in three parts each; one should not offer agaru alone, even when combined with guggulu.
Alternatively, one should give *siddhaka*, or one should give it combined with resin (*sarjarasa*), as well as *niśā*, *kṛṣṭaka*, *kuśīta*, *gandha*, *mura*, and *mada*. (69)
One should perform dry massage (udvartana) daily or once every seven days;
one should perform an oil massage with sesame oil, other unctuous substances, or ghee.
O Śāṅkarī, one should likewise avoid buffalo ghee, as well as curd and milk; [one should offer] with flour made from śāli rice and barley flour.
Then one should perform anointing and bathe Śiva with honey;
first with water, and immediately thereafter with milk. (72)
Then one should perform a bath with the five nectars (pañcāmṛta), or with fresh sugarcane juice,
or a bath with molasses, and one should also cause a stream of milk to fall [upon the deity].
Then one should perform the ritual bath of the jar (*ghaṭasnāna*) one thousand and eight times;
for the middling rite, one hundred times; and for the lowest, twenty-five times. (74)
O Goddess, one should bathe Śiva with a thousand palas for each [deity];
for the middling [rite], with a hundred, and for the lowest, with twenty-five.
Having bathed [the deity] with warm water according to the procedure for the water-conjunction,
one should then perform the *argha* bath, followed again by the *vāruṇa* bath using a water-pot.
In the cold season, one should offer warm water, and at the end of the year, one should discontinue it.
O Goddess, one should bathe [the deity] with the Astra-mantra; this is prescribed as the Great Bath (mahāsnāna).

O Dear One, when a month has passed, one should purge with cow’s urine; O Goddess, one should not employ hot substances for this purpose. When sleep has arrived, one should resort to it for the sake of rest. (78)

One should not perform the *kūrca* rite at night, nor at midnight, nor at the end of a fortnight or its half, nor at the end of a month, O Maheśānī; rather, O beautiful one, one should perform the *kūrca* rite for me [at the proper time]. 79.
One should not brush [the teeth] with yak-tail whisks, nor with cow-hair, nor with horse-hair, nor with the hair of a *māsa* plant;
one should never brush them with the hair of a pig.
One should never bathe the liṅga with wood, bamboo, or hair;
rather, one should bathe it at dawn and immediately thereafter at midday.
Having bathed [the deity] with water at night, immediately thereafter with milk-offerings,
and then at midday and during the final watch of the night at the conclusion of the great worship (mahāpūjā).
One should not bathe Mahādeva with [ordinary water] upon the liṅgas and images;
rather, one should cleanse them with seven bilva leaves and five leaves. (83)
One should never bathe the deity with dry kuśa grass or with silver water;
rather, one should bathe the deity with coconut water as well as with honey.
With a steady hand, one should bathe the Lord of Gods day and night with the pollen of lotus petals or with that produced from cotton cloth. (85)
O beloved, one should move the lamp with sesame oil or ghee measured at four finger-breadths; one should place five [lamps] all around.
One should never worship with only a single lamp or even three lamps;
nor should one do so at the time of bathing or eating, or on the fourteenth and eighth lunar days.
One should gaze [at the deity] for half a night, and at the conclusion of the worship, one should not touch anything at all.
One should wait for only as long as it takes to milk a cow; at the end of the worship, [one may touch] only a tooth-stick.
If the new moon (amāvāsyā) should fall on a Monday at the close of day during the month of Pauṣa,
one should never touch the Divine Lord on that thirteenth lunar day.
We shall go first to Divyeśa, second to Candrabhairava,
third to Kāmaśatru, and fourth indeed to Vikambana.
One should worship these five names, including Gopeśvara, either individually or collectively, each accompanied by "anta-namaḥ" (ending with *namaḥ*).
The worship of each [deity] by its own name has been proclaimed;
it is observed on the full moon day of the month of Māgha when the moon is in the Maghā asterism. (92)
Then one should approach the Liṅga Paśupati with distinction,
quickly through body, speech, and mind, with that disposition and a mind focused on nothing else.

(361) Completely liberated from all dualities, free from passion, and a great festival [of virtue], there stands the lovely *vaṭa* tree, a wish-fulfilling tree (*kalpavṛkṣa*), where Janārdana himself is present. 94.
There, one should perform seven circumambulations with a concentrated mind;
upon seeing him, one is liberated from the sins arising from seven births.
O Śāṅkarī, he who beholds the one named Divya on the third day of Vaiśākha obtains abundant merit and a desired destination.
Liberated from all sins, he goes to the world of Śiva after beholding the god Pinākin on the fourteenth day of the month of Kārtika.
Having extracted twenty-one generations of his lineage, he is glorified in the world of Brahmā;
whatever fruit is obtained through all types of gifts, vows, and religious observances [is attained here]. 98.
A man who beholds the Liṅga even once obtains that fruit;
having seen it, the man should join his palms in reverence and prostrate himself like a staff. || 99 ||
O Daughter of Śaṅkara, by seeing and bowing to this Liṅga, a man obtains the fruit of thousands of horse-sacrifices and attains liberation, which is difficult to achieve. 100.
Freed from sins, pure in soul, for a hundred crores of kalpas he rejoices, endowed with supreme splendor and all delightful virtues. (101)
By means of a resplendent celestial chariot (vimāna) in which all desires are fulfilled,
a man shall uplift twenty-one generations of his lineage and proceed to the city of Śiva.
There, having enjoyed delightful pleasures for as long as a hundred kalpas together with gandharvas and apsarases, he shall become auspicious and four-armed.
Having passed away from there, he comes here to be born into a family preeminent among Brahmins;
he becomes all-knowing, truthful in speech, and free from envy. (104)
Devoted to his own duty, peaceful, self-controlled, and intent on the welfare of all beings, and having practiced the knowledge of Śiva, he shall thereafter attain liberation. || 105 ||
O Śivā, for one who has established the Aśvatīrtha and worships Divyeśa, their desired goals are accomplished; there is no need for deliberation on this matter.
The foot-stool, the trident, the sword, the yellow pigment (rocanā), the jewel, as well as the elixir (rasāyana), the sandals, and the collyrium. || 107 ||
O Maheśānī, [she should carry] a black antelope skin, a *tāḍhaka* stone, red arsenic (*manaḥśilā*), a water-pot together with a rosary, and likewise a staff and a water-strainer. (108)
And having mastered the perfected vidyā along with its ancillaries, Māsakeśvara [performed it] if the three-pronged [vajra], trembling with waves of flaming sparks of fire, [arose]. 109.
Offered but once, it would burn away all the sins born of ten million lifetimes;
just as poison applied to another poison destroys it, so too does it destroy leprosy situated within the body.
Having committed the murder of a fetus or other such sins within one's own body, one does not grieve in the divine state;
[in that case], one should contemplate the blazing [fire] among those seized by the great crocodiles. 111.
Then, indeed, the terrible planets will quickly wail and perish;
this serves as a constant protection for the limbs and hair of children. (112)
It certainly brings about the destruction of those who have died from glandular swellings and carbuncles.
Such, O Consort of Śaṅkara, is the power of the God of gods in that place.
Success is attained even when struck by disease; one should perform oblations with ghee and milk for one month at the three junctions of the day, and all diseases will be destroyed. 114.
One should perform the circumambulation of Śiva along a straight line and must not cross that line;
by crossing the straight line, one incurs the sin of killing a Brahmin. (115)
Then, having gone to the southern direction and touched the bathing water, if one returns there again and makes a residence until that time, [one attains the fruit]. 116.
Having returned once more to that very place, the prostration is proclaimed;
having performed a circumambulation in front of it, the wise man should perform the salutation. (117)
And because it belongs to all other deities as well, one should therefore avoid it;
O Supreme Goddess, this applies to the *nirmālya* and *naivedya* of the Jyotirliṅga.
O Goddess of gods, having offered that food to Hara, the Lord of Tantra, [one should offer it] to other Śambhu-liṅgas that have been installed, O fair-faced one. (119)
One should cast both the food offering (naivedya) and the floral remains (nirmālya) only into wells;
even by means of a bilva fruit, [the merit] may perish, therefore one should avoid that. 120.
Viśveśvara, Nīlakaṇṭha, and likewise the mountain called Kāma; Someśvara, Kedāra, Manīṣa, and Kāmīśvara. || 121 ||
Then [he worshipped] Pāśupata, Nitya, Vyomeśa, Nāgeśvara, Divyeśa, Jalpīśa, Nandīśa, and Kakudeśvara. || 122 ||
The Kṛtrivāseśvara Liṅga, the Kaurakeśvara Liṅga, the great Liṅga named Cyavana, Koṭīśa, and Siddhināyaka. || 123 ||
Campakeśa, Virūpākṣa, Vyādheśa, and Vṛṣadhvaja—
all these Jyotirliṅgas are proclaimed to be made of silver and tin. (124)
One should undertake a pilgrimage every month on the fourteenth and eighth lunar days;
one should lead [the image] to the Saugava-tīrtha and bathe it with waters produced by the ṛṣis. (125)
There, one should worship the God, whether in the form of an image or a linga;
by beholding Him there, a man or a woman shall attain all their desires.
On the thirteenth day of the month of Phālguna, having prepared a swing near the banyan tree, one should worship the God according to the prescribed rites; and then, someone beholds Him there.
One obtains the fruit of a thousand horse-sacrifices, and not otherwise;
one should undertake a pilgrimage toward Nīlācala during the spring equinox.
Having seen Śiva there in his peaceful form, one removes the sin of killing a Brahmin;
indeed, one should undertake the journey on that day, even without wealth or a specific auspicious transit of the sun.
A journey undertaken at nightfall during the evening twilight yields infinite fruit;
on the seventh day of the month of Māgha, one should proceed toward the southern direction.
Having seen [it] there, a man or a woman is liberated from all sins on the fourteenth day at the arrival of day during the four months of the rainy season. || 131 ||
When the sun has grown dim, one should lead [the disciple] toward the abode of the Wheel;
there, one should show him the divine vehicle, and having seen it there, he becomes a partaker of liberation.

And then, O Maheśvarī, having seen [it] on the boat at the end of the Lauhitya river, one obtains that fruit which is remembered as resulting from the gift of a hundred tawny cows at Puṣkara. || 133 ||
Having observed that auspicious fruit [attained] during the rainy season while on a boat,
as well as the fruit obtained by the gift of a hundred maidens when the sun is in Capricorn— 134.

O Śāṅkarī, having observed that auspicious fruit and the face of the palanquin, [consider] the fruit which has been declared as resulting from the ritual offering of the *bali* according to rule. (135)
The fruit of that, as well as the fruit remembered for gifting a hundred gold *niṣkas*, is attained by beholding Śiva at Nīlakūṭa. (136)
Having seen that fruit on the bank of the Nāgara and having bowed to Śambhu,
[one should worship] on the fifth, the new moon day, the tenth, and during eclipses.
During a conflagration of the earth and during an earthquake, one should avoid a pilgrimage to Śiva;
for if [the deity] sees [the pilgrim] there, he destroys all grain and wealth—of this there is no doubt. (138)
At the conclusion of worship, during processions, and in both regular and occasional rites,
one should perform worship with each individual flower using the mantra that will be described hereafter.
Salutations to Bhava, to Rudra, to Sarva, and to the Giver of Boons;
salutations be to you, the Lord of Creatures and the Divine Ishana. 140.

Salutations again and again to the one who has three births, the three-headed one, the bearer of the excellent trident, the three-eyed one, the three-faced one, and the embodiment of sovereign power. 141.
Salutations to Caṇḍa, to Muṇḍa, and to the bearer of the golden staff;
salutations indeed to Daṇḍin, to Śaṅkukarṇa, and to Kāmaratna.
Salutations to the Lord of Arghya-caṇḍikā, to the white one, and to the bull;
salutations again and again to the deep-red one, to the smoky-colored one, and to the lotus-like one. || 143 ||
Homage to the one whose nature is to turn, and to the one who delights in the cremation ground;
homage to the praised one, to the secret one, to the lord of the Gopīs—homage, homage!

Salutation to the All, to the consumer of all, and to the one who dwells within all beings; salutation, repeated salutation, to the Eldest, to the Prosperous, and to the Lord of the Cowherds. || 145 ||
Homage to the Buddha, the fierce one, who delights in sharing;
homage again and again to the divine lord, the five-limbed bird. 146.
Salutations to the Lord of Sacrifice, who is both the created and the uncreated;
salutations again and again to the bearer of sacrifice, to the Staff, and to the Divine Lord. (147)
Thus ends the twelfth chapter in the second part of the section on Kāmarūpa, within the *Yoginītantra*, the great king of tantras consisting of twenty-two thousand verses.
The thirteenth chapter.
The Blessed One said:
Hereafter I shall proclaim the fruit of the Aśvatīrtha; listen.
Whatever fruit is obtained through bathing, giving gifts, and beholding the deity; || 1 ||
Having gone to the lake of Campāvatī at the confluence of the Divyapura,
a pure man, facing north, should bow from afar to that sacred ford.
Having formed the añjali gesture, one should immerse it while reciting this mantra of the earth:
"I am submerged in the ocean of saṃsāra, seized by evil, and devoid of consciousness. (3)
Save me, O Destroyer of Bhaga’s eyes, O Enemy of Tripura; salutations be unto you!
Salutations to Śiva, the peaceful one, the remover of all sins. || 4 ||
"I perform this bath, O Lord of Gods; may my sin be destroyed.
Having stood in water reaching to the navel, one should worship the deities and ancestors according to the prescribed rite.
The wise man should also satisfy the ancestors with sesame seeds and *kuśa* grass;
then, raising his arms, he should stand up and present the *arghya* offering.
O Haṃsa, having worshipped with this mantra using a *karavīra* flower, one should then go to Mānasa, located to the south of Mount Kuvera. (7)
Kandarpa, Kuvera, and Nandin—these are the three rocks there;
and the pool of clear water is known as the auspicious opening of Śiva.
By bathing there, O Lord of Devas, the fear of old age and death shall never exist for me; whatever evil deed I have committed, [may it be purified] by Śivamānasa.
Having bathed according to the prescribed rite in the pure water of this most excellent Mānasa-kuṇḍa, one should offer libations to one's own ancestors. || 10 ||
Thence one should go to the King of Tīrthas; having bathed there, one should satiate the ancestors:
"O Lord of rivers, you are the waters, the most excellent cause of the world. (11)
"O King of Tīrthas, salutations to you; protect me from the ocean of worldly existence and sin.
With this mantra, one should bathe [or cause him to bathe] and offer that [libation]. || 12 ||
O Maheśvarī, to the east of Govindācala and on its southern side,
there is the Vārāṇasīya Kuṇḍa, measuring eight dhanus in extent.
Having gone there and having drunk [it], one purifies one's lineage up to the seventh generation;
for the water from the oceans has been drawn up and united within you.
"O best of lakes at Vārāṇasī, remove my sin; salutations be unto you!
Having bathed according to the rules with this mantra, one should offer the arghya for the sake of prosperity. (15)
He who, having bathed in the lake of Vārāṇasī, worships [or beholds] Divyeśa, shall have his soul purified of all sins and go to the abode of the gods. || 16 ||
Then, having gone to Kāmasaras and bathed, one should mutter the Kāma-mantra; and one should diligently offer libations to all the deities of the sacred seats (pīṭhas) and to all kinsmen. || 17 ||
O illustrious Kāmakuṇḍa, honored by the gods themselves, grant incomparable desires and protect us from all evil. (18)
Having bathed with this mantra, one should present the arghya offering at a spot situated not too far to the northwest of Brahmaśaila. (19)
O Goddess of the gods, a sacrificial pit measuring twelve cubits destroys all sins;
having bathed there with mantras and beheld the Lord Maheśvara, one attains liberation.
A human being obtains the fruit of ten horse-sacrifices.
There, the great-minded Mārkaṇḍeya, the best of sages, performed austerities.
"Today, remove my sin by going to the famous Mārkaṇḍeya-hrada;
then, having gone to the Kalpavṛkṣa, perform a circumambulation once. (22)
One should worship him with supreme devotion while reciting this mantra:
"Obeisance to you whose nature is manifest, who dwells through the great dissolution. (23)
Salutations again and again to the Nyagrodha tree standing above Mahendra; O Vaṭa tree, the abode of Hari, may you always be healthy and grant immortality. (24)
O Nyagrodha, take away my sin; O Kalpavṛkṣa, salutations be unto you!
One shall behold the Lord, the Divine Master; there is no doubt that liberation is attained here. || 25 ||
One should mount the peacock facing toward the eastern direction;
however, mounting it while facing the southern direction will bring about great fear. (26)
Facing west, O beautiful one, one becomes sinful and diseased; it is not otherwise. Facing north, O beautiful one, one is born wealthy. (27)
Having entered the temple and performed three circumambulations,
he worshipped the god Hara, the divine Lord, with the root mantra.
Then, having offered the eightfold respectful oblation (arghya) and prostrated, one should propitiate him:
"O Three-eyed One, salutations to you; salutations to you, whose ornaments are the serpents. (29)
Protect me, O Virūpākṣa; O Mahādeva, salutations be unto you!
Likewise, [protect me] at the lake of Mārkaṇḍeya, O Goddess, and at the lake of Vārāṇasī.
Having performed the tonsure in the forenoon, the Śrāddha is prescribed for the following day;
O Pārvatī, having stepped upon the shadow of that Kalpavṛkṣa tree.
A man would abandon even the sin of killing a Brahmin— what need is there to mention other sins—
upon seeing that supreme [place] born from the body of Kṛṣṇa, which is equal to the water of Brahma.
Having prostrated before Viṣṇu in the form of a banyan tree,
one should recite the Śatarudrīya or some other Vedic hymn according to the prescribed rules.
Yama, Mataṅga, and Mayūra, O Maheśvarī;
Govinda, Brahmā, Pāripātra, and Subhadraka. (34)
Soma, Vijaya, Nāga, and likewise Nandana;
Āditya, Kaseru, Mana, and likewise Mānasa. (35)
In the middle and southern portions, however, these mountains are situated in sequence;
and in the front, in the eastern portion, are Nīla and Kumuda.
Kārttikeya, Bala, and likewise Balabhadra;
Gaya, Vihaga, and the auspicious Makara; [Gomedha and Gavākṣaka;
and Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa, who bestow auspiciousness. || 37 ||
Kaseru, Madhuka, Kuvera, and likewise Hari;
Kuru, Dharmarūpa, Kāhāla, and Lona. (38)
Kaliṅga, Karāla, and likewise the northern mountains;
Kamala, Kāmadhenu, Hara, and Makarandaka. (39)
Rāma, Lakṣmaṇa, Gomedha, and Gavākṣaka—these are proclaimed as being at the end of the Lauhitya [or rather, in its middle and extremities], starting from the west. || 40 ||
In the north is Syandana, and in the west is Piśācaka;
in the southeast is Jālaśaila, and in the northeast is Rākṣasācala. || 41 ||
Combined, three hundred and twenty bows and five thousand [bow-lengths] make one krośa; a thousand of these is the field of Vārāṇasī. Hear now about the inner house, O beloved.
And Vikumbhākṣa, O Goddess of gods, is recited in the north;
one should not ascend Malabhadra, or else one would incur a great sin. (43)
The bow extending from Nīlaśaila to Piśācānta is considered to be five hundred [yojanas] in length;
within this, O Goddess, lies the inner sanctum (antargṛha), which is remembered as containing all sacred fords (tīrthas).
In that regard, O Great Goddess, whatever [act] has been performed there is proclaimed to be inexhaustible;
even a misdeed [committed there], O Maheśānī, is equal to the killing of a Brahmin in a kalpa.
Those who cast off their bodies between the Vaṭa and Mandara trees attain that supreme liberation which is difficult to obtain; of this there is no doubt. (46)
Even that man who, though unwilling, gives up his life there, that man too, being liberated from suffering, attains liberation—[a liberation] difficult to obtain. (47)
Even worms, insects, moths, and others who have entered the wombs of animals, by casting off their bodies here, attain the supreme goal. (48)
Attached neither to the world of mortals, nor to the intermediate space, nor to the abode of Yama, those who are unliberated do not see them; the liberated, however, perceive them with their mind.
Thinking this world to be impermanent, a human being falls into sin;
there, drinking [the wine of worldly pleasure], they do not resort to that which releases one from the fear of saṃsāra. 50.
In this terrible Kali age, O Goddess, men will always follow after sin and will be entirely devoid of refuge in dharma.
I see no other expiation for living beings in the Kali age that so pacifies all sins as the city of Siddheśvarī. (52)
Whatever sin has been previously accumulated over thousands of other births, all of that goes to destruction for one who has entered the Bhadrapīṭha. || 53 ||
Burnt by the fire of the auspicious seat (bhadrapīṭha), like a fortress cast into the flames, one shall obtain the vehicle of merit across thousands of future births. || 54 ||
Whatever wealth and such was sunk in the Bhadrapīṭha, other seats, or at holy fords (tīrtha),
as well as everything previously acquired that had been stolen by a thief— all that [is restored].

O King, whatever has been done unjustly, such as milking many unwilling subjects, that family is submerged in the next world, even if it be of great lineage or established at a great sacred ford. || 56 ||
Those who are perpetrators of the great sins (mahāpātakin), as well as other men who have committed evil deeds—
by entering the inner sanctum (antargṛha), they attain the supreme goal.
On Mount Yama resides Dharmarāja and Yamakūpa;
having bathed there, one shall not see the abode of Yama, but rather the world of Brahmā.
One should worship Mataṅgeśī and Mataṅga, as well as Mataṅgeśa; and on Mayūra, one should worship Divyeśa, Gaṇeśa, and Vṛṣabhadhvaja.
One should worship Nārāyaṇa, Govinda, and Trivikrama on the Brahma-mountain, and Durgā, who resides on the Pāripātra mountain, with her mantra.
In Subhadrā is Kāmapāla, and in Somasomā is Śiva, known as Someśvara;
and in Vijayā is the one called Jayanta, who possesses my own characteristics. || 61 ||
Śakra resides on Nakula, and the leader named Āditya on Āditya [the leader Rudra on Āditya];
the Lord of Yogins is on Kaśeru mountain, and Śivā is with Manas on Mānasa.
In Nīla is the womb of Kāmeśvarī; in Kumuda is Puruṣottama;
and on the great mountain named Kārtika is the exceedingly fierce leader (Nāyaka).
Virūpākṣa is at Vanaśaila, Śatakratu is at Nandabhadra,
Gayāśiras is at Gayāśaila, and there is also the pair of feet of Viṣṇu.
In the sky is Kātyāyanī, the supreme one known as Kāmā;
on the Black Mountain (Kṛṣṇaśaila) stands Kṛṣṇa, and on the Forest Mountain (Vanaśaila) stands Vana.
On Vārāha he is named Varāha; on Dharmaśaila he is Heruka;
on Subhadra he is Nīlavāsī; and on Mandara he is Janārdana. || 66 ||
Kaśeru is on Śaila, and Bhuvaneśī resides on Mātaṅga;
O Padmākṣī, on Kuberaśaila there are two caves of Śiva and Viṣṇu. (67)
On Hariśaila is Śrīdhara, and on Kuruśaila is Jaṭādhara;
on Dharmaśaila at Mahāyūpa resides the goddess Kāmeśvarī.
And on Kailāsa, O Great Goddess, [is Mahābodhi at Rudrācala], as well as in Dharmāraṇya; likewise, at the place called Lolā is Jambhakeśa, and at the Liṅga is Paśupatīśvara. || 69 ||
O Goddess of the gods, Bhuvaneśī resides on Mount Karāla;
in Kamalā there is a lotus-liṅga, and Keśava resides in Kāmadhenu.
Brahmā was situated on Harakūṭa, while Mādhava was in Makaranda;
Sītā was on Kāmaśaila, and the beloved [Lakṣmaṇa] was at Anasūyā’s hermitage. (71)
On the great mountain named Nakula, Dharmāṃśa is the Grandfather (Pitāmaha),
Gomedha is the Great-Grandfather (Prapitāmaha), and the imperishable Viṣṇu is at Gavākṣa.
Whatever fruit one who remains properly engaged in the practice of yoga for three hundred years might obtain, that same fruit one attains by staying to the south of Kāmakuṇḍa. (73)
On the fourteenth day of the month of Kārttika, having worshipped Divyeśvara Umāpati with perfumes, flowers, incense, food offerings, and sandalwood paste; || 74 ||
He who keeps a vigil there with the sounds of song and instrumental music, which are esteemed for the hearing of the Dharma, attains the supreme goal. || 75 ||
To the north of the deity stands a beautiful pond;
by drinking its clear water, one is not subject to rebirth. (76)
Daṇḍapāṇi always guards that water right there,
and likewise, ten million bows are guarded by the leaders of the Gaṇas.
To the northwest of Somakūṭa, established within a cave, the god Kṛttivāseśvara is to be beheld again and again. (78)
He shall attain the saving knowledge, the eternal and esteemed state.
This must be constantly practiced if one desires the eternal state.
They are blessed, they have achieved their purpose, and by them the fruit of birth has been obtained. (79)
Those who behold the supreme Liṅga, the Divine Lord, upon that auspicious pedestal— there, on that very pedestal— are sixty thousand crores and six hundred crores [of others].
O lady of excellent vows, they behold [the deity] on every fortnight, specifically on the fourteenth, the new moon, and the eighth days,
on the western and southern sides of the Blue Mountain.
The sacred field named Dhanur-dvāviṃśaka is the hermitage of Badarikā;
by staying there for even a moment, one obtains the fruit of all sacrifices. 82.
To its western part, however, is the sacred field named Daśāśva;
by residing there, one obtains the fruit of ten horse-sacrifices.
To the northern part of that [region], and further to the north of it, is the Sun;
therefore, among gods and humans, he is celebrated as the "Bridge of Light" (Vārka-setu).
There a pool emerged, born from the essence of all splendors;
it is renowned as Sūryatīrtha, the destroyer of all impurities.
Then one should go to the temple and perform three circumambulations;
and one should offer praise with a hymn to Nīlakaṇṭha at any time.

Salutations to the Liṅga known as Salila, and to the possessor of the Liṅga who exists until the end of the age; salutations to the one wearing a garland of skulls, and repeated salutations to the Divine Lord.
Homage to the Lord of the gods, to Tryambaka, and to Hara;
homage again and again to the divine Lord who dwells in the cave of the peacock. 88.
Salutations indeed to the beloved of Umā, who dwells in Kāmarūpa;
salutations again and again to the divine Lord, whose eyes are the moon and the sun. || 89 ||
Salutations to Rudra, the Vasu; salutations to the one who reclines upon the ocean;
salutations to the bestower of grace and to the sustainer of the world—salutations, salutations!
Homage to the one whose body is like a conch-shell mountain upon a crystal couch;
homage to the one whose arms shine with the khaṭvāṅga staff, the trident, and the ḍamaru drum.
Salutations again and again to you, O Gopeśvara, the bestower of boons, who makes his dwelling in the mountain caves on the waves of the Gaṅgā. 92.
Then, when another day had arrived, the practitioner, having gone to Daṇḍasara in the morning and bathed according to the rules, [should perform the rite] with this mantra: || 93 ||
By merely bathing in this water at Daṇḍatīrtha, a man is freed from the sins arising from birth and goes to a terrible hell. (94)
To the northwest of Hariśaila (Harikūṭa), at a distance of eight dhanus,
there is a pond covered with stones, fifteen cubits in length.
To the east of Mount Govinda is a mountain named Govinda;
directly below it, on the same vertical line, is the Vārāṇasīya Kuṇḍa.
Having bathed in that pool, a man should behold the Lord who wears matted locks;
he is liberated even from terrible sins accumulated over seven lifetimes. (97)
Both are one digit (kalā) in measure; the eight *dhanus* prior to that are the Vāsudeva-saras.
Having bathed there, one obtains the fruit of a sacrifice. (98)
O Lord, one should worship Nārāyaṇa to the east of Govindācala;
then, having gone to Brahmācala, one should honor the Brāhmaṇas there. || 99 ||
To the south, at a distance of nine dhanus, is the lake named Amogha, which arose from the bull;
having bathed there on the ninth lunar day, one is glorified in the world of Brahmā.
The supreme among all sacred fords (tīrthas) is known [or remembered] as the Brahmatīrtha;
it extends for eight dhanvantaras, or likewise five dhanvantaras.
The great sacred site of Kāśyapa is remembered as the primordial sacred site (*āditīrtha*). Having bathed in the primordial pool (*ādikuṇḍa*), O Divine Lord, the man who then worships [the deity]—
Especially on the eighth day, he attains the supreme goal; for him, śrāddha, charity, austerity, burnt offerings, as well as the offering of funeral cakes,
meditation, penance, and self-restraint— all these become inexhaustible.
They know that the lake named Bhāskara is located to the east, measuring one hundred dhanvantaras in length. || 102 ||
One should perform the Śrāddha rite according to the prescribed rules on the full moon and the new moon;
there, the stone in the form of Śakra is situated in its center.
And one should cause the funeral cakes (piṇḍas) to be offered there, especially during the months of Vaiśākha.
Beyond that is the supreme Sārasvata Tīrtha, measuring sixty dhanus.
Having bathed there, O Goddess, a person does not behold rebirth.
There is indeed a lake called Amṛta, extending for twenty-two bow-lengths. (105)
Having bathed there on the Mahāmāghī day, one attains union with Viṣṇu. Following that is the Krauñca Tīrtha, measuring eight bow-lengths.
Having bathed at the close of day in the month of Madhu, one attains the state of Śiva;
thereafter, one reaches the brilliantly radiant Nandikuṇḍa, which extends for eight bow-lengths.
Having bathed there and attained a state equal to Nandin, one attains the status of Rudra at that very moment.
[The lake] extends for seventeen bows in length and is situated on the northern bank.
Having bathed and drunk there, a person shall not go to hell;
by bathing on the thirteenth lunar day, one goes to the world of Śiva.
From there, one should go to the place called Yamunā, which destroys all sins;
there is no sacred ford equal to that of the Yamunā, of this there is no doubt.
To the east of that, at a distance of one *tithi* and one month [from the center], there is a charming pit (*kuṇḍa*) measuring one *dhanus* on each side;
by bathing there, one obtains a fruit equal to that of a sacrifice.
The auspicious lake named Prayāga measures twenty-four *dhanus* in extent;
having bathed there on the Great Eighth (*mahāṣṭamī*), one obtains the fruit of all holy fords (*tīrtha*).
Having bathed at the holy ford named Kanakhala, one shall go to the state of Śiva.
To the east of Ṛṣidhanvantara and to the south of Puṣkarācala. || 113 ||
Śiva, Viṣṇu, as well as Brahmā and Gaṇeśa [are present] due to the transit of the Sun;
the Viṣṇukuṇḍa is to the northeast, while that of Vaṭa is to the southwest;
and the Durgākūpa is in that very place, at a distance of one Kālahasta. || 114 ||
There, having drunk the water from the well, a woman shall become pregnant.
That place is on the eastern mountain, at that very spot where Śrī Puruṣottama resides. (115)
Then one should behold Janārdana to the south of Gayāśiras;
O Goddess, in the water of Gayākuṇḍa, it is indeed the measure of a bow, like an elephant.
Having bathed, one should offer libations to the gods, and worship the ancestors and the sages;
thus liberated from all sins, one is indeed released from the three debts.
To the northeast of Piśāca, however, is the lake named Gaṅgā;
having bathed there, one should worship the Liṅga, and one shall not suffer from the fear of Bhāskari.
That mountain which was previously called Nīlācala is known by the name Madana;
know that the Mānasa-kuṇḍa is located right there, toward the south.
To the northeast of Dharmācala, at a distance of twelve dhanus (or ten darśas), one should behold the Yoni of Siddheśvarī, which has the form of a red stone. || 120 ||
One should worship her on the eighth day and observe a fast;
she is situated not too far and slightly to the south of that [location].
Established in a mortal womb, she possesses a beautiful form like that of a parrot;
by bathing in Kāmakuṇḍa, a man constantly attains his desires.
Having bathed in that pool, a person is liberated from all sins;
the pool measures eight cubits and is situated between three stones.
It is traditionally taught that in the morning the ochre-colored water becomes like milk at midday;
at midday it becomes salty, and in the afternoon it becomes black.
At night, milk and water along with mustard seeds—this is shown as a wondrous sign.
That stream of the Kāmakuṇḍa is proclaimed to be the water of Jaṭā. (125)
Having bathed in that [river], the son of a woman whose children have died never dies anywhere;
that stream which flows to the south of Śivakuṇḍa is the Viyannadī.
By drinking its clear water, one is liberated from the bondage of existence;
it is the stream that issues forth from the mountain in the midst of Vahnikūṭa. || 127 ||
That [river] should be known as Narmadādhārā, the destroyer of great sins;
it flows out from the west of Makaranda and reaches the surface of the earth.
That [stream] is to be known as Sarasvatī; by drinking from it, one becomes a possessor of the Veda.
That which is the stream of Vakrakūṭa is to be known as Gomatī.
Having bathed in that [tirtha] and gone to Brahmayoni, one is released from sin.
To its north, at a distance of three hundred and seventy bows, is Saptadhārā.
At the edge of Varuṇa’s cave, there are two [or three] caves belonging to Agni;
having bathed in the Varuṇa pool, one shall attain the world of Varuṇa.
O Goddess, Trivikrama is situated in Vaṭapūrva (or Vaṭapuṭa), established as the one whose stride overcomes the senses;
his linga measures seven cubits in height and one cubit in width.
O beloved, the face is somewhat red-hued [or endowed with redness], elevated in its anterior portion;
therefore, in the northeast direction, at the peak of fire, is the fire-like Śiva.
One should worship with the seed-syllable of fire (vahnivīja) and various kinds of *bandhūka* flowers according to the rite (*vidhi*).
Having bathed in the Lohitya river and ascended the mountain of fire, one should proceed. (134)
One who worships Valibhi with devotion rejoices in the abode of Viṣṇu.
To the northwest of Vahnikūṭa is the mountain Sarpākāra. (135)
And Sadāśiva is ever present in the form of Caṇḍabhairava;
furthermore, in front of Bhairava is the sacrificial pit known as Mānasa.
Having bathed there, there is no sorrow; even a sinner is released from sin. On its bank stands the excellent mountain Nanda, a vast mountain.
And here Īśāna delights together with all the hosts of gods;
one should worship the Bull-bannered Lord with the single-syllable *Haṃsa*.
One bitten by poison becomes free from it; a fanged creature releases its fangs.
To the northwest of the peacock, at a distance measured by seven bows, [is the location]. 139.
One should recognize Gaṇeśa there and worship him with sweetmeats (laḍḍukas) and other offerings;
thereafter, one should go to Svargadvāra in the north-eastern direction from Kāmadī.
Likewise, at Kumuda to the north, measuring eight bow-lengths, one who fasts for a single night shall obtain the merit of giving a thousand cows. || 141 ||
Then, having gone to Nandana, self-restrained and with his movements controlled, he reached the three bows near Mayūra; this is known as the vicinity of Nandana. || 142 ||
Having touched the waters at Koṭitīrtha, one obtains the fruit of a horse sacrifice.
To its north is Brahmasaras, and the auspicious Mūrtigohrasaras. (143)
Having come to Aśvagotīrtha, one is born handsome;
from there, O Maheśānī, one should go to the two (or three) caves of Varāha.
Having gone there on the fourteenth day, it is celebrated at Lauhitya, where in ancient times Viṣṇu remained in the form of a boar. || 145 ||
In the middle of Indrakūṭa, however, is the famous Candratīrtha;
and the Ekahaṃseśvara Tīrtha is proclaimed to be in its center. (146)
Having bathed there, one obtains that fruit which is the fruit of the Rājasūya sacrifice;
by bathing at Ekahaṃseśvara, one obtains the fruit of a thousand cows.
To the south of Cakratīrtha, extending toward the divine southern and northern directions,
lies there the Rāmahrada Tīrtha, measuring sixty-eight dhanus.
O Goddess, when it has been brought forth by the high-souled Rāma, the son of Jamadagni, one becomes fulfilled in purpose and attains the merit of an Aśvamedha sacrifice. || 149 ||
Five lakes were established by him through the power born of his ascetic merit;
having bathed in those five lakes, one should offer libations to the ancestors and the gods.
One obtains desired objects and attains the heavenly world;
that stream which lies between Ravi and Kandarpa is Sarasvatī. 151.
To the south are both the Yamunā and the Gaṅgā, which carries the wealth of Kubera;
having bathed there on the great full-moon day, one obtains the fruit born of bathing at Prayāga.
At the transition [of the sun], at all times, or during an eclipse of the moon or the sun, one fully attains the fruit of the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice. || 153 ||
From there, one should go to Jāleśvara; Sadāśiva exists there in the form of the Guru.
By bowing down to that Lord of the World, one obtains the fruit of a horse sacrifice.
Having bathed properly in the Rāmahrada lake and beheld Hara [Śiva] Jāleśvara, one should worship Mahādeva while being devoted to fasting. || 155 ||
He attains the Agniṣṭoma sacrifice and goes to the world of Śiva;
from there, he should proceed toward the eastern direction to Mayūra.
One should ascend while wearing a single garment, reciting the mantra very slowly;
at every step, by the nature of dharma, the fruit of a horse sacrifice is obtained. || 157 ||
On Mayūra, the best of mountains, no other destination is pleasing to me.
[I seek] Hari, who assumes the form of a mountain, on Mayūra, the best of mountains. (158)
Having ascended it, a person goes to the stainless world of Brahmā;
he remains there for a hundred crores of kalpas, supported by the wish-fulfilling tree.
Salutations to you, the peacock, the sole repository of nectar!
Having ascended Mayūragiri, I [shall go] to the southern ocean.
Having paid homage and seen him thus, the leader of the pretas was deceived;
"Salutations to you, son of Brahmā! Salutations to the son of Śantanu! (161)
Homage to you, Gaṅgāgarbhā, born from the womb of Amogha;
who, having ascended Mayūragiri, beheld the mountain of birds.

O best of mountains, grant me the supportless Brahmaloka, situated to the north of the divine net, which is eternally produced from the ocean [or: eternally produced from Garuḍa]. When one beholds the Tridhārā at Gayāśiras during the month of Madhu, [one beholds her as] the daughter...
O Goddess of the gods, at that time there will be constant abundance for the Brāhmaṇas on the mountain. || 164 ||
But his stream, O lady, flows toward the south;
then, while Makara rules the kingdom, a cry of "Alas! Alas! arises.
O Goddess of the Gods, when there is prosperity for the four castes, it occurs to the north of Divyamāla and to the west of Mayūra.
But when his sacrificial fee becomes a continuous stream,
O lady, then the Kṣatriya king shall remain firm in his righteous kingdom.
O Goddess, when the ocean flows (or arises) in the vicinity of Caitratīrtha,
after an interval of five years, Jalpīśa becomes exceedingly barbaric.
Then, O Maheśānī, the Yavanas and others will likewise arise;
when a cruel king shall follow him in the south. (169)
Within the mere range of his sight, an extremely cruel spirit is born;
therefore, one should especially avoid wearing garments upon an auspicious seat.
O Goddess, when the ocean of Divyeśa overflows its boundaries, then the earth will undoubtedly become devoid of crops; indeed, the earth will be utterly ruined. || 171 ||
(384) O Goddess, when the ocean shall be at a distance of one *krośa* from the peacock, then the earth will become fit for enjoyment and will abound in its fruits. (172)
O beautiful one, if [the distance] exceeds one krośa, one should know that it falls within my cruel portion;
in such a case, one should duly give a sacrificial fee to a virtuous teacher.
Then one should offer the arghya to the Sun, and thereafter feed the Brāhmaṇas. || 173 ||
Thus ends the thirteenth chapter in the second part of the *Kāmarūpādhikāra* within the twenty-two-thousand-verse *Mahātantrarāja*, the *Yoginītantra*.
The fourteenth chapter.
The Blessed Lord said: To the northeast of the divine waters, there stands a river named Sītā.
O Great Goddess, by bathing there, one is not born again in the womb of an animal.
Hetukā, Śṛṅginī, Ghorā, Satyā, and Tāpasī—
at that very place where there are five streams, by bathing there one shall go to heaven. || 2 ||
To its east, however, is the stream named Kapilā;
by bathing in it on the day of the full moon, one casts off even the sin of killing a Brahmin.
Flowing in five channels, she departed from Cyavana’s hermitage;
having originated at Kapotakuṇḍa, she was brought down by Kapila.
By merely bathing at Mahāmādhya, one beholds the world of Brahmāṇī;
and a krośa to its east lies the Sarasvatī known by a divine name.
And having bathed in that Makara, one obtains the fruit of all sacrifices, especially during the solstices, the equinoxes, and the transits of the sun. (6)
O Maheśānī, having bathed in that [river], one obtains the fruit of an Aśvamedha sacrifice.
When it flows toward the east, there is fear for the Brāhmaṇas. (Note: The reading from "tasyām" up to "labhet" is not present in some versions.)
When it moves toward the south, there is misfortune in the kingdom;
when its movement is in the northeast, then a great pestilence shall arise.
For one whose previous residence was in that [direction], their life is fruitful;
however, for those situated in the west, there will be a loss of wealth and grain. (9)
O beloved, one should not make a dwelling where rivers flow to the east of a city or a village; one should avoid such places from afar.
To its western side, however, it appears in the form of a river;
indeed, by bathing there, one's vital energy (vāyu) and prosperity (lakṣmī) increase. || 11 ||
One should not stop the sound, nor especially the flow of a river;
as long as the binding remains upon the earth, they shall curse the family.
Having incurred bondage through negligence, one should perform an expiation;
likewise, he who performs a ritual bath in water that obstructs a river [should do so]. (13)
A fault arising at all times will undoubtedly occur;
it will be in the western part of that [place], toward the south, O Supreme Goddess. (14)
In the field of the Nāgas, on the seat of the earth, the goddess is known as Trigaṇḍakī;
by worshipping her alone, one shall attain all desires. (15)
To its east, O Great Goddess, is the mountain named Modaka;
by worshipping the Liṅga of Gaṇeśa there, one shall obtain prosperity.
On the north side there should be Brahmā, and on the south side the Kamalā stone;
one intent on devotion should worship Mahāmāyā in the form of the Yoni.
O Great Goddess, in the northeast of that place, situated during the latter half of the watch (yāmārddha), is the river renowned as Dviputra; having bathed there, one shall go to heaven.
O Supreme Goddess, that stream belonging to Dviputra which is in the eastern part is named Tāpinī; by bathing there, one's sin is destroyed.
To the east of that city, at a distance of one krośa, there is a river other than the Sarayū which flows forth, destroying all sins; it is renowned by the name Digvāsā.
O beautiful one, whoever bathes during the months of Māgha, Kumbha, and Mīna—
having bathed there at my temple, he removes even the sin of killing a Brahmin.

That best of men who bathes on the fourteenth day of the bright fortnight shall obtain the fruit of ten horse-sacrifices. And having bathed according to the rules on the full moon day, he goes to the world of Brahmā.
On the full moon day of Kārttika, during an eclipse, and likewise at the solstices and equinoxes. || 23 ||
Having obtained the fruit of all sacrifices, he rejoices like a god in heaven,
O Supreme Goddess, who bathes throughout the entire month of Kārttika.
One who is free from disease, strong, and ever-renowned is born upon this earth on a Thursday coinciding with the fourteenth lunar day, or on a Saturday coinciding with the fourth lunar day. (25)
Having bathed in the Digvāsā, a man is liberated from the bondage of worldly existence.
Salutations to you, O destroyer of all sins, O pure one, O carrier of clear water! (26)
Be gracious, O Subhagāvarta; salutations to you, who are worshipped by the gods!
Likewise, [salutations] to the ever-endless Pārśva, who has increased tenfold.
Endowed with rays and dots, having the luster of the sky and seven colors—one who is composed should bathe with this mantra and offer the arghya water. (28)

One should satisfy the ancestors with devotion and perform the *śrāddha* on the following day. [The reading from "ending with that" (*tadvaśāntam*) up to "on the following day" (*pare'hani*) is an interpolation.
Then one should perform the tonsure and observe a fast. (29)
This most meritorious goddess, served by gods and gandharvas, clad in the directions (naked), world-renowned, is the supreme river among sacred fords. (30)
Clad in the directions, the best of rivers, she has issued forth from the body of Rudra;
O daughter of Śaṅkara, may she deliver all beings, both mobile and immobile.
Whether in a village or in a forest, every direction is meritorious;
for there dwell the sages whose wealth is austerity, together with the gods, asuras, and gandharvas.
And having performed penance, O Goddess of gods, they have attained supreme perfection.
A man who, established in his vows and with senses subdued, bathes in the morning— || 33 ||
Having fasted for a single night, one may deliver a hundred generations of one's lineage;
it is heard that this most excellent river extends for a hundred thousand yojanas.
But in detail, O Goddess of gods, she extends for a hundred yojanas;
one who has become pure, a celibate student, with anger conquered and senses subdued [should go there]. (35)
But he who has desisted from all violence, who is devoted to the welfare of all gambling [and other vices], and who thus practices righteousness, shall abandon all sins. (36)
O Goddess, O lady of excellent vows, hear from me the fruit of his merit:
