O daughter of Śaṅkara, that living being shall rejoice in heaven for a period equal to a hundred years.
Sporting with throngs of Apsarases and attended by hosts of celestial women, he was anointed with divine perfumes and adorned with divine flowers. || 38 ||
He sports in the world of the gods and rejoices with the deities;
thereafter, having descended from heaven, that righteous man shines as a king.
O Goddess, he obtains a house adorned with divine jewels,
featuring pillars made of divine gems and decorated with banners and lapis lazuli.
Accompanied by bright painted vehicles and attended by male and female servants,
the illustrious Lord of Speech, beloved by all women, shone resplendent.
Accompanied by cowherds, he shall live for more than a hundred years;
at that confluence, the king of holy places, he attains both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
The stream that flows to its east is the river Padmāvatī;
having bathed in it according to the prescribed rites, one is glorified in the world of Śiva.
Having bathed there in the highly meritorious Kanyāśrama, one shall go to heaven;
O Supreme Goddess, he who bathes in the Aśoka-soma-kuṇḍa on the tenth lunar day [shall likewise attain that state].
The sin accumulated since birth perishes at that very moment;
she is the daughter of Soma, a maiden protected by Cyavana. (45)
Formerly taken away by Śaṅkara, she remained there after being cursed by Gaurī;
thereafter, that auspicious place named Kaṅgyāśrama became filled with all holy tirthas.
The field measuring two *krośas* is the ground for the altar, half of which indicates the center of the Goddess;
O Maheśvarī, the inner field extends for twelve *dhanus*.
Upon the surface of that stone were placed the footprints of Brahmā, Indra, and Varuṇa;
likewise those of Rudra, Viṣṇu, Krauñca, and the Gaṇa.
O Goddess, the station of Brahmā is red, while the two feet have white parasols;
likewise, O Beloved, that of Vāsava is dark blue, and the supreme [station] has the luster of stone.
When the white *brāhma* square appears, then there shall be the loss of progeny for Vāsava; [this reading from "of Vāsava" up to "there shall be" is an addition].
O Supreme Goddess, when the red *vaiṣṇava* square is seen... (50)
Then, O my beloved, know that there will be famine in the kingdom;
beyond that, however, O beloved, is the highly meritorious abode of Rudra.
A sacred field equal to Vārāṇasī is considered to yield results like Gayā; one should avoid the Virāja-pañca-vidhāna and instead perform the rites prescribed for this place.
Whoever bathes in the Lauhityapāyasa and gratifies the ancestors shall deliver seven lineages and a hundred and one members of their family.
But he who, having especially renounced his life-breaths in that sacred field,
becomes one whose self is purified by all the worlds, is glorified in the world of Brahmā.
O fair-faced one, whether in water, on land, or in the atmosphere, whoever, having attained the Pāśupata knowledge, should cast off the body; || 55 ||
And those who die by hanging shall attain the supreme goal in this field, with one-pointed mind, at the Lauhitya and the Virajas rivers. (56)
O Goddess, one should avoid shaving [the head], especially at Gayā;
O Maheśānī, this also applies at Siddhācala according to the sequence of the Western Tradition.
Having gone to the seven liṅgas within the cave, one should worship them there;
and right there is the most difficult-to-attain tīrtha of Nārada.
O Goddess of gods, by merely bathing there, one obtains the fruit of a thousand cows;
formerly, penance was performed there by the high-souled Nārada, the celestial sage.
Then, the Great Lord Maheśvara, the God of gods, was pleased with his yoga;
therefore, that lake created by Brahmā is known as Brahmasaras (or Brahmeśvara).
Having gone there, O Maheśānī, one attains the world of Brahmā;
then, having gone to Rāmatīrtha, one is liberated from fear by one's own kinsmen.
From there, one should go to Maheśvarī, which yields the fruit of a previous birth;
then one should go to Tāmreśvara (or Bhāseśvara), which destroys all diseases.
Merely by bathing there, a man is liberated from all sins.
Thence he should go to the excellent Piṅgaleśvara in the eastern part.
By fasting for one day and night, one obtains the fruit of a three-night fast;
and he who offers a Kapila cow at that sacred site, O Goddess of the Gods, [obtains the same].
For as many thousands of years as there are hairs on his body and on the families born from him, he is glorified in the world of Rudra.
O Maheśvarī, he who should give up his life there rejoices imperishably in heaven for as long as the moon and sun endure. (66)
And those men who remain taking refuge in the Siddhas,
they are liberated and go to heaven, just like virtuous people who have performed good deeds.
From there, one should go to Dīpeśvara, a sacred place and a holy ford that bestows wealth;
it was there in ancient times that the great river, which was flowing away, was turned back by him.
Having been forbidden by Vyāsa, she then went to the western [direction]. O Maheśvarī, as for that field in which one should perform a circumambulation... (69)
Then Vyāsa was pleased with him, and he obtained his desired fruit.
At a distance of eight throws of an arrow to the northeast of that [place], [is another site]. (70)
The field of Ekāmra is an excellent sacred site measuring two krośas in extent;
there resides Śaṅkara known as Nāga, a charming place abounding in serpents, containing secret holy fords and secret liṅgas, and frequented by the hidden deities.
Surrounded by secret assemblies of the hidden gods and goddesses,
there stands a pool beneath a mango tree, measuring sixteen bow-lengths.
To the south of that place, O Goddess, is the lake named Nāga;
there resides the Lord Śaṅkara, the Supreme Ishvara, situated upon a sacred spot of earth.
Wherein dwell the gods headed by Brahmā, as well as the sages whose ascetic power is dense, along with the Siddhas, Cāraṇas, Gandharvas, Kinnaras, and great serpents (Mahoragas). || 73 ||
Where the god Śaṅkara, known as Nāga and worshipped by the gods, resides;
to the east is the Brahma-lake, and to the north is the Pārvatī-fig tree.
To the south is Viṣṇukuṇḍa, and to the west is Dikkarāyinī;
the sacred field situated between these two is known as Sugandha, though it is not very famous.
Then, on that best of rivers, I bathed Śaṅkara;
having bathed in the Dikkarāyinī, one should touch the Pārvatī-vaṭa tree. (76)
One should bow with devotion to Śaṅkara; he purifies one's lineage up to the seventh generation.
[One should also worship] Tāra, Maṅgala, Haṃsa, and the sounding of the conch.
This mantra of the God of gods was proclaimed by the sage Garga; one should employ it for the purpose of [worship], with Anuṣṭubh as the meter and Bhava as the deity. (78)
He is clothed in variegated garments, dark-complexioned, and has matted hair;
he likewise holds a skull-topped staff (khaṭvāṅga), a trident, and displays the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness.
He has a serpent as his sacred thread and a great bull as his vehicle;
he is endowed with all auspicious marks and adorned with every ornament.
One should worship Rāma and the others, as well as Brahmā and the others, and the Bhairavas such as Niśitāṅga, in front of the pedestal; one should worship the lords of the directions outside.
Then, having offered praise to the mantra, one should offer honeyed milk-rice (madhupāyasa) situated not too far from the northern side of the deity. 82.
Having bathed at that supreme holy site called Triśūla, one attains liberation;
there, devoted to the worship of the ancestors and the gods, one should perform an ablution.
Upon casting off the body, one attains the status of a Gaṇapati; of this there is no doubt—at a distance of sixty bows to the south of the Triśūla Tīrtha.
There, having worshipped the god Mahāliṅga, Kaṅka, Keśa, and Maheśvara, especially during the dark fortnight of the month of Caitra; || 85 ||
On the eighth day of the dark fortnight, one obtains the fruit of an Ashvamedha sacrifice;
however, one should avoid shaving the head on this day, as well as in the hermitages of maidens.
At Lauhitya, Śoṇa, Gaṅgā, and Virajas, one should then proceed to the Kula-field of the Goddess, a field that is very difficult to attain. (87)
There, the goddess Śākambharī, whose very form is the Yonimudrā,
the supreme sovereign, is situated in the northeastern quarter of the Lord.
One should worship the Goddess at nine *dhanvantaras* with the *kāmabīja* mantra;
one obtains the desires prayed for in the mind—of this there is no doubt. (89)
Having gone there, the preceptor, with his hands joined in the añjali gesture and his knees touching the ground, should propitiate the deity with this mantra.
Homage to the infinite God, who brings about dissolution and creation;
homage to the one who bestows grace, the Lord of the Nāgas—homage, homage! 91.
Salutations again and again to the Primal One, the immeasurable Puruṣa;
salutations be to you, the Puruṣa, the Lord of Serpents; salutations again and again. || 92 ||
Homage to the one with a lotus in his hand [with a golden hand], the tusked one, the wielder of the mace;
homage to the Lord of the three worlds, the Lord of the Nāgas, salutations again and again! || 93 ||
Salutations to the Lord of the Universe, who is the primordial Sāṅkhya;
salutations to the one known as Cakreśa, the Lord of the Nāgas—salutations again and again!
Homage to the one whose emblem is free from passion, who wears a necklace of serpents;
homage to the one with the trident in hand, the Lord of Nagas—homage, homage! (95)
Salutations to the Lord of Kalā, who dwells in Kāmarūpa; salutations again and again to Nāgeśa. Salutations again and again to Nāgeśa, the Lord of the Lord of Kalās. (96)
From there, one should go to the sacred field named Naimiṣa in the eastern region.
There, the supreme deity known as Tryambaka resides in the form of a manifested Liṅga. (97)
Having approached, one should worship the God who dwells in the midst of the three desires; one should perform the ritual installation upon the ground-seat with the Tārā mantra. 98.
To the northeast of Traiyambaka is the sacred field named Mārtaṇḍa.
Having gone there, O Maheśvarī, one should worship the Liṅga called Mārtaṇḍa [and his form].
To the west of that field is the river named Marmarā.
She should be known by the name Kalā [or she should be known by the name Kamalā]; one's water should not touch her. || 100 ||
The Sudhāmā river is meritorious and the destroyer of all sins;
by bathing in it, one dispels the sin committed from birth.
O Maheśvarī, one should go to the great field of Dharmāraṇya, located slightly to the west of Dikkariṇī, in the direction of Vāyu. 102.
This is a most meritorious field, frequented by gods and gandharvas,
filled with various trees and creepers, and adorned with diverse flowers.
O Goddess, here Gadādhara is present together with Lakṣmī;
likewise, Viṣṇu alone and Indra surrounded by hosts of Vidyādharas are present. (104)
The one named Ananta and Mādhava of wondrous prowess abide there;
O my beloved, whoever shall behold them on the twelfth day of every month [shall attain their goal].
A person obtains the fruit of the Pauṇḍarīka horse-sacrifice at Viṣṇu’s Puṣkara-tīrtha, located on the western side of the deity. (106)
Having bathed there, one should worship the God and obtain the fruit of a horse-sacrifice;
furthermore, he who performs the pilgrimage on the full moon day of the month of Jyeṣṭha [attains great merit].
Freed from all sins, that man shall go to the city of Viṣṇu;
so too he who beholds Mādhava, the Lord of Men, on the occasion of Mahājyaiṣṭhī.
(At this point, the text appears to be fragmentary.
Thus ends the fourteenth chapter in the second part of the *Kāmarūpādhikāra* within the *Śrīyoginītantra*, the great king of tantras in twenty-two thousand verses.
The fifteenth chapter.
The Blessed One said: In that realm where the Lord [Viṣṇu] shone forth after being created, King Śikhidhvaja [reigned].
At the end of the reign of Śikhidhvaja, there shall be a king named Śāla. || 1 ||
From that lineage were born Kṣatriyas, and after him came Dharmapāla;
while he was still like a child there, a fisherman became his destroyer.
He would have been five years old, and that betrayal was committed by him himself;
this was when Kāmapāla became equal to the moon in luster.
In one or two years, he will be killed by his own malice. || 3 ||
A twice-born man named Vīra, a Śūdra born of the Jaimini gotra, shall again become a king when he is reborn into that very same [family], O King. (4)
At that time, there will be pestilence in the kingdom and the destruction of the Brāhmaṇas;
in that year, known as Rūpaprāya, there will be a path to the gate of heaven.
When the Yavana king [reigns], it shall be the year Vāṇaśūnya.
But then, when there shall be a king born of desire in the Kali age, he will destroy that phallic emblem of Śukra which is as old as the Ṛṣis.
That Śūdra, who reviles the gods and Brāhmaṇas, is celebrated in the world as Samudra;
he shall have a son named Lakṣmīnārāyaṇa, who will cause his lineage to flourish. || 7 ||
While he rules the earth, the Gītikās and the Dharmaśāstras shall arise;
that righteous-souled one shall be born as a king in his own portion,
and from that point on, his entire lineage shall perish.
When the emergence from the Brahma-lake occurred, he arrived from the jeweled pedestal.
Attacked by them, Kali was born under the names Bhāsmagarbha and others;
O Pārvatī, those kings who were mediocre and those who were excellent [were likewise affected].
The sacred fords, the deities, and so forth will become clearly manifest.
O Goddess, whatever sinful king there may be, he shall perish within that kingdom.
In that kingdom where there is the Karmanāśā river or a lake, having built a city on its bank, the king destroys the realm with his sins. (12)
One should avoid the Gītikās, the Dharmaśāstras, and that water at its end;
however, on its western side stands a river which is auspicious. (13)
That meritorious river which formerly existed in its entirety became,
in the year following the Tarkarūpa era, divided from one another due to the weight of the earth.
Then, having ruled the kingdom there during the Nṛgavarṣa, that high-minded one will perish at the end of that year in the Aiśvaryatantra. || 15 ||
Then, in the middle half of that year, one shall encounter great fear;
however, any king who beholds Kāmākhyā during that period will certainly [prosper].
The king shall be deprived of his kingdom, or his wife shall suffer the loss of progeny;
when the king indeed becomes one whose form is subject to desire, with a complexion ranging from white to dark, then Śaṅkara, born at Brahmasaras, shall become Kakudeśvara. || 17 ||
In that [lineage], the Bhārgava clan will not be counted among the middle ranks;
while he rules over the earth, various forms of hostility shall arise. (18)
There, the Sun himself, having been drawn by his own power, [is] the people born therein, the five beginning with the seed-syllable of the Sun (bhānu), and the three seats of desire (kāmapīṭha). 19.
Therefore, the eloquent lord Vyāla, like a bull, shines resplendently;
from the horse-trodden non-dual [source], the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) emerged in its own time.
Once the sacred ford has arisen, all obstacles are swiftly destroyed;
yet while he rules the kingdom, fourfold treachery may arise.

In the great region of Valade, with the syllables of Kāma and Brahmā, joined with Ākāśa and Śaśin, this five-syllable mantra known as the Heart is proclaimed for the sake of accomplishment; it is celebrated as the [mantra] of the Mālā. || 22 ||

One should employ [the mantra] in grasping, establishing, and worshiping; at the end of the recitation, one should place it upon the head, and at the conclusion of the sacrificial session, one should recite the hymn of praise. (23)
One should likewise perform the offering of the sacrificial victim (balidāna) and give away one's own wealth;
one should worship with the root mantra in both direct and reverse order.
With the mantra "Ambe'mbike" and likewise with the Gaurāṇika [mantra]:
"Victory, O Kāmeśī Cāmuṇḍā! Victory, O remover of beings! (25)
Victory to you, O omnipresent Goddess Kāmeśvarī; salutations be unto you!
O you whose form is the universe, auspicious one, pure one, O Virūpākṣī, O three-eyed one! (26)
Obeisance be to you, O Bhīmarūpā, Śivā, Vidyā, Kāmeśvarī;
O Manojavā, Jayā, Jambhā, Bhūtākṣī, Kṣudhitā, and Kṣayā! || 27 ||
O Mahāmāyā, O Maheśānī, O Kāmeśvarī, salutations be unto you!
O Cāmuṇḍā, O Mahākālī, O Kālī, O you who carry away the skull! || 28 ||
O Kāmeśvarī, who holds a noose and a staff in your hands, salutations be to you!
O Cāmuṇḍā, whose face is adorned with a garland of skulls, who possesses sharp fangs and great strength! || 29 ||
O Goddess, you who abide in the place of the corpse, O Kāmeśvarī, salutations be to you!
O Goddess with terrifying eyes, O fearsome one, O destroyer of all beings! || 30 ||
O Karālī, O Vikarālī, O Kāmeśvarī, salutations be unto you! O Kālī, O Karālī, O valiant one, O Kāmeśvarī, beloved of Hara! || 31 ||
O Goddess who embodies all scriptures, O Kāmeśvarī, salutations be to you! O Kāmeśvarī, crusher of Niśumbha and Śumbha, salutations be to you!
O Kāmākhyā, residing in the form of desire, O Kāmeśvarī, beloved of Hara! || 32 ||
Grant me my desires eternally, O Kāmeśvarī; salutations be unto you. (The end of the chapter does not occur here. || 33 ||

Thus ends the fifteenth chapter, and some verses from the sixteenth chapter, in the second part of the section on Kāmarūpa within the *Yoginītantra*, the great king of tantras in twenty-two thousand [verses].
O Mahāmāyā, those who are Brāhmaṇas and Ṛṣis are indeed portions of myself,
intended for the desire to uplift men who are submerged in the mire of sin.
And for the sake of establishing the Dharma, they appear age after age;
therefore, O Goddess, never despise those Brāhmaṇas. || 2 ||

O Supreme Goddess, in order to protect the knowledge that has fallen from the path of the Vedas during the Kali age, You appear as the three incarnations among the three types of those who uphold the Vedas.

O Śivā, they shall gradually manifest through the gateway of the Divine Current (divyaugha) for the purpose of destroying the Buddhists and heretics, and for the sake of the tradition itself. [As published by the Vārāṇaseya Sārvabhauma Pracāraka Kāryālaya]
Verses extracted from the journal titled *Paramārthasudhā*, and also extracted from the commemorative volume of the Indian Philosophy Conference held in the city of Guwahati. [Page 63] || 4 ||
Thus ends the sixteenth chapter in the second part of the *Kāmarūpādhikāra* within the *Yoginītantra*, the great king of tantras consisting of twenty-two thousand verses.
